OLD  RECORDS ¹
By MARTIN  E.  HAWES
Chapter  I
1
One who has occasion now and then to look for some matter of
business  or historic  event in  regard  to  Weymouth is  often  struck
with   the  many  important  and   interesting   events   which  have
happened during our three hundred years of existence and events of
which but little  is  known,   and this  has  led  us  to  an attempt  at
producing or compiling a complete history of the town as far as  it
can be done by any records which are to be obtained.
First,        Weymouth is  in  the  State  of   Massachusetts,     county of
Norfolk,       and situated  on salt-water line  twelve miles  southeast  of
Boston.
What is  Weymouth?   It is a town of fifteen thousand inhabitants.
It has  a school  population  of  over  two  thousand  pupils,      all  in
well- equipped buildings,   including  a high  school  building  with  all
modern conveniences  and appliances.        A superintendent and fifty-
three  teachers  are  employed  and  schools  are  graded  from  one  to
nine below the high.
There are eighteen churches in town,   four Catholic and fourteen
Protestant.
The  town  has   a  well-equipped   municipal  water  plant  with
nearly  a hundred miles  of  main line  pipe  and  water supply  equal
to all  emergencies.      The town has been liberal  in its  equipment of
a fire  department which embraces  steamers,   chemical engine,    hose
carriages and hook and ladder truck.
The town  has  an  extensive  lighting  system,     both  arc  and  in-
candescent,     with  light  taken  from  a  private  company,     the  Wey-
mouth  Electric  Light  and  Power  Company,    which  also  furnishes
light  and power for other purposes.
"Good roads "  has  been  a motto of the town,   and its  one hun-
dred and twenty miles  of  roads  are  one of its  attractive features .
Traveling  facilities   are  good.         Two lines   of  steam  roads  of  the
New York,      New Haven & Hartford  system  are running  through
the  town  and  afford   cheap  and  frequent  service,    and  the  Old
Colony Street  Railway Company have lines  on most of  the princi-
pal  streets,    with good service to all  parts  of the town and also  to
surrounding towns  and cities .
Weymouth is  cosmopolitan,    and  is  both  a  manufacturing  and
residential  town.        Its  nearness  to  Boston,    as well  as  its  cheap and
1 From " Weymouth Gazette."
 - 14 - 
492                                     OLD  RECORDS
frequent  railroad  service,     makes it  a desirable  place  for  city  busi-
ness men to  establish  homes,   and yet it  is  not without advantages
to  the  laboring class.        The American Agricultural  Chemical  Com-
pany,       the  largest  works  of the  kind  in  the  country,      have  their
works  at  North  Weymouth,   and the shoe industry  of  Weymouth
is  not  second  to  that  of  any town in  the  country  in  the  manu-
facture  of  men's high-grade  goods ;       our  manufacturers  and  work-
men have a more than national  reputation for  excellence of work.
We have  a water  front  which  has  many advantages,    is   easy  of
access  and capable  of  a large development,   but we pass  on to  the
third question.
Who made it ?    Some one has said  that "God made the country
and  man made the  town, "  and  when the Great  Creator  divided
the waters from the land there were but few places more artistically
and beautifully finished  than that on which Weymouth is  located.
A long shore front bordering on the ocean with boating and bath-
ing facilities  unexcelled;     the beautiful  Fore River navigable  for  a
long distance and overlooked by equally as beautiful  a landscape ;
Back  River with  its  Hockley Bay stretching  far  inland  and with
scenery  which  vies  with  its  sister   river  in  attractive   features ;
Whitman's  Pond,    which  the  lamented  Archbishop  Williams  said
presented  the most charming view he  had seen  either  in  Europe
or America;       and then streams and brooks which add variety to  the
scenery  and water fertile  valleys .
The  land,          too,     is  not  without  its   many  attractions,       whether
considered  from  aesthetic  points  of  view  or  for  agricultural  pur-
poses,     but we pass from the first  creation to things  more recent .
We can deal but little with  prehistoric races,   but for many years
the red man hunted in the woods,    fished in the ponds and streams,
and dug clams along the beach .
COMING  OF  THE  WHITE  MAN
Next  to  Plymouth,    Weymouth is  the  oldest  settlement  in  the
Old Bay State.
In  the  spring  of  1622  an  expedition  was  fitted   out  by  one
Thomas Weston,   with a view to establishing  a colony and trading
post   somewhere  near  the   Plymouth   Colony.        This   expedition
started   with  two  vessels,      the  " Charity"  of  one  hundred  tons,
and the  " Swan" of thirty  tons.
This  expedition was more fortunate in its  time of arriving  than
the  " Mayflower"  party,      which  first  landed  on the  bleak  sands
of  Cape  Cod in winter,   and then,     amid snow and ice,   were driven
across  the bay to  Plymouth.
The Weston party  arrived  in  August,      and in  their  prospecting
along  the  coast  no  place  was  more  attractive  to  them  than  our
shore  front  and  inland  view.          They  sailed   up  Fore  River,        and,
according   to   all   authorities,     after  coming  to  anchor,      made  their
landing  at what is  now known as  Phillips'     Creek.           After  a month
 - 15 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               493
or  more of  labor  in  establishing  the  colony,    the  " Charity "  with
her  crew  returned  to  England,      leaving   the  smaller   craft,       the
" Swan,  "  for  the use  of  the colony.       The sequel  proves  that  the
adventurers  were a bad lot.       Before  the winter  had fairly  set  in
their provisions  were exhausted,    and they were reduced to  a state
of abject want,    and had also succeeded,   by treachery and theft,     in
incurring  the ill  will  of their  savage  neighbors  to  such  an extent
that before the spring opened it  was learned that the savages  were
plotting  to  massacre the entire colony.        Phineas  Pratt,     one of  the
party,    more daring than the rest,    made his way through the forests
and  swamps  and  succeeded  in  inducing  Myles  Standish  with  a
little  band of eight men to come to  their  aid,    the trip  being made
by water.
Standish  studied  the situation,    and after  one  or  two  interviews
with  the  savages,     among  them  Pecksuot  their  chief,   planned  to
bring matters to a crisis.          His men were assembled in the stockade
and a council  arranged  for  with  the  Indians.         At a given  signal
Standish  sprang  upon  Pecksuot,    grabbed  his  knife from  his  belt
and began the  hand- to- hand fight  which resulted  in the killing  of
the chief and four others,    and the capture of a fifth whom Standish
afterward hung.
The hero of the  Plymouth Colony,  seeing that the people whom
he had come to help were unworthy of  an existence  as  neighbors,
hurried  most of  them on board  their  little  craft  and  dispatched
them to a trading post in Maine;    then,  taking a few whom he had
selected  as  worthy of citizenship with him,   returned to  Plymouth,
and  thus  ended  what is  by  some  called  the  first   settlement  of
Weymouth.
 - 16 - 
Chapter  II
In our last,      we left  the red  man once more in full  possession  of
the territory of his fathers,     or,    at least,    that much of it which then
went by the  name of  Wessaguscus  or  Wessagussett,       but  he  was
not long  to remain so,   as England was ripe for establishing colonies
in  the  New World,    and even while  the  Weston party was in  pos-
session,    the Gorges Company had been organized and had procured
a grant from the Council of New England to  occupy a coast line  of
ten miles  and extend thirty  miles  inland.         This  company was in
command of  Capt.    Robert Gorges .
Captain  Gorges  came,    evidently,     with  great  expectations.          He
held a commission as governor-general.             He also  had as  officers  a
grand admiral  and an organized council for  municipal and judicial
work,        and  in  addition  a clergyman  of  the  Church  of  England,
William Morrill,    for the purpose of establishing  that church in the
colony.
In the early  autumn of the same year which saw the departure
of the last  remnant of the  first  comers,    Gorges made his  landing
somewhere  near  what  is   now  known  as  North  Weymouth,      but
where  there  are  nearly  as  many different  opinions  as  there  are
available  spots  to  land,    the  generally  accepted  theory  is  that  the
landing was somewhere up Fore River rather  than on the outside.
Many of the company had brought  their  families  and their  all
with  them,      and had come to  stay,    and immediately  began  pro-
viding shelter for the coming winter.
Gorges,       however,    made but  little  use  of  his  governor-general
and other  powers,   as he soon tired of the privations  and hardships
of the new life,   and as winter set in sailed again for England,   never
to  return.
Gorges took with him quite a number of the party whose courage
had failed  them;    some went to  Plymouth,   and among them Rev.
Mr.  Morrell,      who returned  to  England the  next year.           A few  re-
mained,     however,    and the real  settlement of Weymouth had begun.
The following  year there  was quite  an addition  to  the settlement
by a  party  from  Weymouth,    Eng.,   who joined  forces  with  those
already developing the wilderness.
Neither  Charles  Francis  Adams,        our  townsman  Gilbert  Nash,
nor  any  other  historian  has  found  much  recorded  history  of  the
Wessagusset  Colony for  the  next  few  years,    but from the  names
we find a little  later on in the first allotment of land to the settlers,
it  is  evident that people continued to come and stay,   as the names,
many of  them,     have  come down through  the  centuries  and  are
 - 17 - 
OLD  RECORDS                              495
still    factors   in  town  affairs.            Another  recorded  fact   as  to  the
growth  of  the  town is  that in  1632  it  was the  second  important
point  in  the  Massachusetts  Bay  Colony,     as  during  that  year  a
tax was levied by the court,   and Boston's portion was £8,     Wessa-
gussett's  £5,      and Salem's £4 10s.
The year  1635 saw a  new era in the history of the town.           Rev.
Joseph Hull with about one hundred people,   among them twenty-
one family  organizations,    came from  Weymouth,     Eng. ,    and were
permitted to join the colony,   and on September 2 of that year  the
town  was  duly  incorporated  and  received  the  name Weymouth.
A commission was appointed to establish  the boundary lines,     and
after  nearly a year's work they reported as follows:     The boundary
line  between  Mount Wollaston  and Weymouth,   on the west,     Fore
River,        then   the  Smelt  Brook,      thence  a  straight   line   running
southerly  to  the line  of the Plymouth  Colony;    on the  east,      Back
River,            Fresh   River  and  then  a  straight   line   parallel   with   the
western line  to  the  Plymouth Colony line,   and these lines  and the
name Weymouth have stood the test of three hundred years,   which
can hardly be said  of any other town in the country.
A NEW ERA
Following the incorporation of the town a new era  dawned upon
the  settlement.           While  the colonists were not communists,    in  the
modern sense of the word,   up to this  date,  from the necessity of the
situation,     things  had been largely  in common,    but  now came the
selling  or allotment of lands to  the settlers  and the formation of a
town government.
Among the landowners  there  were  many whose names  are  still
familiar,        one  being  John  Whitman who came in  possession  of  a
tract of salt  marsh,    and a tract  on the west side of the pond which
still  bears  his  name;    but  there  were  many others  whose  names
have been entirely lost sight of.
We should  have said  more in  our  first  article  in regard  to Wey-
mouth Great  Pond in the extreme southern  part of the town.        It
is   a beautiful  sheet  of  water covering  a large  area,    and  is  at  the
top  of  the  watershed  between  Boston  Bay  and  Buzzards  Bay,
and is  consequently  almost absolutely  free  from marsh and other
drainage,        and  is  a clean,   spring-fed  pond from  which  the  town
derives its  water supply.
The new town must have worked slowly in making records,       as
we find but little  recorded until a town meeting held  Dec.  7,     1641,
when the  town  voted  that  no  man should  fell  any  timber  tree
within six miles of the meeting- house under penalty of 5s.      for  each
tree felled unless first gaining permission from the townsmen.          We
would here  note  that  the  townsmen  seem  to  have been  a  board
somewhat similar to our selectmen,   and at that time were Edward
Bates,         Thomas  Richards,        William   Torrey,       John  Harding   and
John Upham.
 - 18 - 
496                                     OLD  RECORDS
An  interesting  document  about  this  time  is  a deed  from  the
Indians   for   " six   acres   of  ground  impaled  and  broken  up  and
twenty  acres  near  the  same,"  signed  Webcowett,      Nahantum and
Nabscat.                  By bounds  describing  the  same,    this  land  was  near
Whitman's  Pond.
At a meeting  held  April  10,      1643,      it  was  voted  that  all  goats
and great cattle  shall  go under the hand of some sufficient  keeper
from the first  of the third month to the last of the eighth month,
and  the penalty  for  a violation  of  this  was  7s.     for every  head  of
great  cattle and 2s.    for every goat.
At a town meeting held  the  6th  of October  of  the  same year,
Richard Addams was appointed town crier,     and any articles  found
were to be cried by him,   and if  no owner appeared there were to be
sold  after  a stated time for the benefit of the town,   but the crier
was not to receive over 2d.    for crying any one article.        At the same
meeting  it   was voted  that  no  person  should  receive  over  5s.      for
killing any wolf,   unless he had spent time in  making guns or  traps,
and  no  Indian  should  receive over 5s.   for  killing  a wolf,       however
it might be done.
CHURCH AND  STATE
Weymouth  is   a town  of  churches,    and from  the  earliest  days
their  history  has  been  one  of  interest,     and for  the  first  century
church and state,     or rather  town,    were closely  allied.
But little  can  be said  of  the  first  minister,     Rev.  Wm.       Morrill,
who came  in  1623  with  the  Gorges  Colony,   as  he landed  in  the
summer,          and  before  winter  set  in  moved to  Plymouth,      and  the
following  spring  returned  to  England  not  to  come  back.           The
next  party of  comers  brought  a  Rev.  Mr.  Barnard who is  said  to
have been a popular man with the colony,   but died in a few years,
and during  his  ministry  services  were held  among the  people  at
North  Weymouth,    and  after  awhile  more  commodious  quarters
were provided by the  erection of a church edifice on Burying  Hill ,
near where the Soldiers'     Monument now stands.
Rev.  Joseph  Hull of the 1634 or  1635  expedition,     was  the  next
pastor,      but  was  shortly  confronted  by a strong  opposition  on the
part   of   dissenters   from  the   Episcopal   Church,       or   Church  of
England,     which  up to  this  time  had been the leading  factor,      and
a  call  was  extended  to  Rev.  Thomas  Jermer  of  Roxbury.           The
breach,        however,        widened,       and  in   1637   the  Governor  and  his
Council  were  called  in  to  settle  the  difficulty,    and  Rev.   Robert
Lenthal,        a  recent  comer  from  England,     was  placed  in  charge  of
the  church.              Difficulties  failed  to  harmonize  under  Mr.  Lenthal,
as  the  three  ministers,      Hull,     Jermer  and  Lenthal,     all  claimed  the
church,        and  in  1639  Mr.  Hull  retired  in  favor  of  Rev.  Samuel
Newman,      a  recent  graduate  of  Oxford,      Eng. ,     who  succeeded  but
little  better  than his  predecessors,       and  in  three  or four years  took
a few of his  most ardent followers  and moved to  Rehoboth.
 - 19 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               497
Weymouth was now without a pastor  until Jan.  2,  1644.    Rev.
Thomas Thacher,   who had accepted  a call from the people,     came
to  the town,    was here ordained  and installed,    and under him the
First  Congregational  Church of Weymouth was established.           The
little  meeting-house on the hill  became too small,    and  a  new  one
was  erected  on  the  spot  where  the  " Old  North  Church"   now
stands,    and for twenty years Mr. Thacher saw the town and church
grow under his  care,     but a louder call  to  the Old South Church in
Boston  took  him  away,      and  Rev.   Samuel  Torrey  became  his
successor.
 - 20 - 
Chapter  III
There  are  some  questions  we have often  been  called  upon  to
answer  in  regard  to  our  first   chapter  of  this  series,        viz . ,      Where
was the first  church building and why do we place the first  landing
at,       or  near,     Phillips '     Creek?
In regard to the first  church,    we would say that the first  minister
of  whom  there  is   any  mention  was  an  Episcopalian,       or  of  the
Church of England,    Mr.  Morrill,    who came with the Gorges Com-
pany,    but as  he stayed but two or three  months  it  is  presumable
that he did but little.        The next  was also  Episcopalian and lived
with  the  people  some  six  or  seven  years,   and  undoubtedly  held
some services,  and legend says had a place of worship somewhere in
North  Weymouth,     but  no  one knows  where,     yet  it  is  presumed
that it was in the vicinity of where the Pilgrim Church now stands,
but,    as we have before stated,  the first church building of which we
have a written history was on what is  now known as  Burying Hill ,
or the Old North Cemetery.
In  regard  to  the  Phillips'      Creek  location,   we admit that  that,
too,       is  legendary,   some claiming that the landing was on the out-
side  of  Fore  River  rather  than on the inside,    possibly  at  or  near
what is  known as Hunt's Hill.          But it  is a question whether a com-
pany would have gone into  winter  quarters  on the outside  with  a
little  craft  of  thirty  tons  when  they  could  have  found  nice  still
water and a good landing only a mile or two away.
In fact,       there  are many things  in regard to Weymouth,    as  well
as  to  the  whole western  hemisphere,     which  will  never  be known.
We would not detract  from  the  glory  of  Columbus,     but  at New-
port,     in  Maine and the Provinces there are unmistakable evidences
of  an  occupancy  by mill  and  road  builders  of a high  order  long
before  the  day  of  Columbus,      and  the  same thing  is  true  of  the
great  west beyond the " father of waters. "
What we promised  to  do in  these  articles  was to  give a history
of  Weymouth as found in the Town Records,    and we now proceed
with those articles .
Twenty years  from  the  landing  of the Gorges  Company,      Wey-
mouth had  taken the place  of  Wessagussett,    and instead  of being
a place  without  limit  or bounds  it   was  a  well-defined  town  with
fixed   boundary  lines,      a  population  variously  estimated  at  from
three  to  four  hundred  people,    sixty-eight  of  them  holding  titles
to  sundry  parcels  of  land,    and  the  rest  of  the  territory  held  in
common.
Care  of  landed property and control of live  stock seems  to  have
first  engrossed the attention of the townspeople,    and town meetings
 - 21 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               499
were  numerous.                 A singular fact,    however,    is  that while for many
years there were town officials  there  is  no  record  as  to  the time or
manner of their election or appointment.
At a town meeting held Dec. 20,    1643,   it  was ordered that from
henceforth  any person who shall cut or saw any pine,    cedar,     hem-
lock  or spruce boards,    either  to sell or carry hence to any person
or persons to be transported hence,   shall pay for the use and behalf
of the town for every thousand so sawed the several  sums herein-
after named.             Every one that  hath commons for  every thousand,
1s.      6d. ,     and every one that hath  no commons,      2s.       6d.  ,       and  if   any
person shall  presume to  carry away any such boards  without  first
obtaining  permission  from  John  Upham or  John  Hollister,       who
are  deputized  by the town to  see this  order  executed,     it  shall  be
lawful  for  them to  seize  said  boards  for  the use of the  town,  and
they shall receive 6d.    a thousand for their  care.
At the same meeting it was agreed by general consent that those
who have  right  of  common shall  have  swamp  lots  so  it  be  not
within a mile of the meeting-house,  and every one to  the quantity
of two acres.
It  was  further  ordered  that  all  the  unlotted  land  lying  near
the  cedar  swamp by the  Back  River  shall  be  common  pasture
forever  to  the users  only of the lower end of the plantation,      and
they shall  have liberty to  fence it  from any others  " so that it bare
not  to  pass  by the  seaside, " and  that  no  other  person or  persons
turn in any cattle therein,   being intended principally for  the good
of the lower part of the plantation.
On Nov.  20,     1645,     it   was  ordered  that  as  there  was  a  rate
formerly  made amounting  to  £121  for  and toward  the  discharge
of  several   sums  of  money,     which  had  been  borrowed  and  dis-
bursed in money and wheat,    which is  to  be levied  again to  make
satisfaction  that no one man may be eased  and another burdened,
but that  all  may bear their  proportion  in  such  special  levy,      it   is
ordered   that  all   the  inhabitants  in  this  town  shall  make  satis-
faction  to  the  bailiff  who is  authorized  to gather up said  rate  in
money or in wheat before the  9th  of  February,     1645.    (We would
here  state  that as it  may seem strange to some that  January and
February  meetings  came  later  than  other  months  of  the  same
year,     that the O. S.  calendar year began with March. )
On April  6,      1646,     it  was  ordered  that,      " Whereas  we find  by
sad  experience  and  great  inconvenience  that  many  times  have
come to pass by the permitting of strangers to come into the plan-
tation  to  sojourn  for  a  season  and  afterwards  do  account  them-
selves  inhabitants,     no  inhabitant  within  the plantation  shall  take
into his home as  an inmate  or  servant  without giving security  to
the  town for  any loss  or  expense which  may occur  on account  of
the same."
It was further  ordered that no inhabitant should let  or sell  any
house or land to an outside party without first offering  the same at
a public town meeting.
 - 22 - 
500                                           OLD  RECORDS
It would seem that in those days dogs were obliged  to forage  for
themselves,      and we find  that  at a town meeting  held  the  12th  of
February,        1647,    it  was ordered  that  as  dogs had been feeding  on
the  growing  corn,     from  the  sixth  day of August  to  the  29th  of
September,     all  dogs should wear a clog " according  to  the  bigness
of  the  dog, "   under  penalty of 6d.    per  head  when found  at  large
without a suitable clog.
An officer  called  a " hoggard,  "  or  more properly hogward,     seems
to  have  been  quite  a factor  in  looking  after  unyoked  hogs  and
unclogged  dogs,    and  about this  time  he  was  ordered  to  levy  on
Edward Pool,     who was about to  move out of town and had caused
great  inconvenience  to  Widow  Harding  by allowing  five  lengths
of fence to remain down.
On  Feb.  28,         1648,     the  following  fence-viewers  were  appointed:
James Humphrey and Phillip Stainwood,    below the herring bridge;
Thomas  White and John Thomas,      near  King  Oak  Hill;       Thomas
Pratt  and  William Rede,    for the rest  of the town;    and all  fences
were  to  be put in order before the  20th  of the  next  month.           The
fence- viewers  were to  notify  any delinquents,     and after  six  days,
if  not  repaired,   the same was done  by the town and  2d.      per  rod
levied on the owner.
All  udder  cattle  shall  go under the hand  of  a sufficient  keeper
under penalty of 6s.    7d.    per head,   to be collected by the hogwards,
and one- half the fine  shall be his,   the other half to go to  the town.
The town now seems to have gone a whole year without a town
meeting,     but  in  February,     1649,     we find  the  following:         " Every
man person above 16 years  of age after public notice given by the
waywarder  shall   appear  at  the  time  and  place  designated  then
and there to diligently work on the highway."    Any person failing
to do this was fined 5s.    per day unless he gave a reasonable excuse,
when other days were assigned him.
 - 23 - 
Chapter  IV
Those early  settlers  found it  no easy matter to  define boundary
lines  between individuals,   break up the virgin  soil,    produce  crops
and  at  the  same  time  evolve  a  form  of  municipal  government
which should be democratic and just  and equitable  to  all  parties
concerned.
The matter of  taxation was as  serious  a  one in  the early  days  as
it  is   to-day,    and we find  that in March,    1651,   " It  is  ordered and
agreed  upon  by the whole Town that  from  henceforth  whenever
any  Rate  levy  or  assessments  are  to  be  made of  any kind what-
soever  that  public  notice  shall  be given  to  the  whole  town or  as
many as  are  or  may be convenient,    that  upon a certain  day pre-
fixed for that end they shall bring in a list  of the rateable  property
and any one failing  to do so shall be subject  to  a penalty  of 5s.
and any one bringing  in  a wrong statement  shall  pay twice  that
amount."
At the  same meeting  Thomas  Dyer and  William  Torrey  were
appointed  to  mark the boundary line between Hingham and Wey-
mouth,       going  from  Back  River  to  a certain  oak  tree  at  the  end
of the line.         John Oliver and Robert Martin were appointed at  the
same  time  to  mark  the  western  boundary  line  from  high-water
mark on Fore River running south one-half point west to  the  end
of the line.
Evidently the  selectmen,     or townsmen as  they were then called,
were  not  always  on  hand,    as  we find  on  March  11,       1651 ,       that
"owing  to  the  neglect  of  seasonable  appearance  of  townsmen  in
the  meetings  at  the  hour  prefixed  tending  to  the  detriment  of
those who are careful to observe the time,    and retarding  the  labor
of the majority who are present,   all  those who are  late shall forfeit
to the majority who are present  6d.   per hour for  every hour  they
are  absent."
The early settlers  of Weymouth had a thought for education and
employed  a man to " teach  the boys reading,    writing,    arithmetic
and spelling, "   but they had their  troubles  as  we do to-day,     as  is
evidenced by the following record in  1651 :
"Whereas  as  there  is  due our  school  master,     Captain  Perkins,
for  six  months'     salary  10£,     or thereabout,   which must be  speedily
payed  to  prevent further  inconvenience.           Therefore  the  Town do
give order according to the power that is committed to us that there
shall  be appointed  Raters  for  this  purpose  and they  do  speedily
meet  together  and  according  to  directions  address  themselves  to
levy  said  rate  upon  such  inhabitants  as  were  lyable   thereunto
when it was post."
 - 24 - 
502                                        OLD  RECORDS
It  is  further  ordered  that all houses shall  be rated as they are  in
the  last  country rate;      all  single  persons  according  to  the  rate  of
£30;     all  cattle,    meadow and upland shall  be valued  according  as
it was then worth;    and speedily deliver  the  same to the constable
to collect.
Thatched  roofs  were  a feature  of  the  early  days,      and as  there
were complaints  as to the manner of getting it,   the following order
was passed at a meeting in November,    1651 :
" There  shall  be but one way to  sage  flats  and  it  shall  be  16
feet  wide one-half from land of  Richard  Porter  and one-half from
land  of Stephen French and for its  use they were to have the first
rite  to  the  sage growing on the  flats  below their  land  and it  was
further ordered that no thatch should be cut before the 20th day of
the  6th  month and not over  200 pounds shall  be cut by any one
person for  his  own use,    and  there  was a penalty  of  10s.     fixed  for
the  violation of this  order. "
The days of friction  matches had not arrived,   and fire  was pro-
duced by flint  and tinder  or  borrowed from house to  house,     and,
owing to the risk in carrying fire brands and torches,   it  was ordered
that  no inhabitant,    stranger  or  seaman shall  carry  any fire  unless
it  be in a pot or other covered vessel  between the first  day of  the
first  month and the last day of the eighth month,   that is,     from the
first   of  March to  the  last  of  October.        Penalty  for  violation  of
this was 20s. ,   one-half to the complainant.
Up to  1652  gatherings  for  town  business  had  been  frequent,
irregular  and  without  form;     they  now  assumed  a  more definite
character,      as  will be seen in our next chapter.
 - 25 - 
Chapter V
Up to  1651  meetings had been frequent and irregular,   but in this
year it  was ordered that -
Two town meetings in the year should be held,   one on the 1st 2d of the first
month and the last 2d day of the 9th month,   in which the whole town shall  meet
together at 9 o'clock for the choice of Townsmen,  Deputies,   Councillors,    Raters,
Waywarden,       Bayliffs  and all  other  officers  and also  determine  concerning  the
school and the Townsmen shall be accountable to the town for  such  orders  as
they have passed,   what are in  force and what have been repealed,   also what has
been expended on the towns account.
Signed,                HENRY KINGMAN.
THOMAS  WHITE.
JOHN WHITMAN.
THOMAS  DYER.
ROBERT  TUCKER.
The first  town meeting under the  new order  of things was held
on the 26th of November,    1651,   and John Rogers,     Nicholas Byron,
David  Hunt,         John  Burger,        Thomas  Dyer,        William   Reed  and
William   Dyer   were   elected    selectmen,       and   Nicholas   Byron,
Johnathan  Waltham,      Nicholas  Nash,    John  Holbrook  and  James
Nash,       raters .
The duties of selectmen were thus defined : -
" First.                Make such  orders  as  may be for  our interest  in lands,
commons,     grass  or  woods  and  timbers  that  may be  transported
from the town.
" Second.              They shall have power to  see  that all  orders  made by
the General Court shall  be observed  and  also  all  orders  which we
have made or may make which are  not repealed  at  their  meeting
in the first month.
" Third.               It  shall be lawful for them to take course that all dry
cattle shall be herded in the woods,    excepting calves  and yearlings.
" Fourth.               They shall  issue  such  rates  as the town may require
and see that they are gathered.
"Fifth.                They may establish all  grants provided they are satisfied
they  are  in  due order  and  not within  two  miles  of  the  meeting
house.
"Sixth.                     We willingly  grant  they  shall  have  Dyner  upon  the
Town's charge when they meet upon the Town's affairs . "
For the year  1652 John Rogers,    Thomas Hollis,    Henry Kingman,
James Smith and John Holbrook were elected selectmen.
And it   was  voted,     "we  do  elect   Nicholas   Phillips,        Thomas
Dyer and Thomas White,    raters,   to make such rates as  were needed
for the town.  "
 - 26 - 
504                                        OLD  RECORDS
Also voted,    " we do choose Dekon Rogers for  to be recorder  for
the town."
At a general town meeting the  14th of  December,     1652,      Deacon
Rogers,     Sergeant Holbrook,     Thomas Daggett,    Thomas Dyer,     John
Bicknell,       Sergeant  Hunt and William  Torrey  were  chosen  towns-
men,      " and  the same power given  them that  the last  Townsmen
had,      also  to  do what they should judge present necessity requires
about  the  Meeting House and that  they may make it  more com-
fortable  and prevent further decay. "
At a meeting of the selectmen,   Jan. 24,    1652,   John Bicknell " was
chosen Sealer of Weights and Measures and to see to the observance
of the Town's orders  thereto."
At the same meeting " it  was agreed upon that for  seats  for  the
master's  house  that  Sergeant  Holbrook  and John  Bicknell  shall
take care  to  provide such planks,    boards  and other timber as  they
shall  from  time  to  time or  at  any time  have direction  from  the
Townsmen and  to  have full  liberty  for  cutting of timber  on  any
of our commons and also that they keep a true and just account of
what time  they expend in and about the same and to  procure  it
done as cheap as they can.           To give in their account to the Towns-
men who shall  give  immediate  satisfaction  or  they  are  at  liberty
to dispose of the said planks as they shall see cause. "
"March  7th,       1653,      it  was voted  that  there be but five  Towns-
men and Thomas White,     Ensign Whitman,    Thomas Dyer,    William
Torrey and Stephen French were elected and it  was voted that the
same power which was given to the Selectmen in 1651 should con-
tinue."
" It was further voted that the old board of officers  should bring
in a list  of what was due the town for timber and otherwise;    also
what the town owed and the same should be audited. "
It  was also  " voted that the thousand acres  of land formerly set
apart  for  commons be speedily  set  out before any further  grants
are  ratified  and that as  near  and convient for the town as may be
possible  and after  that grants  may be ratified  in order;    and that
being done,     it  was voted that another thousand  acres  of  commons
be  laid  out  which  shall  remain  in  perpetuity  for  the  use  of  the
Town."
"Voted,        that  the  deputies  for  the  town  are  to  have  full  pay
satisfactory for  their expenses at court this year upon a just account
given in by them.  "
Thomas  Dyer  was  appointed  recorder  of  births,      deaths   and
marriages ,        and  William  Torrey  recorder  of  land-bargain  sales  and
"Aleonations. "
" Commons"  and use of " Commons "  seems to  have been a hard
question for  the early  settlers  to  adjust  satisfactorily,    and in  1654
we find  that  John  Lovell,      Edward  Poole,      Lieutenant  Holbrook,
Edward  Kingman,      Thomas  Stevens,     James  Nash,      Thomas  Hol-
brook and  Richard  Bolles  were fined  in sums varying from 1s.     6d.
to £1  15s.    for  cutting cordwood and timber on the Towns Commons,
 - 27 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               505
which led  to  a spirited  discussion,  and at the  next meeting it  was
voted that  all  commons should be immediately laid  out,      and that
every man who is  a commoner shall  have liberty  to  cut wood and
timber,    and any one who is   not  a commoner shall  forfeit  20s.    for
violation of this  rule.
It was also  " voted  by the whole  town  that whereas  there  be
several  in  the lowerpart  of  the town who are  unable  to  make up
their  fences  about  their  commons,    they shall  have liberty  for  the
year to close up the highway.  "
 - 28 - 
Chapter  VI
At the town meeting  in  March,     1655,     " It  was agreed  that the
Pen should be at hither  end of  Pon Plain and that Thomas Pratt
and Hugh Roe shall have 30s.   to make it and the Pen to be 8 poles
one way and 7 poles the other.  "
"Agreement was made with Elder Bates by the town for keeping
of the dry cattle until after  Indian harvest and to begin as  soon as
the Pen is  made for which he is  to have 11s.   to be paid  in  corn at
prices  current.          William Torrey for  the Selectmen of the Town.  "
"Voted,      that  the  Town  Rate  be  collected  and  that  not  any
cattle shall be paid in the rate  nor above one-eighth part in  Indian
Corn  and  that to  be the last  year's  corn  and other  things  to be
valued by independent men according  to the value of prices at 4s.
per bushel for corn and 4s.    6d.    for wheat. "
It  would seem  by  the  above,     and other  things  which  we will
shortly  show,    that  greenbacks,      yellowbacks,    gold  and  silver,     did
not  enter  very much into  mercantile  transactions,   but barter  and
exchange settled accounts.
In accordance with an order by the General Court the selectmen
ordered:
" That  all   fences  about  any  cornfield  whether  general  or  par-
ticular  shall  be made and set  up by each man his  several  portion
from the 20th of the 1st month (March)  if  the weather permits and
the same well  and sufficiently  to  repair and mayntayne against all
orderly  cattle  and yoke  hogs  so  long  as  there  shall  any  kind  of
grayne be remayning in any such cornfield.   "
In  March,       1656,     "Voted  that  all  Rate  men shall  pay for  their
estates  and all  Poles 20s.
"Voted that those persons that have promised to Goodman Hunt
any work that they will give it  in New Corn at  harvest time. "
In March,     1657,   "Voted that the account of the Town Rates be
made to James Nash,   Lieut.    Holbrook,    Nicholas Nash,    Mr. Chard,
William Holbrook and Thomas White who are  hereby empowered
to  equate and discharge upon the same so  far as it  shall  appear to
be just."
Ordered  that  six  acres  of  land be granted to John Taylor,     pro-
vided  he  should  either  build  upon it  or plant it within  one year
of  the date of  the  grant,      and further  provided  that  if  himself or
his  heirs  should hereafter sell it,    it  shall  revert to the town.
Inasmuch  as  many of  the  marked  trees  showed  the  boundary
lines   between  Hingham  and  Weymouth  on  the  one  side,        and
Braintree  and  Weymouth  on  the  other,    parties  were  appointed
to  perambulate  the  line  and  fix  the  bounds  as  per  order  of  the
General  Court.
 - 29 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               507
On Dec.  10,   1657,     as  we have before stated,     Church and Town
were one,     yet  up to  this  time we have found  no mention  of  the
support  of  the  church,   excepting  now and then  a little  in  regard
to the repairs  on the meeting-house.       We now find the following:
"At a meeting of the 20 men who were directed and  empowered
by the Town to  take care  about  Mr.  Thatcher's  (the  minister's)
mayntanance that may be payde both in time and kind according
to  our  agreement  it  was  ordered  by;    then  Mr.  Thatcher's  Rate
shall  be made by the  Selectmen from time to time by the first  of
the first  month and the first  of the second month yearly and that
the said Selectmen shall see that is  payd in either  to  Mr. Thatcher
or the Deacons by the 12th  of the 2d month and the 12th  of the
8th month and in case any shall neglect or refuse to dischargeduty
therein to put forth their power to recover same according to law. "
Preservation  of timber and shade  trees  was one of the burdens
of the times,     and at a meeting held on Feb. 12,   1657,    it would seem
that  the  day  was  devoted  to  this  subject,     which  resulted  in  re-
enacting  laws  and  regulations  previously  stated  in  these  articles,
and adding the following :
"Whoever  shall  presume  to  fell,     kill  or  top  any tree  or  trees
which grow before his  own or his  neighbors  Dore or that stand  in
any place  upon the  common or  highway  which  may be for  the
shade of either  man or beast,     or shelter  of any house or otherwise
for  public use every person so offending shall  be lyable  to pay for
every  such  tree  so  felled,    topped  or  killed   20s.    for  the  Town's
cause."
 - 30 - 
Chapter  VII
At the  annual town meeting for  the election  of  officers  held  on
Nov.  24,     1656,     William Torrey,     Deacon Whitman,    Deacon Rogers ,
Thomas   Dyer,        Stephen   French,      James   Smith,       Sr. ,        and  John
Harding  were  elected  as  selectmen and to  have the  same powers
as  were  established  in  1651 .
At this meeting the lack of restraint upon live stock was one of
the  burdens  of  complaint,      and  in  addition  to  cattle  and  hogs,
sheep came in for a share of the complaint.           Previous  regulations
in  regard  to  cattle  and hogs were re- enacted,    and it  was " ordered
that  as  sheep are  often  found upon men's enclosed  property,     and
where such  fences  are  secure  for  other  cattle,   the  owners  of  such
sheep  shall  be lyable,    provided  the  fence is  sufficient  for  ordinary
cattle,      to a fine of two pence for every sheep or lamb so found and
shall also pay the owner of the land or  crop for  all  damage done. "
At this  time the violation of regulations  in regard to  trees  came
up again,    and about fifteen individuals were fined for cutting lumber
and cordwood on the town's land.
At a meeting held Dec.  17,    1658,     there  was a further  allotment
of  land,        and John Thompson,      Henry Kingman,     Ensign Whitman,
John Burger,     Marcett Pratt,    Richard Newbury,   Richmond Randall.
John  Smith,       John  Harding  and  John Guppie  received  grants  of
additional  acres.
On Jan.  3,       1658,       Elder  Bates  and Thomas  Dyer were granted .
" 20 acres  in  some place near  the  great Rocks.  "
At a town meeting held March 2,   1659,    it was " voted the Serg't .
John  Whitmarsh  shall   have  Huckleberry  pond  and  the  swamp
round  about  the  pond in  full  satisfaction  for  other  land due  his
father."
It  was  also  " ordered  that  the  highway  below  Thomas  Pratt's
house  and  the  house  of  Nicholas  Norton be shut  up during  the
pleasure  of  the  town and they whom it  doth concern  setting  up
sufficient  gate for those who go to  and from the mill. ”
At the  annual  meeting  in  November,       1659,        Henry  Kingman,
Ensign  Whitman,       Deacon  Rogers,        Thomas  White,        Lieutenant
Holbrook,          Mr.  Chard and William  Torrey were elected  selectmen,
with the same powers which had existed since 1651.
"Voted that  Mr.  Thatcher  shall  have granted  his  share  on  a
small  parcel  of land  lying  within  his  fence  near  the  place  where
Gordon  Shopeis'     house  stands,     provided  that  the  highway at  the
brow of  the  hill  be  a little  enlarged  and further  there  is   granted
by his  House and land a small parcel  of land at the foot  of  watch
house hill ."

OLD  RECORDS                               509
"Voted  that  James  Nash and  Lieut.    Holbrook  are  hereby  ap-
pointed by the  town to  lay  out as  much land as  they shall  think
meet  for  such  Highway either for  the Town or  County as shall be
taken  of Stephen  French's  land at the  smelt brook,    Provided  that
the land given by way of allowance intrude not upon the Thousand
acres,    but be taken on the east side of the smelt brook.  "
We would  here  remark  that  this  same land,    after  nearly  two
hundred and fifty  years,    is  still  in the family and being  improved
by Bela  P.  French,    a lineal  descendant in the eighth generation.
The red  man was still  among the people of the town,     and it  is
evident  from  the following,    was something  of a landholder,      as  it
was  ordered at the above meeting
"That  upon  the  motion  of  Nawhantum  that  Thomas  White
and  John  Holbrook should  upon  two days'      notice  from  the  sayd
Indian goe into  the woods with him to  see where the  24 acres  of
land given to the said Indian lyeth or whether any be conveniently
layed out for  him.  "
At a meeting held April 2,    1860,     " Ordered that John Staples  and
be fence viewers for the Neck;      Robert Randall & John Vining
for  the Range & King Oak Hill in the body of the Town;        Richard
Porter & John Harding for  the east  field  and the remaining  fields
of the south end of the Town;     John Smith and James Humphrey
for  the  lower plantation  who are  immediately  after  notice  hereof
to view over the fences  in their several domains and to give notice
to the several owners of any insufficient  or defective fences  and to
act  in all  respects  according as  is  provided  in  the  Towns order  in
regard  to fences. "
At a meeting of the selectmen in  September,     1660,   about a dozen
offenders  against  the rules  in  regard  to  cutting timber  and  cord-
wood  on the  commons  were  brought  before  them  for  trial;       all
pled  guilty  and  were each  fined  10s.    6s.    to be paid  forthwith,     and
the other 4s.      to be paid when the town called  for  it .
There were  government  lands  even  in  Weymouth  in  the  early
days,     and we find  on Nov. 20,     1660,     it  was "Voted  that  whereas
there  was  heretofore  50  acres  of  land  granted  to  James  Parker
and by him sold to  Capt.     Perkins & since been conveyed to Serg't .
Hunt,      but  the  place  for  laying  out  had  not  been  appointed  is
ordered  that  the sayd land shall  be layd out above the  great  lots
on the Hingham side  Provided  there  be taken  not  in  any swamp
land with his assignment above 6 acres. "
The above town meeting was continued to the 27th of November,
when  " The question  was proposed  whither  the 12 hundred  acres
of land formerly set  apart  for  commons,    together  with all  the  rest
of the common,     both  in  the  upper  and  lower  part  of  the  Town
shall  be  divided  and  become  every  man's  proportion  that  hath
rights  to common. "    Voted in  the affirmative.
The  spring  meeting  of 1661  was devoted  almost  wholly  to  the
allotment  of  land,     and  several  hundred  acres  in  all  parts  of  the
town were assigned to different individuals who had rights .

At the November meeting in that year we find but little mention
of  the election  beyond  that of town clerk  and the defining  of his
duties.             " Mr.  Chard  chosen  Town  Clerk  to  record  land  grants
heretofore  made  and  all   manner  of  Aliements  according  as  the
Selectmen shall direct,     who are  hereby empowered thereto.
"Also  to   state  his  fees   and  whatever  else  shall  be  necessary
tending  thereto  so that a fayer  record  may be kept of every mans

drawing up orders,    making of Rates or any other service they shall

"Voted  also  that  the  Townsmen,     together  with  our  Elders  be
instructed  to  overlook our Town Orders,    to correct,   and make new
and repeal what they think are meet and present a draught thereof
to the Town at its meeting in March next. "

Chapter  VIII
We resume these records in March,   1661,    and find that " Liberty
was given  to  Thomas Drake and such persons  as  he shall  like  to
take  in,      to  take  in  100 acres  of  land  above the  great  Pond & are
referred  to  the Selectmen to  make conditions  with them about the
same."
"Voted  that  Captain  Torrey  shall  be  free  from  mayntaining
highway during  the  time  that  he shall sufficiently  keep  in  good
repair  the  highway  between  Corporal  Ludden's  & and  his  own
house."
"Expense acc't.
"Stephen French and John Porter for mending the shed  10s.
"Brother  Bicknell  for  graval  and  making  the  meeting  house
lot £3. "
"Gordon Perkins for his pains in getting powder 4s. "
"John  Harding  for  making  a staple  for  the  Pound,      Hooks  &
Hinges for the meeting house & work about the  Pound,     4s. "
In November,      1662,    it  was  "Agreed on by the  Selectmen  that
Giles Leach shall pay only the sum of sixteen shillings  for  the use
of the Town by way of fine for cutting and carrying away of eight
cords  of  wood from  the  Town common,   with  this  condition  that
the  said Giles  Leach  shall  demand  no  more  concerning  boating
for  carrying  Soldiers  to  Boston or  any other  place  upon that  ac-
count,    being so much deducted;     viz.,   16s.   for that end. "
On Nov. 24,     1662,    at the annual town meeting,   " There is  chosen
for  Town officers  for  the year ensuing  Captain  Torrey,       Thomas
Dyer,           Lieut.          Holbrook,        Ensign  Whitman,      Sergent   Whitmarsh,
Sergent  Hunt & Senior  Nash,   Selectmen;     John Smith & Edward
Kingman,    Constables;    Capt.    Torrey,    Lieut.    Holbrook and Thomas
Dyer,      Commissioners;     Andrew Ford,   James Lovell,   John Thomp-
son and Samuel Butterworth,      Wardens. "
"Voted     That those who did not appear at the mending of the
Highway;      viz. ,      William  Richards,     James  Lovell,     Thomas  Dow,
Thomas Kingman,  Giles  Leach and Philip Read shall  pay to John
Nash 20s.      6d.    to be disposed  of towards  the mending  of  the way
to the mill over the marsh."
At the town meeting,    Nov. 3,    1663,    " James Smith,    Sr. ,    Thomas
Harding,       Thomas White,      Mr.  Chard,      Thomas  Dyer  & Wm.        Fry
elected  Selectmen;      Lieut.    Hunt & James Lovell constables.  "
"Voted that all  the flats  up the Back River shall  be let  out  for
the  towns  use  for  the  year  ensuing  for  the  thatching  of  Houses
and to be done by the Selectmen.         By flats  we understand all those

Chapter  IX
At the town meeting in March,    1664,    the boundary lines between
Braintree and Weymouth,     one side,    and Hingham and Weymouth,
on  the  other,      came  up  for  discussion,       and  John  Holbrook  and
John  Kingman were appointed  to  remark the former,      and James
Lovell  and John Shaw the  Hingham line.
At the  town  meeting  in  November  of  the  same  year  James
Nash,         Thomas   Dyer,        Ephraim   Hunt,       Lieut.      John  Holbrook,
Thomas Pratt and William Torrey were elected Selectmen ;      Robert
Randall  and Thomas Bayley,    constables.
During  this  year  there  came a change  in  the  ministry  of  the
church,       Mr.  Thatcher leaving  for  a Boston field,    and Rev.  Samuel
Torrey  becoming  his  successor  and  remaining  until  his  death  in
1707.
The parsonage  and  some  landed  property  was  evidently  Mr.
Thatcher's  in  his  own right,    for we find  the following  act  at  this
meeting:
" It  is   further  ordered  by  the  Town that  twelve  men under-
mentioned  are  chosen  as   a  committee  to  debate  and  conclude
concerning the house & land formely in the hands of Mr. Thomas
Thatcher.            And now in the hands & disposal of  the purcharsers  in
Town which said  committee are  to  debate  & conclude concerning
the aforesaid  house & land for  disposal of it in the Town as  they,
or ten of them shall  agree the manner and way it  is  to be disposed
of  unto  Mr.  Samuel  Torrey,     now minister  of the Town or other-
wise as they shall think meet.           Elder Bates,    Thomas Pratt,     Thomas
White,       James Smith,    senior,     Richard  Parker,     James  Nash,      Lieut.
Holbrook,    John Bicknell,   James Humphrey,    Thomas Dyer,     Deacon
Whitman,    Sergeant Hunt,    Committee. "
"Voted  that  John  Pratt  & John  Tompson having  formerly  a
Rate  of  £2  10s.     10d.     committed to them to  gather  and there  re-
maining  yet  in  their  hands  the  sum  of  £1  15s.     beside  what  is
allowed  them  for  gathering  the  sayd Rate which  the  Townsmen
do order  to  payd to  Deacon  Dyer who hath accepted of the same
and the sayd John Pratt and John Tompson are hereby discharged."
At the town meeting  in  March,      1665,      there  were a number of
grants of land varying in size from  a quarter of  an acre to thirty or
more,     and among them the following :
"Whereas  as  there  is   a  certain  parcel  of land  lying  near  the
house  of  the  Widow  Poole  containing  about  36  acres  the  right
whereof  is  in  the Town's disposal.              It  is  voted and agreed  upon
by the  Town that  the whole interest  of  the sayd land  is  hereby
 - 37 -

granted  to  Deacon  Thomas  Dyer  with  promise  at  any  time  to
furnish  the sayd Thomas Dyer with all the power to defend himself
against all  manner of persons whichever shall challenge  in  interest
therein & the sayd Thomas  Dyer is   to  pay  Mr. Shimton for  the
lots  now in custody  of one  of  the  Selectmen  for  the  sayd  land,
Provided  that James  Lovell  shall  have one half of the sayd land
if he will,    he paying the one half of the sayd lots within two months.
Provided also  that if a better interest  appear than the Towns that
the Town only to return the sayd pay for  the sayd land. "
"Voted by the  Town that John  Pratt shall  have liberty  to  set
up a gate upon the cart way to the water side below Elder Bates,
his  land and John Haring.          Provided that  no man,    if  the gate be
left  open be accounted  a trespasser.           Only we hope  no man will
take advantage thereof. "
At a meeting of the selectmen  Sept.  11,     1665,    " Information was
given  by James  Smith,     Jr.,    against  John  Pratt,     Thomas  Bayly,
Jr. ,     and John Whitman,  Jr.,  for cutting of thatch with a Sithe upon
the Town's flats  for which according  to  the Town order  they  are
hereby judged  to  pay twenty shillings  apiece,    the  one half  to the
informant and the other half to the Town.  "
" It  was  also  agreed  by the  Selectmen  that  there  should  be  a
Town Rate made to the value of forty pounds for the discharge of
Town debt and for the doing of what was needful to be done about
the meeting  house,      and  Mr.  William  Torrey  is  hereby  desired  to
gett workmen and do what he can for  the finishing  thereof.   "
On Nov.  27,     1665,     Deacon Dyer,     Lieutenant  Holbrook,      Richard
Parker,          James   Humphrey,        John  Bicknell   and  William   Chard
were elected  selectmen,    Captain Torrey,     Lieutenant  Holbrook and
Deacon  Dyer,    commissioners;      Thomas  Dow  and  John  Rogers,
constables.
Voted,     " Whereas there is  necessity that ways shall be settled  so
that the several  inhabitants shall have such  necessary ways to the
water side and as is  needful it  is  hereby ordered by the Town that
Elder  Bates ,       Capt.      Torrey,     Lieut.     Holbrook,     Thomas  White  and
John Bicknell are desired and impowered to lay out and determine
all  ways  within the  bounds  of  the Town for  ways  to  the  several
water  sides  or  as  shall  be  needful  for  the  Town and  the  several
inhabitants  thereof,    and to  mark out such  ways according  to  their
discretion  or the discretion  of the majority part of the committee
chosen,    who are desired to doe it  at or before the last of February
and to bring in a return thereof to be recorded by the Town Clerk. "
"Voted  likewise  by the Town that  the  flats  in  the  Back  River
shall  be the next year and from year to year until  the Town shall
order otherwise for proper use of William Chard,    Schoolmaster.  "
"Voted  likewise,    that  John  Vining  shall  have  the  Town  flats
up the  Back River the year ensuing  to  be paid to  William  Chard,

"Voted that Joseph Green shall have a place  to  dig a well  in  a

"At a  meeting  of the  Selectmen  and  Commissioner  held  June
8th,    1667,      with reference to  an order from the General Court held
in  Boston,       May last.           It is  agreed that there be raised  by way of

Back River  side  near John Pratt's house at that landing and John
Staples,         Jr. ,        is  empowered and directed  to cord  the  said  wood so
gathered."

Chapter X
We resume with a meeting of the selectmen held in April,    1667,
when we find the following :
" It  is  agreed by the Selectmen and Militia with reference to  the
fortification  for  the  management  thereof that  the  same  be  com-
mitted to  Capt.    William Torrey to act in that matter."
" It  is  agreed the Selectmen shall  make a Rate of thirty shillings
to make up for the past year and it  is  to be added to  the County
Rate to be gathered by the constable. "
At the town meeting,  November,    1667,    Captain Torrey,     Thomas
White,      Sergeant  Hunt,     John  Kingman,     John  Bicknell,       William
Holbrook   and  William   Charde   were   elected   selectmen;         John
Kingman and John Shaw,    constables.
"Voted by the  Town that there be three sides of the meeting
house  galleyed  with  two  seats  next  the  wall  as  already  begun.
Committee  chosen  to  carry  out  the  above  Capt.       Torrey,       Lieut.
Holbrook & James Nash,   senior.  "
"Voted that what expense be necessary for repairing the Meeting
House & hanging up a Bell is  to be raysed and payd by a Town
Rate."
At a meeting of the selectmen,   held Dec. 10,    1667,     the following
vote was passed :
"The  Town  Clerk,      William  Chard,     or  his  successor  shall   be
allowed  for  every entry of any grant of land in the Town's  Books
one shilling,    for every copy of any record  or grant  or  searching  of
the records six pence,   to be payd by him or them that shall demand
the same.          For  every  Rate  committed to  him  to  be  made three
shillings  and fower pence."
At the March meeting  in  1668  the  county  and  town  rates  for

constables,      for  collection,    and were to  be payed as follows :

Fences at this time,   March,   1669,   came in for an overhauling,    and
several  committees  were  appointed  for  the  different  parts  of  the
town to see that the town laws in regard to fences were enforced.
Captain  Torrey,        Lieutenant  Holbrook  and  Deacon  Whitman
were appointed commissioners  to settle  small cases for the year.
The town  was  warned  to  bring  in  all  their  horses  above  two
years  old  to  be  viewed  according  to  the  law  passed  by the  last
General Court.
"Voted  that  Deacon  Whitman  shall  have  ten  acres   of  land
within  the  circumference  of  the  300  by  the  Common and  is  in
full  satisfaction of the said Deacon Whitman's several  lots. "
In  November,      1669,      at  the  annual  meeting,     Captain  Torrey,
Lieutenant  Hunt,      Deacon  Dyer,      John  Bicknell,   John  King,      Sr. ,
John  Pratt  and  James  Lovell  were  elected   selectmen;           Stephen
French and Thomas Kingman,    constables.
"Voted that  the Selectmen are  directed  and improved for  year
following  and from year to  year to  see  that the Minister's  Rates
for mayntance be made gathered & payd & satisfied,   to our present
minister,       Mr.  Samuel  Torrey  according  to  day specie  and agree-
ment once in each year.  "
"Voted that William
liam Chard be Schoolmaster to such as shall be
sent  to him being children belonging  to the Town for  which he is
to  have yearly  ten  pounds in  good  pay for  the Town.         And the
benefit  according  by scholars  as  aforesaid  both  of  this  town and
strangers."
Thomas Dyer,    treasurer,    reported due the selectmen 8s.  ,      and all
accounts were balanced.

At the annual meeting,    November,    1670,    Lieut.    John Holbrook,
Deacon Dyer,     Thomas Dean,    Sergeant White,    John Pratt,    Stephen
French  and  John  Bayley  were  elected   selectmen;     James  Nash
and Samuel Pratt,    constables.
Several grants of land were made to Thomas Deon,   John Taylor
and  James  Lovell,    but  there  was  some  subsequent  trouble  about
the latter,      and  at  a meeting  of  the  selectmen  in  December  the
town clerk  was instructed  to  issue  a warrant to  the constables  for
the  arrest  of James Lovell  for  abusive language  to  the  selectmen
and  snatching  a deed  from  the  hands  of  Lieutenant  Holbrook,
and he was fined  19s.
On March 11,    " Voted by the Town that  Samuel  Pratt & John
Nash or either of them are directed in behalf of the Town to request
the  next Honorable Court to  appoint  a commission to  end  small
cases  for  the ensuing year. "
"Voted by the Town in reference to some land that was formerly
granted  to  Henry  Kingman,     deceased,     which  grant  doth  appear
how much for the settling whereof of the Town but committed the
matter  to  Thomas White senior  & Lieut.   John Holbrook to  settle
the  land and stake  it  out to  Thomas Kingman according  to  the

best descretion,    lying  near the highway between the high  heap  of

In November,     1671,     Capt.     Wm.     Torrey,     Ensign John Whitman,
Deacon Dyer,    Thomas White,   Sr.,    John King,  Sergeant Whitmarsh
and  James  Humphrey  were  elected  selectmen;      John  Pratt  and
Phillip King,     constables.
"Voted that  the Selectmen's expenses for  the year past shall be
added on & gathered with  the County Rate and paid unto Deacon
Dyer the  same being  about twenty- six shillings."
"A vote  passed  by  the  Selectmen  to  choose  a  committee  to
negotiate with our Rev.  Pastor to  treate with him and to conclude
concerning fower particulars mentioned.
" 1st.              How much Panum.
" 2d.            In what particular specie.
" 3d.             When it  shall be payd.
" 4th.                 That some particular men shall undertake to pay it. "
Under  the  above  vote  a  committee  of  twenty  was  appointed,
and they  met on the 30th of November,   with the following result :
" 1st.              Fifty pounds P anum in specie.
" 2d.                By  the  free   vote  an  engagement  of  Lieut.        Holbrook,
Serg't.         Whitmarsh,      John  Pratt,     Stephen  French  & Jacob  Nash

" 3d.               The committee hath full  faith  agreed  that the Selectmen

of New England according to each man's proportion to our pastor's
Rate to be paid into those men who disbursed the money which is
to  be  intended  such  pay from each  inhabitant  as  may be  fit   for
Wood or  Clothing,   also provided that any inhabitant may if  he see
fit  pay his Rate in Money."
"And further  the  committee  agreed  that  each  Inhabitant  that
hath a Team is  to bring in  a load  of  wood to  Mr.  Torrey  and  all

In  November,       1672,       Capt.        Wm.       Torrey,     Lieutenant Holbrook,

Jr. ,      constables .
The same  parties  as  for  the  previous  year  became  responsible
for  the minister's  salary .
At the March meeting in 1673 much was done in small grants  of
land  along  the  highways  and  between  individuals   in   order   to
straighteń  lines  and settle  " small differences, "  and in  addition  was

"Voted that  whereas  the  Town passed  a vote that John Rone
shall  have two acres  of land somewhere above the  upper division
of  the commons to make him a commoner and the vote passed  in
the affirmative the land be set off."
At a general town meeting in March,    1673,    we find  as follows :
 - 43 -

"Whereas  the keeping  of  sheep  is  of  great  advantage  to  any
Commonwealth especially  to such a place as our Town is  and for
the  encouragement  of  the  Inhabitants  so  to  do  and  for  the pre-
vention of  much damage in  cornfields  and  pastures  by the  great
company  of  horses  and  mares  kept  by  the  Inhabitants.           It  is
ordered,     therefore,   and agreed upon the order of Town that thence-
forth  no  Inhabitant shall  keep more than one horse or one mare
&colt upon the Towns Commons except said person has 100 acres
of land of their  property  lying  on  Common and  such  Inhabitant
as  that  100  acres  or  above shall  not keep  above  two  mares  and
colts  on the  commons.            Under penalty  of five  shillings,     one  half
of which  shall  go  to  the  complainant  and  the  other  half  to  the
Towns benefit ."

Chapter  XII
At the annual town meeting,    in November,     1673,    Capt.     William
Torrey,        Dea.         Thomas  Dyer,      Stephen  French,      Sr. ,      James  Lovell,
John Rane and  Corporal  Vining were elected  selectmen;      Thomas
White,       Jr. ,       and Richard Phillips,     constables.
"With  reference  to  the  procuring  of  our  Pastor's   wood,      the
Town hath passed a vote that there  must be ten pounds added to
the  Rate  for  the  procuring  sufficient  wood for  the  year  ensuing;
viz. ,      twenty cords of wood."
The pastor's  salary  remained  the  same as  before      £50,      -and
Stephen  French,     Jr.,      Sergeant  White,      Deacon  Dyer,      John  Pratt
and  John Vining  were paid  the  same  in  money,    taking  as  their
pay the  £80 rate,    in  good pay,     as  assessed  by the town.           As good
pay in  those days  meant wood,     corn and other  commodities,     it  is
hard to  tell  how much graft there was in the transaction.
"Voted  that  William  Chard shall  ring  the  bell  and  sweep  the
meeting house for which he is  to have thirty shillings for the year. "
"The Town agreed  that  the twenty men who agreed  to  bring in
a cord  of wood each,   to the  Pastor for his  supply shall have seven
shilling  a cord.  "
At a meeting  of the selectmen,    in January,    1673,     the  following
rate was assessed:

There  came  this  year  several  more  grants  of  town  land,        and
Grape  Island  became  the  property  of  George  Fry,     James  Smith,
Sr. ,      James Ludden,   Sr.,    John King,  James Smith,    James Humphrey
and  Richard  Phillips,      and  according  to  the  allotment  the  island
must then have contained about fifty acres.
Andrew  Ford  at  this  time  put  in  a claim  that  he,     being  an
original   inhabitant  and  one  of  the  purchasers  of  the  town,      was
entitled  to  more land,     and was granted  a few  acres  in  the  Cedar
Swamp .
The meeting-house  now came  in  for  repairs,     and  we  find   the
"Selectmen  agree  with  Samuel White to  clapboard  the  north  side
of the meeting house and all  other places  as they shall  be needful
of clapboards for which he shall receive twelve shillings  P thousand
and  the  said  Samuel White is  further  obliged  to  lay  a  Flower  in
the  said  meeting house with sound,    sizable,    pine boards  for  which
he is  to  be paid six shillings  P hundred for all so  laid and the said
Samuel White is  empowered to cut so much stuff as may be needed
from the Town Commons. "

In   November,         1675,           Deacon   Dyer,        Lieutenant   Holbrook,
Sergeant  White,    John  Bicknell,    James  Humphrey,     Thomas  Dane
and  Stephen  French  were  elected  selectmen;      Sergeant  Pratt  and
Wm.    Reed,     constables.
At a meeting  of the  selectmen,    Dec.  4,    1676,      " The  matter  of
Town  record  with  Joseph  Dyer  as  executor  of  Deacon  Thomas
Dyer,      lately  deceased,     and  his  final  dues  for  securing  the Town's
powder for  nine years  at ten shillings  P annum at the full  sum of
four pounds."
"The  Selectmen  hereby  agree  the  same  day  and  date  above
with Serg't .      White for the securing and renewing  the Town Powder
the next year following  the sum of  ten shillings  and further  they
have  agreed  that  Joseph  Dyer deliver  the said  powder which  is
143 pounds  into  the custody  of  the  said  Serg't.       White  and  580
bullets  and  14 pounds  of  Swivel  shells  & 128  flints  which  is  de-
livered to him by the Selectmen.  "
The town rate  was considered  heavy for  the year  1676,     it  being
£170 13s.      4d.      on  account  of  repairs   on  the  meeting-house  and
other  matters,     but as  this  was only  a  few  cents  over  $882  of  the
currency of this day,    what would those hardy pioneers have thought
of the town of Weymouth raising  over  $169,000  in  one year,     and
having  out  bonds  exceeding  the  entire  valuation  of  the  State  at
that  time?     The town,   however,    was  not  discouraged  at  the  big
rate,    but went on with improvements,     as we find in this  year  1676:
"The Selectmen contracted with Jacob Nash to make and erect  a
new  Pound where  the  Selectmen  shall  appoint  said  pound to  be
eighty  rayles,       six  rayles  to  each  post,     the  rayles  to  be  sawed  six
inches wide and 21½ inches  thick.         The posts  to  be of  substancial
white oak nine feet  long  and  three  feet  set  in  the ground and  for
this   service   Mr.  Nash  was  to  receive  six   pounds  and  the  old
Pound."
On Jan.  24,       1676,    " with  reference  to  the  order  Enacted by the
General  Court  for  the  choosing  of  meet  persons  to  inspect  the
several  Inhabitants  of  the Town that shall  keep houses  of  Enter-
tainment  without  license.           In  observance  thereof  the  Selectmen
have  chosen  and  appointed   William   Holbrook  senior,       William
Torrey junior,   James Lovell & John Kingman to inspect the  several
Inhabitants of the Town of Weymouth according to the  Honorable
Courts act & Order. "

Chapter  XIII
At  the  March  meeting,      1677,       fences   and  walls  were  still   the
burden,     and the following fence- viewers  were appointed :        “ William
Torrey junior & Phillip King for the lower end of the Town below
the meeting house and the east field & King Oak Hill  field  and all
the  Elder  Bates  mill.         John  Pratt  & Thomas Bayley Jr. ,       Samuel
Pratt & John Shaw senior,   for the range field & Deacon Whitman's
field  and all  the  fences  belonging  to  the  Pond field.        Jacob  Nash
& Thomas White,   Jr.,   for  all the Neck fields  and William  Reed &
Increase Bates for all  the fences  lying beyond the river. "
At the annual meeting,     November,    1677,    Capt.     Torrey,   Thomas
White,           Sr. ,           Deacon  Whitman,     John  King,       Thomas  Dun,        Jacob
Nash and Lieutenant  White were elected  selectmen.
At this  meeting  it  was  "Voted  and  hereby  duly  ordered  that
Stephen  French jr.   be Clerk of the writs  to  record  Births,       Deaths
& marriages  and whatelse pertaineth  to  that office  as  also  that  he
be Town Clerk  and  recorder  of  the  Town with  respect  to  Town
acts and grants and that he attend the Selectmen at their meetings
and safely  to keep the Town Book and other matter committed to
him."
At the March meeting,    1678,     Lieutenant  Holbrook and Sergeant
White were appointed to  attend the honorable county court.
"Voted  that  the  minister's   Rate  be  made  in   October  next
ensuing and so from year to  year and to  be gathered with all con-
venient speed and none to delay  the payment of their  proportion
until the first  of March next. "
The town rate,    or tax,    for this year was £27 06s.
At a meeting on April 29,   1678,   " It is  ordered that the constables
appoint  the watchmen to begin the  first  of  May according  to  Law
& to see that the watchmen are provided with Muskets,      Powder &
Bullets  and  begin  the  watch  as  the  law  directs  & continue  the
watch till  sun rising & that two for the present & till  further orders
shall  suffice  as to watch. "
At a  town  meeting  held the  18th of September,     1678,       " It  was
voted by the  Town that  a  Schoolmaster  shall  be procured  for  to
teach children to  Read & Write & Casting of accounts. "
" It was voted that  Mr. Chard shall have a call  to this  work. "
" It  was  voted  that  the  Schoolmaster  shall   have  twenty- five
pounds  per  annum,      the  one-third  in  money and the  rest  in  good
pay."
" It  was voted that  the  Selectmen shall  have full  power to  raise
the above named sum for the use of the Schoolmaster proportionally
upon the  several  Inhabitants  by way of Rate  from  year  to  year
until the Town shall see  cause to  take further order. "

OLD  RECORDS                               525
Further,     " It was voted that the Selectmen shall have full  power
to  provide a house and such accommodations  as  they shall  need
for  the use of the Schoolmaster at  the Town's Charge. "
At the  town  meeting,     November,      1679,       Lieutenant  Holbrook,
Deacon   Whitman,        Deacon   Humphrey,     Jacob   Nash,         Sergeant
White,       Stephen  French  and  John  Rogers  were  elected  selectmen.
The selectmen reported  that they had hired  the house and grounds
of James Stewart for the use of the school for 35s.    per annum.          The
rest  of the year was devoted in the main to  the allotment of land,
laying out a road,    and building  fences .
At the annual meeting  in  November,     1680,     the  school  question
was up again,    and it  was "Voted to  purchase the house and land
of  James Stewart for  the use of the Town and the sum to be paid
was forty pounds.  "
At a meeting in December,    1680,     a feature not before mentioned
but which must have existed came to  the front,    as we find :      "Voted
that  Richard  Phillips   be  clerk  of  the  Market  for  the  Town  of
Weymouth and the Selectmen  provide  him with one half  bushel,
one  peck,     one  half  peck,     one  payer  brass  skales,       a  four  pound
weight,    a one pound weight,   one half pound and one quarter pound,
one  ell,     one  yard  and  two  letters   to  mark  the  measures  & one
quart,    one pint,    and one half pint.  "
Agood financial showing was made at this  time,  the town debt
being £15 14s.
In March,     1681,    the town passed a vote " That Capt.     Holbrook,
Serg't.       White and Stephen  French to  join with the  Selectmen  for
the building speedily of a School House. "
The town also  voted " That the Rate shall be ten pounds added
to the minister's salary and be paid in money."
The selectmen  did  also  mutually  agree  " That  the  3s.         P head
for  those  that are  appointed  to  go to  school  are  to  be added  each
scholar  to  his  parents  Rate for the year. "

Chapter  XIV
At  a meeting  of  the  selectmen,     on  Aug.   16,      1681,      " It  was
ordered  that   on  account  of  repeated  injury  to  Inhabitants  on
account  of  open wells  and water holes  that  all  such  shall  be  im-
mediately  filled  up or timbered. "
The schedule  of indebtedness  of  the town for  the annual  town
meeting,       November,     1681,    was  £45  05s.           Captain  Holbrook  was
chosen  moderator  and  Lieutenant  White,      Jacob  Nash,       Stephen
French,      John Kingman,     John  Shaw,     Sr. ,    William Reed and James
Smith  were  elected  selectmen,   and John Hunt and John Randall,
constables.
At  the  March  meeting,     1682,        Captain  Holbrook,        Lieutenant
White  and  Captain  Torrey  were  appointed  commissioners  to  the
honorable court.
At this  meeting there were further  allotments  of land  to  James
Lovell,           Micajah  Torrey,      William  Richards,       Nicholas  Whitmarsh
and John Vining,   a part of  which was for land taken to  build  the
road  near " Webb's Puddle."
At a meeting of the selectmen in April,   1682,    it  was ordered that
those  who  had  neglected  the  order  about  wells  and  water  holes
be fined 20s.     each,    and the same be gathered at once.
The  rate  or  tax  levy  for  this  year  was  £39  00s.       00d.             for  all
expenses  reported,    and  at  a  meeting  held  in January,        1682,        the
following  highway was  reported  and accepted :
"A Highway two poles  wide from  the  Smelt  Brook  to  Rockey
Swamp in  the  same place  the  cartway  now is,    then  over  and by
land of Jacob Tyler,     William  Richards,     Isaac Poole & Jacob  Poole
to  the  Town  Commons,      then  by  the  great  marsh  to  Plymouth
line [now Abington]  .  "
At  the   town  meeting,      Nov.   27,         1682,          Captain   Holbrook,
moderator,       Dea.      James Humphrey,    Lieutenant  Whitmarsh,     Jacob
Nash,           Captain   French,         Captain   Torrey,         Micajah   Torrey   and
Ebiza  White  were  elected   selectmen;      Samuel  King  and  Abiah
Whitman,     constables.
This ,        according  to  the  town  clerk's   record,       was  a  live  town

Meeting  house,     the  following  committee  was  chosen  to  act  in  all

Joseph  Patty,   James Lovell,  John Shaw,  sen. ,  Joseph Pratt William

RECORD  OF  COMMITTEE
"The committee met the  18th  of  Dec.,    1682,     reviewed  the  old
Meeting  house and find  the said  meeting house to be very  rotten
in many parts  & defective  both for  strength  and  likeness  for  ac-
comodation  to  little  to  supply  the  people  for  comfortable  room
and light  in  the  worship  of  God.            Upon debate  about  it  at  the
Parson's  house,    the  committee with  a plurality  of consent  passed
a vote that there  shall  be a new Meeting house built. "
"2d  ly  the  committee past  a vote  that the meeting house shall
be 45 feet  in length,  40 feet  in breadth and 20 feet  stud between
joist."
"3d  They voted that there shall be four gable ends of convenient
height to make it  uniform. "
"4th   Voted that the platform on the top shall be covered with
lead."
"Voted that the place where the Meeting house is  to be raised  is
upon  the  land  which  they  lately  purchased  of  Capt.         Holbrook
near  the School house."
"The walls on the outside to be boarded and clapboarded on the
studs  and filled with brick up to the plate. "
" Clapboarded or plastered with lime on the inside. "
"The sills   to  be raised  a foot above the  ground upon stone wall
laid  in lime. "
" With  Belcony  proportionate  & suitable  for  said  house & to
hang the Bell & to  suite the  said  house with seats  convenient.  "
"The  said  committee  ordered  that  the  pay for  the building  of
the  Meeting house & Furnishing  the  same is  one third  in  money
& the other two thirds in good pay at current money prices,    Viz
corn,       timber  clapboards,      shingles,      work  or  any  good  provisions
such  as  Pork,    Beef,      Lard,      Wood or  the  like.      The one half when
the meeting  house is  raised  and the other  half within  one month
after  the house is  finished. "
The said  committee voted that Jacob Nash shall be the man to
build   and  finish   said  meeting-house,      and  agreed   with  him  for
£280 and the Old Meeting- House.

Up to  date  the  rate  for  the  year  1683  was  the largest  in  the

There were  this  year  many additional  grants  of  land,      some of
which were for  other  land  taken for  highways,    and among those
receiving  the  same  were  Stephen  French,      Abiah  Whitman,     John
Richards ,             William   Bicknell,      John  Bicknell   and  Widow  Mary
