At the town meeting  in  November,     1683,      Captain  Torrey  was
chosen  moderator,       and  Lieutenant  White,      Sergeant  Whitmarsh,
Ensign  Hunt,      Abiah  Whitman,       Sergeant  Phillips,     James  Lovell
and John Rogers were elected  selectmen.
" It was voted for the future time to choose Selectmen by paper
and each  Inhabitant that is  in  a capacity by law to bring in their
several  votes  & make their  choice as  the law provides  for  in  that
respect."
"Agreed with  Henry Cote to sweep the Meeting House and ring
the bell for thirty shillings per annum and to dig graves for eighteen
pence for all under 12 years of age and two shillings  per grave for
those over 12 years ."
"Voted  that  the  tithing  men  shall  be  Samuel  Humphrey  &
Nathaniel   Ford  for  the  lower  plantation;           Wm.        Reed  & Wm.
French for the middle of the Town & Thomas Richards & Benjamin
Ludden for  the Neck. "
"Voted that  Richard Gurney shall have six  acres  of  the Town's
Common land  to  build  a  house  and  fence  to  dwell  thereon  with
his  family  in  an  absolute  state  of  Inheritance.        On  the  Town
Common on the west side of the Pond . "
A new road was laid  out from the meeting-house to  the landing
in  the  spring  of  1684,     and  also  a new  road  in  South  Weymouth,

There  was  a  wide  margin  in  1684  between  current  pay  and

pounds being according in money to 66£ 05s. "
Captain  Holbrook,     Sergeant  Whitmarsh,    Jacob  Nash,     Corporal

"The  town  passed  a vote  that  any inhabitant  or inhabitants

At  the  March  meeting  in  1684  a committee  of  fourteen  was

An interesting  document  from  the  minister  finds  place  in  the

Know all  men that I,  Samuel Torrey,   do hereby forever acquit  and discharge

Among the grants of land in 1685 was one to John Hollis .
The town passed  a vote  " that  John  Hollis  shall  have as  his  &
his  heirs  and  assigns  forever  all  that  orchard  and  land  which  he
hath fenced  in along  the highway  on the  west  side  of  the  way.

The town passed  a  vote  " that  the  present  Schoolmaster,       Wm.

teach  all  children  & servants  belonging  to the Town that  are  sent

Chapter  XVI
In  March,       1686,    " The town passed  a vote that our pastor  Mr.
Samuel  Torrey  have  liberty  to  fence  in  the  Town burying  yard
place  to  straighten  his  fence  Provided  he  doth  not  prejudice  to
Town  way  nor  hinder  or  obstruct  thereby  convenient  passage
for  the burying of deceased,  from time to time.     And so to  remain
until  the Town see cause to  alter  it. "
" The Town passed  a vote that  our Pastor,     Mr.  Samuel Torrey
is  to have the use and benefit of that house,    orchard & land which
is  now in the occupancy of Samuel Humphrey and to hold it  during
his  ministry  in  Weymouth,   or  until  the  Town shall  see  cause  to
alter  it."
This  was a year for  several  grants  of  land,    most of which were
in  small  lots,        but  Capt.      William  Torrey  received  a grant  of  one
hundred acres  which  placed  him among the largest  landowners  in
town.
In  addition  to  grants  of  land  the  selectmen  were  authorized  to
lease  land for  breaking up and planting or cutting timber.
The poor account was small in those days,    and we find  that  the
one  town charge was boarded with  "John Shaw for  three shillings
a week in money or its  equivalent  in Town Pay.  "
In  1686  the  selectmen  were  authorized  to  contract  with  the
minister and the schoolmaster at the same price as before.
Following  is   an  order  of  the  selectmen  at  this  time:     " To  the
Constables   of   Weymouth.        You  are   hereby   required   in   Her
Magestys name forthwith to  repair unto the house as  was formerly
Thomas  Whites  and  notify  Caleb  Littlefield  that  liveth  in  said
house that he doe depart the Town,     and to declare to him that  he
is  not looked upon as an Inhabitant of the Town.          Or else  to bring
security  to  be  bound for  the  Town security  to  the  Selectman  of
Weymouth. "
In  1687  the  question  of  the  ownership  of  the  flats   on  the
" northerly side of  Hockly on the  Back River, "  which had been in
dispute  between  the  town  and  Stephen  French  for  twenty years,
was  settled  by acknowledging  the  claim  of  Mr.  French  and dis-
charging him from all trespass and damage.
In  November,       1687,        Captain   Holbrook,        Jacob   Nash,        Abiah
Whitman,        Ebeneazer  White,     Lieutenant  White,    Joseph  Dyer  and
William Reed were elected selectmen.
"The Town past a vote not to  continue Mr.  Chard in  the work
of  public School  Master upon the public charge of  the Town. "
The  town voted  "that  Mr.  Chard  hath  liberty  to  continue  in
the dwelling  house he now dwelleth in and to  improve the School

"General Town Meeting first Monday in  March,   1688. "

This is  the first  mention we find of any supervision of the schools

We are not going much into English history in these articles,    but
evidently  there was a change across  the water about this  time,    as
we find,      instead  of  State  and  county  orders  being  issued  in  Her
Majesty's name,    they are now issued in His Majesty's name,    and a
special  county (Suffolk)  rate for the year  1688 was £24  15s. ,   and in
December of the same year the regular county rate was £154,     the
one- third in money and the other  two- thirds in town pay.
" March  1690,    Voted  that  Mr.  Chard  shall  have  the  improve-

Evidently  Mr.  Chard was keeping school  on his  own account at
this time.
"There  is  also  appointed  Jacob  Nash,     Jr.,    & Jonathan  Torrey

Chapter  XVII
At the general  town meeting  in  March,    1691,     Lieutenant  Reed,
Captain  White,      Ebenezer  White,     Abiah  Whitman,     Captain  Hunt,
John Smith,     Sr.,    and John Smith were elected selectmen.
The town was now nearly seventy years  old,    and still  had but
the  one  church  and  one  school,      and  for  this  year  voted  to  con-
tinue  Mr.  Chard as  teacher,    with  a salary  of  £26 and the use  of
the  house,      garden,      orchard  and  income  from  the  flats.               For  the
minister's   maintenance  the  rate  was  £109  8s.    7d. ,       of  which  £3
were  to  go  to  the  sexton  for  ringing  the  bell  and  sweeping  the
meeting- house.
"Voted to pay Mr.  Drake fifteen  shillings  per month for keeping
the one town pauper.        Settled  with  Capt.      White for  keeping  the
Town's powder and shot. "
Wewould here answer some questions which we are often asked:
"Why  so   many  military  titles   and  why  so  much  powder  and
bullets ? "     We of to-day little  realize the condition of those times.
We read about our frontier  and the border wars,    not thinking that
this was once the frontier and the seat of the border or King Philip's
War.           Men went to  the  fields  with  the hoe in one hand and  the
flintlock  in  the other.         They went to  church carrying  their  trusty
muskets,     and  never  retired  at  night without putting  new priming
in the pan and repicking the flint  of the musket.         Weymouth had
its  mounted cavalry and its  marching infantry,    and the  situation
may be better understood by reading the following reply of Captain
Torrey to  the Governor in a demand for  more troops :
To the  much  bonored  Governor  and  Council  now in  Boston.              The  bumble  petition  of
the Committee of Militia for  Waymouth.
Humbly showeth,     that  your  poor  petitioners  have this  morning  received  a
warrant from the honorable Major for the impressing  of six able  men fitted  for
service  both  with  arms,     ammunition,
mmunition,   and provision,  which  we shall  endeavor
to do,  and are in the execution of said warrant,    but we most humbly beseech
your honors to consider of our present  distressed and distracted condition,    who
when we are most,   are but a small company,  and we have ten men out already,
and have the enemy appearing daily at our very doors,   four killed by the enemy,
already,      all  in danger  wheresoever  we go,   unlike  to  have any help  from  any
other,    in expectation  every day and hour,    of being assaulted,    stand continually
upon  our  guard,     whereby  planting  is  obstructed,    and  all  things  turning  into
confusion and destruction,   not knowing how to dispose of our cattle,    which were
wont to go into the woods,    now cannot;      they will starve  us,    or  we shall  starve
them,   and this is  a little  of our deplorable condition.
Wherefore our  humble petition  and request  to  your  Honors,      is,     that  if  you
cannot afford  us any help,  for  the  preservation  of  our lives,    which now are  in
danger  (and  which  is  the only thing  we have care  of) ,    that  you will  please  to
 - 55 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               533
pity us,   and so far to lend an ear to our humble request,  as that our men now
impressed,    may be discharged and returned to us  again,  and we hope we shall
respectfully acknowledge it,   as a great favor and still remain your honors'   humble
servants.
WM.       TORREY.
In the name of,    and by  the order  of the
Committee of Militia for  Weymouth.
At the  March meeting  in  1693,       Wm.      Chard  was  elected  town
clerk;        Edward  Bates,        Albert   Whitman,       Serg't.        Thomas  Reed,
William  Torrey,     James  Lovell,      Sr.,     Joseph  Dyer  and  Nathaniel
Humphrey,     selectmen.
By order  of  the selectmen the following persons were warned to
leave town in the month of April  and May of the year 1693 :         Abia
Blancher,       Thomas Mayer,     Widow Benson,     Elias  Monk,    an inmate
at  Samuel  Holbrook's and Cornelius Thomson.
At the same meeting  of the selectmen  there  were a number of
grants of land,   and,    as will be seen by the following,     a movement
made to get back lands which had been illegally  taken.
"There has been past a vote that it is left to the Selectmen who
have  legal  power  to  preserve  the  Town's  interest  that  all  such
persons  as  have fenced  in  and  improved  any of  the  Town land
are  to  repair  to  the  Selectmen  at the  next  meeting  to  treat  with
them concerning  it  or else  such  fences  upon the Town Commons
will be pulled down that there  may be no longer wronged of  the
people's rights and interests."
Captain   Holbrook,       Lieutenant   Whitman,        Lieutenant   White,
Joseph  Pratt,       Sr. ,      William  Reed,    Joseph  Green,   John  Rogers  and
Captain  Hunt were  added  to  the  selectmen  as  a  committee  to
relocate  the  roads  in  town,    and  in  1693  there  was much done for
roads,     and among the land damages granted was the following  to
Gideon Tirrell :      " The liberty of the river in the Towns Commons
in  a place called the blades mill to set up a fulling mill and to have
one acre of land. "   And it  was voted that all  town ways should be
two poles wide.
John  Rogers  was  the  Representative  to  the  General  Court  in
1693,     and for eighty- five days'     service he was paid  £1  10s.
At the town meeting in November,    1693,      " The Town passed  a
vote  that  the  Selectmen prepare  and present  in writing  such by-
laws  and orders  which concern  the  prudential  affairs  of  the Town
unto  the  Court  to  be  holden  in   Boston  to  be  by  such  court
approved."
At the town meeting in November,     1694,     it  was voted  to  have
but five  selectmen,   and Capt.      Ephriam  Hunt,   Lieutenant  White,
William  Reed,    Joseph  Green  and  Edward  Bates  were  elected  by
"written vote."
The following  document presented  at  this  meeting  speaks  of  a
long pastorate :

Chapter  XVIII
The size  of  town  meetings  in  Weymouth  two  hundred  years
ago may be estimated by the vote cast at the annual meeting held
March 2,      1696.
Major Hunt was elected  moderator,   and the meeting proceeded
to ballot for  selectmen,   and the  elected  ones were Edward Bates,
33  votes ;       Lieutenant  White,     14;    and Major Hunt,  Joseph  Dyer
and William Reed,   12 each.
A new man in town history  seems  to  have come to  the  front
this year in the person of John Copp,  who was elected town clerk.
The town voted to employ a schoolmaster,    and the selectmen were
authorized  to " raise his salary by polls & Estates the same as they
do other town Charges,"  and John Copp was employed at a salary
of30£.
"Voted to build  a new pound at some convenient  point  to be
selected by the Selectmen,   and Maj.  Ephraim Hunt was authorized
to sell  the land on which the old pound was located,   at the rate of
10£ per acre.  "
"Aug.  12,       1696,    delivered  to  Carnet White the town's  stock  of
powder,      bullets  & flints,    viz.:     92  pounds  of  powder,      271  pounds
and a half of bullets,  628 flints  and agreed with the said White to
secure  the stock and what may be added to it  by the Town for ten
shillings  in money a year annually as long as the said stock shall be
kept by him. "
At this August meeting the selectmen,    acting  as  assessors,    made
the following rate:
"County,    seventy-six  pounds;     Maintenance of Minister,   106£,
16s.    in goods,    or 86£ in money;     Town Rate,    112£ in Town Pay."
The town was  without  a  schoolmaster  for  the  winter  term  of
1697,        and " Joseph Dyer & Edward Bates were employed to instruct
children  to  read and write and cipher from the 2d day in  January
to  the next  March meeting.      Joseph  Dyer to  keep  at  the Town's
schoolhouse and Edward Bates at his  own home,    and  all  scholars
from  Thomas Porter's  up  shall  go  to  Edward Bates  and  the  rest
of the Town to  Joseph  Dyer.        And we have  ordered  John  King
to  be helpful  to  assist  Joseph  Dyer  in  that  work to  teach  and
instruct  the children and youth that shall come to him. "
At the March meeting,   1698,      Major Hunt,    moderator,    Sergeant
Pratt,          Samuel  Humphrey,       John  Bicknell,       John  Richards   and
Stephen  French were elected  selectmen.
"Voted  that  Rev.  Samuel  Torrey  shall  have besides  his  salary
out of the town Treasury twelve pounds in money.  "
"Voted that John Torrey,   Tanner,   for the encouragement of his

business  shall  have  twelve poles of land joining  to his  father's  lot

"Voted that  the Selectmen shall  have power to obtain a school

The  last  part  of  the  above  vote  was  reconsidered  at  a  town

At the annual town meeting,   March 6,   1699,    officers  and boards
of  officers  elected  by vote were:       selectmen,   constables,       surveyors
of highways,     fence-viewers,    haywardens,    tithingmen,   treasurer and

was  incorporated.        Most of the business done at this  meeting and
by the  several  boards  of officers  up to  the November meeting was

At the town meeting Nov. 13,     1699,     " The town voted to  have a

At a meeting of the above board held the fourth day of December

Chapter  XIX
On Dec.  12,      1699,       it   was  " concluded  by  the  Selectmen  and
committee  that  there  be  five  women agreed  with  in  the  several
parts  of  the  Town to  teach  school  from  the last  of  March  until
the last of September and that they shall have twenty-five  shillings
apiece  in  or  as  monhy out of the town's  Rate beside  what those
that send children to the school shall pay by the week which is to be
the usual rate."
The  committee  further  agreed  with  Edward  Bates  and  John
Torrey  to  teach  school from  December to  March,     Mr.  Torrey  to
teach in the town's schoolhouse and Mr. Bates at his  own home.
At the annual  March meeting,   1700,   the usual boards  of officers
were elected,      and as  usual  quite a number of assignments of  land
in small lots  to  different  parties .
The real  business  of  the  day was  a discussion  of the  boundary
line  between Weymouth and  Braintree  which had always been in
dispute,       and a committee was  appointed  to  meet  a similar  com-
mittee from Braintree and try to locate the proper line.
The  school  question  was  the  only  one  of  importance  at  the
March meeting in 1701,  and we find the following :
"After much debate about settling  a School in Weymouth they,
by their vote chose Lieut.    Nash,    Wm.     Reed,    Serg't  Thomas Reed,
Wm.     Torrey,      Joseph Green,    Samuel Andrews & Wm.     Petty  to  be
a committee when they did by their  vote  impower  to  treat  with
persons  and settle  a school master according to  law in the town of
Weymouth for the year ensuing. "
The committee later reported :
"Have treated  with  Samuel Hunt for  one whole year  from  the
15th of October until the full time of a year for  thirty five pounds
in or as money."
The town rate for 1702 was £39 19s. ,    and the selectmen,     acting
as  assessors,    divided the town into two districts  and committed the
rate  for  the  First  District  to  Capt.     Nathaniel  Shaw,      £20 9s.;     the
Second District to Joseph Nash,     £19  10s.
At a special  town meeting  in  April,    1702,    the  town " voted  to
rescind  the power of  the committee chosen  at  the  March meeting
to  settle  school  master  and  a new committee  appointed  of which
Rev.  Samuel Torrey was one. "
At this meeting  Capt.   Stephen French was elected  to  represent
the  town in  a Great  and  General  Court  to  be  held  in  Boston  in
May.
"Chose Lt.  Col.  Ephraim  Hunt a  committee  to join with  the
Selectmen in making a valuation of the Town.   "

538                                         OLD  RECORDS
Military  matters  were  a disturbing  element  in  1703  and  1704,
and  the  town defaulted in furnishing  troops  as  called  for  by the
general  government,     and Colonel  Hunt was censured  by  His  Ex-
cellency,       and  Colonel  Hobby  was  dispatched  from  Boston  with
ten men of  the guards with orders  to  make a draft of twenty men
from Weymouth.
At the  annual  meeting  in  November,      1704,       Lieutenant  Nash,
Ensign Hunt,       Sergeant Richards,    Joseph  Pool  and Sergeant Tirrell
were added  to  the selectmen to make a town rate.           Colonel Hunt,
Captain  French,      Elder  Rogers,      William  Torrey,     Lieutenant  Reed
were elected as a committee to draft  new by-laws.
At this  meeting it was voted to build a new barn for the pastor,
and  he  donated  a balance  of  £20 which  was due him  on salary
toward the object.
Enforcement of regulation  in  regard  to cutting  wood and hoop
poles  came up,   and a number of people  were fined  for  thus  tres-
passing upon what was known as the minister's woodland.
It  was also  voted that  any person  pasturing  sheep  or  rams  for
others  than residents of the town should pay a fine of 5s.   for every
sheep or  ram so pastured.
It was also voted to  pay a bounty of 10s.   for every wolf killed  in
town.
At the March meeting in 1707 it  was voted by the town to grant
£5  to  encourage  women's  schools,     and  to  pay 20s.     each  to  five
women to teach.
At this meeting the following order was drawn :
To the Selectmen of Weymouth,   Greeting:     You are hereby desired to pay to
Thomas Thurston  twenty- five  pounds  in  money at  fifteen  pence which  we the
committee of Weymouth have agreed to pay to said Thurston for keeping of the
Schools  of Weymouth.
JOHN PRATT,
JOSEPH  HUNT,
JAMES RICHARDS,
GIDEON  TIRRELL,
Committee.

Chapter  XX
The town suffered  a severe  loss  April  21,    1707,    in  the death of
the  pastor,       Rev.  Samuel  Torrey,      who had held  the  position  con-
tinuously  since  his  ordination  in  1665,    and was considered  one of
the most able  preachers  of his  time,    and much of the time of  the
inhabitants  for  the  next  six  months  was  devoted  to  securing  and
settling  his  successor.
At the town meeting held on the 11th  of August following  the
death of Mr. Torrey,   we find the following :
"Whereas the  Church of Christ in Weymouth did on the 21st of
July,  1707,    meet together and did Elect and Choose Peter Thatcher,
of  Boston,      to  be their Minister.       At the town meeting Aug.  11th,
1707,        the  town  of  Weymouth did  indicate  by  vote  their  concur-
rence  with  the  church  in  the  election  and  choice  of  Mr.  Peter
Thatcher to become their  minister. "
"Voted by the  Town to  choose a committee to  the  number of
nine men to  treat  with  Mr.  Thatcher about his  settlement  in  the
work of the ministry in the town.  "
"Voted by the Town at the same time to give Mr. Thatcher 70£
a year  in  money annually and a convenient settlement for  his  im-
provement while  he shall  continue in  the  work of  the ministry  in
this place."
On Aug.  19,      1707,      the  selectmen  delivered  unto  the  custodian
"the  Town's  stock  of  Ammunition     viz .:      Powder  two  Caggs,
one of ninety pounds with the cask and one of fifty  pounds with
the cask;     Bullets 271 pounds,     flints  617."
At the town meeting,    Oct.  16,      1707,     "Voted to  add  10£ to  the
70£  already  voted  for  the  minister  and  convenient  firewood  for
his  fuel when he has a family of his own,    or as soon  thereafter  as
he shall  call for the same."
"Voted that  Mr.  Thatcher  shall  have his  pay quarterly,     voted
also to have a weekly contribution for the collection  of said Rate. "
At the  town meeting,   Feb. 4,     1708,     " Voted to  sell  the  Town's
commons lying by the Back River -viz.   the Old Seder Swamp &
Common land  near  and  adjoining  & voted  to  sell  the  land  by
Micajah  Torreys  lately  improved  by our  late   Rev.  Pastor  Mr.
Samuel Torrey. "
At a town  meeting  held  Sept.   13,        1708,       "after  much  debate
about the land  of Joseph Green,    Capt.    Hunt & Zeckham Bicknell
as  a  settlement  for  the minister  the town voted  to  purchase  the
land of Mr.  Bicknell  under protest of  Mr. Green and Capt.     Hunt.
"Voted  the  Selectmen  have  power  to  employ  a school  master
for  the year. "

At the town meeting,    Nov. 29,   1707,    the committee  on  sale  of
town  land  reported  a  number  of  sales,     and  among  the  rest   12
acres  of  Huckleberry Swamp to Sergeant Tirrell,    and at a meeting
the following April they reported the sale of the flats above Hockley
in  ten lots  to  run from a given point to  the channel:      first  lot  to
Stephen French;      second,   Ezra Whitmarsh;   third,  John French,    Jr. ,
and  William   Petty;         fourth,          Ebenezer   Whitmarsh   and   John
Richards ;        fifth,   Jacob  Turner  and John Vining;       sixth,     Nicholas

Ezra Whitmarsh and Samuel Porter ;       tenth,    Sergeant  Porter.
Other  town lots  were sold,    and it  was voted  that  the  proceeds
shall  remain in  the hands of  the committee to pay for  the  settle-
ment of the minister in Weymouth.
 - 63 - 
Chapter  XXI
At the March meeting,    1709,      Captain  Hunt was elected  moder-
ator;     Edward Bates,    town clerk;     Captain  Hunt,    Captain  French,
James  Humphrey,    John  Shaw  and  Edward  Bates,     selectmen ;
James Humphrey,     treasurer;     and James  Lovell  and John Green,
constables.             In  addition  to   these   there  were  tithingmen,       hay-
wardens,    hogwardens,   fence-viewers and special committees to look
after  the cutting of wood,  timber,   hoop poles and stakes from the
town's commons in violation of regulations governing the same.
At a special  town meeting,    Sept.  19,     1709,   "Voted that  money
that  is  due to  the  Town for  ten  lots  sold  be  paid  to  the  Town
Treasurer,      James Humphrey,   for  them that it  is due unto for  the
purchase  of  settlement  for  the  Minister  and  for  the  charge  of
building and furnishing a house."
Further   grants   of  land   this   year   were   made  to   Ebenezer
Whitman,     John  Randall,    John  Blanchard,     William Torrey,      James
Richards,         Joseph  Lovell,     Samuel  Pratt,     Abijah  Torrey,     Ebenezer
Pratt,      Sergt.      Gideon  Tirrell,      Colonel  Hunt,     Captain  Hunt,       Ezra
Whitmarsh and Lieutenant Nash.
At a meeting of the selectmen held in  December " it  was agreed
with  John Torrey  to  keep  school  for  the  town from the  first  of
Jan.  to  the last of March,   three months in all,  for  fifty  shillings  a
week."
The  selectmen  assessed  a  county  rate  of  £6  18s.       and  issued
warrants  to John Green and James Lovell to collect the same and
pay it  to Jeremiah Deemon,     Esq. ,   county treasurer.
"Voted that John  Pratt  and James Lovell shall  have power  to
seize  for  the use of the Town any timber already cut on the Town
Commons."
"Voted  that  any  person  that  shall  carry  any  stone  from  the
Town Common shall  pay for  every  Boat Load one shilling  for  the
use of the town. "
In  March,      1710,     the  settlement  of the  minister  was  completed
for the time being by the following act :      " Voted that Mr. Thatcher
shall  have the improvement of the house where he now lives  and
the  barn  and all  the  upland  and  some  part  of  the  salt  medder
which was purchased of  Mr.  Zechara  Bicknell and all  the  medder
on the  easterly  side  of a ditch or dam made by said  Bicknell  on
the salt  marsh and one acre  below it on the  north  side  ditch  ad-
joining  to the other before named. "
Upon the request  of John Nash,    who was chosen  constable,     the
town by vote released him from that office  on condition that unless
 - 64 - 
542                                      OLD  RECORDS
he left  Weymouth before winter he was to pay the regular  fine  of
constable for not serving,   viz.  ,      £5 .
At the March meeting in 1711,   among other officers  elected  was
James  Humphrey,     treasurer,    and for  the  first  time in the  history
of Weymouth we find  a salary attached to that office  and for  the
year it  was 40s.
Movable  schools  are  not  an invention  of the latter  day school
scientists  or  school  necessities,    as we find at this time "The town
by a vote  impowered the Selectmen to  agree with or settle  with  a
School  Master and to order his  removal to several  places  in  town
for  the benefit of the several inhabitants at the town charge."
The year  1712 was  not marked by any special  events outside of
the protracted  fight with Braintree in regard to the  Perambulating
line,    and the following  vote was passed:        " That the  Town would
stand  by the  selectmen  in prosecuting  the Selectmen of  Braintree
according to law for refusing to run the Perambulating line between
their  town and ours as the law directs."
For this  year  the tax levy was £143 for the maintenance of the
ministry,          school,       poor   and  defraying   other   necessary  charges.
Warrants  for  collecting  this  were  delivered  to  constables  in  two
districts,    John Turner one,    and the other to  Israel  Ford.
 - 65 - 
Chapter  XXII
At a  legally  called  town meeting  of the  freeholders  and  other
voters of the town,  Jan. 23,    1713,    the main business was in relation
to town commons and use of the same.            Several  people were fined
for  trespass  on the  Cedar Swamp,   and it  was voted to divide the
great swamp into parts and then stake it  off into lots  and convey
them to " house holders  in Town. "
A committee was chosen to make this division  and assignment,
and  by  the  result  of  their  work  one  hundred  and  eight  people
became owners of small lots  in  the great  Cedar Swamp extending
to the Hingham line.
It was also voted that no sheep should be at large on the town's
commons between  May and  November under penalty  of  3d.       per
day;         no  geese  at  any  time  under  penalty  of  1s.     and  no  horse,
gelding or mare over two years of age under penalty of 5s.
A tax levy for  the year of  £147 was made for the support of the
ministry,     school,   poor and other town charges.
At the  town meeting  in  March,      1714,     regular  boards  of  town
officers  were elected,    and among them Samuel  White and Joseph
Torrey  as  constables.             Mr.  Torrey declined  to  qualify,     stepped
up to  the  treasurer,    paid  the  £5  penalty,   and Samuel  Pratt  was
elected in his place.
Other business  of  the  year  was  mostly  assignment  and  sale  of
public lands.
At the  March  meeting  in  1715,     Captain  French  was  elected
moderator;      James  Humphrey,   clerk  and  treasurer;       John  Shaw,
Nicholas   Shaw,       Ezra  Whitmarsh,      James  Humphrey  and  John
Vining,    selectmen;      and  it  was  voted  to  pay  Mr.  Humphrey  £5
for his  services .
"At said meeting John Torrey,  James Humphrey, Joseph Torrey,
Ezra Whitmarsh,    Enoch Lovell,     Eben Pratt and divers other their
partners  who had  agreed  to begin  a  fishing  trade  to  Cape  Sable
requested  of  the Town that they might have that  piece  or  parcel
of  land  at  the  mouth  of  Fore  river   in  the  northerly  part  of
Weymouth,        called  and  known  as  Hunt's  Hill  and  the  low  land
and beach  appertaining  thereunto,    that  is,      as  much as  they shall
need for  the management of said  fishing  trade.         The  Town after
consideration  thereof  voted  that  they  shall  have  the  said  land
& beach to manage their  fishing trade.
"Lt.   Jacob  Nash  & Nicholas  Phillips  entering  their  contrary
dissent to the aforesaid  vote relating to Hunt's Hill & Beach.  "
At a meeting  in  May,     1715,      Nicholas  Shaw  and  John  Porter
were appointed to run the line between Weymouth and Hingham,
 - 66 - 
544                                      OLD  RECORDS
and the same was accomplished with a similar committee from the
latter  town.           John Vining  and Sergeant  Torrey were  appointed  to
run the line between Weymouth and Brantry,   but the selectmen of
the latter  town refused  to meet them and once more nothing  was
done.
At a meeting in  March,     1716,    the  meeting-house was the main
topic.         It  did  not  meet  the  requirements  of  the  growing  town,
and more room was  needed,  and it  was voted  to  allow those who
wanted  the  room  to  build  another  row  of  galleries  above  those
already  in  use at  their  own charge,   said  work to  be done under
the  supervision  of  Captain  French,      Lieutenant  Nash,        Captain
Hunt and Nicholas Phillip.
In  March,       1717,    James Humphrey was again elected  clerk  and
treasurer ;           James  Humphrey,      Lieut.    John  Hunt,       John  Vining,
Edward  Derby  and  Samuel  White,      selectmen;          Captain  Hunt,
representative to General Court.
"Voted that the school be removed and kept four months in the
year in each school house."    This is  the first  mention we find  of a
second  schoolhouse  in  Weymouth.          The tax levy  for  all  expenses
this  year was £176 15s.
"Voted to  approve of the action of the selectmen in hiring  John
Galt as school  master for  a  quarter  of a year and they shall  have
power  to  agree  with  him or  some other  schoolmaster  for  further
time."
The year  1718 was not a specially happy one for the town.           It
lost  one of  its  most  valuable  citizens  in  the death of selectman,
town  clerk  and  treasurer  James  Humphrey,     and  trouble  began
in  regard to  Mr. Thatcher,    the minister.       It was in the air that he
was wanted in or was looking  for a Boston pulpit,   and some of the
hasty  ones  pushed his  premature  resignation  or  discharge,     and in
March,     1719,     we find the following  record :
" Whereas,         the  church  of  Christ   in   Weymouth  did  meet  to-
gether  on  Feb.  26th  and did choose and elect  Mr.  Thomas  Paine
of  Barnstable  to  be  their  minister,     the  Town did  at  a  General
town  meeting   held  the  27th  day  of   March  vote  their  general
consent  and  concurrence  together  with  the  church  in  the  choice
of Mr. Thomas Paine to become their  minister as  aforesaid.
"Voted that the Town will pay 20s.     Per week to  Mr.  Paine and
his  board and keep for his horse so long as he shall preach for  us,
viz.     before he shall settle  in the work of the ministry with us.  "
 - 67 - 
Chapter  XXIII
At a town meeting held May 7,    1719,    Captain Hunt was chosen
moderator ;          John Torrey was elected  to  represent  the town at  the
General  Court;      Captain Hunt,    Edward Bates,     Lieutenant Torrey,
Lieutenant Lovell,    Lieutenant Nash,   Sergeant Whitmarsh,    Sergeant
Tirrell  and Stephen French were authorized to make the following
proposal  to  Mr.  Thomas  Paine  to  become the settled  minister  of
the town:       " At a salary of ninety pounds a year the Town to  put
the  house,      barn  and  land  in good tenable  order  and  the  same to
be kept so by the minister. "
At a special  town meeting  held  July  2 of  the  above year  the
committee  reported  that  they  had negotiated  with  Mr.  Paine  as
per vote of the town.        A special committee was appointed to make
arrangements  for  the ordination,   and the  meeting voted  to  appro-
priate  £20 for the expense of the same.
The selectmen reported that they had agreed with  Mr.  Ebenezer
Rolie  to  keep school  for  the year,     with  a salary  of  £42 10s.
The  selectmen  acting  as  assessors  reported  in  December  that
they  had  completed  their  work with  a tax  rate  of  £206  for  the
ministry,       schools,    poor  and  all  other  town  charges  for  the  year.
The same was  committed  to  the  two constables  to  gather  in  and
pay,    the one-half the  next February,     and all  before the next June.
On  March  7,     1720,     at  the  annual  meeting  held  on  this  date,
Captain  Hunt  was  chosen   moderator ;          Micajah  Torrey,        clerk;
Captain Hunt,      Lieut.   John Torrey,    Sergt.     Ezra Whitmarsh,     Sergt.
John Porter and Micajah Torrey,    selectmen.
They had trouble  with  taxes  in  the early  days,      as  we do  now,
and we find  that  a special  town meeting was called for April  27,
when the following vote was passed :
"Voted by the Town that the Selectmen should in behalf of the
Town  petition   the   Honorable  General   Court  to   impower  the
Constables   to  gather  the   Rate  already  committed  to   them  to
gather  which  the  people  refused  to  pay  because  the  Selectmen
had neglected  to  take  the  assessors   oath  before  they  made  the
said Rate."
At the annual town meeting in  March,    1721,    Enoch Lovell  was
elected  moderator;       Ezra  Whitmarsh,    town  clerk  and  treasurer ;
Captain  Hunt,      Dea.     Edward  Bates,       Dea.        Micajah  Torrey  and
John Vinson,    selectmen.
The town had still  a large lot  of common land on its  hands,      and
much of the time of this  meeting was devoted to  the  sale  of  land
and regulations for town's commons.
 - 68 - 
546                                      OLD  RECORDS
We have now covered  nearly  a hundred years  of  town history
and find the first  doctor's bill in this year's  expenditures :
"Voted  Mr.  Sargent  shall   have  three  pounds  for   doctoring
Samuel  Holes  and wife. "
"Voted  to build  a convenient barn for  Mr.  Paine and the same
to be completed before 1722."
We come now to  a very  interesting  act  in  regard  to  building
new  pews  in  the  meeting-house  which  was  the  last  before  the
establishment  of  a second  church,     for  many years  known as  the
"Old South."
" It  was voted  that           to sit  in  the pew with his family,     the
Town to have the refusal,   if sold the bidder to have the preference,
Samuel Badlam to have the north east  corner behind the minister's
pew,      he  paying  nine  pounds;        Abiah  Whitman  to  have  a  pew
between the pulpit  and the minister's  pew,   he paying  four pounds
and  twelve  shillings;      Benjamin  Bicknell  to  have  a pew between
Col. Hunt's and the pulpit, he paying two pounds and ten shillings ;
Samuel  French  to  have  a  pew over  the  stairs  in  the  south  east
corner  provided he doth not dew no damage to  the  stairs,     for  one
pound;     John Torrey to  have a pew in the sow west corner  above
the stairs,     he paying one pound if he do no damage to  the stairs ;
Thomas White to  have a pew on the  east  side  of the  great door,
he paying four  pounds  and ten shillings ;      Ebenezer  Pratt  to  have
a pew on the west  side of the great door,     he  paying four  pounds
and five  shillings ;       Joseph  Torrey to  have a pew in  the south  east
corner,        he  paying  three  pounds  five  shillings ;       Lt.  John  Pratt  to
have a  pew on the west side  of the great  door  next  the woman's
stairs,     he paying three pounds.  "
There were several dissenters  to  the above arrangement.
We now  arrive  at   a  condition  on  State  finances  which  then
existed  but would be an impossibility  to-day,    which  may be seen
in the following :
"At a general  town meeting of the inhabitants  of the Town of
Weymouth held on the 19th  of Sept.  1721,    and adjourned  to  Oct.
2d when it  was  enacted,    voted  and ordered  by said  meeting  and
unanimously  agreed  on  by  them  that  Deacon  Edward  Bates,
Stephen  French  and  Ezra  Whitmarsh shall  be  trustees  to  let  out
to the several inhabitants of said town the sum of 368£ 10s.     which
was allowed  by the General  Court  unto the said  town in manner
and  form  as  follows,       viz.:      ' Voted  that  the  trustees  shall  have
power to  let  out said  money for  the Town's  use  after  the  rate  of
six per cent per year and so  yearly,    year by year,   until the term of
time is  expired that it  was allowed to said town,   viz.    ten years. '
"Voted that  the  trustees  shall not let  above five  pounds to  each
man the  first  week and ten pounds the second week and also voted
that  whoever taketh  any of this money shall give good  bond with
sufficient  bondsmen if required by the trustees of said town. "
 - 69 - 
Chapter  XXIV
We now arrive at the town meeting of  March,    1722.   This meet-
ing  lasted  two days,    and  was the  beginning  of  a new era  which
eventuated in the separation of  church and State,    or rather  church
and town,    and nearly eventuated in  a  town division.
Abijah  Torrey  was  elected   town  clerk;        Dea.       Edward  Bates,
Lieut.       John  Torrey,       John  Porter,      Thomas  White  and  Micajah
Torrey,      selectmen.         Ebenezer  Vinton,    Josiah  Waterman,      Samuel
Bedlam  and John  Pratt  were elected  constables,  but declined  to
qualify and were fined  £5 each,   which they paid.     John Torrey and
Samuel Kingman were then elected and took the oath,     and  Enoch
Lovell  was elected  treasurer  and the meeting  voted to buy a new
law book for the town.
The protracted  March meeting  was  renewed  under  a  new call
May 22.     Lieut.    John Torrey  was  elected  moderator,     and  Capt.
Joseph White representative to  the General Court.
There were  things  in the  air  at this  meeting  and  another  was
called  June 6,    which  voted  " That  Capt.     Hunt,     Lt.  John Torrey,
Dea.      Edward Bates,  John Pratt and Sergt.    Ezra Whitmarsh should
go up to Boston to  the General  Court on the 8th of this  instant ,
June,     then and there  to  answer in the behalf of the town relative
to  a petition  put in  to  the  court  by the  people  of  the  upper,      or
Southerly  End  of  the  town,    concerning  a  new  precinct  or  new
township to be granted.  "
If  the  town was to  be divided  it  now became a question  of  a
dividing  line,    and as  a step  toward it  a special  town meeting was
called  July  27,   1722,    when the " Town voted that there shall be a
plot  of the Town taken and  that  Col.  Thaxter  shall  be procured,
if  he will,    to survey the Town and take a plot of it. "
"Voted that  Lt.  John Torrey,     Lt.  Enoch  Lovell & Sergt.       Ezra
Whitmarsh shall be committee to get a surveyor to  take such  plot
& to be helpful to the surveyor to  take such Plott of the Town. "
"Voted also  that Benjamin White shall  entertain the committee
of the General Court at the charge of the Town.  "
"Voted further  that Lt. John Torrey & John Vinson shall  meet
the committee of  the  General  Court when sent  here  to  acquaint
them with the state of the Town. "
At a special town meeting,   October 15,   " Voted that  the  select-
men have power to  treat with those who had fenced in town lands
or sue them out of possession.  "
The  above  meeting  was  adjourned   to   the   first   Monday  in
November,        when the following  instructions  were  given  to  Capt.
John White,       representative  to  the  General  Court :           " That you do
 - 70 - 
548                                       OLD  RECORDS
not  for  the  future  use  any  means  to  prevail  with  the  General
Court  to grant a precinct  to  Weymouth Petitioners  as the  affair
now  lyes  in  said  court  but  that  you  use your  influence  and  best
endeavor in all  proper ways and by the use of all  proper means to
prevail  with  said  Honorable  General  Court  to  delay  passing  an
act  or resolve  relating  to the affair of the Precinct  until  the Town
hath  used  their  best  endeavor  to   accommodate  affairs   among
themselves  either  by the  proposal  now  on foot  or other  proposal
that may promote and preserve  harmony,  unity and peace in  the
Town.              And if  all  your  endeavors  fail  of  success  you  use  your
uttermost  endeavor that the petitioner for  precinct  may not have
more than the half set off upon a square from one side of the town-
ship to the other side line of the town thereof and that you deliver
these  instructions  to  Mr.  Paine,     clerk  of  the  House  of  Repre-
sentatives  and that you use your best endeavor to have them read
in public in said  House.  "
The meeting  adjourned  to  November  9,     when  it  was  " Voted
that  the petitioners  for  a precinct  or  township shall have half  the
precinct  of  Weymouth at  the upper end of said  town  set  off  to
them  by  a square  dividing  line  running  directly  athwart  such
dividing  line  of said Town.  "
"Also all  the  income of  Weymouth part of the fifty  thousand
pounds loan  money,   less  the charges which are or shall  arise  from
the  management  of  said  money,    until  the  Town  of  Weymouth
shall  be discharged from the whole of said  money by the  Province
or  in  any  other  way by  the  General  Court.           Provided  the  said
High  & General  Court  shall  see  cause  to  set  them off  a precinct
conformable to  the above mentioned square line. "

Chapter  XXV
On March  11,      1723,      at  a  town meeting  held  this  day,      Justin
White was elected  moderator;      Benjamin White,    town clerk ;   Justin
White,    Col.  Enoch Lovell and Lieut.   John Torrey,    selectmen.
The time of  this  meeting  was spent  in adjusting  land  claims,
suits  for  trespass,   the  church  question,   and  finally  adjourned  to
meet again on the 18th,   and the record is  as follows :
"At a general  Town Meeting  of  the  freeholders  and  other  in-
habitants  after considerable debate concerning of the Town Meet-
ing House there was a vote called by bringing in their votes on paper
and there was a majority vote for the meeting house to  stay. "
At the  town  meeting,    April  22,     1723,      " Joseph  White  elected
representative to the General  Court.         On the same day voted that
the  Selectmen  shall  have  power  to   agree  with  Mr.  Calder  our
schoolmaster  for  to  teach  school for  this  town one year  provided
he would take forty two pounds and ten shillings  or else  to  agree
with another. "
On July 1,   1723,  "Voted to build one school house for the benefit
of the whole town of Weymouth. "
"Voted  that  the  said  school  house  shall  be  between  Joseph
Lovell's  and John Shaw's.  "
At  an  adjourned   meeting,       July  22,        " Voted  that  Benjamin
White,     John Torrey and Abiah Whitman be a committee to  make
up the account of the treasurer  and to give it in at the next meet-
ing. "    Also,     "Voted that  the same committee shall  take care  that
a school  house be built for the town."
"Voted the  same day that  there  shall  be two hundred  pounds
raised  for  to pay the Town's charges this year. "
On March 2,     1724,     "Voted  to  pay  Rev.  Mr.  Paine out of the
town treasury  ninety  pounds  for  his  salary  to be paid  quarterly
beginning April  1st and forty pounds to be paid the South  Parish
of said  town out of the treasury  quarterly. "
"Voted to allow the account that was brought in for  building the
Town School house,   viz.,  42£ 7s.    11d. "
At an adjourned  meeting,     March  15,      " Voted  Mr.  Calder  our
present  schoolmaster  may  have  forty   pounds  and  ten  shillings
provided he keep school this year. "
"Voted  the  school  shall  be  kept  in  the  south  precinct   four
months  in  a year,     two  months  in  one  of  the  school  houses  and
two  months  in  the  other. "      (Evidently  there  were  two  school-
houses somewhere in the south part of the town at this  time. )
In  March,         1725,      John  Torrey,       moderator,     John  Torrey,       town
clerk;     John Torrey,    Benjamin Dyer and James Beale,    selectmen.

"Voted that  Capt.    Enoch  Lovell,    Ensign  Ezra Whitmarsh  and
John  Randall be a committee to  treat with the proprietors  of  the
mills  on the  river  by  Bateses  to  make a convenient  passage  for
the fish  up into Whitman's pond if  they can agree with them not
exceeding  five  pounds price securing  said  passage for  the fish  for
the Town's use forever."
We digress  a little  here to  tell  a fish  story but it has  the  merit
of being  more true  than  most fish  stories.        From the above date
for  nearly  a hundred and twenty-five years  the  fish  were a factor
which entered into the debates of nearly every town meeting,    and
in  1847,      through a committee or commission,   the town sold  them
to  the Weymouth Iron  Company for  a  little  over  $4,700,    subject
to certain conditions of preservation  or propagation.
The money received  went into  the town treasury and was used
for  current  expenses,    but for  more than  half  a century  the  town
continued  to  appropriate  the  income  from  the  alewife  fund  for
school  purposes,     when,      as  a  matter  of  fact,      there  never  was  an
alewife fund;      the  money was simply  taken out of  something  else.
There  is,         however,     more  to  this  fish  story.         The fish  were and
still  might be  made a  source  of  profit  and a food  supply,     and  it
is  up to  some one to  see that the terms  of sale  are  complied with.
Wehave,   however,    digressed enough from our regular story and will
take up the thread.

care of the meeting house for sixteen  weeks. "

"Voted that the  assessors  shall  have  five  pounds  for  making
up the Rates for this year. "

Chapter  XXVI
At the town meeting in  March,     1726,     John Torrey was  elected
clerk  and treasurer ;        Ensign Ezra Whitmarsh,     John Torrey,     Sergt.
John Vining,      Thomas White and Samuel White,   selectmen.
"Voted  to  instruct  the Trustees  of  the  Province  Loan  Fund  to
proceed  to  collect  the  interest  on money loaned from it  and that
there  be  paid  to the  Province  Treasurer  seventy- three  pounds  of
the loan."
On May 17,        1726,     Gideon Tirrell  was  elected  representative  to
the General Court,   and the vote of the previous year was repeated
in regard  to  schools,     i.e. ,     one school  in the town schoolhouse,    and
Mr. Calder  to have £42 10s.   for teaching the same.
The record  of  a town  meeting  held  in November  of  the  year
1726 shows a  new move on foot.         "Voted that  the country towns
in the county of Suffolk shall be separated from the town of Boston
and formed into a county by themselves;     passed in the negative. "
The following vote was passed :         " Instructions  to the  representa-
tive  of  Weymouth in  the General  Court  respecting  a new county
made of  the towns  round about Weymouth,     Provided the county
seat shall be within five or six miles of Weymouth or in Weymouth
then you are to  use your best endeavor to bring it  to pass.
"Voted at  the  aforesaid  meeting  to give  Dr.  White  four  acres
of land below         Hill that was formerly granted to John Vinson
provided  the  said  Dr.  White continue in  the  town of  Weymouth
and  in  practice  of  physick  but in  the event  of  his  removal  from
town the  land reverts  to  Weymouth unless  he chooses  to  buy the
same."
Dr.  Nathaniel  White was born in  1690,   according  to Alden's  Early  History of
the Medical  Profession,    in the county of Norfolk,    Mass. ,    and to the inscription
on his tombstone,    or in  1701,     as  stated by Vinton,    in  his  "White Genealogy. "
He graduated from Harvard College in  1725,    and was a man of much talent and
eminent in his  profession,    although a very eccentric person.          It  is  asserted  that
when he was summoned to a patient  in stormy weather,    he  frequently  would
refuse  to go,    saying, "the weather was not fit  for any one to go out;  "   but the
messenger  on his return  usually found him,    with his saddlebags,    at  the  bedside
of his patient.  -NASH'S  " HISTORY. "
"Voted that  the  south  precinct  shall  have the  Old  Law Book
and the north precinct the new one. "

On March  13,       1727,       "Voted  that  the  wood  of  the  woodland
which lyes  below  the  great  marsh  on Great Marsh river and held
and  preserved  for  the  ministry  shall  henceforth  belong  to  the
north  parish  in the town of Weymouth and shall be made use  of
for the ministry of said parish for the time being in such proportions
and quantities  of wood yearly  as  the said  north parish  shall  order
and appoint.            And the south parish shall  have thirty  acres  of  the
wood of the woodland in the southeast part of said town for the use
of the ministry for the time being of the precinct in such proportions
and quantities of wood yearly as the precinct shall order. "
There was evidently a warm debate on this  matter,    and twenty
men registered  their  names as  opposed to  the vote.

Chapter  XXVII
At the  town  meeting,     May 8,     1727,    Joseph  White was  chosen
moderator.              Several  small  parcels  of  town's common lands  were
allotted  to  individuals who had already fenced them in for various
considerations,    and the  following  committee  was  chosen " to  lay
out the wood lot which was voted to the South Parish in Weymouth
for  the  ministry  in said  parish: "   John Vining,    Jr.,    John Vinson
and William Reed.
A motion was  made that  £60 be raised  for  the maintenance  of
schools,       of  which  £40  should  be  for  a  grammar  school  for   the
whole  town  and  £20  for  a  writing  school  in  the  South  parish.
After much discussion  a negative  vote decided  the  question,      and
the  meeting adjourned  to  the  15th,     when it  was "voted  that  the
school should be kept in the same place as last year.  "
At the special  town meeting,    February,    1728,      Ezra  Whitmarsh
was chosen  moderator  and the day was spent in discussing  wood
and  timber  lands,     with  the  following   result:        "Voted  that   the
Town will  protect  the  wood standing  or  lying  upon  the  Town's
Commons or  undivided lands  and chose a committee consisting  of
Joseph  White,     Esq.,    John Torrey,   and John Randall to  prosecute
all  trespassers. "
On March  4,        1728,     at  the  general  town  meeting  of  the  Free-
holders   and  other  inhabitants,     Joshua  Torrey  was  elected  town
clerk;       Joseph  White,     Esq. ,    treasurer;      Joseph  White,     Esq. ,      John
Torrey  and  Samuel  White,    selectmen.         The meeting  also  elected
a long list of minor officers.
At a special  town meeting,    March 29,    " Chosen  for  trustees  to
receive  the  Town's part of the  sixty  thousand pounds of bills  of
credit  to be issued  out to the Towns in proportion to  their  taxes.
Joseph White,     Esq. ,    Ebenezer Vinson and Abiah Whitmarsh.  "
"Voted that  the trustees  shall  let  out of the Town's part of the
sixty  thousand  pounds  to  the  inhabitants  of  Weymouth on  the
first  day  five  pounds.      And ten  pounds  on  the  second  day  that
shall be appointed for that business. "
"Voted  that  the  trustees  shall  have  ten  pounds  allowed  them
by the town for their trouble in letting out and taking in the Town's
part of said money and whole management of the affair.  "
On May 13,       1728,     Gideon Tirrell  was  elected  representative  to
the General Court.
"Voted that the school shall  not be moved.  "    (There was a  large
amount of school talk then as  now. )
"Voted for a committee to lay out the land granted to Dr. White
and to lay out Nathaniel Ford's grant  of a piece of land  on Smelt

Chapter  XXVIII
In December,   1730,     " Voted to  raise  fifty  pounds to defray  the
charge for  schools. "
"Voted that  the school  shall  be kept eight  months in  the  year
in the North precinct  and be kept where  the  selectmen  shall  see
cause to keep it,   and that the South precinct  shall have the school
kept in the South precinct four months where they shall  see  cause
to keep it. "
"Voted  that  Abiah  Whitman,     Benjamin  Richards  and  Samuel
Badlam  be a committee  to  prosecute  any person  or  persons  that
incroach  on the town's highway."
" Chosen Representative in the room of Gideon Tirrell,    deceased,
Stephen   French  who  refused   to   serve   as   Representative,       and
Thomas White was elected. "     (Things  are different  now,      as  there
are  several  who are waiting for the position to come their way. )
"Voted  that  the  schoolhouse  by John  Reed's  shall  be moved
down to the meeting house hill in the first  precinct for  the school
to be kept in while it  is kept in said first precinct if the Town will

At  the  March  meeting,     1730,      John  Torrey  was  elected   town
clerk,     and after  most of the day had been spent in discussing  the
question  of having  three or  five  selectmen,    it  was voted  to  have
five,       and the  following  were elected:      John  Vinson,      John Vining,
Capt.       Joseph  White,      Adam Cushing  and  Abiah  Whitman.           This
meeting  and one  or  two  adjourned  ones  for  the  month were de-
voted mostly  to settling land claims.
Town meetings  in  May,     1731,      were  quite  frequent,    and at  the
first  one a motion to  raise  £75  for  school  purposes,      £50 of which
should be for  the North  Precinct  and  £25 for  the South,   was de-
feated,        as  was  also  a  motion to  state  the commons and undivided
lands,     and the schools were continued as they were the year before.
In  March,       1732,    the town voted  to go back to three selectmen,
and  Thomas White,     Philip  Torrey and John Beale were elected.
This  year  it  was  "Voted  that  the  South  parish  in  Weymouth
should have their proportion of the school  in that parish according
to what they pay toward the school for  the year.   "
Another commission was chosen to fix  the boundary line between
Weymouth and Braintree.
At the  March meeting  in  1733,      in  addition  to  routine  business
it  was "Voted that  Dr.  Nathaniel  White draw 13£ 13s.    00d.      of  the
Town Treasury for his curing Betty Shanks an old  Indian squaw of
her lameness."
"Voted  that  Epharm  Porter,     Jr.,      shall  be  allowed  ten  pounds

out  of  the  Town Treasury  for  his  charge  and  boarding  of  Betty
Shanks an old  Indian squaw which lay lame at his house. "
In  March,          1734,      John  Torrey  was  elected  town  clerk;      Adam
Cushing,    John Beal and Philip Torrey,    selectmen.
This  year  there came the culmination of a difficulty  which had
existed   since  the  formation  of  the  South  Parish.          For  lack  of
financial  support,   and other reasons,   Mr. Paine,   the minister,    who
for  some time had been doing his ministerial work from his  home
in  Boston,      to  which place he had moved,   dissolved  his  connection
entirely  with  the  people  and  also  the  ministry  and  engaged  in
mercantile pursuits,   and we find the following vote:
"Voted that  the Housing and land  belonging  to the town that
Mr.  Paine  lately  improved  shall  be let  out until  the  5th day of
March next,    and the rent be improved for the use of the town. "
"Voted  that  Capt.      Adam Cushing  shall  have fourteen  shillings

"Voted that Ebenezer Humphrey,    E. Vining and John Tirrell be

spring of the year. "
"Voted that the town's stock of powder be sold and a new stock
of powder bought.  "

Chapter  XXIX
The year  1735  opened with  a somewhat disturbed  condition  in
church  matters,      the  Old  North,      or  First   Parish,      property  still
belonging to the whole town.
Rev.  William Smith had succeeded  Mr. Paine,   and his pastorate
extended  from  1734 until  his  death  in  1783,     during  which  time
among other  children  which  were  born  to  him was Abigail,      who
became the wife of John Adams of historic  fame and the  second
President  of  the  United States,     and  no  names will  live  longer  in
American history  than those of John Adams and his wife Abigail
(Smith)   Adams whose memory the historic  societies  of Weymouth
cherish and will pass down to future generations.
What to do with the property in which there was so much joint
ownership  and  so  little  common interest   now  became  a serious
one,      and  at  a special  town  meeting  held  in  June,     1735,       it   was
"Voted that  the town's housing and land purchased of Zechariah
Bicknell  shall  be sold  and the money go to  such  use as  the town
doth see fit ."
"Voted  that  the  money which  the  town's  housings  and  land
brings  shall  be divided  between  the  two  parishes  in  proportion
according  to  the tax that each parish bears in the Province Tax in
the present year.  "
While  this  motion  passed  in  the  affirmative,      there  was  a  hot
debate,       and nine men signed  a protest  against  the action  of  the
meeting.
At the March 3,    1735,    town meeting,   John Torrey was  elected
town  clerk;        Capt.        Adam  Cushing,     John  Vining  and  Nathaniel
Ford,   selectmen;    Benjamin Dyer,    treasurer.
"Voted  that  the present  minister of the town shall  receive  the
possession  of  the  parsonage  according  to  the  terms  of  the  deed
ofthe same."
The meeting  then  adjourned  to  the  next  day,    when the  first
business taken up was the election of constables.        One after another
ten men were elected,   eight of whom declined  and paid the fine  of
£5,      two  were excused,    and at  last  James  Humphrey was  elected
and qualified.
"Voted that  the town confirm the way laid out from the South
meeting house to the Widow Sarah Turner's.  "
"Voted  that  there  shall  be  a way laid  out  from  the  meeting
house  in  the  South  Parish  to  the  Commons  or  undivided  lands
that lieth  at the thicket."
"Voted  that  the  constables'     fines  be  paid  unto  each  precinct
treasury  to which precinct it  belongs. "

558                                              OLD  RECORDS
Lieut .         Eben Hunt,    John Vining  and Ensign  Hunt were  chosen
to lay out the new way to  the  thicket.
"Voted  to  State  the  Common or  undivided  lands, "  and a  com-
mittee  of  twenty-five  was  appointed  to  divide  the  lands  among
the householders.
At a town meeting held May 12,    1735,  Adam Cushing was elected
representative to the General Court.
"Voted that there  shall  be but one school in the town and  said
school  shall  be kept  in  each  precinct  in  proportion  to  the  taxes
they pay. "
In  1735 Weymouth occupied the same place on the map which
it  had for  more than a century,    and which it has occupied for  one
hundred and seventy- three years  since,     but at  that  time it  was a
part  of  Suffolk  County,    and we find  in September of that  year  a
second  attempt was  made to  form  new county  alliances,       and  at
a special  meeting held  in September it  was  "Voted to join  with
Roxbury  and  Dorchester  in  a petition  to  the  Great  and  General
Court that Boston be an entire countyby itself and the rest of the
towns in  said county be by themselves. "
For  the  years  1736  and  1737  the  town meetings  were  devoted
largely  to  making titles  to  the  new allotments  of  lands,       building
and straightening of public highways,   with an occasional discussion
of schools,     the latter  of which remained as for  the previous year.
The March meeting for 1738 elected  the usual board of officers ,
and  Capt.         Adam Cushing  as  representative,    with  special  instruc-
tions  to  bring about a new county.
At a town meeting in May of this year the school appropriation
was  raised  to   £100,     with  a vote  " That each  precinct draw from
the treasury in proportion to  the tax they pay for  a school  in  that
precinct."
A meeting  was  called  August  12  to  settle  the  housing  at  the
parsonage  in  the  North  Precinct.            A motion  to  repair  the  said
house went in the negative.
Next came a motion to tear the house down,    and it was negatived
and then came the following:       " Voted that the selectmen prosecute
any person or persons who shall attempt to pull down the parsonage
house, "   forty  persons  signing  a  protest  against  the  latter  vote,
but the house stood  the heat of the contest  and the historic  house
in  which  Abigail  (Smith)   Adams was  born  now  stands  on  Bridge
Street,      North Weymouth.

Chapter  XXX
At the  annual  town meeting,     March 5,    1739,    John Torrey  was
elected  town  clerk;     Capt.       Adam Cushing,     Dr.  Nathaniel  White,
Dea.        Samuel  Whitman,     John  Reed and James Humphrey,     select-
men.
There  was  the  usual  contest  on  constables,     and  ten  men were
elected  and declined,    paying  the  fine  of  £5  rather  than  to  serve
in that capacity.
The day was spent  in  making rules  in regard  to  cattle  running
at  large,      awards for killing  black birds  and crows,     and penalty  for
killing  deer.             The meeting  adjourned  to  the  7th  of  March,     when
the following was passed :        " Voted to  raise  one hundred pounds for
schooling  in the town the present year,    each precinct  to have their
portion  of  said   money,      provided  they  improve  said  money  in
schooling  in  said  precinct;      provided  also  each  precinct  keep  a
grammar school  in  proportion to the money drawn for  schooling. "
The warm days of August in this year,   1739,     were chosen  for  a
warm meeting in regard to the joint ownership of church property,
and at  a special  town meeting on the  13th  we find  the following :
"Voted,        whether  the  town  would  allow  anything  to  the  South
precinct  in  lieu  of their interest  in the minister's  land  in  this  pre-
cinct.         And it  passed in the negative.  "
"Voted  to  choose  a committee,     part  of  said  committee  to  be
chosen  in  each  precinct,      to  consider  what  may be  done  to   ac-
commodate the controversy between said  precincts  respecting  the
ministerial land."
The  committee   chosen   were   Capt.          Adam  Cushing,          Capt.
Nathaniel  White,     Capt.      Eben  Hunt,     Philip  Torrey,      Dea.      Samuel
Whitman,    John Hunt,  John Pratt,   Jr.,    and Ebenezer Burrell .
This   matter   was  up  again   at   a  special   town   meeting   in
September,       when " It  was  put  to  a  vote  whether  the  South  pre-
cinct  should have the  improvement of  sixty  acres  of  the  common
land  in  the  Beach  Thicket joining  to  the  wood lot  belonging  to
said  precinct  to  help  support  the  publick  worship  of  God among
them.          It passed in the negative. "
There was  nothing special  in the several  early  town meetings  in
1740.     There  was  the  usual  election  of  town  officers   in   March,
and  the  regular  £100 for  schools  was voted  in  May,    the  same to
bedivided among the two precincts for two schools.
In our last  we said  that the historic  birthplace of  Abigail  Smith
Adams was  still  standing,    and we now get a little  light  on how it
came to be moved from the original spot.
During  the  year  1739  a  committee  with  Benjamin  Bicknell  at

the  head  (records  do not tell  by what authority)  moved the par-
sonage to a new location,    and we find the following vote at a special
town meeting held Sept. 27,    1840:
"Voted that  Deacon Josiah  Waterman,    Captain Adam Cushing

In  1741  the  money question  seemed  to  be of the  most  impor-
tance,       and the town voted that the taxes  for  that year should  be
paid  in  manufacturers'     bills.         We hope  no one  will  ask  us  what
kind  of  currency  " manufacturers'      bills "   was  because  we do  not
know.
In  1742  the  new  county  was  again  agitated,      and  the  repre-
sentative  to  the  General  Court  was  specially  instructed   to   try
and bring  about a separation from Boston.
At a special  town meeting  held  on the  sixteenth  day of  April
in this  year  it  was "Voted that there be four days in a week ap-
pointed for the inhabitants of the town to  take or catch shad and
alewives in the river by Samuel Bateses,   viz.:    Monday,    Wednesday,
Friday and Saturday and from the pond up the river  by John Tir-
rell's  upon the aforesaid days. "
"Voted  that  Samuel Bates,    Jr. ,   shall  have liberty  to  fish  from
the fish  gate down the river to the salt water,    who is  to fish for the
town for  sale."

Chapter  XXXI
There  were  no special  features  to  the  March meeting  of  1743.
The day was spent  in  electing  the usual long  list  of town officers
and hearing  reports  of  committees  on  new  roads  and  relocating
old ones.
At the May meeting  Capt.      Adam Cushing  was  chosen  repre-
sentative to the General Court,   and the new county question seems
to have been dropped for  the time being  and Weymouth was still
a part  of Suffolk County.
The school  question  passed off  very quietly at this  meeting,     as
did also  the matter of other  town charges,     as  the following  vote
indicates :
"Voted  to  make a  Rate of  one  hundred  and  forty  pounds  in
old  currency  to defray  charges.        One hundred  pounds  to  be  ap-
propriated  for schooling  in said town and that each  precinct draw
their  proportion  of  the  same  according  to  their  tax  rate,      and  it
be applied to schooling  as  the precinct thinks proper. "
"Voted  that  Samuel  Bates  shall  be  free  from  paying  of  rates
for  his  Grist Mill this year in consideration of its  lying  idle a con-
siderable time for the fish  to  pass up to the pond. "
Like  1743,          the   March  meeting  of  1744  was  without  special
interest,      but  after  quite  a debate  as  to  certain  animals  going  at
large,       it  was voted that hogs  may go at  large,    provided they  be
yoked and ringed.
The school  board  did  not  ask  for  an  increase  of  two  or  three
thousand dollars  each year for  schooling,    and we find  the  regular
£100 ($500)   to be divided as usual between the two precincts .
We have  not  seen  the  red  man mentioned  for  several  years ,
with  the  exception  of  the  single  instance  where  medical  aid  and
board  was  paid  for  an  " Old  Indian  Squaw,"  but  now  a  special
town meeting was called  for July 25.    Capt.      Ebenezer  Hunt was
elected  moderator  and  " It  was put  to  a vote  whether  the  town
are  willing  that  the  Pegnacket  Indians  that  are  now  in  Boston
should be placed in Weymouth.       Said vote was unanimously in  the
negative."
" It  was  also  voted  that  Ezra  Whitmarsh,      Jr. ,      James  Pettie,
Capt.        Ebenezer  Hunt,      Capt.      John  Vinson  and  Ebenezer  White
be a committee to meet the General Court committee and acquaint
them of said  vote  and to  use their  endeavor with them that  said
Indians may not be placed  in said  town.  "
On March 4,    1745,   there  was  an election  of the usual  board  of
officers,     and Captain Vinson,    Captain Whitman and Gideon Tirrell

were appointed a committee to lay out a way from Captain Vinson
to  the Braintree line.
On  May 14  Adam Cushing  was  again  elected  representative,
which was his fifth  consecutive year.
The meeting  also  voted the  usual  £100 for  schools  and  £40  for
all  other charges.
At the  March meeting,      1746,     Joshua  Torrey  was  elected  town
clerk;     Adam  Cushing,      James  Humphrey  and  Ebenezer  White,
selectmen  and assessors ;      Abiah Whitman,     treasurer.
Voted,      " The towns  people  might take  alewives  above  the  fish
Gate Monday,      Wednesday,      Fridays  & Saturdays  and that  David
Rice might have the water for his fulling mill the other two days.  "
The  parsonage  question  was  not  brought  up  this  year,        and
harmony prevailed in  the division of the regular  £100 for schooling
and £40 for  other town charges.
In  March,         1747,     there  was  routine  business  and  another  new
road,       as  per  the  following  vote:       " Chosen  Capt.      Vinson,        Justin
Dyer & Capt.     White a committee to  agree with Thomas Hollis  to

Fore  River,          the  water  front  and  the  landing  were  no  small
factors  in  those early days,    as  a large part  of  Weymouth business
and outside  social  life  was done by way of its  two rivers,   and we
find  in  this  year something doing in the way of its  development.
"Voted to  grant  a landing place and highway to it  to  Nicholas

The  regular   £100  was  raised  and  appropriated  for  school  and
divided  between  the  two  precincts   according  to   the  rate  they
paid.
Town charges  were  increased  this  year from  £40  to  £100,      but
as  this  made but $1,000 for  schools  and all  other  charges,      it  would
be  but  a drop in  the bucket  these  days of  New Town ( ?)   houses
