Chapter  XLVI
At a special  town meeting  held April  5,      1790,      " called  in  con-
formity  of  many towns  to  fix  the  pay  of  representatives  to  the
General  Court. "     " It  was  voted  to  allow  the  representative  4s.
per day for  the ensuing year. "
It  is  evident that the town still  held some proprietorship  in the
North  Meeting-House,    as  they  sold  a pew at  public  sale  at  this
meeting for  $150.
The May meeting was no doubt an interesting one to the people
ofthat day.
The  committee  appointed  at  a  previous  meeting  to  report  in
regard  to   schoolhouses   reported  that   " the  following  places  are
best  suited  for  the  purpose: "    viz. ,     first   at  the  schoolhouse  on
King Oak Hill;     second,  between Mr. Waterman's and Mr. Turner's
house;       third,     near the  house of  Mr.  Nathaniel  Richards,       Jr. ,        on
the west side of the way;     fourth,    near  Mr. John Vinson's mill  lane
on the main road.
"Voted to  instruct  the  representative  to  use his  efforts  for  es-
tablishing  a new county."
"Voted  to  raise  150£ to  defray  the  town's  charges  and  build
two school houses. "
"Voted  to  let  out  Rockweed below  Great  Hill  and  Hunt's  Hill
to the highest  bidder. "
At a town meeting  held  October  4,      Urban Bates,   John Tirrell,
Thomas  Vinson,      Josiah  Waterman  and  James  Humphrey  were
appointed  a committee to build two schoolhouses,    one near Josiah
Waterman's,     and the other near Nathaniel Richards'  .
In  March,        1791,    after  the  usual  election  of  town  officers,      and
re-enacting  many rules  and regulations  in regard  to  town govern-
ment,      it  was " Voted that the town clerk be directed  to  lay before
the town the laws of the Commonwealth and they be read in  the
next town meeting after he has received  said laws. "
No man living  would dare  attempt  the  above feat  in  the  year
of our Lord 1908.
The  committee  on  rockweed  reported  that  they  had  sold  the
same  to  David Blanchard for  a term of ten years for  £4 15s.
Lemuel  Torrey  was  granted permission  to  lay  stones  along  the
beach in front of his land for the purpose of growing rockweed.
On  May 9,       " Voted to  raise  80£ for  schools  and  50£ for  other
town charges."
"Voted that  the selectmen  provide women schools  the  ensuing
year."
At  the  March  meeting,    1792,      the  collection  of  taxes  was  the
 - 118 - 
596                                        OLD  RECORDS
vexed  question  of  the  meeting,     and  it  was  voted  to  put  up the
collection  at vendue to be sold  to the  lowest bidder,   he to  put up
$5  as  earnest  money until he shall have secured satisfactory bonds ,
and  the  North  Parish  went  to  Joshua  Torrey  for  51½  pence  per
pound;     the  South  Parish  to  Josiah  Blanchard for  54 pence  per
pound.
At the  state  election  in  April,      John  Hancock received  all  the
votes  but  one  for  Governor,      and  Samuel Adams  the  entire  vote
for  Lieutenant Governor.
At this  meeting  it  was voted to build  a stone pound near  the
residence  of  John  Tirrell,    but it  is  evident  from  future  records
that this  pound was never built.
At the  May meeting  a request  was  received  by the  following
petitioners  of Abington asking  to be taken in by Weymouth,    pro-
vided  the  General Court would grant the petition to be separated
from   Abington :          Josiah    White,          Labulan   Paine,         Ezra   Tirrell,
Labulan  Paine,     Jr. ,    Abiah  Shaw,    Joshua  Curtis,     Abiah Shaw,     Jr. ,
Thomas Hunt,    Jeremiah White,    John White and Benjamin White.
"Voted to grant the petition."
A request   was   received   from   Scituate,       in   the   county   of
Plymouth,      for  a new county of towns  south  of  Boston,      and John
Tirrell  was appointed a committee to take counsel with them.
The county was made in  1793,    and it was a sad disappointment
to Weymouth and other towns in the immediate vicinity,    as  it  was
hoped to have Weymouth or Quincy the " shire town, "  but it  went
to  Dedham,     and efforts  were shortly made to get back into  Suffolk
County,    but without  effect,    and we of  this  generation  can  only
accomplish  it  by becoming a part of "Greater Boston. "
The only  thing  out of the ordinary  at  the  March meeting was,
"Voted  to  give  permission  to   erect  a  hospital  for  innoculating
with the small pox under the supervision of the selectmen. "
At the  May meeting  it  was voted  not  to  send a representative
to the General Court.
The town election  of  March,     1794,     the  state  election  in April
and May business meeting were all  without marked incidents.
At a special  meeting held  in August of that year it  was voted
to  take  a plan  of  the  town agreeable  to  a  request  of  the General
Court,     and the selectmen  were appointed as  a committee to  carry
the same into effect.
There was a  special meeting held November 3 of this year,      1794,
to  take  action  in  regard  to  a call  for  soldiers,      and  it  was "Voted
to  join  the  captains  of  militia  in  hiring  the  men that  they  are
called  upon to detach from their companies."
"Voted that the soldiers'    wages be made up to  $15  a month for
each month in service and $1  per year for  one day's service  if  the
regiment  meets one day in  a year,    and $ 10  to  each man when he
shall  enlist  or be detached,   as a bounty. "
On Dec.  11 ,       1794,    "Voted to  raise  the sum of 93£ for  the pur-
pose of paying the soldiers'     bounty as  per vote of  Nov.  3rd. "

Chapter  XLVII
At the  March meeting  in  1795,    John Tirrell  was  elected  town
clerk;      Urban  Bates,     John  Tirrell  and  James  Humphrey,       select-
men;     and  Joshua  Humphrey,    treasurer.          The other  list  of town
officers  and committees came in regular  order,    and then the topic
of the day was  Fore River,     Back River and the wharves and land-
ing  places,        and  the  discussion  terminated  in  the  following  vote
and result :
"Voted  to  let  out  the  landing  places  and  wharfs  for  one  year
from the 5th day of April next to the highest bidder.      The vendue
was held and Capt.  Joshua Bates bid off  Back River for  six dollars
and  fifty  cents  and  paid  two dollars  to  bind  the  bargain.            Ezra
Bicknell bid  off  Fore  River  for  thirty-two dollars  and fifty  cents
and paid eleven dollars  earnest money. "
At the May meeting Asa White was elected  representative.
There was some school  business  done,    but most of the day was
devoted to roads.
In  March,      1796,    with  the exception  of  a few minor officers,       the
same parties  were elected as in  1795.
The fishery was the main topic of this meeting,   and it  was " Voted
to  sell  them by the barrell  to the highest  bidder at the rate of 700
fish  per  barrel  and fish  to  be taken between sunrise and sunset  on
but three days in the week. "
"Voted that the highways be repaired by a tax of 4s.     on a poll
and in proportion on real estate given a poll  the  privilege of sub-
stituting  a day's work for  the 4s. "
"Voted to raise $500 for schooling . "
The rivers  were again sold  by vendue,   and Capt.    Joshua Bates
bought  Back  River for  the  year  for  $6;     Lieut.    John White,       Fore
River for  $11.
At  the  state  election   in  April   the  town  cast  69  votes   for
Governor,     all but one of which were for Samuel Adams.
Washington  was  now  in  the  last  year  of  his  second  term  as
President,     and  had  publicly  declared  himself  as   opposed  to   a
third  term and would not accept  another election.          The campaign
was on for  a President of the United States for the next four years,
but it  is  apparent  that Weymouth took but little  interest  in the
matter,     as  it  cast but 17 votes at  the  November election for mem-
bers  of  Congress  and  the presidential  electors.         Rev.  John  Reed
received 13 votes for member of Congress,    and Edward H. Robinson,
4;     for presidential electors,   Hon.   Wm.    Seaver,     13,     and Edward H.
Robinson,    4.
At the  annual  meeting  in  March,      1797,     the  same  officers   for
 - 120 - 
598                                         OLD  RECORDS
town clerk,      selectmen,     assessors  and  town  treasurer  were  elected
as  in  the  two  previous  years,    and the  all-important  fish  question
was disposed of as in the last  year.
The  landing  places  and  wharves  on  Back  River  were  sold  to
Capt.       Joshua  Bates for  the  year for  $20.50;      those on  Fore  River
to  Jacob  Loud for  $29.
The school  question was the one of the day,   and while in many
of the previous years there had been committees chosen for specific
school  purposes,     or  the  matter had  been left  in the  hands  of  the
selectmen,        we now come to  the  first  time when a committee was
chosen and designated as the  " School  Committee, "  and the  sequel
proves that trouble in the school committee is  no new thing.          Hon.
Cotton   Tufts,         Asa   White,       Esq. ,         Capt.         Joshua   Bates,          Hon.
Nathaniel  Bayley and  Eliphalet  Loud,    Esq. ,    were chosen  as  school
committee.
State election occurred on the 3d of April,   and 38 votes were cast
at this meeting.
The school  question  was again  brought  up,   and it  was " Voted
to  empower and authorize the school committee to  provide  school-
masters  and  schoolmistresses,       assign  districts   and  places  for  the
several  schools,    give  directions  with  reference  to  the management
of them and that for  the expense of  schooling,    the selectmen  shall
draw  orders  on  the  treasurer  for  the  same certified  by said  com-
mittee."
If  there  were  shorthand  reporters  at  that  meeting  their  notes
are  not  recorded  in the  Town Records,      and the next thing we find
is :          " Nathaniel  Bayley,     one  of  the  committee,     excused  himself
from  further  service  and  the  meeting  voted  to  excuse  the  whole
committee. "

Chapter  XLVIII
The question  of  a division  of the  town came up again  early  in
January,       1798,      and  a  special  meeting  of the  freeholders  and  in-
habitants  of  Weymouth was called for January 29,    " For the  pur-
pose of taking  into consideration  a petition of the North Parish  of
said  Town,       Praying to be incorporated  into  a separate Town with
an  order  of  the  General  Court  therein,   for  any  person  to  show
cause,      if  any they have,   why the prayer of said petitioners  should
not be granted. "
Urban Bates  was moderator of the meeting,    and  " The question
was put whither it  is  the sense of the Town that the North Parish
should  be  incorporated   into   a  separate   Town -   Passed   in  the
affirmative.              Meeting Dissolved. "
On March 12,    1798,    John Tirrell was chosen town clerk;         Urban
Bates,    John Tirrell,  James Humphrey,   Samuel Badlam and Eliphalet
Loud,    selectmen and assessors;    Josiah Humphrey,    treasurer.
"Voted to  sell  the alewives at public vendue provided  the pur-
chaser  shall  furnish  the  inhabitants  of  the  town  with  fish   at  20
cents a hundred. "
Wharves and landing places were sold in open meeting.          Samuel
Dyer  bought  Back  River  for   $9,       and  John  White  bought  Fore
River (price not recorded) .
On April 17 the town accepted the report of a committee laying
out  a  road  from  the  foot  of  Great  Pond  to  the  Randolph  line,
and the abutters were to give the land and build the road.
At  the  May meeting  the  town  voted  to  raise  $600  for  town
charges  for  the year.
At  the  March  meeting  in  1799  John  Tirrell  was  chosen  town
clerk;      Urban  Bates,      James  Humphrey and John Turner,       select-
men and assessors ;       Josiah  Humphrey,   treasurer .
"Voted that a committee be appointed  to divide the town into
school districts  and report  to  the town at the next April meeting. "
Hon.            Cotton  Tufts,       Asa  White,       Zadock  Nash,     John  Tirrell,
Joshua  Bates,     Joseph  Torrey  and  David  Joy  appointed  a  com-
mittee for  the above.
The  wharf  and  landing  places  on  Back  River  were  sold   to
Joshua  Bates  for  the  year  for  $9,      and  Fore  River  went  to  Levi
Bates  for  $25.
Nothing special at the April meeting.
May 13th.                    "Voted to  raise  $550 for  town charges."
Committee  on dividing  the  Town into  school  districts   recom-
mended it  be divided into  eight districts  and it  was so  done.           In
the town records  the  lines  of  these  districts  are  definitely  defined

* 600                                          OLD  RECORDS
but as  many of the locations would not be familiar with the people
of to- day we omit them in detail,   but they have stood through all
the  years  since  as  town  lines   for  specific  purposes.             Districts   1
and  2  are  now Ward One,     District  3  is  Ward Two,    District  4 is
Ward  Three,      Districts  5  and  6  are  Ward  Four,      and 7 and  8  are
Ward Five.
(We would  here  state  that  some  of  these  districts   were  sub-
divided  into  other districts  before  becoming Wards. )
"Voted that  the money be divided  among the districts  in  pro-
portion  to  their  Tax.   "
"Voted  that  each  district   should  build  and  maintain  its   own
School  Houses.  "

Chapter  XLIX
Town division had failed  to materialize,    efforts  for  a  new county
had been abandoned,    and Weymouth began the  nineteenth century
in  a quiet way by electing  the same board of town officers  for  the
year  1800  as  had  served  the  previous  year,      viz .:      John  Tirrell,
town  clerk;        Urban  Bates,      John  Tirrell   and  James  Humphrey,
selectmen and assessors ;       Joshua Humphrey,    treasurer.
Collection   of   taxes   was   sold   in   open   meeting,         and   Wm.
Humphrey bid off  the  North  Parish  for  71½ pence per pound,   and
the South Parish went to  Mathew Pratt at the same price.
A highway tax of 50 cents  on all  polls  was voted  and the  same
ratio  on estates.             It  was also  voted  to  allow $1  a day for  work on
the highways.
At the April meeting $700 was raised  for  schools,    to  be divided
among  the  eight  districts   according  to  the  number  of   teachers
employed in  each .
"Voted  to  lease  the  taking  of  Rockweed  on  the  beach  for  a
term of  ten years,     excepting  that  much which belongs  to  Lemuel
Torrey and  David Blanchard.  "
This  being  a state election  day Weymouth  polled  84 votes  for
Governor,       55 of which were for Elbridge Gerry .
The year  1801  was without special  incidents .
They took a new interest in roads in the year 1802,   as after voting
$600 for schooling they passed a vote raising  $150 in  addition to  the
district   highway  expenditure,      to  be  expended  on  the  road  from
Fore River  to  the Abington line,  $ 100 of the same to be expended
on  the  road  and  $50  on  the  bridges,      and  a  special   committee,
consisting   of   Nathaniel   Bayley,        Eliphalet   Loud,      John  Vinson,
S.   Blanchard,      E.  Hunt,      Thomas  Nash  and  Samuel Arnold,     was
appointed  to  supervise the work.
In the early part of 1803 we find the first  record of  any effort  to
bridge  Back River and Fore River at tidewater.
Up to  this   time  all  of  the  travel  from  the  South  Shore  had
crossed  the  rivers  by ferry  or  come  and  gone  by  way  of  East
Weymouth,     and the  building  now occupied by Willard  J.  Dunbar
and  Miss  Ellen  Parrott,     in  the  olden  times  known  as  the  " Rice
Tavern, "    was  one  of  the  most  popular  and  well-known  places
from Plymouth to  Boston.
Early  in   1803  Benjamin  Lincoln  and  others  petitioned  to   the
General  Court to build  bridges  across  the  two  rivers  substantially
where the existing  bridges  are,     and  at  a  special  town meeting held
on  February 3,     Hon.       Cotton Tufts,     Eliphalet  Loud and  Nathaniel
Bayley were appointed as a committee to appear before the General
 - 124 - 
602                                      OLD  RECORDS
Court  and  remonstrate  against  the  granting  of  the  petition  on
account  of Weymouth shipping interests .
We do not find in the immediate record what the result was at
the time,    but those of us who are now alive know that the bridges
are there.
The next  item  of interest  for  the  year  was  also  in  relation  to
roads.           We find  that  on April  2 the  town voted  to  build  a road
from  a point  near  Mr.  Noah  Tirrell's  barn to  Peter Whitmarsh's.
The road  was built,     and  that much of it  extending  from Middle
Street  to  a point near the Franklin schoolhouse is  a part of Broad
Street.        The rest of it for many years was known as  Drury Lane,
but is now Madison Street.
The town was  now fast  approaching  the two  hundredth  anni-
versary  of  its  existence,  and up to  this  time the only allusion  we
have  seen  to  any  postal  service  is  that  to  the  repair  of  " Post
Roads" in connection with other roads.         We now find the following :
"Voted that  there shall be a Post  Office  in  said  Weymouth at
or  near the head of navigation in the Province of Weymouth. "
"Voted  that  the  Selectmen  be  directed  to  petition  the   Post
Master General for  said  Post Office."
Other events of the year were simply routine.
 - 125 - 
Chapter  L
At the  annual  meeting  in  March,     1805,    John Tirrell  was  again
elected  town  clerk;     Dea.        Elnathan  Bates,     John  Tirrell  and  Dr.
James  Lovell,      selectmen  and  assessors ;      and  Josiah  Humphrey,
treasurer .
The  collection   of   taxes   was   sold   at  vendue,         and   William
Humphrey bid off the North Parish for  2 pence and 8 mills  on the
dollar,     and the South  Parish  was  bid  off  by Mathew Pratt  at  the
same  price,      each depositing  $5 earnest  money until his  bond was
approved by the selectmen.
The  meeting  voted  $800  for  schooling  and  appointed  a  com-
mittee of eight,    one from each district,     to equalize the money.
The  selectmen  were  authorized  to  hire  out  the  wharves  and
landing places and make rules  in regard to the same.
Much of the time of this  meeting and the following  one in May
was devoted to roads.          Many roads were widened and straightened,
and some new ones  voted,    among them the following,     which may
be of interest  to  the  Village  Improvement Society  of Weymouth
Heights just at this  time:
"Voted to  widen the North Meeting house lane and to choose a
committee to  lay  out said  road so  as  to  be sufficient  for  passing. "
Dr.  Cotton Tufts,    Capt.    Elliot  Loud and Asa White,    Esq. ,   were
chosen a committee for the laying out of said road.
The much discussed  bridge  question  for  Fore  River  and  Back
River was again before the General  Court,   and this  time on peti-
tion of Elisha Done and others,     and a special  meeting was called
for August  19  to  remonstrate on account of  its  " Serious injury  to
Trade,     Navigation and the Industries of the  town.  "
Once  more  the  iron  ore  of  Great  Pond  became  a  source  of
revenue,      and  the selectmen were authorized  to  lease  the privilege
for  the year.
There  were  no  marked events  in  the  year  1806;      substantially
the  same  officers   were  elected,    the  same routine  votes  in  regard
to  schools,      roads,   iron ore,   etc.,   and 1807 began in  nearly the same
way.               But some of the people got busy before the March meeting
was  over  and it  began with  a discussion  of  the  poor  which  had
cost  the  town  $600  in  the  year  past,     and John  Dyer  raised  the
question  how better  to  employ  the  idle  and  assist  the  helpless,
and the question once raised was carried  into  adjourned and other
meetings  until the town voted to expend $2,500 in building  a new
workhouse and enclosure,    the same to  be built  on the  town's land
near  Levi  Bates' .
Captain Tufts,     Eliphalet  Loud,    Levi  Bates,     Ebenezer Hunt and
 - 126 - 
604                                     OLD  RECORDS
Nathaniel  Bayley were appointed as  a building  committee,      and to
place them  in funds  the  treasurer  was  authorized  to  sell   at  the
best  advantage the 6 per cent  United States  bonds  owned by the
town.
The Revolutionary War was long past,    but there had never been
real  peace,      and we were then fast  approaching what is  now called
the  War of  1812,   but it  had already  begun in  1807.     American
sailors   and  fishermen  were being  seized  on the  sea  and  impressed
into  foreign  service,     and  fears  were  entertained  of  coast  disturb-
ances,        and  a  special  town  meeting  was  called  for  August  11  to
make  arrangements  for  " minute  men,"  and  the  meeting  " Voted
that  should  a quota be called  for  by order  of  the  Commonwealth
to  pay a bounty of $5 when mustered in and also a sum equal  to
$1  a day with  that  paid by the  Commonwealth for men while  in
the service."
The  call   came  and  we  now  get  an  idea  of  Weymouth  as  a
military  town in  the early  part of the  last  century.         There was  a
battery of light artillery,   a company of horse and two companies of
infantry,    and following is  the draft made on those companies :
Captain  Thayer's  company     one  sergeant,    one drummer,      one
fifer  and six  privates.
Captain  Webb's  company     one  sergeant,     one  drummer,     one
fifer  and ten privates.
Captain  Shaw's  company     one  sergeant,      one  fifer   and   nine
privates.
Captain   Jones'         company -one   sergeant,       one  corporal,         one
trumpeter and nine rank and file .
The  bridge  question  was  up again  this   year,      and  Theopalus
Cushing  and others  were petitioners  to  the General  Court  for  the
two bridges.             A special meeting was held in September,    and Cotton
Tufts,        Eliphalet  Loud and  Elijah  Bates  were chosen  to appear at
the  General  Court  with  Weymouth  representatives   and  remon
strate.
 - 127 - 
Chapter  LI
The year  1808  was  a  comparatively  quiet  one  as  far  as  town
matters   went.                   At  the   annual   meeting   in   March  Nathaniel
Blanchard was elected town clerk;     Eliphalet  Loud,   Lifee Holbrook
and   Levi   Bates,       selectmen   and   assessors ;         Josiah   Humphrey,
treasurer ;              and  in  addition  to  the  other  list   of  officers   ten  men
were  elected  on  the  board  of  school  committee,      one  from  each
school  district  and two at  large.
At the  state election in April there were two parties in the field,
Republican  and  Federalist.         James  Sullivan,     the   Republican
candidate,       received  136 votes,     and David Cobb,    Federalist,     95.
Some may wonder why,   as  late as  1808 and still  later,    Weymouth
cast  so  small a vote,    and the answer may be found in the fact that
there was a property  qualification  for  voters  at that  time,     and  to
be voters  in  state and national  matters  one must have a personal
property giving at least  £5 a year  income,    or  real  estate  not  less
than £60 in value.
The year 1809 opened with a little increase in  the war excitement,
and as  there was an early draft for soldiers  it  was " voted to  make
the pay of  those who should be detailed  from their  companies  for
active  service  $15.     a month including  Commonwealth pay. "
Wharves,        landing  places   on  the  rivers,     and  herring  were  still
town property and disposed of in  open town meeting.
There are  also  some quite interesting  records  at this  time to  be
found  in  regard  to  sale  of  pews in the meeting-houses  of both  the
South  and North parishes,    as  there  was a small fraction  of  a pew
sold,     and one could hardly tell who his  pew neighbor  would be at
the next sale.
The collection of taxes was the leading  subject for 1810.    Money
was  scarce,      and  poor at  that.           The collection  of  the South  Parish
tax was bid off at 4 cents  on the dollar,    and the  North Parish  at
2 cents and 9 mills,     and later  in the meeting it  was voted that the
selectmen  at  their  discretion  might make good  any poor bills   the
collectors  might take.
"Voted to  raise  $800 for  school  purposes. "
"Voted  that  we  authorize  and  direct  the  school  committee  to
supply  Latin and Greek school  masters  to  teach  in  the Grammar
School,      also  to teach English Grammar.  "
It  is  evident  by the  records  of these  times  that the town looked
after  the  spiritual  welfare  of its  citizens,     or  at  least,      their  church
relationship,     as we find  the following record :
To Mr.  NATHANIEL  BLANCHARD,     Clerk of the  Town of  Weymouth.
SIR:  -We have joined  ourselves  to  the  Protestant  Episcopal  church at  St.
Andrews in  Scituate  and hereby express  our desire  to  be set  off  from the  First
Parish  in Weymouth to that end with our Polls  and Estates.
JAMES LOVELL,
WILLIAM  WILDE.
WEYMOUTH,     Feb.  22,     1811.
 - 128 - 
Chapter  LII
There  was  a  still  further  withdrawal from  the church  relations
of  Weymouth in  the  early  part  of  1811,      and  Cotton  Tufts  filed
with the town clerk a notice of his affiliation  with the " Protestant
Episcopal church St. Andrews of Scituate and adjoining town. "
At the  March meeting  Nathaniel  Blanchard  was  again  elected
as  town  clerk,    but  there  came an  entire  change in  the  board  of
selectmen  and  assessors,       and  John  Vinson,      Jr.,       Dea.          Ebenezer
Hunt and Samuel Webb were elected .
The  sum  of  $800  was  raised   and  appropriated  for   schools.
Roads  were repaired  by the  district  system,    and the  old  rate  for
labor  continued,   viz.:     $1  a day for men and $1.25  a day for  yoke
of oxen and cart.
In connection with the road business  it  was voted to repair  the
footbridge  across   Back  River,     and we would  here  state  that  this
" foot  bridge "  was  near  where  the  railroad  now crosses  the  river.
From  the  earliest   time  this  footbridge  was  the  only  means  the
people in the lower eastern part of the village had of getting across
without  coming  around  Commercial  Street.          With the  coming  of
the  Weymouth  Iron   Company  a  more  substantial  but  private
team-way was established,    but this  has long since been abandoned,
and up to date the people in that vicinity can get  to  the depot and
other  near-by places  only  by crossing  the railroad  in  violation  of
law,    or going around three-quarters  of a mile to get but a few rods.
From time to time efforts  have been made to remedy this difficulty,
but thus far they have failed  for various reasons.
At the May meeting it was voted to send but one representative
to  the General  Court,      and Christopher Webb was elected.
"Voted  to  lease  the  Rockweed privilege  for a  term of  ten years .
The lessee  to  pay one- third  in advance and balance in such periods
as  shall  be determined by the selectmen. "
"Voted that all  paupers in town whose expense to the town have
been more than 40 cents per week shall  be let  out at public vendue
to the lowest bidder,    to be maintained at the work house and the
bidder have  the use  of  the house  and  the  benefit  of  the paupers'
labor."
Among the sales  of pews in the North Meeting- House which are
recorded  this  year  there  is  the  sale  of  pew No.  72  to  Dr.  Noah
Fifield.               The deed  of  one-half  is  from Joseph  Nash,    Jr. ,      and the
price $75.              The other half was bought from Eben Hunt,    Jr.,  Betsy
Hunt,    Emma Nash and Jas.    F. Nash,   and the price was the same as
for the other half.
 - 129 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               607
At the town meeting,    Dec.  9,     1811,     " Voted not to sell  the hoop
poles on the Town's land. "
There  were  no  marked  events  in  1812  beyond  the  raising  of
soldiers  for  the war which was then on,    and it  was voted  to  pay a
bounty  of $5 for  those  who were  detached from  their  companies
for  military duty and $10 a month while in active service.
The events  of  1813  were a repetition  of other years.                Wharves
and landing  places  on the rivers,   herring  in  Back River,      and iron
ore  at  Great  Pond were still  sources  of  income to  the  town,   and
they were severally  assigned to committees for disposal.
The menu of  the workhouse was a subject of  debate  and was
referred  to  a committee which reported as follows :
"Breakfast  and  supper      milk or  milk  porridge with  good  rye
or   Indian  bread.         Dinner      soup  two  days  a  week,      if   suitable
meat can be obtained;      fish  and pork one day;     Indian pudding and
beef  one day;      the  other  three,     pork  and beef,    or either,     and all
inmates who are able to work shall be stinted by the master. "
There was but little  change in the several boards of town officers
for  the year  1814,    excepting  an addition  to  the school  committee
which was increased  to  eleven  members.         Collection  of  taxes  was
sold to the lowest bidder,    the South Parish going to Mathew Pratt
and  the  North  to Benjamin Dyer at  2 cents and 8 mills  on the
dollar.
At this  March meeting  the town voted to  build  a magazine  to
keep  the  town's  powder,    bullets  and military  equipments,     and a
committee,      consisting   of  Capt.      Nathaniel  Shaw,       Capt.          Joseph
Harding,     Maj .    Samuel Bayley,   Eliphalet Loud and Jacob  Richards,
was appointed to submit plans for the same,    and at a  later meeting
recommended a structure of brick and lime  with  stone  foundation
and outside  retaining wall,  the same to be ten feet in diameter and
twelve feet  elevation.
As far as we get in our research we find no evidence of this  build-
ing ever having been constructed,    but the writer recollects  full well
when  there  was  the  remnant  of  a wooden " powder  house"  on
Middle  Street,    and  if  it  were standing  to- day it  would  be  in  or
quite near the St.  Francis Xavier Cemetery.
A special  town  meeting was called  later  in  the year on petition
of  John  Dyer and others  to  make arrangements  for  the  payment
of soldiers.
There are  many interesting  legends  of the  Weymouth  soldiers
who were drafted  to  go to  Cohasset to  repel  foreign invasion,    and
we find  that  the town voted  to  pay the  men who were detached
from  their  companies  and  stationed  at  Cohasset  a  sum which,
added  to  the  State  pay,    should  be  $15  a month,    and  $1,200 was
raised  for  that purpose.

Chapter  LIII
At the  annual  meeting  in  March,       1816,       Nathaniel  Blanchard
was elected  town clerk,   John Vinson,    Samuel Webb and Nathaniel
Blanchard,        selectmen,     assessors   and  overseers  of  the  poor;      and
Josiah Humphrey,    treasurer.
Up to  this  time  Weymouth may have  paid  some  attention  to
fire  protection,    as  there  are here and there to be found one of  the
old  leather  fire  buckets  of which every  householder  was  supposed
to  have  one  or  more  hanging  handily  about his  house  or  shop.
We find in this year for  the first  time an election of special  officers
for  fire  purposes,    and  Maj.    John White and Starks  Whitten were
elected  " Fire  Wardens. "
At the meeting  in May it was " voted to raise $1,000  for  school-
ing,      and subsequently  there  was  added  to  it  the  proceeds  of  the
sale  of  alewives."
The  year  1817  was  without  marked  events  in  the  municipal
affairs  of  the town.
There was  a general  overturn  of  town officers  in  1818,       and evi-
dently the military department of the town had formed a " Trust,  "
as   Capt.          Joseph   Loud,      Capt.       Benjamin  Derby  and  Capt.        Levi
Bates were elected  as  selectmen,    assessors,    etc.,    and Maj .      Ebenezer
Hunt,         treasurer.
The  running  at  large  of  neat  cattle,     horses  and  swine  was  a
topic of discussion,    and it  was voted to prohibit the same.
By the following  report,    which is  recorded at this time,    it  would
seem  that  the  brick,      stone  and  lime  magazine  which  was  voted
three  years   previous  was  never  built   according   to   the  original
vote:
We,     the  subscribers,    appointed a committee by the  Town of Weymouth for
the purpose of building  a magazine and procuring  a suitable  place to  erect  the
same,      have attended that  service  and beg leave to  submit as  follows :         Viz,      We
agree  with  Mr.  Thomas Webb for a place  to set  said building on his  land about
twenty rods westwards  of the town pound for  three dollars  and took a lease  of
the same in behalf of the town for  ninety-nine  years.           We also  agree with Mr.
Nathan  Pratt  to  furnish  material  and  complete  the  carpenter  work  of  said
building  together with  the  painting of the same for sixty- eight dollars and forty-
eight  cents.             Bill for hinges,     bolts,    etc.,    $4.54,    locks  $3,    making the whole cost
$79.02.
SAMUEL  WEBB,
LEVI  BATES,
NATHANIEL  BLANCHARD,
Committee.
There was a  little  more doing in 1819 than in the previous year.
Nathaniel   Blanchard   was   elected   town   clerk;        Levi   Bates,
 - 131 - 
OLD  RECORDS                               609
Ebenezer   Humphrey  and   Capt.         Noah  Torrey,        selectmen   and
assessors .
The school  question came in for a good share of attention,     and it
was  voted  that  each  school  district  should  have  the  liberty   to
declare the school age and other qualifications for that district .
District  No.  4 filed  a complaint that  it  was  not getting  a fair
proportion of the school money as it  had one hundred and sixty- nine
scholars  of  school  age,     four  to  sixteen,     and  in  addition  had  the
children  from  the  poorhouse,    and it  was voted  to  allow  them $30
extra.
The town was nearly two hundred years old,    and by the  records
of  this meeting it would seem that it  never had a barn or owned a
cow,      and it  was voted  that in view of the fact  that the town had
sufficient  land  on which  to  pasture  a cow,     and that  hay could be
bought cheap in its season,   the town build  a barn and keep a cow,
and John  Bates  was  appointed  to  submit  plan and probable  cost
of a suitable  barn at the meeting in May.
At the May meeting the town economized by voting not to send
a representative to the General Court.            We would here note that in
those days the cities  and towns paid for  their  own representative.
At this  meeting  John  Bates  submitted  his  specifications  for  a
town barn,     and its  building was sold at vendue and went to  Capt.
Benjamin Dyer for $114.
 - 132 - 
Chapter  LIV
For the year  1820 the same town clerk,     selectmen,    assessors  and
treasurer  were elected  as in the previous one.
Schools were quite a subject of discussion at the March meeting,
and " Capt.       Levi  Bates,     Richard Burrell,  John Vinson and the two
ministers  in town were elected  School Committee. "
"Voted that  each school district  have liberty  to  fix  the  age  for
scholars  for the winter  term. "
The  state  election was  still  held  in  April,    and at  this  meeting
245 votes were cast for Governor.
At the meeting in  May it  was voted  to  raise  $1,600  for  support
of  the poor and other town  charges.
By an  act  of  the  Legislature  the  " Hingham & Quincy  Bridge
and  Turnpike  Co."   had  been  incorporated,     and  the  bridges  and
turnpike were opened for  travel,   but the company discovered  that
one  clause  in  the  franchise  was  a  heavy  burden,     and  were  now
petitioning  to  have it  removed;     i.e. ,   the company were  to  pay a
bounty on all  vessels  passing  up or down Weymouth Fore  River
or  Back River.          A special  town meeting was called for August 21
to  remonstrate  against  granting  the petition for  its  removal,     and
at  this  meeting  the  Weymouth  representatives   were  instructed
to  use all  lawful means to keep the bounty in force,   and the follow-
ing resolution was passed :
" Whereas  we  consider  the  Town  of  Weymouth  has  suffered
great  injury  and  inconvenience by the construction of the bridges
over  Rivers  in  said Town notwithstanding the small bounty which
is  allowed  to  loaded  vessels  for  passing  said bridges  and  whereas
the proprietors  of said  bridges  have petitioned  the  General  Court
to  repeal  that part of the Act of  Incorporation which obliges  them .
to pay the Indemnification.          Therefore,   '  Voted that a committee of
three be appointed  to  assist  the  Representatives  in  their  work at
the General Court.  '"
The  March  meeting  for   1821   had  some  particular   features,
notably  so  when the  collection  of  taxes  was  sold  at  vendue,      and
spirited  bidding brought the rate from 3 cents on the dollar down
to 9 mills.
The meeting,      however,     made it  a little   easier  for  the  tax  col-
lector by voting " that he need not pay interest on his  bond given
to  the  town, "  and still  later  by instructing  the  treasurer  to  make
good to him a poor $5 bill  he had taken in collecting  taxes.
The school  committee was increased  to  eight,    and an addition,
as before,     of the " two ministers in town. "
The  meeting  also  voted  that  the  schoolmasters  employed  by
the committee shall  teach twenty- six days in each month.
 - 133 -

It  also  voted  that  there  be  an  enrollment  of  the  families   in
town and number of pupils  between the ages  of four and eighteen
years of age.

Some  people  who are  now living  may ask  how about  the  9th
and 10th district,    and we would say that they did not then exist,
but were made later from those already mentioned.
There may be others who are  curious  to  know where these dis-
tricts  were,       and we explain  that  District  Nos.   1  and  2  are  now
Ward 1 ;     No. 3 is Ward 2;     No. 4 is  Ward 3;    Nos.   5 and 6 are Ward
4;    and Nos.     7 and 8 are Ward 5.
The year  1822 was without special  features of interest.      A com-
mittee  was  appointed  to  mark  more  definitely   the  boundaries
between  Weymouth  and  adjoining   towns  by  setting   up  stone
markers.
The  rockweed  on  our  beaches  was  still   considered  a  valuable
asset,     and  the  treasurer  was  authorized  to  lease  it  for  another
term of  ten years.
The fishery  was  also  a  factor,      and a  special  town meeting  was
called  in August to  consider a  proposal  of  one " Samuel  Hubbard
Esq. "  to  purchase  the  same,    and when the question  of  sale  came
up there was a unanimous  No,   and at the  November meeting  the
representative was instructed to use his influence for more strenuous
laws protecting Weymouth fisheries.
The foregoing  records have taken our readers  through  two hun-
dred years of the most important part of Weymouth history.           We
have seen the beginning and ending of the first  attempt at a settle-
ment on our shores ;        we have seen this  little  failure  followed  by  a
more  substantial  coming;      we have  seen  a permanent  settlement
made,        treaties  with  the  " Red Men,"  reclaiming  of  a  wilderness,
wars with the natives,    wars with the  mother country,  the building
up of town,     state  and nation,   and the  establishment  of  churches
and schools.

ANCIENT  RECORDS
The following  is  a record  kept by Col.  Asa White of  this  town,
father  to  Deacon Abiel,     and grandfather to  the  late  Enos White,
Esq. ,       which  I  have been  permitted  to  copy.              It  is   of  special  in-
terest,       as,      having  been written  by an actor  in  the  stirring  scenes
that  tried  men's  souls, "   and  one  who  was  a  fellow  townsman,
it  is  one of  those  documents  that  are  well  worth  preserving.            It
is   of  special  interest  to  the  public  because  it  opens  the  curtain
and lets  us  into  the  private  meetings  of patriots who initiated  the
movement which  resulted  in  our  national  independence.            It  tells
us  the  names  of  those  to  whom the  town  entrusted  this  difficult
and important duty.           The names of  the committee of correspond-
ence and selectmen of our town are familiar  to  a large  part  of  our
present  citizens,      and  they  have  but  to  be  named  to  command
instant  attention  and  respect;        but  where  are  their  descendants?
It  is   a  curious  study  to  follow  that  question.            Of  Cotton Tufts,
whose name is  common property  and  needs  no prefix,      there  is  no
one  to  call   him  ancestor.                Gen.  Solomon  Lovell  has  no  one  to
bear  his  name.                Of  Col.   Asa  White's  descendants  there  are  but
two  in  Weymouth  to  recall  his  name.             Maj.         John Vining  leaves
no  male  posterity,    and,    as  far  as  the  writer  is  aware,       the  Colsons
have  none;      and it  remains  for  the  families  of  Major Humphrey,
Colonel   White  and  Mr.  Kingman  (if   the  latter  can  claim  the
privilege)    to  bear the honors descending from that committee.
We may also  be  permitted  to  infer  that  the  Weymouth  com-
mittee  was  no insignificant  one,   and that  the combination  of  the
towns  mentioned  grew upon its  suggestion,   and that  the meetings
in  the old Arnold tavern were guided and inspired to a great extent
by its  wise counsels.

MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
By JOHN  CHISHOLM  FRASER,     A.M.,     M.D.
For  the  earlier  material  facts  in this  chapter,    the writer  is  in-
debted to  the compilation by Francis Flint Forsaith,    M.D.,     late  of
Weymouth,    deceased,   and published in the history  of the  town by
Gilbert  Nash in  1885.    In preparing  the  medical  history  of any
old  community from its  settlement there  are several difficulties  in-
evitably  encountered.        First,     as  in this  instance,    the practice  of
medicine was not  on so  recognized  a basis as  at  the present time,
and secondly,    there  were no medical schools  or  universities  in  the
county,    each doctor being  isolated and independent,   while the fact
that there was no authorized power for conferring degrees gave any
man,     no matter how incompetent,   the right to assume the title  of
" doctor.  "    Again,  occasionally the clerical and medical professions
were  united  in  the same  individual,     and  as  that  individual  was
usually  recognized  in  the  community as  a minister  rather  than  a
doctor,     his  name would not  appear  as  a physician.      Still,    with  the
exception  of   Plymouth,     Wessagusset  claims   priority,       as  to   the
presence of a physician,    over any place in New England.
In  April,           1622,        Thomas  Weston's  company  of  "Merchant  ad-
venturees "  came from England under the command of his  brother-
in- law,       Richard Green.         Among these courageous  men was a Mr.
Salisbury,       a  surgeon,     who,      as  far  as  can be ascertained,     was  the
first   representative  of  the  medical  profession  in  Weymouth.         In
the  " Annals "   of  Dr.  Samuel  Fuller  of  Plymouth,    who wrote  to
Governor  Bradford June 28,    1630,    we find  an interesting  item
that  at  the  request  of  Mr.  Warham he " had been  to  Mattapan
and let  some twenty of these people blood,"  proving  satisfactorily
to  one historian  that the people of  Plymouth did not lack medical
attention from their  very arrival  in  America.         History gives us  no
information  concerning  Dr.  Salisbury's  success  in  his  profession,
or what became of  him.
NICHOLAS  BYRAM
Dr.  Byram was the  son  of  an  English  gentleman who came to
Weymouth in 1638,    and remained until  1662,   when he removed  to
Bridgewater,        Mass.        According  to  family  tradition  Dr.  Byram's
father,       a  native  of  Kent,     removed  to   Ireland   about  the  time
Nicholas  was  born.            His father sent him to  England when sixteen
years  of  age  to  visit  friends,     in  charge of  a supposed  friend,     who
robbed him of his  money,    and sent him to the West Indies,     where
 - 137 - 
MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH             615
he was sold  to  service  to  pay for  his  passage.           When his  term  of
service expired he came to  Weymouth.
He married  Susannah,     daughter  of  Abraham Shaw of  Dedham,
with  issue,       eight  children,    six  of  whom were born in  Weymouth,
viz.:
I.      Nicholas.
II.           Abigal,    who married Thomas Whitman.
III .              Deliverance,   who married John Porter.
IV.              Experience,    who married John Willis .
V.    Susannah,    who married Samuel Edson.
VI.           Mary,    who married Samuel Leach.
Dr.  Byram died in 1727.
THOMAS  THACHER
The Rev.  Thomas Thacher was born  May 1,     1620,    son  of  Rev.
Peter  Thacher,     rector  of   St.   Edmunds,      Salisbury,     County Wilts,
England.           He came to this country with his uncle Anthony in  the
ship " James "  from Southampton,    arriving in Boston June 4,     1635,
Hewas taken to  Ipswich  by his  uncle and placed in charge of  the
Rev.  Charles  Chauncy of Scituate,   who prepared him for  his  pro-
fession " with great diligence, "  as it  is  said.          He also instructed him
in  the  science  of  medicine,   as  he himself  was  celebrated  for  his
knowledge and success as  a medical practitioner as well as a divine .
Mr.  Thacher  became  a great  success  as  a  physician,     and  was
noted for his knowledge in other directions than that of a physician
and divine,     for  Mather says that he " composed a Hebrew Lexicon,
so  compressed  that within one sheet  of paper he had given  every
considerable word in the language. "
He came to  Weymouth in  January,      1645,      and had charge  of  a
church.            He remained  in  Weymouth  for  twenty  years,       removed
to  Boston  and joined  the  First  Church there Aug. 4,       1667.     On
Feb.  16,      1670,   he was installed  as  pastor over what is  now the Old
South  Church,     and  is  supposed  to  have  been  the  first   minister
ordained in America.         It is  also said he was the author of the first
medical  work  ever  published  in America,      a  small  tract  entitled
"A Brief  Guide  to  the  Common  People,    in  the  Small- pox  and
Measles, "  first  published in  Boston in  1677,     and a second  edition
in  1702.   Cotton Mather informs us that " having preached for  my
father,    he visited a sick person after going out of the church,   whereby
he got some harm,   which turned into a fever of which he died Oct.
15,      1678,     aged fifty- eight years.  "

BENJAMIN RICHARDS

treatment   of   " throat   distempers "    and  "bloody   flux, "   which
raged in  the years  1746 to  1749.

Carter.

LAZARUS  ANDREWS  BEALE
There  is   considerable  mix-up  among  writers  in  re  Dr.  Beale's
birth and subsequent life.       He is  reported to have lived in Newton,
and  other  places,     and  to  have  sustained  a " good  character  as  a
citizen  and  physician,"   and  resided  in  the  North  Parish,      Wey-
mouth.               Whatever  difference  of  opinion  regarding  his  life   and
places  of  residence  existed,    we know by  the  Town Record  that
he married,     Oct.  29,    1776,    Bethiah  Lewis,    who died Aug.  5,     1809,
aged forty- nine years,    leaving him with four children:
I.       Lydia,     born in Weymouth June 10,   1782.
II.              Elizabeth,    born in Weymouth July 11,     1785.
III .              Lewis,      born in Weymouth Oct. 13,    1793.
IV.              Elias,       born in Weymouth Nov. 13,    1796.
In the opinion of the late  Solomon J.  Beale,    Esq.,    he  removed
to  Weymouth from  Cohasset,    and the Town Records  indicate  his
death as  occurring Nov. 23,      1822.
COTTON TUFTS,      A.M.,       M.D.,       M.M.S. ,         A.A.S.
Dr.  Tufts  was  born  in  Medford,       Mass. ,     May 31,      1731,       son  of
Dr.  Simon Tufts.           His family was one of the first  who settled  in
that  town and held  many prominent  positions.        His  great-grand-
father  was  its   representative  at  the  General   Court  about  1684.
and some others  were graduates  of  Harvard.       At the age of four-
teen  he  entered   Harvard  College,       graduated  in  1749,        and  took
his  second  degree  in  1752.    He  then  taught  school  for  a time,
after  which  he began  the  study  of  medicine  under  the  direction
of his  brother,      Dr.  Simon Tufts,    Jr. ,     then practicing  in his  native
town.              After  his  graduation  he  settled  in  Weymouth  and  lived
near  the  North  Weymouth depot,    not far  from  the present  resi-
dence  of  the  family  of  the  late Judge James  Humphrey.           As  a
 - 141 - 
MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH             619
physician  he  was  described  as  " courteous,    sympathetic,     faithful,
considerate  and  kind. "     He was  always  considerate  of  his  pro-
fessional  brethren,   especially of the younger members,     and we are
told  he " labored  for  the spiritual  as  well  as  the  temporal good of
his  patients,  "   and  was a  deacon  for  more than forty  years  of  the
Old North Church.
He was one of the original members of the Massachusetts Medical
Society,      and was its  president from  1787  to  1793.    He held many
positions  in civil  life,   being one of the trustees  of  Derby Academy,
Hingham;      president  of  a  society  for  moral  reform;      an  honored
member of  the  American Academy of Arts  and Sciences;       a state
senator  for  many years,   and a member of the convention for adopt-
ing  the constitution of the United States.           He was a gentleman of
culture  and  refinement,     and  left  his  impress  on  the  community
in which he lived.     His funeral  sermon was preached by his  pastor,
Rev.   Jacob   Norton,      who  said   in   part:             " He  was  a  man  of
general  erudition  and attainments of  considerable eminence.        His
researches   were  various   and  extended,        judicious   and  accurate.
He was an ardent Federalist,   and happy had it  been for our country
in times past had its  citizens  in general been  Federalists,    or,    to use
a  more  appropriate  term,      Federal   Republicans,    of  this   descrip-
tion."
He was married twice,   first,    on Dec.  2,    1755,    to Lucy Quincy of
Braintree  with  issue,    Cotton,    born  in  Weymouth  Aug.  4,     1758.
Second,      to  Mrs.  Susanna Warner of Gloucester on Oct.  22,     1789.
He died Dec. 8,   1815,   in his eighty-fifth year.
JAMES  TORREY
Dr.  Torrey was born in Ashford,    Conn. ,    in 1756,    son  of  James
and  Sarah  (Nash)   Torrey,     and was  the  great-grandson  of  Capt.
William Torrey,    who settled in Weymouth in  1640,   a distinguished
citizen,     and " clerk of the deputies "  for  many years.           We are  told
that  his  first  occupation  was  that  of  tanning  hides,     and  that  he
studied  medicine  afterwards.            We are  not  told  when  he  studied
medicine,     but he began its  practice  in  Lebanon,    Conn. ,    and later
removed  to  Nantucket,    from which place  he came to  South Wey-
mouth  in  the  year  1783,      and settled  in  a house at  the corner  of
Pleasant  and  Union  streets .                He served  for  a  short  time  as  sur-
geon's  mate in the War of the Revolution,   and at one time as  sur-
geon of  the  Second Regiment,    First  Brigade,     First  Division,     Mas-
sachusetts   Militia,      commission  dated  Sept.   3,      1800;         discharged
June 16,      1812.    He was  a  " seventh  son,"  and at that  time  was
supposed  to  possess  most extraordinary  powers in healing  " Kings
Evil, "   " Throat-ail "   and  other  indefinite  diseases.        We have  no
information  that  he himself  believed  in  this  mode of  treatment,
although  he  practiced  it  to  some  extent  in  his  earliest  years  of
practice.            He was the only physician in South Weymouth for more
than thirty years .

THOMAS VINSON
Dr.  Vinson  was  born  in  Weymouth June  8,     1756,     son  of  John
and  Sarah  ( Colson)   Vinson,   and died Jan.  12,     1841,   at  the age of
eighty- five years.         His forbears were prominent people in the town
who came from London in the latter half of the seventeenth century.
Very few  facts  can  be  ascertained  in  regard  to  him,     but it  is  re-
corded that he lived in South Weymouth and was successor  to  Dr.
Torrey and lived  on  Pleasant Street on the spot now occupied by
the house built  by Mr.  Edward  Rosenfeld  and opposite the house
occupied  by  the  late  Dr.  Greeley.          It  is  recorded  that  he  was  a
colonel  in  the Revolutionary Army,    and was a  " mathematician of
no mean ability,    and made the calculations for almanacs for several
years.   "     He was also said " to have been a learned man and acquired
a large  practice. "
He married,      Jan.   27,       1782,      Hannah,     daughter  of  Samuel  and
Elizabeth  (Shaw)   Holbrook,     with issue:
I.      Warren,     born in Weymouth Oct. 5,    1782.
II .             Sussanna,   born in Weymouth Jan. 1,     1784.
III.     Betsey,  born in Weymouth Dec. 25,   1785.
IV.          Thomas Warren,    born in Weymouth Nov. 28,    1788.
JAMES  LOVELL
Dr.  Lovell was born Jan.  1,    1768,    son of General Solomon Lovell
and Hannah  (Pittey)   Lovell,      and  a descendant  of  Robert  Lovell,
who came to  Weymouth in  1635 with Rev. Joseph Hull.          He lived
on Neck Street,     near the junction of that street  with Green Street,
North Weymouth,   in the house where he was born  and died.        He
" inherited his  father's  homestead  and  one  of  the  finest  properties
of that time in the town."   He entered  Harvard College,   but never
completed  the  course.          He studied  medicine  with  Dr.  Thaxter  of
 - 143 - 
MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH             621
Hingham,    but never practiced  much,   as he was wealthy.             He occu-
pied himself in farming and in town affairs.
He married,       Nov.  8,     1798,      Widow Winch,    whose maiden  name
was Priscilla  Ford.         They had no children.
He died April 8,    1820,    and the body is in the family tomb in the
Old North  Cemetery.
NOAH  FIFIELD
Dr.  Fifield  was born July  10,      1783,     at East  Kingston,     N.  Η.  ,
son  of  Ebenezer  and Mary (Sanborn)    Fifield.         He was descended
from  English  stock  (Fyfields,      Oxfordshire).     He began  the  study
of  medicine  with  his  uncle,        Dr.  Wm.      Sanborn  of  Portland,    then
Falmouth,       and  later  with  the  famous  Dr.  Nathan  McKinstry,       a
Scotch  surgeon  of  Newbury,      Vt. ,       and  later,      1804,      attended  the
Harvard  medical  lectures  at  Boston,      a course  of  two  years,       after
which  he practiced  for  a short  time in  Maine.           While  attending
the medical lectures  at  Boston he formed the  acquaintance of Dr.
Cotton  Tufts,    who induced  him  to  come  to  Weymouth in  1806.
After  Dr.  Tufts'    death,    in  1815,     he became  the  most  prominent
and  influential  physician  of  the  South  Shore.          One  of  his  con-
temporaries,       Dr.  Howe,    says of him:   "As a citizen and a neighbor
it  is  believed  that he sustained  a character above reproach.            As a
physician he brought to the aid of his patients a sound and vigorous
mind,      well  stored  with  professional  knowledge  and an aptness  in
the  investigation  of disease  which  rendered  his  opinions  of  great
value  to  the  sick  and  of  great  weight  with  the  members  of  the
profession .   "      He  was  a  man  of  dignified   bearing  and  pleasing
address.              In  addition  to  eminence in his  profession,     he  was  fore-
most  in  all  public  affairs  for  the  betterment  of  the  community,
and  was  the  practical  founder  of  the  Weymouth  Academy.             In
1814 he purchased the homestead on the corner of  Front and  Elliot
streets,         and  here   brought  his   wife   Hannah  Cranch   Bond  of
Dorchester.             Not only was he  a success  as  a physician,      but  also
as  a business  man,   believing  that his  exertions  were  worthy  of  a
just  and  honest  remuneration.         He was  admitted  to  the  Massa-
chusetts  Medical Society in  1807,    and was for several  years  one of
its  councillors.        The Fifield  Memorial  Room at the  Boston  Medi-
cal  Library  has  many professional  relics  of  the  three  Drs .         Fifield
as well  as  of Dr.  Cotton Tufts.          Other historical  material is  in the
Fifield  collection,   Tufts Library,     Weymouth.
He married,     July 30,    1820,      Hannah Cranch Bond of  Dorchester,
with issue:
I.      George Fordyce,    born April,     1822;    died Nov. 15,    1846.
II .             Mary Sanborn,    born  March 27,    1824;      died Aug. 17,    1845.
III .             William C.  B.,    born Aug. 27,   1828;    died in  Dorchester,    1896.
He died Oct.  21 ,    1867,     and was buried in  the family lot  in  the
Village  Cemetery,   Weymouth.

APPLETON  HOWE,        A.B.
Dr.  Howe was  born  Nov.  26,     1792,     in  the  town of  Hopkinton,
Mass.   ,       the  son  of  Rev.  Nathaniel  and  Olive  Howe of  that town.
He was  prepared  for  college  at  Phillips  Academy,     Andover,       and
entered  Harvard College in  1811,    graduating from that  institution
Dr. AppletonHowe
in   1815,     after  which he studied  medicine at  the  Harvard  Medical
School,        under  the  supervision  of  Dr.  John  C.  Warren,     receiving
his diploma in 1819.    That same year he came to South Weymouth,
being invited  by a committee of twelve men of that place to settle
with  them  " in   the  practice  of  physic  and  surgery, "   where  he
practiced  his  profession  for  fifty  years.         He was  a  member of  the
 - 145 - 
MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH              623
Massachusetts  Medical  Society,     and  at  one time president  of  the
Norfolk  District  Medical Society.        He held many prominent posi-
tions  in  military  life.          He was  surgeon  of  the  Second  Regiment,
First   Brigade,        Second   Division,        of   the   Massachusetts   Militia ;
also  adjutant  and colonel  of  the  same.         He was brigadier  of  the
First  Brigade,     and afterwards  major-general of the  First  Division
of Massachusetts  Militia.       He was  also  a  member of  the Ancient
and  Honorable  Artillery   Company,       and  at  one  time  its   com-
mander.            In 1841-43  he  served  as  state  senator,     Norfolk  County.
He served  on the school  board for  many years,    was  its  chairman
for  several,       and on retirement  received  a vote  of  thanks from  the
town.        He was  a sincere  anti-slavery  man,    and  it  is  related  of
him  that  he refused  to  order  the  officers  of the  First  Division  of
Militia,      when  he was its  commander,    to  attend  the  funeral  of  an
officer   from   Massachusetts  who  died   fighting   in  the  Mexican
War.              His  reason  was  that  he  considered  the  object  of  that  war
to  be the extension  of slavery.        It was said  of  him that he was a
man of great  mental and physical power,     and was able  to  perform
work that few members of  the medical  profession were able  to do.
He had one  sensible  characteristic,    that  of  taking  things  easily,
which allowed him to rest when not in active work,    and yet nothing
was left  undone.       Before  the study of  medicine he taught  school
in many places,    the  " Iron  works  district,  "   Braintree,      being  one,
where  he  boarded  with  Col.   Minot  Thayer,       by  whom in  later
years he was introduced to the citizens  of South Weymouth.
He was married twice,   first  on Dec. 12,   1821,    to Harriet,    daughter
of  Eliphalet  and  Anna  Loud,     born  in  Weymouth  Feb.  8,        1795,
and died  Nov.  16,     1848 ;     second,     to  Eliza,    daughter of  Joseph  and
Thankful  (Bates)   Loud  of  North Weymouth,    born  May 9,        1812,
with issue:
I.      Hattie,   born Dec. 18,   1852.
II .          Appleton L.,   born Feb. 20,   1854;    died Nov. 23,    1856.
Dr.  Howe died  in his  residence,     Columbia  Street,     South  Wey-
mouth,        Oct.  10,     1870,     and was  buried  in  the  family  lot  in  the
Highland Cemetery.
JACOB  RICHARDS,    A.B.
Dr.  Richards was born in Weymouth June 24,    1795,   son of Jacob
and  Lydia  ( Colson)    Richards.          His  early  education  was obtained
in  the Weymouth public  schools.        He entered  Brown  University
in 1820,     and graduated from that institution four years later.        While
in college,    and for some time after  his  graduation,    he taught  school
in the winter months.        He then began the study of medicine with
Dr.  John  C.   Warren  of  Boston,    receiving  a diploma.           He began
the practice of medicine in  Hanover,      Mass.,   about the year  1833.
From  there  he  came to  Weymouth in  1856,     remaining  one year,
then removed to  East Braintree,    where he lived and died.

DAVID  TORREY,   A.B.
Dr.  Torrey  was  born in  Weymouth June 29,     1793,    son  of  Dea.
Samuel  and  Dolly  (Blanchard)   Torrey.        His  preparatory  educa-

Brown  University  in  1819.    It  is  not  recorded  when he  studied
medicine,      but he practiced in  Holbrook and Hanover,    and came to
South Weymouth in  1840,    where he  remained for  fifteen  years  and
then removed to Joliet,   Ill. ,    where he died Aug. 14,   1870.

TIMOTHY GORDON,     A.M.
Dr.  Gordon was born at  Newbury,    Mass. ,    March 10,      1795.    It
is   supposed  he was  prepared  for  college  at  Exeter,    N.  H.    He re-
ceived  his  A.  M. degree from Amherst in  1868,     and graduated  in
medicine  from  Bowdoin  in  1825.    He came to  North Weymouth
in  the same year  and lived  for  twelve years  in  a house at the foot
of King Oak Hill,    lately  occupied by the children of the late Henry
A.  Nash,    Esq. ,    and then removed to  Plymouth,    where he remained
until  his  death,    Nov. 5,   1877.    He was a man of  firm  convictions,
always holding to his opinions when he considered he was in the right.
He  married,         May  12,      1825,       Jane  Binney  Jones  of  Hingham,
daughter of Solomon Jones,    with issue :
I.       Solomon J.,    born in  Weymouth Sept.  24,     1826.
II.           Timothy,    born in Weymouth April 16,    1836;    died April,    1836.
JOSEPH  DOW
Dr.  Dow came to Weymouth in  1836,    remained but a short  time
and boarded with Capt.    Harvey Cushing,   North Weymouth.          Little
is  known of his  antecedents.            What practice he had,   he sold  to Dr.
Learned and removed to  Philadelphia,    where he died.
He married  the  widow of  Mr.  Robert  Bicknell.         They had  no
children.

CHARLES  COFFERAN
Dr.  Cofferan was born in Thomaston,    Me. ,    about the year  1817 .
He studied medicine with Dr. Jackson of Boston,    and later  gradu-
ated from  the Harvard  Medical School.      He came to  South Wey-
mouth in  1845,    where he remained for about five years,    then return-
ing to his native town.         He remained there for a time,    after which
he went to Riverside,     Cal. ,    where he died in 1879.    Little is  known
about him or his family.
He was married and had two children,    a boy and a girl,     born in
Weymouth.
EBENEZER  TURELL  LEARNED
Dr.  Learned  was  born  in  Gardner,       Mass. ,    July  19,     1812.    He
came to  North Weymouth in  1836 and bought out the practice  of
Dr.  Dow.            He had a common school education and received private
instruction  in  advance  studies.          His  medical  degree  was  received
in   1836.     He studied  at  both  Harvard  Medical  School  and  the
medical  department  of  Dartmouth College.         He was a member of
the  Massachusetts  Medical  Society,    a  councillor  for  some  years,
and  for  two years  was  president  of  the  Bristol  South  District  So-
ciety.             He remained in North Weymouth for ten years,    and in  1846
removed to  Fall River,   where he died.
He married  Mary Matilda  White of  Ashburnham,     Mass. ,       May
14,     1835,      with issue:

GEORGE  FORDYCE  FIFIELD,     A.B.
Dr.  Fifield  was born in  Weymouth April 18,    1822,   eldest  son  of
Dr.  Noah and Hannah Fifield.       He attended the public schools  of
Weymouth after which he entered  Harvard College and graduated
from  there  in  1841.    He then  commenced the  study  of  medicine
and practiced  in  the  State  of  Maine,    where he gave promise of  a
useful  and successful  career,    but suddenly developed  an incurable
disease  from which he died  at  his  old  home in  Weymouth,      Nov.
15,   1846,    and is buried in the family lot in the village cemetery.

DANIEL  LEWIS  GIBBONS
Dr.  Gibbons was born in Boston Jan.  29,    1824.    Little  is  known
of  his  parentage.       He was  educated  in  the  Boston  schools  and
graduated in  medicine from Harvard in  1847,    and became a mem-
ber  of  the  Massachusetts  Medical Society  in  1848.    He practiced
for  a few months in Wrentham and came to  North Weymouth the
year  of  his  graduation.         He  remained  there  five  years,      and  then
removed to  New Orleans,    where he died Dec. 3,     1865.

JOSIAH  BALL
Dr.  Ball was born in  Milford,    Mass.,  in 1828.   He took a course
of study at Holliston Academy,    and graduated in  medicine at  Har-
vard  Medical School.          He located  in  Weymouth in  1847,    and be-
sides  practicing his  profession he engaged in the drug business,    his

was a member of the school board for  two years.
He married,     in  1846,     Sarah Taylor of  Mattapoisett,     Mass. ,    with

IRA  H.   PERRY,     A.B.
Dr.  Perry was born in  Natick,    Mass. ,     March 23,    1819.    He was
educated  at  Wesleyan University,    Middletown,     Conn. ,    and gradu-
ated  in  1842.    In 1845 he received  the degree  of  M.D.,       Berkshire
Medical  College,     Pittsfield,    Mass.         He practiced  in West Medway
and  Weymouth from  1845  to  1856.    The  next  year  he  went  to
Minnesota,      and with a few others founded the town of Zumbrota.
He was  assistant  surgeon in  the  United  States  army  in  Virginia
and  Washington  from  1862  to   1863;       assistant   surgeon,         Ninth
Regiment,       United  States  Colored  Troops,   from  1863  to  1866;       and
was  surgeon,     with rank of  brevet  major,    United States Volunteers,
in 1866 and 1867.
He married,       April 26,   1849,    Joanna Bullard of Wayland,      Mass.  ,

HENRY E.   WESTON,       A.Β.
Dr.  Weston was born in  Weymouth June 21,    1817.    He was  a
graduate  of  Yale  College  in  1839,     and  received  his  diploma  in
medicine from  Harvard.         He spent  a few years in medical  studies
in  Paris  and returned  to  Weymouth in  1847.    He resided  in  the
beautiful  old  homestead on Washington Street which  his  relatives
still   possess .                 In  1859 he joined  members  of  his  family  then  re-
siding in  Italy,   and returned to Weymouth in 1861.   He practiced
in  Weymouth  for  several  years,      and  also  for  a time  in  Boston.
His practice in Weymouth was devoted,   in a great measure,     to the
poor who could  not afford  to pay for  the  services  of a physician.
He was ever  ready to  answer to  their  calls,    and many times  acted
as  nurse as well as physician.         Many years  ago  I  was  greatly  en-
tertained  by a woman who was his  patient when she was ten  years
old,      who related many of his  acts  of kindness  and devotion.         He
was an invalid  for  several years before his death,    but retained his
vigorous  intellect  to  the  end.        He was  a  good  classical   scholar
and much interested  in archaeological  and neurosismatic researches
which he studied  to  a considerable extent while in Italy.       He died
in the Weston home July 31,   1882.   He never married.
EPHRAIM  LEWIS  WARREN
Dr.  Warren  was  born  in  Lunenburg,    Mass. ,    in  1823,          received
his   preparatory  training  at  Phillips   Academy,      Andover,        Mass. ,
and  graduated  from  the  Berkshire  Medical  College  in  1849.    He
came  to  Weymouth  in  1850  and  entered  on  the  practice  of  his
profession.            In  October,     1861,    he entered  the  army  as   surgeon
in  the  Twenty- second   Regiment,       Massachusetts  Volunteers,      and
received  his   honorable  discharge  June  10,      1862.     In  December
of  the  same year  he  re-enlisted  in the  Fifth  Rhode  Island  Vol-
unteers,      and in  December  of  the  following  year  was  discharged
for  physical  disability.          He held  the  position  of  inspector  in  the
Sanitary  Commission,   with the rank of major.        He was a member
of  the  Weymouth school  board,     and  succeeded  Dr.  Ball  in  that
office.        After  leaving  the  army  he  returned  to  Weymouth,       pur-
chased  the  " Weymouth  Drug  Store, "   and after  practicing  medi-
cine  for a few years removed to  Medford,     Mass.
He married the widow of Dr. Ball,   with issue:
Anna A. ,    born Jan. 11,   1870.
WILLIAM  CRANCH  BOND  FIFIELD
Dr.  Fifield,       second  son  of  Dr.  Noah  Fifield,     was born in  Wey-
mouth Aug. 27,   1828.    He attended the schools of the town,   and at
an early age was sent  to  Phillips  Exeter Academy,   where he finished
his   academic  education.              He  returned   to   Weymouth  after   his
 - 150 - 
628                       MEDICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
brother's  death,  and began the study of medicine with his  father.
Shortly  after,        he entered  the  Harvard  Medical School  and gradu-
ated from that institution  in  1848.    He was then sent to complete
his   medical  education  in  the  hospitals  of  England  and  France,
spending  four  years  there.             He graduated from the  Royal  College
of   Surgeons,            England ;         was  house  officer   in  London  Hospital;
licentiate of the Royal Ophthalmic Hospital;     and a member of the
American  Medical  Society,     Paris.           On his  return  from Europe  he
located in Weymouth and practiced for a few years with his father,
and then removed to  Harrison  Square,     Dorchester,   in  1861,   where
he  remained  until  his  death  in  1896.     He was  a  member of  the
Obstetric   Society,        an   honorary  member  of   the   Improvement
Society,            Boston,     and  surgeon  on  the  staff   of  the  Boston  City
Hospital,       which  position  he  held  for  eighteen  years  with  great
honor  to  himself  and the institution,    and was consulting  surgeon
at the  time  of  his  death.              He became a fellow  of  the  Massachu-
setts  Medical  Society  in  1858,       and was  at  one  time  president  of
the  Norfolk  Medical  Society.         It  was  my privilege  to  know  Dr.
Fifield  in  the  height  of  his   success,      and  can  recall   in  grateful
memory many acts  of  kindness  and assistance  at his  hands.           He
was ever ready to advise the younger members of the profession in
difficult  cases,    and seemed to  take great  pleasure in imparting  his
knowledge on such occasions.          He had a rare  personality,     of large
proportions,        handsome  face,      and  a low,       melodious  voice,      which
drew  the  attention  of  everybody.       He had  remarkable  skill   in
diagnosis,         and  noted  deftness  in  operation;       and  besides  all   that
had a marvellous  memory in  other  matters  than that  of his  pro-
fession .             Many years  ago,   while  riding  with him on some of  the
principal  streets  of  Weymouth,      I  was  much  impressed  by  that
fact  in hearing him relate  the  history  of the different  old  houses
and  the  people  who occupied  them  when  they  were  first   built,
their  notable characteristics,    and their manner of living.          He was
indeed a delightful  entertainer.
He married,   May 13,     1856,     Emily A.,   daughter of Thomas B.  and
Emily (Vining)  Porter of Weymouth,    with issue :
I.      Mary Sanborn,     born  March 29,     1857;     married a Mr.  King,     now resid-
ing in Milton,    Mass.
II.          George F.,  born July 1,  1859;      died September,     1860.
III .              Charles B.,   born Sept. 5,  1861;  died March 4,   1877.
LEMUEL  FULLER

of  Dr.   Lemuel  Fuller  of  Attleboro,       Mass.           He had  a common
school   education  and  graduated  in  medicine  from  the  Vermont
Medical  College.      He practiced  for  a time at  Milton,      Mass. ,      and
removed  to  North Weymouth,    on  " receiving  a call  from  a  com-
mittee of the citizens of the village,   Jan.  9,      1853."
He  practiced   there  for   about  ten  years,      when  sickness   com

pelled  him to  relinquish  his  business,   and he died  in  Harvard  on

At  Concord,       Mass.,     he  married  Catherine  Pallisseuir   Barrett.
They had no children.
CHARLES  CARROLL TOWER,     A.B.
Dr.  Tower was  born in  Cohasset,      Mass. ,   Sept.  26,    1833.    After
a  preparatory  course  of  study under  private  instruction,       he  en-
tered   Harvard  University  in  1852  and  finished  in  1856.    In  the
same year he entered  the Harvard  Medical School  and  graduated
therefrom in  1859.    That same year he came to  South Weymouth,
where  he  practiced  his   profession  for  the  remainder  of  his   life,
with the exception of his service in the Civil War from September,
1862,        to  January,       1863,      as  assistant  surgeon,     U.  S.   A.,     on duty
at  Emory  Hospital,      near  Washington,     D.  C.    He  served  on  the
Weymouth  school  board  for  many years,      and  at  one  time  was
its  chairman.         He filled  the position  of Medical Examiner for  the
Fourth  District  of  Norfolk  County  from  the  passing  of  the  act
establishing  that office  until  his  death.           He was a  member of  the
following   medical   societies:       the   Massachusetts   Medical,       being
one  of  its   councillors ;        the  American  Medical  Association;       the
Massachusetts  Medico- Legal  Society,     acting  as  secretary  for  the
latter  for  many years,     and holding  the position at the time of  his
death;    also  a prominent and useful member of the South Norfolk
District  Medical Society.
Dr.  Tower  was greatly beloved  by his  patients  and the  towns-
people.           He always  continued  his  work faithfully,   was  ever  pro-
gressive for the best interests of his patients,    a careful diagnostician,
and  a good adviser.       He was a man of  much ability  and had  the
health of the community at heart.      He was good to the poor  and
unfortunate,     and ever  ready  to  help  them in  their  troubles.           His
professional  standing  was  of  the  best,      and  his  character  above
reproach.           He  died   May  29,       1893,       and  is   buried  in  Highland
Cemetery,    South Weymouth.
He married,     Nov. 29,    1860,      Clarissa  Lothrop Pratt of  Cohasset,
with issue:
I.       Carrie A.,   born July 18,    1862.
II .              Charlotte B.,  born Nov. 22,   1863.
III.     HelenM.,  bornAug. 8,  1868.
IV.            Ruth N.,   born Nov. 15,    1873.
JOSEPH  CORLIEU

six  years.           He came  to  South Weymouth from  Millbury,     Mass. ,
and returned there in  1862,    where he died  after  practicing  in  that
town for over twenty- five years.        He had two children :
I.     Joseph.

FRANCIS  FLINT  FORSAITH,      Α.Β.
Dr.   Forsaith  was  born  May 8,       1824,      in  Deering,     N.   H.    He
received  his  academic  education  in  the  schools  of  that  town  and
in  academies  of  Hancock  and  Francestown,      N.  H.    He entered
Dartmouth  College  in  1843,      and  received  his  degree  from  that
institution  in  1847.    He received  his  medical degree in  1852 from
Vermont  University.          He came to  Weymouth in  1861 ,      where  he
practiced  his  profession  for  about  thirty  years.         He died  March
11,       1894,      and is  buried in  the  Village  Cemetery,     Weymouth.             He
took  an  active  part  in  town  affairs   and  contributed  a chapter,
covering  an outline  of  the  medical  profession,     to  the  History  of
Weymouth by Gilbert  Nash,   published in  1885.
He was admitted to the Massachusetts  Medical Society in  1856,
and for  some years  was one of its  councillors .
He married  Sarah Jane  Dickerman of  Providence,      R.  I. ,       Nov.
25,    1851 ,      with issue :
I.      Frank L.,  born Feb. 13,   1854;   died May 11,    1895.
II.                  Walter G.,    born Oct.  20,   1865;    died Dec. 27,    1921 .
III .           Eva M.,   born Sept.  13,   1869;     died when quite young.
Dr.  Forsaith  was  a  successful  physician  and a tireless   worker.
He had the respect and confidence of his medical brothers,     and was
ever ready to help in difficult  cases .
JOSEPH  PORTER  HODGDON
Dr.   Hodgdon  was  born  in  Kensington,   N.  H.,     June  9,       1825.
He had  a  common school  education  and was graduated from  the
Eclectic  Medical  School,         Worcester,        Mass.           He  came  to   Wey- .
mouth in  1852 and remained seven years .
OLIVER  PERRY  PIPER,      A.Β.
Dr.  Piper was  born April 18,    1848,    in Northumberland County,
Pa.                  He received  his  academic degree  from  Princeton  College  in
1868,           and  M.D.  from  Jefferson   College,        Philadelphia,        Pa.             He
practiced  for  about  one year  in  Schuylkill  Haven,    Pa. ,     and came
to North Weymouth in March,    1873.   He returned to Pennsylvania
after practicing in North Weymouth for three years,   and held many
positions  of trust in that state.
He married Anna Eliza Eshleman,   with issue:

MOSES  REUBEN GREELY
Dr.  Greely  was  born  Aug.  13,      1826,      in  Hudson,      N.   H.    His
academic  education  was  obtained  at  the  schools  of  Nashua,    New
