NORTON QUINCY TIRRELL
Dr.  Tirrell was  born  in  East  Weymouth  Nov.  20,       1817.    He
attended   the   public   schools   of   Weymouth,       Warren  Academy,
Wilbraham,         Mass. ,      and  later  studied  at  a  Washington,        D.   C. ,
University   to   which   he  was  appointed  by  the   Hon.        Daniel
Webster,      who at  that  time  was  representative  to  Congress  from
Massachusetts.             In  Dr.  Forsaith's  compilation  it  is  stated  that
he  obtained  his   medical  education  "in  the  regular  process   of
study, "  which is  not exactly correct.       Although not a graduate of
a medical  school,     he  was  articled  with  a  Dr.   Prescott  of  Pitts-
field,      N.  H. ,     with whom he studied for  a few years.          After that he
began  practice  in  Sharon,      Mass.            He was  the  only  physician  in
that  town for  several  years,     and  then  removed  to  North  Wey-
mouth  in  1852,     and  succeeded  Dr.  Gibbens.        He occupied  the
house  now owned  by  Mr.  Parker  T.  Pearson  on King  Oak Hill,
and  later  moved  to  Broad  Street  where he lived  and  died  in  the
house I  now occupy.         He was a man of  many parts and enjoyed a
large  and lucrative practice.
He married May 12,     1842,   Susan Jane French of London,    N.  H.,
with issue:
I.      Frederick N.,  born June 30,   1843.

V.   Norton,    born March 2,    1855 ;       deceased.
VI.             Georgie E.,   born Aug.
g.   4,  1856,   deceased.
Dr. Tirrell died Oct.  19,   1882.

JOHN HENRY Gilbert
Dr.  Gilbert  was born in Atkinson,     N.  H.,     Nov.  11,     1826.    His
academic  education  was  obtained  at  Atkinson  Academy,      and his
medical   education  began  at   Harvard  Medical  School   and  was
completed  there  in  1853.     He came  to  East  Weymouth  in  the
same year,     and remained  three years.         His next place of practice
was in Huntington,    Mass. ,    where he remained for  about one year
and a half,     and then returned  to  East Weymouth,    where he prac-
ticed  for  five  years  more,     and in  1862 removed to Quincy,     Mass. ,
and continued there in  practice.      He died there several  years  ago.
He was  admitted  a fellow  of  the  Massachusetts  Medical  Society
in  1854 and was one of its  councillors .
He  married  Jane  Copeland  of  Huntington,       Mass. ,       Nov.   27,
1856,      with issue :
John H.,    born Sept.  3,    1870.
Dr.  Gilbert  had  many of  the  characteristics  of  the  successful
physician,   -faithful,      progressive,     and  was  a  calm  and  tireless
worker.
GEORGE  WYMAN FAY
Dr.  Fay was  born  in Grafton,     Mass. ,     Feb.  9,      1834.    His   pre-
paratory  education  was  obtained  at  Leicester  Academy,       and  he
was  graduated  from  the  Harvard  Medical  School  in  1863.    He
came to  East Weymouth in  1857,    and continued in practice  there
until  his  death,     Feb.  5,    1889.    For several years he was a member
of  the  school  board  of  Weymouth,    and at one time served  on the
board  of   selectmen.              He  was  admitted   to   the   Massachusetts
Medical Society in  1866,    and was one of its  councillors.            He served
for  two  years  as  president  of  the  Union  Medical  and  Surgical
Association.
He married,       March  21,   1857,     Jane Louise  Mowry of  Worcester,
Mass.  ,      with  issue :
I.       Frank G.,    born Feb. 1,     1859.
II .                 George W.,    born Jan. 6,    1861;      deceased.
III.           Florence J.,  born June 30,      1864.
IV.           Blanche M.,   born Dec. 16,    1865;    deceased.
V.    E.  Louise,   born June 10,    1870.
VI.             M. Fanny,    born Oct.  12,    1871.
Dr.  Fay  was  greatly  beloved  by his  patients.          He was  a  man
of  sterling   qualities,     upright  and  honorable  in  his  dealings,       and
strictly  ethical in his  profession.

JOHN  CHISHOLM  FRASER,      A.M.
Dr.  Fraser  was born in Antigonish,     N.  S.,    Aug.  2,     1853,       son  of
John  and  Mary Chisholm  Fraser.          He was educated  at  the  Uni-
versity of St.  Francis Xavier of that place in the years  from  1868
to  1872.    In 1873 he matriculated at the Harvard Medical School,
where he remained one term,    after  which he continued his studies
at  Bellevue  Hospital  Medical  College,    New York,    and graduated
from that institution in the class  of 1876,   and came to  East Wey-
mouth  in  May of  the  same year.          He served  on the  Weymouth
school  board  for  six  years.               In  1893  he  was  appointed  medical
examiner for  the Fourth  District  of  Norfolk County by Governor
Russell,        a  position  which he still holds.     He was admitted  to  the
Massachusetts  Medical  Society in  1880,     and was one of its  coun-
cillors .            He is   a member of  the  South  Norfolk  District  Medical
Society  and  was  its   president  for  two  years;       a  member  of  the
American Medical Association,   and of the  Massachusetts  Medico-
Legal  Society.        He is  at  the  present  time  president  of  the  latter
society.             He was the medical member of  Exemption Board No. 36
during the World War.
He married,       July 20,    1880,       Mary A.  Boyle  of  East  Weymouth,
with issue:
I.      Mary G.,   born July 18,   1881.
II.          Archibald McKay,   born May 22,   1883.
III.           Katherine E.,   born Jan.  21,    1885.
IV.              Somers,     born Jan. 28,    1887.
V.    Irene A.,    born Aug. 22,     1888.

ROSCOE  ELLSWORTH  BROWN
Dr.   Brown  was  a native  of  Lynn,     Mass. ,   where  he was born
May 18,     1851.    He received his  preparatory education in  Bridgton
High School  and Bridgton Academy,     Bridgton,     Me.         His  medical
education was obtained in the Portland Medical School,    the Maine
General  Hospital,     and  the  medical  school   of   Bowdoin  College,
from which  he was graduated  in  July,   1876.    He came to  North
Weymouth  in  September  of  the  same year,     afterwards  removing
to East Weymouth,  where he practiced for several years,   after which
he  went  to  Everett,       Mass. ,    where  he died  some  years  ago.          He
joined the Massachusetts Medical Society in 1879.
He was  twice  married,    first  to  Mary E.  Wilson  of  Brunswick,
Me.   ,      Feb.  2,       1877,    with  issue :
Roscoe B.,        born Sept. 11,   1882;     deceased.
Dr.  Brown was  a genial  man,    always  kind  and  considerate  in
the sick room and faithful to his patients.
WM.         FALES  HATHAWAY
Dr.  Hathaway was  born at  Northbridge,     Mass.,    Oct.  4,      1843.

in  the battles  around  and at  the  siege  of Vicksburg,       Miss.            He

Infantry.           He came to  Weymouth in  1871  and practiced  his  pro-

JOSEPH  CHASE
Dr.  Chase  was  born  in  Boston,      son  of  Joseph  and  Clara  d'A.
(Luce)    Chase,       Nov.  25,      1851.     He was  educated  in  the  public
schools  of  Boston,     graduating  from  the  English  High  School  in
1870,        and  then  entered  business.       Subsequently  he  received  in-
struction  under  private  tutelage  and  entered  Boston  University
School  of  Medicine in  1875,     from which he graduated  in  1878  as
class  valedictorian.           Further  medical  studies  were pursued  at  the
Harvard  Medical  School  and  the  Post- Graduate  School  of  New
York.           Before  coming  to  East  Weymouth  in  March,        1887,          he
practiced  in  Hingham,      Boston,       New York,         and  Concord,       N.  Η.
He is   a  member of  the  American  Medical  Association,      American
Institute  of  Homoeopathy,     Massachusetts  Medical Society,      Massa-
chusetts  Homoeopathic  Society,      Norfolk  District  Medical  Society,
Boston  Homoeopathic  Society,      and  the   Massachusetts   Surgical
and Gynaecological Society.     He served six years on the Weymouth
school  board,    and is  now a trustee of Tufts Library.
He married,      June 2,   1884,    Carrie A.  Blaisdell of Concord,      N.  H.;
no children.
On August  6,     1910,     he  married  Emma W.  Raymond  of  East
Weymouth,    with issue:
Joseph,    3d,    born Feb.  28,      1912.
Dr.  Chase died at Vineyard Haven,     Mass. ,  Aug. 23,    1923.
EDWIN MAYBURY
Dr.  Maybury was born in  1827,    in Windham,    Me. ,    son of Daniel
and  Hannah  Craig  Maybury.            He practiced  in  East  Weymouth
for  about  ten  years,     succeeding  Dr.  Brown.           He was  a gentleman
of  the old  school,    kindly  and dignified.       He died suddenly  from  a
cerebral embolism,   and is buried in Waltham,      Mass.
He  married   Lenora  Hall  of  Windham,     Me.            They  had  four
children,      two of whom became physicians.
GEORGE  DEXTER  BULLOCK
Dr.  Bullock  was  born in  Taunton,      Mass. ,     Dec.  6,      1859,    son  of
Dr.  Andrew  D.  and  Love  F.  Bullock of that city.        After receiving
his  elementary  education  in  Taunton  and  Providence,        R.  I. ,      he
entered  the  New  Hampton  Literary  Institution  of  New Hamp-
ton,      N.  H. ,      in  1878,    from which he graduated  in June,       1881.    He
then entered the Jefferson  Medical  College of  Philadelphia,     gradu-
ating  in  1886.    The following  year he came to  Weymouth,     where
he practiced his profession until the year of his death,    Dec.  6,     1914.
He was a member of the  Massachusetts Medical Society,    the South
Norfolk   District   Medical   Society   and  the  American   Medical
Association.

FRANKLIN  PIERCE  VIRGIN,       B.A.
Dr.  Virgin  was  born  at  Rumford,      Me.  ,     Oct.   13,       1850,       son  of
Benjamin  F.   and  Eunice  (Kyle)   Virgin.           Shortly  after  the  Civil
War the family moved to Lewiston,    Me. ,    where he fitted for college
at the Lewiston High School.        In 1871 he entered  Bowdoin College,
from  which  he graduated  in  1875.    That  same  year  he  entered
the office  of Drs.     Gage and Cowe at  Concord,     N.  H.,     for  the study
of medicine,     and attended lectures at the Bowdoin College Medical
School.               Subsequently  he  entered  the  office   of   Dr.   George  W.
Jenks  of  Detroit,        Mich. ,       matriculated   at  the   Detroit   Medical
College  and  graduated  from  that  institution  in  1878.    He  then
settled  for  the practice of his  profession at Rochester,     N.  H.,    where
he spent  twelve years.           He came to  Weymouth in  1890 and  took
over  the  practice of  the late  Dr.  F.  F.  Forsaith.             He is  a member
of the New Hampshire  Medical Society.      In 1898 he took a post-
graduate  course  on the  eye  at  the  Carney  Hospital,     Boston,       also

WEYMOUTH HOSPITAL
On May 22,       1922,     the Weymouth Hospital  opened its  doors  to
the public,    and now for  a year has continued its  work with remark-
able   success.           An institution of this kind was much needed in the
town,   and with the co-operation of citizens and others,   it  is  destined
to become one of the most serviceable in the state.        It  is  already
equipped with  full  sets  of  surgical  instruments,      X- ray  machine,
lung-motor,   etc.

SCHOOLS
The government of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay was prompt
in  recognizing  the  need  of  schools.        By a  vote  passed  Nov.  11 ,
1647,     it  was  ordered  that  every  " Towneship,                                after  the  Lord
hath  increased them to  the number of 50 house holders,   shall then
forthwith  appoint  one  within  their  towne to  teach  all  such  chil-
dren as  shall  resort  to him to write & reade,    whose wages shall  be
paid either  by the parents or  masters of such children or by the in-
habitants in generall,    by way of supply,    as the major part of those
that  order  the  prudentials  of  the towne shall  appoint;        provided,
those that  send  their children be not oppressed by paying  much
more than they can have them taught for in other townes.
It  was further  ordered that in towns of over one hundred house-
holders  " they shall  set up a grammar schoole,    the  master  thereof
being  able  to  instruct  youth so  farr  as  they may be fited  for  the
university. "
Of the  General  Court which  passed this  vote,  quoted  above  in
part,    was Thomas  Dyer of  Weymouth.¹
Whether at  this time the town of Weymouth possessed a school-
master  may not certainly be known.         Our early  town and  parish
records  are  meager  in  this  respect,    and  practically  all  important
matters  of  record  regarding the history  of  our schools  for  the  first
one hundred and fifty years of the town's history are cited  by Mr.
Gilbert  Nash in  Chapter  VII  of  his  " Sketch  of Weymouth.  "     A
lengthy excerpt therefrom is  here in order :
Next to  importance to the ecclesiastical  interests  come those of education,     of
which the  public  schools  form the  prominent  feature,     and  for  these  the  town
has always  taken  special  care.             In the early  days  of  its  history  the  records  are
exceedingly brief,   and only slight and incidental  mention is  made of many things
upon which now there  is  great  need  of  fuller  information.         The  first  notice  of
matters  connected with schools occurs on March 10,    1651,    when the town voted
to pay Captain  Perkins  ten pounds for  six  months'     schooling.        Capt.     William
Perkins was a prominent  man in town in  those  days,     being " townsman, "  and
probably held other impor
important offices.       In subsequent history it was found that
it  was to  men of  this  character  that  the  town  intrusted  the  education  of  its
children.
It  is  a singular  fact,     and one which shows that the  interest  of the  town in
education was not confined to its  own borders,     that  the  second  mention should
be that  of  a  subscription  of ten pounds sixteen  shillings  and sixpence  by Wey-
mouth to  Cambridge  College,    in  1652.    After  Captain Perkins,    the next  school-
master  named is  William  Chard,    who was also  town clerk,    and attended to the
drawing up of such legal  instruments  as  the necessities  of the people demanded.
1 See Records of the Governor and Company of  the Massachusetts  Bay in  New England,     Nov.
11,    1647,    Vol.     2,    p.  682;      Colonial  Laws of  Massachusetts,    reprinted from the edition of  1660,   pp.
190,  191.
 - 167 - 
SCHOOLS                                     645
He is  first  mentioned in that  capacity April  10,     1667,    when the town voted him
three pounds and ten shillings,   the rent of the  flats,    in addition to  his  other pay.
On the  25th of August,    thirty  shillings  was  also  added.           On Nov.  29,       1669,       he
was  engaged at ten pounds per  year,     probably  employed only  a portion  of  the
time.       He was also  sexton,     and the pay of  both offices  was sometimes included
in  one vote.          On Sept.  18,      1678,       his  pay had advanced to  twenty-four  pounds,
and the town was to furnish  a schoolroom.               The selectmen with the elders  were
also  " to  rate  each  pay-scholar  for  his  benefit. "    The next  year  a  house  and
orchard  were rented for  him at  forty- five  shillings,     and  in  1680,    the  house  of
James  Stewart  was bought  for  forty  pounds for  the  use  of the  schoolmaster ;
this was to be paid for by subscription,    which failed,   and a tax was laid  for it.
In the following year,     1681,    a schoolhouse was built on a part of the land bought
of  Capt.      John  Holbrook,     and the  other  part  of which was afterwards  occupied
by the new meeting-house,     erected  in  1682.     The house with  the  furnishings
cost  thirty-six  pounds.          In  1684,       Mr.  Chard's  salary  was  advanced  to  thirty-
three  pounds  and fourteen  shillings.         His  duties  were "to  keep  a  free- school
and teach all children  and servants sent him to read,    write,    and cast  accounts. "
On Nov. 28,    1687,    for some reason the town voted " not to continue Mr. Chard
in the work of a public schoolmaster  at  the public charge,   but he is  at  liberty
to  use  the  dwelling  and schoolhouse  until  next  March  meeting,     for  which  he
is  to ring the bell and sweep the meeting-house. "    Probably this  was for want of
funds,     as  he was in  office  during the  year  1689  and  continued  a town school-
master  until  1696,      when  he  removed  to  Abington.            Mr.  John  Copp was  ap-
pointed  to succeed him,    at  thirty pounds per year,    and he was also chosen town
clerk the same year.       Mr. Copp does not appear to have remained in his position
quite  two  years.          At the  March  meeting,    1697,     the  town voted  that " parents
shall  pay three shillings  for  each child  sent  to  school  between the  ages  of  eight
and fourteen  years. "    This was to  pay in  part  the  schoolmaster's  salary,      the
remainder to  be made up by a tax upon all who lived within two miles  of the
schoolhouse.          By this  time the increase  of scholars  was  so  large  that  the  town
found  it  necessary  to  employ  more teachers,      and  Joseph  Dyer  was  employed
to teach in  the schoolhouse,    with John King as  assistant,    and Edward Bate was
to teach in his own house.        To follow the precedent,    now well established,    Edward
Bate was elected town clerk.        The pay of schoolmaster was to be not over thirty
pounds,  one-third  of which was  to  be  paid by those who sent  their  children  to
school,    and the remainder by tax.           The next  year the whole was raised by tax.
and John Torrey was employed,    probably in the place of John King,     as  Edward
Bate still  retained his  position the following  year,     1699,    and later  Torrey appears
as Bate's  assistant.
During the summer of 1700,    five  women were engaged to teach  school  for  six
months,     at twenty- five  shillings  each,     besides the usual rate  paid by those  who
sent children.               On the 21st of October of that year Samuel Hunt,   son of Colonel
Hunt,      was hired as schoolmaster at  fifteen  pounds ten shillings  in money for  six
months,    or twenty- three pounds,  ' as the rates run.   "   In January,  1705,     Ebenezer
White of Dorchester was appointed schoolmaster for half a year at fifteen pounds,
and on March 3,     1707,    Thomas Thornton  was  engaged at twenty- five  pounds,
of fifteen pennyweights each  (silver) .          To him,   in  1709,    succeeded John Torrey,
at fifty  shillings  per month.      In 1717 school was kept in each  schoolhouse  four
months,      and it seemed that now there  was  a schoolhouse  in  the  south  part  of
the town.          John Galt was teacher for  a part of this  year.         In September,     1719,
Ebenezer Rolie was hired for a year at forty- two pounds ten shillings,    and Mr.
Calder in  1723  at  the  same price.      And this  year,     1723,     a new schoolhouse was
built  at a cost  of forty-two pounds seven shillings  eleven pence,    between Joseph
Lovell's  and John Shaw's.      Mr. Calder taught two months here and two months
in the North schoolhouse.        In  1729 it  was voted that the South  Precinct  should
have a school one-third of the year,    and be at the charge of having a schoolhouse,
and the  North,    two-thirds  of the year.          In May,    1730,   Joseph Torrey was hired
as  schoolmaster at fifty  pounds.
After  the division  of the town into  two  precincts,     a large  part of the school
business was transacted at  the  precinct  meeting,   the town appropriating  money
and dividing  it  between  them  according  to  the  amount  paid  by  each.               The
 - 168 -

appropriations commencing in 1733,    at seventy- five  pounds,    had risen,    in  1800,

Jan. 24,    1785,    Nathaniel Bayley,    Esq. ,   was appointed to answer to the General
Court on behalf of the town for neglecting to keep a grammar school;       thus it
appears that the town had become a delinquent in this  matter,    but the lesson
was a good one,  and did not need to be repeated.
After the  close  of the  war,     prosperity  began to  dawn upon the town;      the
schools  soon  felt  the impetus,    and new houses were built and new schools  estab-
lished in  various parts.            Samuel Reed and James Humphrey,   3d,    were employed
at two pounds per week,   and the latter to have three shillings  per week extra,
"he having been at the expense of fitting  himself for  a grammar school teacher."
Both of these were men of mark in town,    as well as schoolmasters,    having been
town clerks,     selectmen,    and also village notaries.       Both held long terms of service
as  school  teachers,    with excellent  reputation.                   GILBERT  NASH,    Sketch  of  Wey-
mouth,    pp.      125-129.
By chapter  19  of the Acts of 1789  the  General  Court  again de-
fined  the duties of the schoolmaster and his  qualifications .
The teaching of religion  is  no longer emphasized,     but the master
was to  " teach  children  to  read and write,     and to  instruct them in
the  English  language,     as  well  as  in  arithmetic,   orthography,      and
decent behavior. "
This  chapter  also  authorized  towns to  determine and define  the
limits  of school districts.
At about  this  period it  is  apparent from the Town Records  that
school  facilities   in  Weymouth were  inadequate.          The  old  parish
system was becoming outgrown.
At the March meeting of  1790 a committee composed of  Cotton
Tufts,        John  Tirrell,    Josiah  Waterman,     Capt.      Eliphalet  Loud,     and
Capt.       Elliot  Loud was directed  to " consider the method of school-
ing  and to  adopt such  measures as  shall be most beneficial  to  the
Town and agreeable to the laws of the Commonwealth. "    All of the
above  committee did  not  serve  thereon,     others  apparently  being
appointed in their stead;     and this committee reported to  a meeting
of the town on April 5,    1790,     and their  report was rejected.
It  was,    however,    voted  at  this  meeting  that " there shall  be four
schools   kept  six   months  each,      through  the  winter  season,       one
Grammar and one  English  school  for  each  Parish "  and  £100  was
appropriated  therefor.
It  was also  voted  to  choose  a committee " to  consider  the  most

It does not appear what was done under their vote,   but for some
years  the  Parish  seems  to  have remained the school unit,    and the
money appropriated by the town for schooling to have been divided
between  the  two  parishes.           But  that  the  matter  of  the  schools
during this period was a live,   unsettled issue is very clear.
The  first   mention  of  a  " school   committee"  is   found  in  the
record  of  town meeting held in  March,     1797,     when Cotton Tufts,
Asa  White,          Capt.       Joshua  Bates,      Nathaniel  Bayley  and  Capt.
Eliphalet   Loud  were  chosen,     and  $550  were  appropriated   for
schooling.            But at  the  April  meeting  (and  town  meetings  were
very  frequent  in those  days) ,    when  Nathaniel  Bayley  "excuseth
himself  from  serving in that office,"  it  was voted " to  excuse  the
whole of the School Committee. "
In 1799 the old system of schools,    marking the first  period of the
town's  history,     came to an end,   and definite  advantage was taken
of the law allowing the establishment of school districts .
At the March meeting in  1799  it  was voted " to  choose  a com-
mittee  to  divide  the town into  school  districts  and report  to  the
town  at  the  next  April   meeting."     Cotton  Tufts,      Asa  White,
Zadok  Nash,      John Tirrell,    Col.  Joshua  Bates,      Dr.  James  Torrey
and  Lieut.     David Joy were so chosen.          Their  report,    written  and
signed  by  Cotton  Tufts,     was  made  to  the  meeting  of  May 13,

school  districts  were set  out and defined in detail,   the first four in
the  North  Parish,    and  districts   numbered  five  to  eight  in  the
South  Parish.
At this  meeting it was also voted to divide the school  money be-
tween the school districts  in proportion to each district's  taxes,    and
"that  each  District  provide  its  own school  houses  and  that  each
school  shall be considered  a free  school."

The  nineteenth  century,    therefore,      saw  the  district  school  es-
tablished,        and  seventy  years  ran  on  before  this  system  became
outworn,       ill-functioning  and  finally  abolished.        The  eight  school
districts  remained,    with  some minor changes  in  their  limits,      until
the  year  1845,   when the ninth district was made from the easterly
portion of the fourth.        In the year 1847 a tenth district was formed
from  the second,    with its  school  located  at or  near the location of
the  Jefferson  School  or  Middle  Street,     near  Broad,     and  in  1857
the  eleventh  district  was  formed  from  the  eighth  and  in  Pond
Plain,     but it  disappears in  1865 along with the eighth,   being merged
into  the seventh,   after  the " Center School, "  later called  the Bates,
was  constructed.
Originally,     the local  prudential committee had full  charge of all
school  matters within  its  district.            Later,    with the definite  estab-
lishment  of  a town  school  committee,    called  for  many years  the
" High  Committee, "  the local  prudential committee would usually
consist  of  one person  whose duties  were  to  provide  and maintain
the schoolhouse,    and pay,     and frequently provide a boarding place
for,         the  teacher.             The  " High  Committee"  would  examine  and
approve
ove  the  teachers  and  supervise  the  curriculum  and  teaching
in the schools.        From the so-called " High Committee" the present-
day school  committee has developed,    and the duties of such com-
mittee have been well defined  by statute.        The result  now is that
the  school  committee perform  all  the duties  formerly  assigned  to
the  prudential  committee  of  each  district,     and  have  as  well  the
final   word  as  to  the  curriculum,     methods  of  teaching,      and  the
choosing  of  instructors .             The immediate contact  with  and super
 - 171 - 
SCHOOLS                                    649
vision over the schools has,   during the last  two generations,    become
definitely  delegated  to  the  superintendent  of schools,     now a well-
established   and  necessary  profession.             Originally  our  town  had
one,     then  two,    schools  kept  by a schoolmaster,    to  whom resorted
those  whose  parents   or   " masters "   wished  them  to  be  funda-
mentally  instructed,    and who usually  paid  a small  fee  therefor.
Later,       " women  schools"   were  added  for  the  smaller   children .
Then  came  the  district,      whereby  each  defined  neighborhood,       as
distinct  from  the  parish,     provided  quarters  for  schooling,      usually
in  houses  owned by the district,    but often  rented,    while the town
provided the teachers.       School was kept six days in the week,    with
a half  holiday  on  Saturdays.          In  the  district  schools  the  terms
were always  summer and winter,   the winter  term,    so called,    being
usually  the  longer.         Even  after  the  abolition  of  the  school  dis-
tricts  the idea of the summer and winter terms survived as " first"
and " second "  terms ;     formerly,  the school year began with August 1 ,
and ended with July 31 .
About  1880  the  school  year,      September  to  June,    became  ac-
cepted,       and  schools  have  generally  been  kept  for  forty  weeks.
School  had  long since been compulsory for  the younger scholars,
and in the early 80's free  textbooks were available  to all.
As the  old  district  schoolhouses  wore out or became too  small,
schools  were centralized  in a greater  degree,     so  that  to-day,     with
twice  as  many scholars  in  attendance  at our  schools  than in  the
middle 70's,       there are considerably fewer schoolhouses.
After  abolition of the school districts  the town in the year  1871
was in the possession  and use of the following  schools :         the North
High,         South  High,    the  Athens,    High Street,      Broad  Street,      Pratt,
Main Street and Central Street schools of grammar grade;       and for
intermediate  and  primary  grades  were  used  the  Athens,      Adams,
Broad Street ,       Middle Street,    High Street,   Pleasant Street,     Perkins,
Mount  Pleasant,    Main Street,     Central  Street,    Union Street,      Pond
Street,       Randolph  Street,    Grant  Street,     Commercial Street,      Pratt,
and Washington Street schools .
The  Athens  School  has  since  been replaced  by another  of  the
same name,    the Adams is still in use,   as is  the Broad Street School,
now called  the  Lincoln,   and which was built by the  town.            The
Middle  Street  School has been  replaced by the Jefferson,    and the
High,        Pleasant  and  Grant  Street   schools   by  the  Washington.
The  Hunt School  (old)   replaced  the  Perkins,    which  was  located
near by,     on Front Street.          The Mount Pleasant was used for years
by the town as  the  Tufts  School,    and was discontinued  upon the
erection of the New Hunt.           The Main Street School was replaced
by  the  Shaw;     the  Central  Street  School,     originally   called   the
" Center  School,"   then  long  known  as  the  Bates,     in  memory  of
Gen.  James  L.   Bates,       who,      as  a  young  man,    for  several  years
successfully   taught  in  this  district,    and  who was  later   actively
interested  in  the  construction  of  this   school,     was  discontinued
on the erection of the Edward B. Nevin School,   as  was the Torry
 - 172 - 
650                                               SCHOOLS
Street School,    or Howe,   named for Dr. Appleton Howe,   later built.
The  Pond  Street  School  is   still   used,     and  the  Randolph  Street
(Hollis)   School is  available for use.        The Commercial Street School
(the  Bicknell)   is  now Grand Army Hall.          The Pratt has been re-
placed  by another of  the same name,    and  the Washington Street
School,     later  called  the " Holbrook, " near Lovell's  Corner,     has been
discontinued.        At intervals,      also,    a  mixed  school was kept in  the
old  town hall on Middle and Washington Streets.
The old Union Street  School,    in  the  " Boxberry"  neighborhood,
later  called   the  Thomas,      was  discontinued  nearly  twenty  years
ago,     and  is   now  a  residence.            Many persons  remember  the  old
Pratt  School,       once the school of the sixth  district,   popularly called
the  " Globe "  School,    from the peculiar window in the front gable.
This  school  was named in memory of  Lois Pratt,   who by her will,
probated  in  1810,      provided  a fund  to  be devoted  to  educational
interests  in  the  sixth  school  district.           The original  school  of  the
sixth  district  was  on  Pleasant  or  " Sheep"  Street  near  Pine.            It
was a " little  Red School house, "  and was destroyed by fire in 1845.
The " Globe"  School,     a  two- room  building,    was  erected  with  the
aid of  the  Pratt fund,    but the present Pratt School was erected by
the  town.                  The  Pratt  fund,     however,       is   still   in  existence,      con-
siderably   increased,     and  the  income  therefrom  has  consistently
been devoted to  educational  purposes  for the benefit of the neigh-
borhood,      for  many years  supporting  the  manual  training  depart-
ment of  the  Pratt School .
Mention should be made also  of  the River Street  School  of  one
room for  the smaller pupils living  near the fertilizer works in North
Weymouth.            It was erected in 1876 on land purchased of the (then)
Bradley  Fertilizer  Company for  $100,     and the  total  cost  to  the
town for  the  erection  of  the  school  was  $1,913.29.            It  has  been
discontinued as a school since 1905.    Subsequent to its  discontinu-
ance  it   was  abandoned  to   the  American  Agricultural  Chemical
Company,       the  successor  of  the  Bradley  Company,     possibly  by
reason  of  some reservation in the original deed to  the town.         Its
thirty-year  history  is  remarkable in  this  respect :        when opened in
1876,      its  teacher  was  Clarabelle  Pratt;       when  closed  in  1905,     its
teacher  was Clarabelle Pratt.
THE  SUPERINTENDENT  OF  SCHOOLS
Rev.   Calvin  Terry  was  the  first   regularly  employed  superin-
tendent of schools.         He served for the year  1862-63,    and his  salary
was $400 per year.          He had previously been a member of the school
committee.
The  next  year  Rev.   D.  F.   Goddard  was  superintendent  at  a
like  salary,       and was  re-elected  for  the  year  1864-65  at  a salary  of
$500,       but  shortly  resigned,     and Mr.  Terry,     then  chairman of the
school  committee,   was chosen for  the vacancy.
For the year  1865-66 the committee voted not to employ a super-
 - 173 - 
SCHOOLS                                     651
intendent,    but performed such duty themselves in  accordance with
the early practice.
For the years 1866 to  1870 Francis M. Dodge was superintendent.
His salary started at $1,000 and ended at $1,350.
During  the  next  three  years  the  duties  of  superintendent  were
performed  by the  school  committee,   for  which services  they were
severally paid.
In  1873  Arthur G.  Lewis became superintendent for  about  two
years,       at  a  salary  of  about  $1,500.           He was  succeeded  by  F.   B.
Gamwell,     formerly principal  of the South High School,    until  1877,
at a salary  of  $1,340.             W. G.  Nowell completed  the year  1877  as
superintendent,   and was so  engaged in  1878 at a salary of $1,200.
For  the years  1879 to  1881  the duties  of a superintendent were
again performed by the committee,    but most of this work was done
by Mrs. Elizabeth C. Hawes,    who was for many years a member of
the school  committee.
In  1882 Mr. Gilman C. Fisher became superintendent at a salary
of  $1,800  a year,     and served until June,     1890.    Mr.  Fisher  was a
most  successful  educator  and  administrator  and  his  resignation
was much regretted.
Succeeding  superintendents  have  been:     I.    M.  Norcross,        1890-
1900;     Andrew S.  Thompson,     1901 ;        Elmer  E.  Sherman,       1902-04;
John  C.  Anthony,    four months,   1904-05;     Abner A. Badger,      1905-
09;    and Parker T.  Pearson,    1909 to date.
The spirit of good- will  and loyalty to the town that has developed
within the constantly increasing teaching force has been one of the
conspicuous  achievements  of the administration  of Superintendent
Pearson.
THE EARLY HIGH SCHOOL
The high  school,     or,    as it  meant then and still  in part  means,      a
school  qualified  to  prepare  scholars  for  college  or university,     was
first  established in the year 1853.   Joseph Dow was the first teacher,
and for the year 1853-54 he was paid $480.25.        The course of study
included arithmetic,    algebra,   bookkeeping,  anatomy and physiology,
Watts  on  " The  Mind,"   natural  philosophy,      United  States   and
general history,     French and Latin,    as principal subjects,   with minor
attention  to  geography,      English  grammar,     parsing,     composition,
reading,      spelling,   declamation and penmanship.
The Town House,     erected  in  1852 at a cost  of  $6,342,     including
$50 for  " entertainment at the raising, "  and located in the so-called
"geographic  center"  at  Middle  and  Washington  Streets ,      housed
this  school.               In  1854 the school  committee was directed  to  open a
high  school,      but not "at the  Town House,    where it  was kept the
last  year.   "    Such a school was established for  ten months,    the first
five months in South Weymouth and the  last  five  at  the Landing.
The South Weymouth school,   held in the hall of J.  G. Rogers,    well
remembered  by many in  Columbian  Square,      opened  with  forty-
one scholars,      but closed with but eighteen,   " most of the absentees
 - 174 - 
652                                            SCHOOLS
having left  at  the close  of the  week's  vacation  about the  1st  of
July.  "     The second  term opened October 5 in the ninth district,
with fifty-three  scholars,    nearly all of whom continued through the
term.             Mr.  Jonathan  C.  Brown was teacher  in  both schools,      and
his  salary  was $700 for  the year.¹
The town evidently recognized the difficulty  of keeping success-
fully  a high  school during the  summer months,    as was shown by
the experience in South Weymouth,     and at the  March meeting of
1855 it  was voted to open one high school in East Weymouth.        School
commenced  April  9  in  the  grammar  schoolhouse  with  fifty- four
pupils  under  Mr.  S.  S.   Marston,   whose  salary  was  $700  for  the
year.             Crowded  conditions   soon  compelled  the  removal  to  the
grammar school  in the tenth district.          Mr.  Marston soon resigned
by reason of ill  health,   and Mr. Loring Johnson was elected to take
his  place.                 The  first   term  ended  with  the  loss  of  about  twenty
scholars  during the term,   and the second  term  commenced  Octo-
ber 8 in the new house in the second district  (North  Weymouth) ,
with  twenty-nine pupils,    most of whom regularly attended.
The years  1856  to  1859  saw the  high  school  again  established
in  the  Town Hall  with  the  customary  two  terms  (summer  and
winter) ,      under  Mr.  W.  K.  Fletcher.          Attendance  was  large,      and
continued  large  during  all  this  period,     and  admission  had to  be
refused to many applicants for lack of room.          Record and tradition
both proclaim  Mr.  Fletcher  to  have  been an exceptional  teacher.
The high  average  attendance  records  attest  to  this.           He was  as-
sisted  during his last year at the Town House by Miss  Mary Poor
for  sixteen  weeks,   for which she was paid  $124;      and then by Miss
R.  V.  Humphrey of Dorchester,    who went with him the next year
to  the " North Weymouth High School "  in the building now called
the Adams School.
The curriculum at the high school at  this time included arithme-
tic,     algebra,       bookkeeping,   geometry,    rhetoric,    astronomy,      French,
Latin,      English grammar,   chemistry,    declamation  and composition.
The period  commencing with  the spring  of 1859 and ending  in
March,      1862,      again saw two high schools,   -   at  North Weymouth,
in  the  present  Adams  School;      and  the  South  Weymouth  High
School,    first  in the vestry of the  Universalist  Church,     and later  in
" Rachel  Rogers  room. "    At North Weymouth the school  was  for
one year  under  Mr.  Fletcher,    and for  the  next  two  years  under
Mr.  L.  Z.  Ferris,     assisted during the last year by Mary E.  Dowse.
At  South  Weymouth,      for   the  first   two  years,        Mr.   Elbridge
Torrey,       then  a young  man,    who later  became a very  well-known
merchant  of  Boston,     was  the  teacher.          He was  followed  by Mr.
A.  H.  Davis.             Of  Mr.  Torrey  it  has  been many times  said,      " He
was an inspiration  to  his  pupils."    It  may well  be  recorded  that
during all  his  life  Mr. Torrey retained  a great interest in his  native
South Weymouth.

In  1862  the high  school was again  transferred  to  the  town hall,
with an enrollment  for  the summer term of sixty-nine,     and thirty-
three  in  the winter  term.       Mr.  Ferris  was the  master,    assisted  by
Miss E.  P.  Hammatt.
This  arrangement  continued  during  1863  and  1864  under  the
same master,      with  attendance in these years of about forty pupils.
There  is   no  doubt  that  this  attendance  would  have  been  much
larger  but for  the  Civil  War in  which  many of  our  boys  of  high
school  age were  engaged.

THE  PERIOD  OF  TWO  HIGH  SCHOOLS
In  1865  again  two  high  schools,      North  and  South,      were  estab-
lished,        and  there  remained  two  separate  high  schools   until  the
building of  the  present school  in  1898 .
The  North  High  School  now  used,      as  it   had  before,      the  room
in  the  house of  the  second  district  (the  Adams) ,    and  in  1865  Mr.
Ferris  was  the  principal.            The  standard  of  admission  was  some-
what  lowered,     and  the  course  extended  from  three  to  four  years .
Before  the  end  of  the  school  year  Mr.  Ferris   resigned  and  was
followed  by Mr.  Nathan E.  Willis,      who served  as the teacher  until
1868,      being  succeeded  by  Mr.  Alfred  Bunker,     who  remained  for
about one year.          Then followed as principal  George  W. Shaw,    who
remained in  charge of the North High School  until June,      1882 .
 - 176 - 
654                                           SCHOOLS
In  1876 the  North High School  was relocated  in the new build-
ing erected  therefor  on Tremont Street in Weymouth Landing.
Succeeding  principals  of  this  school  were  Robert  E.   Denfield,
1882-84,        and Frank H.  Beede,    1884-88;    L.  Herbert Owen,   1888-
92 ;        A.   C.  Russell,      1892-94;       Charles  F.  Abbott,     1894-96;          and
Edmund J.  Bugbee,    1896-98.
The  South  High  School  during  the  years  1865-68  was  estab-
lished in the vestry of the Union Congregational Society,   on Pleasant
Street,      but was,    in  1868,     removed to  Rogers Hall,   so called,    where
it  remained until the completion of the South High School  build-
ing,    later called the Howe School,    in  1875.
The principals  of the South High School were George A.  Willis ,
1865-66;        F.   B.  Gamwell,      1866-73 ;      George  F.   Chace,       1873-74;
George  B.  Vose,     1874-82;      Nathaniel  S.  French,     1882-86 ;        Edgar
R.  Downs,       1886-92 ;     Albert  E.  Kingsbury,     1892-96;      and William
D. Mackintosh,      1896-98.
The present  high school,    for which an appropriation  of $50,000
was made at the annual town meeting in 1897,   was completed and
ready  for   occupancy  with  the  beginning  of  the  school  year  in
September,       1898.    The following  committee carried  out  the  vote
of the town in its  erection:    Dr.  Wm.    A.  Drake,    James Humphrey,
Wm.     Hyde,      Jr.,      Dr.  Joseph  Chase,    Jr. ,     Chas.      B.  Cushing,     Martin
E.  Hawes,       Henry A.  Thomas,    Augustus J.  Richards,     Dr.  John H.
Fraser,      Bradford Hawes,    Wilton A.  Loud and Herbert W. Sears.
George C.  Torrey was later  appointed to  this  committee in place
of  Henry A. Thomas,    resigned.
Loring  & Phipps  of  Boston were the architects.           P.  H.  Jackson
of Brockton was the general  contractor,     with a bid  of  $35,636.75 .
Heating was installed  by L.  E.  Smith of Gloucester,     with a bid of
$3,775.                The building  was  erected  within  the  appropriation,      and
has,     during the past twenty-six  years,    proved to  be a  satisfactory
building for the high school.
The average membership of the two high  schools  had been  240
in  1898;        in  1899 in  the  new high  school  it  was 239.   Attendance
now fell   off  for  a few  years  and  a  period  of  very  slow  growth
ensued.          In 1908 average membership was 268;    in  1914,     265;     but
in 1915 it  reached 300.
The following year saw a membership of 348,   but in 1918 it  had
fallen  to  302  and in  1919  to  291.    The World War had the  same
effect upon high school  attendance as did the Civil  War.
In the school year of  1921  average membership reached 331 ;     in
1922,      for  the year ending in June,  it was 417;      and for  the  school
year  1922-23,    up to  January,    530,    and  to  June,   560 scholars  had
enrolled,       necessitating  the division of the school  into  morning and
afternoon divisions.
A portable schoolhouse of two rooms has,   since  1921 ,      materially
assisted  in housing  the increased  number of scholars.         A few years
ago  the  proportion  of  high  school  scholars  to  the  whole  number
in  school  had  been  for  a  long  period  generally  about  1  in  10;

to-day it  is  about  1  in  6,     and  the  fraction  still  tends  to  become
larger,     due  to  the  raising  of  the compulsory  school  age.            At this
time proper provision is  being made to care for this  increased  and
growing  attendance by the erection  of  an addition  to  the present
high  school,      more than doubling its  capacity  in  schoolrooms,     and
substituting  for  the  small  hall  now therein  one of  larger  propor-
tions,      capable  of  seating  a  school  of  900  in  assembly,      and  with
exits  and other  safety  factors  amply provided.       The appropriation
for  this,        made in  February,      1923,     allows  $300,000  for  this  work.
Bids  so  far  received  and  accepted  warrant  the  expectation  that
this  sum will  be  ample.         A comparison  between  the  original  ap-
propriation and the later one is  inevitable;     but the old days,    when
the dollar purchased  much in labor and material,   seem to be gone
forever.
The principals  of the  present high school have been Edmund J.
Bugbee,       1898-1904 ;        Edwin R.  Sampson,      1904-10;      and  Frederick

EVENING SCHOOLS
From  time  to  time,     as  occasion  required,   the  town  has  main-
tained evening schools.          The percentage of adult illiterates  needing
education has never been great in our town.        Considerable numbers
of  foreign-born  adults  have  at  times desired  instruction  in  the
English  language,     and  opportunity  has  been  afforded  therefor  in
the most convenient places.
At the  present  time the greater part of evening school  work is
in  the  way of  practical  arts  for  women,   including  instruction  in
dressmaking  and  cooking,    for  which  purposes  the  state  furnishes
instructors.
CONTINUATION  SCHOOL
For the  past  few years  the town has maintained,    as required by
law,    a continuation school for the instruction  of minors under the
age of  sixteen  who are lawfully  employed in mercantile  or manu-
facturing   establishments.             At  the  present  time  the  number  of
such  scholars  is  small,     since  the  number of  minors  of  school  age
employed in town is  small.
Although   the   Commonwealth  pays  one-half   the  expense   of
maintaining  the continuation school,  the cost  to  the town and to
the state per pupil is  many times the cost per pupil of the regular
scholar.                This is due in large  part  to  a continually  changing  and
fluctuating membership.

PRIVATE  SCHOOLS
As  early  as   1827,        Edwards  A.   Park,       whom  the  writer  well
remembers  in  the  early   90's   as   a  very  aged   professor   in   the
Andover  Theological  Seminary,    had  conducted  a classical  school
in Weymouth Landing .
The success of his school induced many citizens of that neighbor-
hood  to  undertake  the establishment  of  an incorporated  academy.
In  February  of  1828,      Cotton  Tufts,     Joseph  Loud,      Noah  Fifield
and  Ezra W. Sampson,   and their associates,   who,    in fact,     numbered
about  forty,       were  incorporated  under  the  name and  style  of  The
Proprietors  of  the  Weymouth  and  Braintree  Academy.          Shortly
thereafter  a lot of land was purchased of Warren Weston,    who was
one of  the  associates,     on Washington Street,   then called  the Queen
Anne's  turnpike,    and a schoolhouse of  two stories,    thirty  by forty
feet,     was erected.     It also had a cupola and a bell.          For about five
years   a  classical   academy  was  maintained,      with  scholars   from
many of the near-by towns.
Its  principals,    in order,    were Thomas Douglass Gregg,   Amherst,
1828 ;            Erasmus Darwin Eldridge,     Amherst,    1829;      Samuel Thomas
Worcester,         Harvard,     1830,    a brother  of Joseph  E.  Worcester,      the
lexicographer;         Calvin  Emmons Park,     Amherst,     1821 ,        a  brother
of   Edwards  A.  Park;       Joseph  Brewster  Walker,       Harvard,         1832 ;
and  Charles  Dickson,     Yale,       1832.
Financially,     the Academy was not successful,     and after  the close
of  the  term  in  December,     1833,    the  school  was  closed,     and later
the schoolhouse was sold.           With the closing  of the Academy there
was no regularly established school  prepared to  fit  boys for  college
until   the  opening  of  the  high  school  some  twenty  years  later .
The word boys is  used here correctly,    since at that time there were
no collegiate institutions  open to  girls.¹
The  parochial  school  for  children  of  the  grades  in  Weymouth
Landing  was  established  in  a small  way a few  years  ago  by the
Rev.  John  B.  Holland  in  quarters  near  the  Church  of  the  Sacred
Heart.                 This   school  has  rapidly  grown,    and  to-day  has  enrolled
more  than  250  pupils,     mostly  in the lower  grades,    but  includes
scholars  in  all  grades  up to and including the eighth.
In  East  Weymouth  a  parochial  school  for  the  parish  of  the
Church of  the  Immaculate  Conception  is  in  process  of  construc-
tion,     but no school has as yet been opened.
Generally  speaking,   the  schools  of  Weymouth have  given  the
boys  and girls  of the town a sound and thorough  training  in  the
education  required  by  the  average  man.               For  more  than half  a
1 Vid.  Samuel W. Reed,    a paper  for Weymouth Historical  Society,   1885.    Weymouth Gazette,
July 24,   31,   1885.
 - 187 - 
SCHOOLS                                     665
century  any boy or girl  wishing  to  be prepared  for  the  college,
university,      or  even,    in  some  instances,      the  professional  school,
has  received  such  preparation   in  the  Weymouth  High  School.
The average  record  of  its  graduates  in college  is  good;      in many
cases  it  has been exceptional.
With  the  increase  in  the  compulsory  school  age,   the  demand
that  the  school  definitely  prepare  for  a given  trade,    business  or
career  will  be more insistent,   for  the years  of youth must not be
wasted.            Many of the simplest  looking problems  of education  are
the  hardest,     and in Weymouth,    as  elsewhere,   they  remain  still  in
process of solution.

LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
Compiled by KARLE H. GRANGER,    M.D.
In the  records  of every community,    and aside from its  religious
history  or  its   military  organizations,     there  is   always  its   social
history.             As the numbers grow there is  sure to develop the tendency
towards  a  friendship  or  some concerted  understanding  which  ex-
presses   its   loyalty  one  to  another  by  acts   of  brotherhood  and
esteem.             It  is  then that men begin to fraternize.        Familiar  spirits
meet in  varying  numbers,    and behold,     the fraternity  exists,     good-
will appears,      and some definite object at once becomes an incentive,
and the concerted  effort  of many minds  serves  to  accomplish  the
work  for  which  the  fraternity   was  formed.       Weymouth  is   no
exception,       and  many  secret   orders   and  brotherly   bands   have
flourished ;    many have,      from early days,   been a force  in  the  com-
munity;     many have played their parts and are now only a memory.
It  is  a strange  fact  that  a  reviewer  of  an article  bearing  on this
subject  will  invariably give to his special  lodge his  first  attention.
He turns  to  the  page,   finds  his  lodge  history,    reads  it  carefully,
criticizes  it ,      reads a little  more,    and turns  the page,    thinking later
to  return and finish  all of them.      It should be the effort,    therefore,
of  the historian  to give each  reader  something  in an entertaining
way,      and at the same time to  record  a correct  and general history
of the organization  under consideration.     Several clubs exist  in the
several   villages   of  the  town,     and  the  membership  rolls   always
include  the  keenest  of men,          - business,     professional,    and men of
leisure,     who co-operate with  a definite  purpose,   and their  associa-
tion is  known as  a lodge,      a society,     a club,    or a fraternal  order.
All such efforts  are  praiseworthy,    representing effort for lightening
burdens,    co-operating  in relief  of distress,    or  broadening  the  fields
of education.
Beneficial  orders,    ever  in  the greatest  numbers,   have  always
flourished;        comradeship,     inbred  in  all  of  us,    calls  imperatively
for  acts  of fellowship,   and the creation of the order seems to furnish
an  arrangement  by  which  such  objects   may  be  accomplished.
Sociability  and lodge  life  combine to  extend  relief  where  needed,
and  to  guard  us  against  pitfalls,    which,    without  warning,      might
engulf us.
Again,        and  still  in  the  interest  of  its   associates ,        we find  the
beginning  of  the  Union  movement,     where  one  whose  only  crime
consisted  in refusing to accept  a lowered wage for identical service
performed by a coworker in the shoe shops  fifty  years  ago  seems
to be the forerunner of our present-day labor unions .
Others formed military,   religious,    political bands,    each  organized
and having some plan or object as a working principle.

THE WEYMOUTH HISTORICAL  SOCIETY
The Weymouth Historical Society was organized April_12,      1879,
and was incorporated on July 19,    1886.                                                                                                                                  K
Elias   Richards  was  chosen  President  at  the  time  the  Society
was organized,   and served in that office for several years.
The officers  elected for  1879 were
President,     Elias  Richards.
Vice- President,   John J.  Loud.
Recording  Secretary,    Gilbert  Nash.
Corresponding Secretary,   Rev. Anson Titus.
Treasurer,      William H. Clapp.
Librarian,         Samuel W. Reed,    who held the office  for  one year,    and it  was then
filled by Miss Carrie A.  Blanchard.
In explanation  of the need of a Historical  Society,    and why it
came to exist,    a quotation from the first  entry on the record books
bears  full  testimony and follows,    thus:
The absence of any historical  organization in the town of Weymouth for  the
collection  and  preservation  of  records,      traditions  and facts,     historical,      genea-
logical  and geographical,   led  to the  preparation  of the  following  paper  which
explains itself,   and which was circulated inMarch,1879.
We,      the  subscribers,      believing  it  to  be of the highest  importance that  the
ancient  records  should  be collected and preserved,   and that the time has  fully
come when some systematic  effort  should  be made to  do this,   recommend the
organization  of an association having such an object in view,   its  meetings to be
held in some convenient  place,    as  often  as  may be  necessary  to  carry out  the
contemplated  object,    and we agree  to  do what we can to  further  the  interests
of  such  an association  by aiding  in  its  formation  and support,    by gathering
records  and  traditions  to  be  considered  at  its   meetings  and placed  upon  its
records  or  files,      or  published  as  deemed the  most expedient,    and to  encourage
by whatever  means  we  may,     the  objects  of  its   organization,     and  we  further
suggest  that  an initiatory  meeting be called  as soon as ten names are obtained
to this paper.
The signers  to  this  paper  were the following  interested  gentle-
men:       Gilbert  Nash,     Frank  W.  Lewis,     Samuel  W.  Reed,    John J.
Loud,       Anson  Titus,       Jr.,        Charles   G.   Easterbrook,           Everett   C.
Bumpus,         Elias  Richards,      Wm.      H.  Clapp,     Lucien  H.  Frary,     J.   W.
Armington,     and F.  P.  Chapin.
Immediately  after,      on  March  29,      1879,     in  the  office  of  Elias
Richards,       Esq.,   a plan for  a permanent organization was presented
by  Rev.  Anson Titus,    Jr. ,      which  was  referred  to  a  committee  of
Messrs.         Titus,     Lewis  and Nash,    with instructions  to  report  at  the
next  meeting.          At this  second  meeting,    April  12,   1879,      the  Wey-
mouth  Historical  Society  was  formed,    a constitution  adopted and
officers  elected.
The Society  was thus  fully  organized  and placed  on a working
basis,         regular  meetings  held  and  much  interest  manifested,         not
alone by the members but by townspeople and  historical  students

elsewhere,       and  others  interested  in  historical  matters  in  different
parts of the country.
Many  valuable  papers  were  prepared  by the  members  of  the
Society,      and  the  first  year  of  organization  gave great  encourage-
ment to  them.          Success  crowned their efforts  beyond anticipation,
and  much  historical   material  otherwise  lost   has  been  collated,
recorded  and put into  condition  for preservation;       also  a new and
growing interest  for  research  and study  of  historical  subjects  was
being exhibited by coworkers in  special lines  of study.
Later  the  meetings  of  the  Society  were held in Tufts  Library,
Weymouth,      and on April  7,    1880,    the historical  library  and papers
were removed  to  that  building  and arranged  so  that  they  would
be  more  accessible  to  the  public.        During  the  later   years   the
Society  has  held  monthly  meetings  in  the  Fogg  Library,        South
Weymouth.
Many and varied were the subjects considered,    and it  is  perhaps
a  document  of   most  general   interest   which   the   Society   has
published in  a volume entitled " Private Diary of General Solomon
Lovell,  "   and kept by him during  the  unfortunate  Penobscot  Ex-
pedition of 1779.
Also of most intense interest and importance is  a volume entitled
" Historical  Sketch  of  the  Town  of   Weymouth,       Massachusetts,
from  1622  to  1884, "   compiled  by  Mr.  Gilbert  Nash,       the  first  re-
cording secretary of the Society.       This work was published in  1885
under  the  auspices   of  the   Weymouth  Historical   Society,         and
forms  the  nucleus  for  the  recorded  history  of  the  town.           Special
mention may be made of the very excellent and complete index in
this  volume,    and the entire  work deserves unqualified  approval.
Weymouth  has  a history  second  in  importance  to  few,      if  any,
towns  in  New  England,     and  the  present  undertaking  is  largely
sponsored  by  its   Historical  Society.        The  material  is  being  col-
lected  and is  to be written  into  several  volumes and arranged  in
graphic form,    and the three hundred years of our past seem to cry
for  recognition  of  its   history  from  Weston,      through  the  savage
wars,      through the Revolution,     Civil War and reconstruction period
to  the  present,    tracing  events,    ancestry  and  happenings  to   our
present day.
The Weymouth  Historical  Society,     therefore,     asks  your  special
recognition  for  this  effort,      and  much credit  is  due those  collabo-
rators  who have worked so untiringly in their efforts  to  present the
present volumes.
The Society  has  a fine  collection  of  historical  matter,      and has
recorded  in  print  many  abstracts,      pamphlets  and  papers  dealing
with  earlier  history.        They also have many deeds,     maps and plans
which may be consulted upon application.
Of special  mention is  a  Bible  dated  1691 ;       English  Dictionary,
1702;      a  Columbian  Orator,     1799;       New Art  of  Gardening,    1652 ;
Bolton's   Sermons,        1625 ;        eighteen   volumes   of  biography,         one
written  on  Paul  Revere;      seventeen  volumes  on  Boston;     descrip

tions  of Old State House,  King's Chapel,   Bulfinch  Front,     Railroad
Jubilee,      Boston,    Records of Selectmen,    1634 to  1880;        thirty- three
volumes  on  Massachusetts,    History of Massachusetts Bay Colony,
1630 to  1692 ;     Weymouth Ways and  Peoples,    Homes of  our  Fore-
fathers;      fifteen  volumes on miscellaneous  subjects ;       genealogies  of

A very important feature of the Society is  its museum,    an ever-
growing  collection  which  occupies  the  second  floor  of  the  Fogg
Library,        which  is    the   present   home  of  the   Society.             Brought
together  by  many  people,    donated  by  Weymouth  citizens   and
others,      this  collection  is  on exhibition daily during library hours.
Herein  are  contained  the  original  deed  given by Wampatuck;
also  one signed  by Peregrine White.         Complete  files   of  the Wey-
mouth Gazette,     Vital  Records  of one hundred twenty-four  Massa-
chusetts towns,    gathered from church,   baptismal and town records.
Original  signatures  of  one hundred enlisted  men from Weymouth
in  reponse to Lincoln's call  for troops in  1861.
The membership of the Society is  about eighty,   and the present
executive officers  are  Howard H. Joy,    President,   South Weymouth,
and Rev. Wm.    Hyde,    Secretary,    Weymouth.
GRAND ARMY OF  THE  REPUBLIC
The military history has been assigned to  a special  chapter,     and
only a passing mention will be made of the G. A.  R.   The primary
object  of  the  body  is  the  relief  of  soldiers,    sailors   and  marines,
together  with  the  social  organization,     and in  the  years  following
the  Civil  War it  formed  one  of  the  greatest  factors  possible  in
Weymouth history.        The G. A.  R.  originated in Decatur,     Ill. ,     and
the  first  meeting  of  the  organization  was  held  at  that  place  on
April  6,     1866.    Its  aims  are many and varied,   -" to  collect  and
preserve  historic  relics  and documents pertaining  to  the  war;         to
aid  and  assist   sick  and  disabled   Union  veterans,      their   widows
and  orphans ;         to   observe   Memorial  Day by  suitable   patriotic
exercises  and the  decoration of the graves  of  fallen  comrades ;        to
keep  alive  the  cherished  incidents   of  the  camp  and  campaign;
and to teach lessons  of  patriotism to  the rising generation.  "
The  earliest   Post  in  Weymouth was  organized  in  North  Wey-
mouth,      Jan.  2,    1868,    and was named Lincoln  Post  No.  40,     having
for  its  first  Commander Gen.  B.  F.  Pratt,     a comrade from Post  15
in  Boston.             In August,   1873,   it  surrendered  its  charter,    and forty
of its members united with Post 58.
Reynolds  Post  58 was formed July  14,    1864,    and in five  years
numbered three hundred and nineteen members.            It was named in

whom many of  its  comrades  had  served.          The  names  of  the  ten

The highest  membership was  in  1883 when three  hundred  and
twenty- five  Comrades belonged  to  the Post.           It numbered,    Dec. 1,
1920,     fifty- two members.         The Post became a corporation Aug.  21,
1883 .
The social  history  of  the  G.  A.  R.  is   a  wonderful  chapter,     and
with it  goes  memories  of fairs,     parades,     Memorial  Day exercises,
flag  raisings ,      monument dedication,    patriotic  services  for  children,
etc.
At the  old   Town  House,     corner   of  Washington  and  Middle
Streets,      were  held  the  G.  A.  R.  fairs   of  Weymouth,      always  the
great event of the year,    and many of the most distinguished singers
and  entertainers   in  the  country  appeared  on  these  occasions.
Races  were run,   one,   which required four hundred laps  for  twenty
miles,      won by  Patsey Slattery  of  Hollis  Street,    South  Weymouth.
Rifle  practice  and  contests  of  all  sorts  filled  every  corner  of  the
big  building,     wonderfully  decorated,    and  with  such  attractions  it
was most profitable  to the Post.
Memorial Day is   always  observed  by the  Post,   and up to  1912
a grand dress  parade  was always held  on the green in front of the
Old South Church.

RELIEF  CORPS
Closely associated with the work of the G. A.  R.  is  the Woman's
Relief  Corps,            a company of ladies  enlisted  from  every  section  of
the  town,       whose  activities   consist  in  rendering  aid  to  those  in
need,        helping  those  whose  burdens  were  results  of  war  service,
also  directing  social   entertainments  and  helping  by  cash  dona-
tions  in  administration  of relief.       All loyal women are  eligible  to
membership.               Their meeting place is  in the G.  A.  R.  Hall at  East
Weymouth.
Reynolds  Corps  102 of Weymouth was organized Jan.  31,      1893,
with  Mrs.   Marion  Hastings  as  President,     and  with  74 charter
members.                   The  following  persons  have  served  as   presidents   of
the Relief Corps :
Marion E.  Hastings,   1893-94.
Sara E.  Cain,     1895-96.
Mary E.  Holbrook,     1897–98.
Margaret E.  Culley,     1899.
Flora D. Bicknell,    1900.
Helen C.  Cushing,     1901.
Junie E.  Morrill,    1902-03.
Addie W. Raymond,   1904-05.
Emeline Vining,     1906-07.
Carrie F.  Loring,    1908-09.
Mary E.  Mahoney,     1910–11.
Agnes F.  Baldwin,    1912-13.
Annie E. Jordan,    1914.
Ida L.  Keene,    1915-16.
Charlotte B. Stoddard,   1917-18.
Estelle W. Richards,     1919.
Mary E.  Brassil,     1920.
The Roll  Book bears four hundred and eighty- two names.
Mrs.  Mary  E.  Holbrook  of South  Weymouth was  Department
President  in   1912,      and  has  held  office   of  Department  Patriotic
Instructor  under two administrations.
The Woman's Relief  Corps was the pioneer in patriotic work in
our  schools.                The floating  of  a  flag  over  every  public  school  was
the  result  of its  work.           Each school  in  Weymouth has  been pre-
sented a  flag  by them,   the high school receiving  a large silk  parade
flag .               The  Corps  visits   schools   on  Memorial  Days,       enlists   the
children  in  patriotic  exercises,      provides  dinners  for  veterans  on
that  day,      distributes  flowers  and baskets,    and with  money brings
needed relief  to the veteran or the dependent ones.
The Corps  has  furnished  a room in the  Chelsea  Soldiers'     Home
and delegations often visit  the veterans  there,     and since the World
War they have sent  help  and wearing  apparel  to  the  boys  in  the
Parker  Hill  Hospital,      Brookline.          During the war the  Corps  had
its    preparedness   aides,        which  now  is   the   reconstruction   aides.
The President  visited  the  Food  Economy Kitchen,     North  Street,
Boston,      and Corps 102 extends  its  work and contributes  money to
the splendid work for undernourished children at the South End.
The  Corps  bought  liberally  of  Liberty  and  Victory  Bonds,      and
disbursed money to the G. A.  R.  Post  and for  flowers .
Corps  102 has done its  work so quietly that few outside the  Post
and  Corps  know of  its   many deeds  of  kindness,     of  its  splendid
patriotic work,     or  its  contributions  to  the calls  from  the  National
Department Headquarters to carry on the work for which they are
 - 199 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           677
banded  together.         The  interest   maintained  and  the  wonderful
results  obtained  stamp the work as  of the highest  order  and  one
worthy of all encouragement.
