Their  principles  are  along  the same lines  as  the G. A.  R.,       with
special reference to perpetuating the memory,   sacrifices and services
of  our  ancestors  for  the  preservation  of  the  Union;      inculcating
patriotism;    teaching truthful history and spreading and sustaining
the doctrine of equal rights,     universal liberty and justice to all.
They also band themselves together to  assist the G. A.  R. ,    extend
aid  to  the  widows  and  orphans,      and  give  proper  observance  of
Memorial Day and Union Defenders Day (February 12) .
To these younger men have descended the matter of service,    and
to them in the fullest  measure of responsibility  they  are  concerned
with  the  perpetuation  of  the  glorious  traditions  and  memories  of
the Grand Army of the Republic.
DAUGHTERS  OF  VETERANS
Dorothy  L.  Dix Tent 32  Daughters  of Veterans  was instituted
Oct.   30,     1906,     with  sixty- two  charter  members.            The  Tent  was
named Dorothy L. Dix in honor of the first  volunteer nurse accepted
by the government.
 - 200 - 
678                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
All   daughters   of   honorably  discharged   soldiers,        sailors   and
marines  who served  in the Union Army or  Navy during  the  Re-
bellion  of  1861-65,    whether members of the G.  A.  R.  or  not,     who
have reached  the age of fifteen  years,     are eligible for membership.
The object of this organization is  to aid and assist Union veterans
of  the  Civil  War,     their  widows  or  orphans,    and  to  cheer  them in
their declining years .
The  present  membership  is  one  hundred  and  forty-five,       this
being the largest Tent in  Massachusetts .
HISTORY  OF  SCOUTING  IN  WEYMOUTH
In  1911  Rev.  Walter  H.  Commons,      who was  then  the  pastor
of  the  Congregational  Church,      East Weymouth,    after  reading  the
Boy Scout Handbook,    edited by Gen. Baden Powell,   decided that
such  an  organization  would  be  valuable  training  for  the  young
boys  in  his   parish.         He  therefore  organized  a  scout  troop  and
asked  Mr.  Ernest  C.  Smith of  East Weymouth to  be scoutmaster.
Rev.  Robert  Cochran,     pastor of the Union Congregational Church
of  Weymouth  and  Braintree,      had,      however,     applied  for  a com-
mission previous to  this.         He never got to the point of organizing
a troop,     but his  commission was issued  before that of  Mr.  Smith.
The troop in  the East Weymouth Congregational Church was num-
bered  Troop  2,     although  it  is  really  the  oldest  organized  troop
in  town.            Troop  2  has  a  continued  existence  up  to  the  present
day,      and  now has  twenty- two  boys,    with  Mr.  Albin  Johnson  as
scoutmaster.
Mr.   Francis   Vaughan,       Weymouth  Landing,    applied  for  com-
mission  as  scoutmaster  in  1912,   and organized  a second  troop  in
Weymouth  in   1914.     He  resigned  to  take  commission  with  the
Sea  Scout  Organization.              Mr.  Howard  M.  Clark  of  Weymouth
Landing  succeeded him.         In  1917  Weymouth was joined with the
towns  of  Avon,          Braintree,        Cohasset,        Hingham,        Hull,         Scituate,
Randolph and Holbrook,    and formed the Old Colony Council with
an  employed  executive,        Mr.   Harold   Converse.              Mr.   Converse
was  succeeded  by Mr.  Howard  M.  Clark,      who was  in  turn  suc-
ceeded  by  Mr.  Duncan  MacKellar.         Under  the  present  council
management  scouting  has  increased  rapidly,     and  there  are  now
seven troops in Weymouth with a membership of 200 boys:      Troop
1 meets  in  the  Baptist  Church,      Weymouth  Landing,     and has  35
boys ;          Troop  2 meets  in  the  Weymouth  Congregational  Church,
with  25  boys;         Troop  3  meets  in  the  East  Weymouth Methodist
Church,         with  25  boys;        Troop  4  meets  in  the  Congregational
Church, Weymouth Heights,   with Frederick E. Lunt as scoutmaster ;
Troop 5  meets  in  the  Howe School,     South  Weymouth,      with  Mr.
Arthur  Sargeant  as  scoutmaster ;           Troop  6 meets  in  the  Congre-
gational   Church,       North  Weymouth,      with  Mr.  John  Tower  as
scoutmaster ;         Troop 7 meets in  the  Catholic Church of the Sacred
Heart Parish,    Weymouth Landing .
 - 201 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            679
The " major objectives "  of the Scout Organization are  character
building  and American citizenship  training.             This  organization  is
certainly doing its  good turn to the town of Weymouth in reducing
juvenile  crime and  making  better  citizens.           A camp  is   operated
at  Manomet,      Mass.,      every  year.              Here  one  hundred  and  sixty
boys  a week are  entertained.           The Scout  Organization  has  taken
an  active  part  in  all  movements  in  the  town,     such  as   Liberty
Loans,         War Saving Stamps,     etc.
Troop  5  Boy Scouts  of  America  of  South  Weymouth was  first
started by Charles  F.  Brown,    scoutmaster.
Permission  was  secured  of  the  Norfolk  Club  to  use  the  Fogg
Opera  House for  the opening meeting.          Troops  already formed  in
Weymouth  were  invited  to  demonstrate  to  the  gathering.          The
W.  R.  C.  were,    as  ever,     on hand and presented  Old Glory  to  the
new Troop 5.
Eight  boys  were enrolled  and started  to  hold  meetings  in  the
anteroom of the Opera House,    but soon this  was not large  enough
to  accommodate the troop,   as it  had grown to  a full  troop of thirty-
two members.          Sometimes  as  many as  forty  boys  attended  meet-
ings.            Charter members of Troop 5 were
William Ralph.
Elmer Grundstrom.
Otto Zwecker.
Earl Holbrook.
Leon Record.
William Hill .
Adrian Barnes .
Harold  Mowry.
Mr.  Brown,       not  being  able  to  continue  work  after  four  years
of  service,      secured  Mr.  Walter  Reed.            Later  Mr.  Harry  Granger
took  the  position,    and at the present  writing  Mr.  Arthur Sargent
has the troop,    holding meetings in the old  Howe School building.
Mr.  Ernest  Mowry was  assistant  scoutmaster  to  Troop 5 until
the World War started.         He then left the troop and enlisted in the
Marines,       and was killed in action in France.
AMERICAN  LEGION
The Order of  the American Legion  is  composed  of  the soldiers ,
sailors   and  Marines  who  were  members  of  the  American  Army
during the World War.
Weymouth Post  79 was organized June 27,     1919,    with  William
A.   Connell,           commander,        C.    Parker   Whittle,         vice- commander,
Pasquale   Santa   Croce,       adjutant,        Norman  A.   Walker,         finance
officer,          Charles   W.  Burton,       historian,        and  William   R.   Duffy,
chaplain.
Preamble to the Constitution :
For God and Country,    we associate  ourselves  together for  the following  pur-
poses:     To uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States  of America;
to  preserve  the  memories  and  incidents  of  our  association  in  the  Great  War;
to inculcate a sense of individual obligation to the Community,   State and Nation ;
to  combat the autocracy of both the classes  and the  masses;      to  make right the
 - 202 - 
680                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
master of might;      to  promote peace and good-will  on earth;     to safeguard  and
transmit   to  posterity  the  principles   of  justice,      freedom  and  democracy;         to
consecrate and sanctify our comradeship by our devotion to mutual helpfulness.
Weymouth  Post  meets  in  G.  A.  R.  Hall,      East Weymouth,      the
first  and third  Monday nights of each month,  is  uniformed accord-
ing  to  United States  Army regulations,    and has  a band composed
of  its  own members.           At present  (1920)   it  has  four  hundred  and
sixty-four members.
DAUGHTERS  OF  THE  REVOLUTION
A Chapter of  the Daughters of the  Revolution was organized  at
North  Weymouth March 8,    1898.    The organization  meeting  was
held in the ancient dwelling- house at  " Old Spain,"  which was once
the  parsonage  of  the  old  First  Church,    which  stood  at that  time
under  the  lee  of  Burying  Hill.          It  was  sold  and  removed  to  an-
other  site  about sixty years  ago.         This  probably was the house in
which  Abigail  Smith,      the  daughter  of  Rev.  William  Smith  and
Elizabeth   ( Quincy)   Smith,     was  born  and  reared.          She  afterward
became the wife of John Adams,    the patriot and President,    and the
mother  of  John  Quincy  Adams,       who  also  was  President  of  the
United  States.              The State  regent,     Miss  Sarah  E.  Hunt,      presided
and   appointed    the   following-named   officers:           Regent,           Miss
Georgiana   A.   Robbins;         recording   secretary,         Miss   Antoinette
Pray;         corresponding  secretary,       Miss  Dora  E.  Smith;          treasurer,
Miss Josie Cummings.      The Chapter has taken the name of Abigail
Smith  Chapter,       D.  R.    So large  was  the  attendance  that  it  was
thought  best  to  adjourn  to  the parlors  of the Universalist  Church
near   by  for   the  addresses   which  were  made  by  Hon.          Charles
Francis   Adams,      a  great-grandson  of  Abigail  Smith  Adams;       the
president   of   the  Weymouth  Historical   Society,    John  J.    Loud;
Rev.  Edward E.  Morris,    pastor of the Universalist  Church,     North
Weymouth;       Mrs.  Emma O.  Perkins,      Miss  Clara  B.  Adams  and
Miss  Hunt.             A gavel  made of  wood  from  the belfry  of  the  old
North   Church,         Boston,         was   presented   to   the   Chapter.             The
different  parts  of Weymouth are  represented in the Chapter mem-
bership.              Besides the State regent there  were present  Mrs. Dudley
R.  Child,     the  State treasurer,    and Mrs. John A. Heath of the State
council.            Representatives   from  the  Adams  Chapter  of  Quincy
also  came,       bringing  congratulations  to  their  sister  Chapter.           The
occasion  was  one of  great  interest,     serving  to  inspire  Weymouth
women with new zeal in  patriotic work.
SUSANNAH  TUFTS  CHAPTER,        D.  A.  R.
Susannah  Tufts  Chapter,      Daughters  American  Revolution,        of
Weymouth,         was  organized  in  January,      1899.     In  naming  this
Chapter  the  members  decided  to  honor  one  of  the  citizens   of
Weymouth,    -conspicuous  during  the  Revolutionary  War for  his
 - 203 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           681
ardor,      activity and zeal,    and a liberal  contributor in  money,     -so
bestowed upon it the name of Susannah Tufts,    wife of Dr.  Cotton
Tufts,     who was an ardent supporter of the cause of liberty.
Susannah  Tufts  was  one  of  eleven  children  of  Maj.          Philemon
Warner and  Mary Prince,    and was born in Gloucester  March 20,
1745.
The Chapter  received  its  charter  Oct.  25,     1900.    Meetings  are
held  regularly  each  month  from  September  to   May,       inclusive.
Many of  the  members are  from Weymouth Landing,    and latterly
the meetings  have been held  at the homes of the members.             The
Chapter   furnished   a  " Susannah  Tufts "   bed  in  the  maternity
hospital  at  San  Juan,       P.   R. ,     and  has  contributed  money  to  the
McKinley and the Walcott Memorials,   the Spanish War Fund for
nurses,     and  to  the Memorial  Continental  Hall.          The  Chapter  has
for   many  years   been  interested   in   the   Hindman  School   in
Kentucky,    and has provided money for  two scholarships  besides
help  in  other ways.         The International  College  at  Springfield  has
also been the recipient of ample gifts.
HISTORICAL  RECORD OF  THE AMERICAN  LEGION  AUXILIARY  FROM
ITS  ORGANIZATION  TO  APRIL 3,      1922
In  the Assembly  Hall  of  the Weymouth High School,       on Sept.
19,      1920,     at  3  o'clock  P.M. ,    a public meeting was held  to  organize
a women's auxiliary unit to Weymouth Post 79,  American Legion.
Post   Commander  Bryan  Leonard  opened  the  meeting  and  in-
troduced  Mr. J.  J.  Mullin,   Jr.,   State organizer,   who explained the
object  and the work of an auxiliary.        Post  Commander Leonard
asked  Mrs.  K.  B.   Howley,    chairman  of  the  Women's  Auxiliary
Committee,      to take the chair,    but she wished to be excused.          Mrs.
J.   Herbert  Libby of  East Weymouth was elected acting president,
and  Mrs.  Philip  Haviland  of  Weymouth  was  elected  secretary.
There was  a good  attendance  from all  parts  of the  town at  this
meeting,       and much enthusiasm  was shown.         It was decided  that
the  first  regular  meeting  of the  newly  organized  unit  should  be
held  in  G.  A.  R.  Hall,    East Weymouth,   on the evening of Oct.  4,
1920.
The  first   regular  meeting  of  the  Unit  was  held  on  Monday
evening,    Oct. 4,   1920,    at  8  o'clock  P.M. ,    at  G. A.  R.  Hall,     and the
following  officers  were elected:
President,    Mrs. J.  Herbert Libby,    East Weymouth.
Vice-President,  Mrs. Egbert V. Warren,   East Weymouth.
Secretary,   Mrs. Philip Haviland,   Weymouth.
Treasurer,    Miss Hazel Dexheimer,    Weymouth.
Mrs.  Mary  J.   Reilley  of  Weymouth  was  elected  chairman  of
the Executive Board,    with Mrs.  Leah Rockwood and Miss  Pauline
Dowd as  members of the  Board.
A temporary  charter  of the  Unit was granted  on Oct.  8,      1920,
 - 204 - 
682                             LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
by which  the  " Auxiliary  acknowledges  jurisdiction  and  declares
itself to be in all things subject to the constitution of the American
Legion and the rules,    regulations,    orders  and laws  promulgated  in
pursuance thereof.... Each Auxiliary  Unit pledges itself  through
its  members to  uphold,    protect,      and defend the Constitution of the
United  States  and  the  principles   of  true  Americanism,      for   the
common welfare  of  the  living  and  in  solemn  commemoration  of
those who died that Liberty might not perish from the earth. "
American  women  have  always   confronted   the  terrible   after-
effects  of war with  wonderful love and earnestness,     and this  Unit
started  on  its   work  with  the  feeling  that  its  members  could  by
steady  persistence  mitigate,     to  some extent,     at  least,       the  horrors
of  the  World War and bring  to  those  in hospitals  and to the sick
and disabled at home as many comforts as possible,   together with a
vast amount of sympathy for  and interest  in  all those who served,
either directly or indirectly,   and sacrificed  so much for the common
good.               The members of the Unit aim for  the  same attributes  that
the colors  of our American flag signify,   viz. ,   courage,    zeal,    fervency,
purity,      cleanness  of  life,     rectitude  of  conduct,   loyalty,     devotion,
friendship,    justice  and truth.
Mrs.  Christine Flynn,    at the meeting held on Nov. 1,      1920,     sug-
gested  that  the  Unit should  hold  a  candy sale  at the  dance to  be
given  by Legion Post 79,   the proceeds  to be donated to  the  Post.
This  suggestion  resulted in the Unit's  first  financial offering  to the
Post;       $50  was  presented  by  the  President,      Mrs.  Libby,       to   Post
Commander Leonard,     at  the  meeting of  Dec.  6,     1920,     to  be used
as  the Post should deem advisable.
At the November,     1920,    meeting  Mrs.  Katherine  Peers  of  East
Weymouth was chosen guard,    and Mrs.  Drusilla  Davis,    conductor.
Miss  Lillian  Smith was chosen pianist.
It  had  become apparent  that a  Relief  Committee should be ap-
pointed,       and  at  the  third   regular  meeting,       Dec.  6,          1920,          the
following  members were  appointed  to  act  on this  committee :
Mrs. Leah Rockwood,    Chairman.
Mrs.  Laura Rand,     North Weymouth.
Miss Marion Melville,    South Weymouth.
Mrs. Mary Reilley,    Weymouth.
Mrs. Emma Hawkesworth,    East Weymouth.
The President gave a very interesting talk on the " get- together "
meeting  held in the  Public  Library,      Boston,    at  the  Unit's  regular
meeting  on  Jan.  3,       1921.    She  urged  each  and  every  member  to
attend  these  meetings  at  the  Public Library,     in  Boston,    whenever
possible.             Mrs.  Libby  also  told  how generously  the  people  of  the
town  had  contributed  in  response  to  the  call  for  candies,       fruits,
cakes,      etc. ,      at  Christmas  for  the  boys  at  West  Roxbury  Hospital.
She  especially  mentioned  the  fact  that  Miss  Clara  Tanguy  had
solicited  among the young ladies  at the local  Telephone  Exchange
seventeen  pounds  of  homemade candy.        Three  pairs  of  hand-knit

At this  meeting  the  matter  of  procuring  and presenting  Wey-
mouth  Post  79  with  a  Legion  flag   was  taken  up.          Mrs.  Delia
Caulfield  was  appointed  to  get  what  assistance  possible  from  the
other patriotic  organizations  of the  town,   and the Auxiliary  would
help  out when she  reported  back,     inasmuch  as  the  price  of  the
flag   was  prohibitive  for  so  youthful  an  organization.         This  flag
was  presented  at  a special  meeting  of  Weymouth Post,     so  that  it
could be used by the Post on Memorial  Day.
The first  installation  of  Weymouth  Post  79 was  on  March  11,
1921 ,       and  supper  was  provided  by  the  ladies  of  the  Auxiliary,
after which came the installation  and dancing.
At the April,     1921 ,      meeting of the  Unit,      Mrs.  Leah  Rockwood
and Miss  Pauline  Dowd resigned  from the  Executive  Committee.
Mrs.   Laura  Rand  of  North  Weymouth  and  Mrs.  Alys  Hall  of

Daughters  of  Veterans,     through  Mrs.  Jennie  Morton,      Patriotic
Instructor,         presented   the   Auxiliary   Unit  with  four   beautiful

American  flags,     similar  to  the  flags  used  by  their  color  bearers.
This gift  was greatly appreciated by the Unit,    as it showed  such a

A successful  whist party and candy sale  held on May 11,     1921 ,
in the afternoon,     at G. A.  R.  Hall,     netted about $46.
The Auxiliary  made  an  especial  effort  to  assist  in  every  way
possible  on  Memorial  Day.               Mrs.  Warren  efficiently  directed  an
able  corps  of  assistants  in  preparing  and  serving  a dinner  for  the
members  of  Weymouth  Post  79,      in  Odd  Fellows  Opera  House.
Food  left   over  from  this  dinner  was  sold  by Mrs.  Warren,       who
proved herself a good  saleswoman,    as  well  as  eager to care for  the
financial  interests of the Unit and  not waste.
On Saturday  prior  to  Memorial  Day,      May 28,       1921 ,        the  Unit
held  a  tag  day,     in  co-operation  with  the  Legion,    to  sell  poppies
to  be worn on  Memorial Day in memory of those now sleeping  in
Flanders field.        The poppies were made by French women and were
sold for  the benefit of the orphaned children of France.
On Memorial  Day the  Unit  provided  wreaths  to  decorate  the
graves  of  those  who had made the  supreme sacrifice.               Up to  this
time two of the members of the Unit had passed on,          -Mrs. Mary
Slattery   and  Mrs.   Elizabeth  Wrinn,       and  a  committee  was  ap-
pointed  to  place  wreaths  on  their  graves.           Mrs.  Bessie  Edwards,
State President of the Women's Auxiliary,   requested that each Unit
should  present  to  all  gold  star  mothers,      or  to  those  who filled  the
place of mothers,     bouquets of pansies.          Twenty-one bouquets  were
presented by this  Unit .
At the June meeting,    a check of $10 from the Special Aid Society
of  the  Old  South  Church  of  South  Weymouth,    for  welfare  work
at  West Roxbury Hospital,    was gratefully acknowledged.
The July  meeting  of  the  Norfolk  County  Council  was  held  at
the  home  of  Mrs.  Egbert  Warren,      on  Middle  Street,      East  Wey-
mouth.              Miss Verzari,    representative of the North American Civic
League  for   Immigrants,    told  in  a very interesting  way the  tribu-
lations  and  struggles  of the immigrants  who come to  the  United
States.
In July the Unit donated $10 to the moving-picture fund of the
Norfolk County Tubercular Hospital  at  Braintree.
Aug.  6,       1921,     the  Field  Day of  the  Weymouth  Post,       will  long
be remembered by both the Post and the Auxiliary  as  an exceed-
ingly warm,    busy day,    but O Boys !      what a success  it  was !         In the
morning the boys  were getting  everything  on the field  ready,     and
many of  the  Auxiliary  members  were  busy  making  pies  for  the
supper,     which  was  served  so  efficiently  and  successfully  by Mrs.
Warren,       assisted  by  many  of  the  members  of  the  Unit.               This
supper  netted  $170 which was turned over to the  Post.          Mrs. Leah
Rockwood reported  $31.05  realized from the grabs.

The first  grand minstrel show and bazaar of the American Legion
Auxiliary  was  produced  on  Feb.  16,      1922,      at  Odd  Fellows  Hall,
East Weymouth.        A splendid  vaudeville  program  was  composed
of  an  overture  by  Tower's  Orchestra,       and  orchestra   selections ;
reading  by  Catherine  Kelchner;      violin  selections  by Hazel  Clark
Leonard;    and  the  Trowbridge  Sisters   entertained  with  " some
jazz. "    Then came the  minstrel  program,       which was greatly  en-
joyed.            The idea of  the minstrel  show originated with  Mrs.  Libby,
who  was  chairman  of  committee.            Mrs.  Libby  threw  her  home
open for  rehearsals,     and in  every way was influential  in making an
immense success  of  not  only the minstrel  show but the  bazaar  as
well.          The welfare fund was helped greatly by the financial  success
of this  entertainment,     as  between $500 and $600 was the net sum
realized.
The daisy drive carried  on by the American Legion on February
24 and 25,    for their unfortunate comrades,    out of employment,    sick
or needy,    was enthusiastically and actively  supported by the  Unit.
Captains  were appointed to  cover the different  parts  of  the town,
with the Unit president as chief of the captains.         The response was
most  gratifying.         The total  receipts  for  the daisy drive netted  the
American Legion $375.36,    of which 40 per cent went to State head-
quarters  and 60 per cent,     or  $225.22,    to  Weymouth Post 79,    to  be
used  for   the  relief   and  care  of   needy  veterans   of   Weymouth,
whether Legion members or  not.
At the meeting of March 6,   1922,    the  following committees were
appointed for the year :
Finance Committee,     Mrs. Alys Hall.
Refreshment Committee,    Mrs. Mary Talbot.

Announcement was made at the regular meeting of April 3,      1922,
that a store was to be opened April 10,   1922,   at 443 Boylston Street,
Boston,   for  the sale of articles  made by disabled ex-service men of
Massachusetts  or  any  member of  their  families.         This  store  will
offer  to  the  disabled  man receiving  vocational  training,       or  any
other  veteran,     an  opportunity  to  sell  the  articles  that  he makes
and thereby increase his income,   which in many instances  is  insuffi-
cient.        Massachusetts  is  the  first  State  to  take  this  step,    and  the
new store is  only the first of what the Auxiliary to the Legion hopes
will be a series  of small stores.        The result will be to encourage the
unfortunate  victims  of the  World  War more than  any words  can
do,      as  actions  speak louder than words .
At the April  meeting  Mrs.  Libby  announced  her  appointment
by Mrs.  Bishop,     President  of  the  State  Department,      as  welfare
worker  for   the  towns  of  Avon,       Braintree,       Cohasset,      Holbrook,
Quincy and Weymouth.
The  charter  of  the  American  Legion  Auxiliary  to  Weymouth
Post  79 was  closed  at the January,     1922,     meeting,    at which  time
there  were  one  hundred  and  six  members.          The Unit's  gold  star
mothers are Mrs. Mary Talbot,    Mrs. Charles Mowry,    Mrs. Klinge-
man  and  Mrs.  Wellbrock.         This  Unit  was  one  of the  first   to  be
organized in  Massachusetts.
WEYMOUTH  CHAPTER,       AMERICAN  RED  CROSS
In  the  early  days  of  the  World  War various  associations  were
formed for  the production of  surgical  dressings  and garments.            Of
these,      the one best known on the South Shore was the  Special Aid
Society  which  organized  groups  in  all  of  the  towns.         After  the
United States entered the war it  was the  Red Cross which the gov
 - 210 - 
688                               LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
ernment recognized,    and it became necessary that all  articles should
meet the  requirements specified by the Red Cross.            This led  to  the
formation of  Red Cross units  or chapters  all  over  the country,     and
most  chapters  had numerous  branches  in their  adjacent towns.
Thus  when  the  Metropolitan  Chapter  was  formed  in  Boston,
her  branches  developed  in all  the smaller  cities  and  towns  of the
metropolitan district.
The Weymouth branch came into  being at a meeting held at  the
Fogg  Library  in  South  Weymouth in  November,      1917,       at  which
time there were officially  only 147  Red Cross members;       but at the
end  of  the  first  year  4,000  members  had been  added.            The  first
officers   to  be  elected  were  Mrs.  Freeman  Putney,    Jr. ,      chairman;
Dr.  Rudolph  Jacoby,    vice- chairman;            Mrs.  Walter  R.  Field,      sec-
retary;       and  Mr.   Edwin  R.  Sampson,     treasurer,      an  office  which
he has held continuously  since that time.
The Red Cross work was begun at once in the workrooms of the
Special  Aid Society,    already  well established  in  the four  villages .
A joint  committee was appointed for  conference,    consisting of  the
officers  of the  Red Cross,      the chairman of the Special Aid and the
four  workroom  chairmen,     Mrs.  Elbridge  Nash,    Mrs.  Kate  Pierce
Thayer,        Miss  Lillian  Curtis  and Miss  Katherine  Fraser;       also  Mr.
W. Carlton Barnes and Mr.  Prince H. Tirrell.
During that  first  year,     through the combined efforts  of the Red
Cross  and  the  Special  Aid,    the  following  articles  were  sent  forth
from those four workrooms:        10,042  pieces  of sewing,   4,888 knitted
garments,     and 163,457 surgical dressings.
Shortly  after  the  United States  entered  the  war and  our young
men entered  the  service,      there  came the  realization  that  as  these
young  men left  home,    it  frequently  meant that  the  chief  bread-
winner was taken away,   leaving a family with the problem of  re-
adjustment  to  face,      and  often  causing  much  suffering,     increased
by the worry for  those who had gone.         It was then that the Red
Cross  instituted  its  Home Service  through which an endeavor was
made to  reach  every  man and the family  of  every  man who en-
listed;         financial  assistance  was given  when  needed,     and friendly
services  of  every variety  were rendered.           It was not meant that  a
single family should be the worse for giving its  members to the war.
To be sure,       the government insisted  that  every  man with depend-
ents  should  make an  allotment  of  his  pay which the  government
would supplement if  necessary with an allowance.          With the rapid
movement of troops and the enormity of the proposition,   the money
did not come through  immediately,     so  that if  it  had not been for
the ample resources  of  the  Red Cross  and their immediate service,
the results  might have been unfortunate.
This all had its  bearing upon the men as members of the National
forces.                Having confidence  in  the  Red Cross,     which they felt  was
present  to  meet any situation in their families,    they  were relieved
of  worry and thus  enabled to give themselves  up to  being  efficient
soldiers  and sailors .
 - 211 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           689
At first  this  work was handled by the  Chapter,   but in October,
1918,       a committee was  appointed  to  consider  Home Service  as  a
branch activity,    and in February,    1919,    a Home Service Committee
was appointed with Mr.  Edwin R. Sampson chairman.            The other
members were Mrs. J.  Herbert  Libby  and Miss Katherine  Fraser
for  East  Weymouth,     Dr.  Rudolph Jacoby  and Mr. Joseph  Kelly
for   Weymouth,      and Mr.   Prince   H.   Tirrell   with   Mr.  Matthew
O'Dowd for  South Weymouth.            The executive and clerical  work of
the committee was to be done through the established office  of the
Quincy branch.
To be sure,    this  was after  the Armistice,   but the troops  were re-
turning;        men did  not  find  immediate  employment  and  become
readjusted;       besides,    there were the sick and wounded troops  being
returned  to  their  families.      These  men  were  to  be  followed  until
they recovered,     and were able to take their places in the community
as  self- supporting citizens.           The government had made plans  that
the  Public Health  Department should attend to the further physi-
cal  needs  of  the  men;   that  compensation  should be given  to  men
not able to work,    and where men were unable to pursue their former
occupations  they should be trained in some line  that would insure
for  them  independence  and  self- respect  in  the  future.           Again,      it
seemed  necessary for the Red Cross  to  grease the wheels of govern-
ment  procedure  and assist  the men in making  their  connections
with  the  proper  government  agencies.            The  problem  grew  very
rapidly,       beyond all  expectations,     and  the  problem still  continues.
The  Home Service  makes  no  decisions  upon  men's  claims  upon
the government,   but every chapter and branch feels  that in order
to  fulfill  the  sacred  responsibility  assumed  under  the  Red  Cross
Charter,     they must continue until the last  man is  satisfied.
While the  Home Service  was becoming very active  the produc-
tion  still  continued on through  the  year  1920,     and large  consign-
ments were sent  out for hospital  work as  well as  for  people  in  the
stricken  countries.       In the  spring  and fall  of 1919  the  branch  re-
sponded  generously  to  the  call  for  used  garments  to  be  sent  to
Belgium and northern  France.
Following  the close  of  the  war,    the  National  Red Cross  made
plans for continuing work,    developing a Peace Time Program which
should  endeavor  to  " conserve  the   vitality  of  the  Nation. "     In
accordance with this plan,   on Dec. 30,    1919,    the Weymouth branch
appointed  a  Public  Health  Committee  which  was  given  power
whereby they should secure  a  nurse at a salary of $1,200 per year ;
such a nurse was installed as nurse in the schools of Weymouth for
the year  1919-20.
In the  fall  of  1920  membership  returns  were  greatly  reduced,
with the result that the branch now felt it was able to meet only its
Home Service obligations.
On April  12,     1921 ,    after  due consideration,    the branch voted  to
petition the New England Division of the  Red Cross  to  become  a
chapter,       thus  separating  itself   from  the  Metropolitan  Chapter;
 - 212 - 
690                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
this  petition was acceded to and a charter was granted on Sept.  9,
1921.
Up to  March  1,    1922,    however,     the  Home Service  work of  the
Chapter  was carried  at the office  of the  Quincy Red Cross,     where
a full- time  worker  was  maintained  and  the  Weymouth  Chapter
assumed  its  proportion  of  the  overhead  expenses.        Upon inquiry
it  was  discovered  that  Weymouth could  manage a less  expensive
way of  having  her  work done,    and,     it  was  believed,      a  more  ad-
vantageous  way.         The services  of  a worker were procured  for  one
day a week,    and she was established for work,    with desk room in the
town office at East Weymouth on March 1,    1922.
During  the  year  the  Home  Service  work  has  been  followed
closely;    there have been some demands for  material  relief  to  tide
over  short  periods;      numerous  men have been given  assistance  in
the  technicalities  of  prosecuting  their  compensation  claims  upon
the  government;          one  or  two  old  allotment  and  allowance  diffi-
culties  required  attention;      help was given in making proper  appli-
cation  for  State  bonuses ;        and  what  seems  very  important  is   the
service which we are at times called  upon to  render  to  the doctors
and workers  in  hospitals  where our men are  receiving  treatment;
they depend largely  upon this .
The  past  fall   and  winter  the  Chapter  has  filled   its   quota  of
layettes  assigned  to  it,    and made a  contribution  of  used  clothing
for  the  refugees who fled  to  Greece after the burning of  Smyrna.
An information  service  has  been offered  to all  requiring  this  in
any line whatsoever.
More recently  it  has been deemed possible  to  render  assistance
in a few  civilian  families,    particularly  where  there was  a special
health  problem,    and the  Chapter is  at  this  time considering a con-
tinued program and how it  may make the largest  offering  towards
" conserving  the  vitality  of the  Nation. "
THE  SPECIAL  AID  SOCIETY  OF  AMERICAN  PREPAREDNESS
In  February,        1917,     fully  two months  before  the  United  States
entered  the  World  War,       a  meeting  of  representative  women  of
Weymouth  was  called  at  the  home  of  Mrs.  Albert  Worthen  of
Weymouth,       for  the  purpose  of  forming  a  branch  of  the  Massa-
chusetts  Special Aid Society of American Preparedness.           A society
with a long  name,    but every word of it  with a vital  and farseeing
purpose.
Mrs.  Barrett Wendell of Boston,  President of the Massachusetts
S.  A.  S.  A.  P.,    made those present  realize  the  need  of  such  an or-
ganization  in  Weymouth,     and  a  general  chairman  for  the  town
was chosen that day,              Mrs.  Carleton Barnes of South Weymouth.
The local   chairmen  were  selected  also,                         Mrs.  Elbridge  Nash
for   South  Weymouth  and  Miss  Lillian   Curtis   (afterwards  Mrs.
Albert Gladwin)  for North Weymouth.         These two chairmen served
during  the  existence  of  the  Society.           Mrs.  Kate  Pierce  Thayer
 - 213 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           691
for  Weymouth,     and  Miss  Katherine  Fraser  in  East  Weymouth,
brought  their  respective  organizations  through the  first  hard  year
of  the  war  period,     and  were  succeeded  in  Weymouth  by  Mrs.
Elmer Alexander and  Mrs.  Jennie  B.  Worster,     and  in  East Wey-
mouth by Mrs. George W. Perry .
Meetings  in  each  part  of  the  town  were  called  within  a  few
days,       in  order  to  perfect  the  local  organizations  and  chairmen  of
sewing,      knitting,   outfit,   bandage,   and ways and means committees
were then appointed.
The significant  fact  of the geographical location of  Weymouth,
being next to the Hingham Arsenal and on the coast brought home
to its  women the especial  need of "preparedness,  "  and as the men
had their Home Guards and Public Safety Committees,    the women
met at  first  to sew and prepare for any local emergency or disaster
that  might  occur.              A regular   first-aid   medicinal  and  hospital
outfit  was purchased and kept on hand in case of need.
Thus  when  the  United  States,      on  April  6,      1917,     did  actually
enter the war,    the Special Aid Society was in working order,      ready
to  help  the  men of  Weymouth.         This was pre-eminently  its  pur-
pose for  the  next  few years,                     to  see  that  not  a  man went  into
the  army or  navy without  a warm and  serviceable  outfit,      which
included a sweater,    socks,    helmet,    wristers,    handy kit and pajamas.
Of course this took money,    and as  the dues were very small,     the
finance,     ways and means  committees,     and men of  the  town were
constantly  arranging  pop  concerts,      card  parties,     mammoth  lawn
fêtes,             moving-picture   shows,       dances,         childrens'       entertainments,
etc.,       to  raise  the  necessary  funds.       Finally  a system  of donations
by " systematic giving " was worked out.        A large corps  of women
and  girls   divided  into  squads,       made  a  house  to  house  canvass
every week,    collecting pledges made to the  S.  A. S.  of sums varying
from  10 cents  a week to  $5 from men,   women and children.          This
ensured  the  society  a definite income,   amounting to  several  thou-
sands  of  dollars  yearly.            Every contributor  thus became a member
of  the Special Aid,    working for the men of Weymouth.
The first few who went across  before  December,    1917,    were sent
Christmas  gift  boxes,    and in  1918 the  many abroad  were  remem-
bered with Christmas cards and $2 bills,  -the first  cash that some
of them had seen for many a long day.
Each  part  of  Weymouth had its  separate  Special  Aid  Society,
workroom,      chairman,     and committees,    but they all united in their
desire  to  help  the home boys,    wherever  they  were,                    in camps in
the  United States,   on the warships,    or in foreign  service.           Besides
two  or  more days  of  serving  a week,     they  met for  several  after-
noons  and  evenings  to  make surgical  dressings,    in  churches,      halls
and engine houses.    And everywhere and at all  times the knitters
plied  their  busy needles.          The total output was truly  enormous.
The scope  of  the  work of  the  S.  A.  S.  was  varied,   -" Special
Aid "   wherever  needed.           They  answered  calls  from  ships  leaving
port  for  warm knitted  garments,     and  gave pajamas  to  hospitals.
 - 214 - 
692                               LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
The sailors  of  Camp Hingham were given  a mammoth husking
bee,     supper  and  dance,    besides  being  entertained  by individuals
in their own homes at various  times.          The S.  A. S.  helped support
the  Officers '             House  at  Camp Devens,    the  Major  Willard  House,
and  the  one towards  the close of the war located  in  Boston.              The
societies  gave war- time courses  in  food  conservation  and cookery,
and organized  to  cook  and  carry  food  to  families  laid  low by the
dreaded  flu   epidemic.         They  contributed   tons  of  clothing  and
several hundreds of dollars  to the Halifax relief fund.          They partici-
pated  in  the   Fifth  Victory  Liberty  Loan  parade  and  also   the
Armistice  torchlight  parade,    and its  members  helped  the men in
all  the drives during the war.
They sewed for the American Fund for  French  Wounded,       Bel-
gian Relief and American Red Cross.         They made surgical dressings
by the thousands  for  the  Peter  Bent  Brigham  Hospital  Unit  and
the  Red  Cross.             Even  the  school  children  were  organized   into
Junior Special Aid Societies.
When the men began to  come back the Special  Aid gave them
banquets,   entertainments,     welcome  home  greetings  and  gifts   of
money.            The Massachusetts  S.  A.  S.  A.  P.  supported the Wendell
House  in  Boston,      a  house  with  a home atmosphere  for  soldiers
and sailors.            Weymouth furnished one of its  rooms,    and Weymouth
women acted  as  hostesses for  one afternoon and evening a week.
The situation  in  Weymouth  in  regard  to  the  relation  between
the  Special  Aid and Red Cross  was  unique to  Weymouth.           There
was  a  Central  Red Cross  chairman and committee for  the  town as
a whole,      but automatically the local  S.  A.  S.  chairmen became also
the  local  Red Cross  chairmen,    as  the  Special  Aid workrooms  did
also  the  Red  Cross  work.            This was possible because the personnel
and membership of the two organizations  were one and the  same,
carrying  on  both  Special  Aid  and  Red  Cross  work.            Each  local
society  had its  treasury with  Red Cross  money used only for  Red
Cross  work,      and Special  Aid money used for the "Special Aid "  of
its   own  Weymouth  service  men,   -an  amiable  and  convenient .
arrangement,        as  it  fulfilled  the  very  vitally  broad  scope  of  the
American  Red Cross  program,    and yet the women of  Weymouth
had the honor of  providing for the individual  needs of  every man
who  served  Weymouth in  the  World  War,      and  of  reserving  part
of  the  S.  A.  S.  funds  for  a memorial  or  memorials  to  those  who
sacrificed  their lives in that war.
POLITICAL
The political  history of Weymouth has played its  part in as  full
measure  as  any town in  the  Commonwealth.        From  the  earliest
times down to and through the Rebellion we have had our share.
We had the Abolitionists  and the anti- slavery camps,    the differ-
ence  being  that  the  former were  much  more  radical  in  that they
used every means against slavery and were absolutely uncompromis-
 - 215 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           693
ing,     and their  rabid  attitude drove many eminent men from  their
ranks.             They held that  " immediate,    unconditional  emancipation,
without  expatriation,    was  the  right  of  every  slave  and  could  not
be withheld by his master without sin.  "
The chief exponent in New England was the editor of the Boston
paper,        " The  Liberator, "   William  Lloyd  Garrison,       who  in   1831
advocated the " liberation of slaves  regardless  of  all  laws or  consti-
tutional  provisions to  the contrary. "
In  Weymouth,      Garrison   made  several   speeches,      and  in   the
years  following  1831  a  society  gained  headway with  the  above
tenets  as  their guide.     In his efforts  he was seconded by such able
speakers  as  Wendell  Phillips,     Parker  Pillsbury,    Edwin Thompson
and  Theodore  Parker.        All  of  these  men  delivered  speeches  in
Weymouth,      several  of  which  were  made in  the  new  Universalist
Church at Weymouth Landing.
Gradually  the  anti-slavery  feeling  grew,    and  the  years  of  the
early  fifties   saw  further  aggressive  tactics  of  northern  statesmen
and parties,     and the political  movement of 1854 can never be for-
gotten.           It was at this  time that Weymouth,    as well as the whole
country,     organized  a great  secret  society  called  the " Know Noth-
ings. "     Secret  lodges  were  formed  everywhere,      with  passwords,
grips  and  solemn  initiations.           The  candidate  took  his  oath  of
secrecy  on the  Bible.       Required  age was twenty-one years.             Born
in  the United States,    and neither himself,   his  parents  nor his  wife
were  Roman  Catholics,     but  had  been  reared   under  Protestant
influences.           After  affirming  these  facts  he  was  conducted  to  an
inner chamber where on a raised  platform sat the worthy president,
and  there  he took  the  oath  of  secrecy  and  swore  to  vote  for  no
man other than a Protestant American citizen.
Its  further  aim  was  to  pass  very  stringent  naturalization  laws
in order to make practically powerless the large number of emigrants
then  settling  in the  United  States,     and  through  other  means  to
check the growth of foreign influences and ideas.
Passwords,      grips  and signs  were given to the new member,    and
he was  taught  the  challenge.      Meeting  a  brother  he  must  ask,
" What time? "     The answer  would  be given,     " Time for  work. "
Next he would  say,   "Are you? "    And the  answer  would  come,
" We are. "
The great  mystery was the name of the organization;      this  the
president  alone could  give.           At the  proper  time  he solemnly de-
clared,        " Brothers,     you  are  now  members  in  full  fellowship  with
the  Supreme  Order  of  the  Star  Spangled  Banner. "     The  official
name was  " The American Party. "    When one inquired of a member
of  the  party  what its  principles  were,   the  answer  was,     " I   know
nothing, "  and from this  the  party was  named  in  derision,       " The
Know Nothings. "
In Weymouth the Order met in the Town Hall,   and Mr.  Abner
Holbrook and  Mr.  Daniel  Dyer were very prominent.         They were
the candidates  nominated for  the General  Court,     and were chosen
 - 216 - 
694                             LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
by  an  almost  unanimous  vote,    and  were  re-elected   the  second
year.
In  1854,        Horace  Greeley,    editor  of  the  New York Tribune,     was
foremost  in  the formation of the Republican party.           He was  anti-
slavery and prohibitionist,    but strongly opposed to Know Nothing-
ism.                Henry  Ward  Beecher's  political   articles   appeared  in  the
" New York  Independent, "  and he also  was  opposed  to  the  prin-
ciples  of  the  Know Nothing party.         In  1858  the  Know Nothing
deluge had in  a great  degree  subsided,    and soon  after  the  party
great
passed out of existence.
THE WIDE-AWAKES
A peculiar feature  of  the  1860 campaign was  the  development
of a new spirit  in the North that was  quickened by the organiza-
tion known as  the  "Wide-Awakes. "     This  was a Republican  or-
ganization uniformed by white caps and white capes,   and each one
carrying  a  torch  in  night  processions.            Many of  these  drilled  as
military  companies,     for  the  threat  of  war came  up with  almost
every echo from the South.        The young men,  and especially  those
just from our colleges,   entered largely into the Lincoln Wide-Awake
ranks.           It  is   related  by  eyewitnesses  that  much  ceremony  was
observed  at  the  night  parades,      and  that  during  these  times  the
houses  of the village  were decorated and lighted up along the line
of the parade.
One of  their  trips  was by horseback to  hear Belva  Lockwood,     a
presidential candidate,   speak in Braintree.           They were accompanied
by  the  Weymouth  band  and  were  greeted  by  cheers  along  the
route  of  procession.
The  Wide-Awakes  existed  only  a  short  time  about  1860,        and
were working  on the  Republican side for  the election  of Abraham
Lincoln to his  second term .
DEMOCRATIC  ASSOCIATION
The Democratic citizens of Weymouth met on Thursday evening,
Feb.  14,      1839,     for  the purpose of organizing  a Democratic associa-
tion.              Fisher  A.  Kingsbury,      Esq.  ,     was  chosen  chairman  and  Mr.
Allen Vining appointed secretary.
At this  meeting it  was voted to form a Democratic Association,
and a committee of  one  person  from  each  school  district  was  ap-
pointed  to  obtain  signatures  to   the   Constitution,      the  following
persons  comprising  the  committee :            James  Torrey,      Daniel  Dyer,
Alvah  Raymond,        Elias   Hunt,        Edwin  Shaw,       Thomas  Harding,
Jason Pratt,     Abner W. Paine.
The object  of  this Association  shall be to  disseminate principles
by lectures ,     addresses,    and such other means as  may be expedient ;
to  form as  complete an organization  as  possible of the Democratic
young men of  Weymouth;     and to  recommend and encourage  the
formation of  similar societies throughout the State.

WOMEN'S  CHRISTIAN  TEMPERANCE  UNION
This   organization  had  its   origin  during  the  great  temperance
crusade  of  1874.    Each  member was required  to  sign  a pledge  of
total  abstinence  and to  pay dues  of 50 cents  a year.            This  money
 - 219 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           697
was spent  in  local  work,      and  a part  used  as  fee  to  the  State and
national unions.
The membership badge was a bow of  white ribbon,   and it  is  in
the memory of many of this  late day how proud the wearer of the
insignia was.
Throughout  the United States  this  Union has  the largest  mem-
bership  of  any woman's  society  in  the  world,    managed  and  con-
trolled  by them.        Frances  Willard  was  its   second  President  for
nineteen years,    succeeding Mrs. Annie Wittmayer.
In  April,       1876,      Mrs.  Ward,    agent  of  the  Massachusetts  W.  C.
T.  U.  addressed  the women of  South  Weymouth in  the  vestry  of
the  Old South  Church,    when it  was voted  to  organize a Union in
South  Weymouth.        A constitution  was framed  and adopted,     and
a committee appointed  to  nominate officers.          Twenty- nine women
became  members  and  expressed  their  willingness   to  aid  in  any
way.            The organization of men known as  the  Reform  Club offered
the  Union  the  use of  their  reading  room  as  a  place  of  meeting.
This   room,         Clapp's  Hall,      was  thereafter  used  as  their  meeting
place.
The women of  the Union furnished  entertainments,    social  sup-
pers,     and maintained the rooms as  a place for  reading  and recrea-
tion.               A Bible was presented to  the  Reform Club  for  use in their
meetings.
The first  anniversary  was  appropriately  observed  by a  supper
and postprandial  exercises.         Mrs.  Mercy Littlefield,   the  President,
introduced  Mr.  S.   Murray  as  toastmaster,      and  the  Rev.  Elmer
Hewitt,       the  Rev.  George Stanton,     the  Rev.  George  Marden  and
Louis  Cook  responded  to  his  calls.          About sixty men and women
were  present.
During  the  year  the  cause  of  temperance had  advanced,     much
personal  effort  had been put forth,    public  sentiment  aroused  and
some money collected for temperance uses.
In  the  spring  of 1877  petitions  for " no license"  were circulated
and sent  to other  parts of Weymouth.
A Cold Water Army was formed,    with good success,    also a Home
Guard,       and  later  the  Loyal  Temperance Legion,   whose work was
carried on for  some years.
The  President,     Mrs.  Littlefield,     assisted  in  freeing  the  Reform
Club  from  debt.          The sum of  $150  was  collected  by her  in  one
afternoon,            Josiah   Reed,     Albert  Tirrell   and  Prince  Tirrell   each
giving $50.
In after  years  the Union paid  the  rent  of the Reform Club,     and
in   1882,         when  they  disbanded,      purchased  their   furniture   and
continued to use the room as their own headquarters.
The  school  work  required  much  care.            A superintendent  was
appointed  and  the  children  were  greatly  interested   in  the  self-
sacrifice  and zeal of the women whose names we honor to-day.
Mrs.   Mary  Clark,       Mrs.   H.  C.  Alvord,       Mrs.  Ezra  Reed  and
Mrs.  Prince Tirrell  each filled  the office  of President in turn.
 - 220 - 
698                                LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
Mrs.  Murray Whitcomb was its  Treasurer during its  existence,
and  at  its   twenty-fifth    anniversary   reported   that   $1,481   had
passed through her hands in the cause of the Union.
For  a  number  of  years  this  Union  in  the  town  furnished  the
voters  at  the  annual  town meeting with  coffee,   120 gallons  being
served  according  to  one  record,      thereby  serving  the cause  of  " no
license."
While carrying  on their  regular  work the women had numerous
lectures   and  addresses   given  in  churches  on  Sunday  evenings.
After one of these,   given by Gov. John D.  Long,    the Union called
a meeting  in  their  rooms  where  a  " Law and  Order  League "  was
formed which did effective work,    and its  influence is  felt  to-day.
The  Reform  Club  was  in  existence  during  the  years  following
1870 and until its  succession by the  W. C.  T.  U.
The  Reform  Club  was  one  of  the  most  important  temperance
societies   in  Weymouth,     and  its   workers  were  very  active  in  the
cause.               Their meetings were held in the old Clapp Hall,   the mem-
bers on several occasions preparing the banquets for the Wednesday
Night  Club,     which also  held its  meetings at that time in the same
hall.            At last  it  was merged into  the  W. C.  T.  U.,       which  society,
with  the  increased  membership,     continued  the  special  work along
the line of temperance reform.
SONS  OF  TEMPERANCE
The Order was represented in South Weymouth under the name
of  Old  Colony  Division.           The meeting place was in  the vestry  of
the  Universalist  Church,     which was  at that time known as  Union
Hall.
The  Old  Colony  Division  was  organized  about  1859-60,        with
its  chief officer,    the Worthy Patriarch,    represented by D. S.  Murray,
and  associated  with  them,     but  having  a  special  organization  of
its  own affiliated  with  the  " Sons,"  were  the  Lady Visitors  of  the
Old  Colony  Division,     Sons  of  Temperance,    whose initiations  and
installations   were  held  in  conjunction  with  those  of  the  main
society of the Sons of Temperance.
The  society  started  with  great  activity,    and with  such  leaders
as  Father Elmer Hewitt,    J.  Murray Whitcomb,   Tyler Poole,    James
L.   Bates ,          George  Sargent,       William  Sargent,      Ephraim  Bradford,
Seth Vining and George R.  Bowker.
The age limit  was fourteen years,    and the  members were obliged
to  sign  the  pledge.        The society  had  a ritual,     and  regalias  were
worn  by  the  officers.             Father  Hewitt  acted  as   Chaplain,       D.  S.
Murray,          Worthy  Patriarch,        and  Ephraim  Bradford,        Secretary.
The Lady Visitors  had  special  duties,     the object  of which was to
gather  the  youth  into  the  temperance  ranks,       and  the  Band  of
Hope was  organized for the school  children to join by signing  the
pledge  to  banish  intoxicating  liquors.           The children  were  adorned
with  sashes  and  badges,      and held  meetings  and exercises,      met  at
 - 221 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           699
picnics  and  accompanied  by  their  elders  on  several  consecutive
Fourth  of  July's  enjoyed  games  and  sports  at  Island  Grove  in
Abington.
When  the  Civil  War broke  out  many of  the  members  of  the
order joined the ranks,  and the charter  was  surrendered about six
years after  its  institution.
WASHINGTON  TOTAL  ABSTINENCE  SOCIETY   OF   WEYMOUTH  AND
BRAINTREE
This  Society  was,     as  its  name implies,    an organization for  the
suppression  of the use of liquor  personally,   as well  as  limiting  the
traffic  therein.
Its    constitution   expressly   affirms   that   the   members  of   the
Society  solemnly  agree  that  they will  entirely  abstain  from  the
use  of  all  intoxicating  liquors  as  a  beverage,       that  they  will  not
provide them for friends  or persons  in  their employ,  that they will
in  all  suitable  ways discontinue the  traffic  and use  of  them in  the
community,       and,      above  all,     that  they  will  use  their  utmost  en-
deavors  to  reclaim  and restore  to  temperance those who are unfor-
tunately addicted to the use of intoxicating liquors .
One of  the most striking  incidents  in connection with the above
was the discontinuing of the sale of liquor by Asa B. Wales,    a prom-
inent  hotel  keeper  at  Weymouth  Landing,     which  was  in  those
days a most heroic act.
Officers  of  the  Society  were  elected,      a  visiting  committee  ap
pointed  to  work in  their  respective  neighborhoods  and  to  devise
ways  and means to  carry on the work of the Society.         There was
also  a section  in the by-laws  which provided for the relief  of  fam-
ilies  in  need and to furnish  the  immediate  necessities  required  by
them.
No dues were required.          A person  became a member by simply
signing  the Total Abstinence Pledge.        Their records show 639 names
on its  roll  of membership.
At a meeting  of  the  Friends  of  Temperance,       March  7,         1842,
several   addresses  were  made  and  Elias   Richards  was  chosen  as
temporary chairman,   and Peter H.  Cushing as  temporary secretary.
A committee  of  seven  was  chosen  to  draft  a  constitution,     and  at
an adjourned  meeting held  March  15,      1842,     the  following  officers
were chosen :
Edward Pray,     President.
Darius Smith,   Vice- President.
Hiram Cushing,   Vice- President.
John Cushing,    Recording Secretary.
Ebed S. Stoddar,    Corresponding Secretary.
Samuel Cook,   Treasurer.
Simeon Cushing,      Adoram  Clapp,     John  P.  Nash,      Daniel  P.  Edson,     Robert  W.
Lincoln,         Mrs.   Mary  Cook,       John  Burrell,          Mrs.   Deborah  Cushing,        Isaac
Binney,    Mrs. Betsey Pray,    Mrs.  Susan Coolidge,   Visiting  Committee.

700                                   LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
The meeting  place was in  the  Universalist  Vestry,      Weymouth.
Committees were chosen to  visit  similar  meetings  in  other  places,
-on  March 16,    1842,    at North Weymouth;      March 29 at Stough-
ton.         At one  time  Dedham sent  an invitation  to  Weymouth  to
participate  in  honoring  William  Smith,      a  hotel  keeper,      who  had
relinquished   the  sale   of  intoxicating   liquor.            This  Temperance
Festival  was  held  June  23,       1842,      and  was  under  the  charge  of
Edwin Thompson.            The Cold Water  Parade held in Boston on the
Fourth  of  July  was  known  as   the  Temperance  Jubilee.          The
Weymouth  Washingtonians,      with  Maj.       Elias  Hunt  as  marshal,
visited Hingham July 4,    1842.
Darius  Smith was the  second  President  and R.  K.  Trott,      H. J.
Gardner and C.  C. Jordan,    Secretaries .
In  1846-47  John O.  Foye was President  and M. K.  Pratt,       Sec-
retary,      the  meetings being held in Liberty Hall.
In 1848 J.  Hunt was President and E.  Evans,    Secretary.
In   1849   William   Bartlett   was  President  and  John  O.   Foye,
Secretary.
On Oct.  26,      1849,    the last meeting of the Society was held.
The workers  were earnest  and many burdens  were taken up by
them  in  their  struggles  against  intemperance.         Many were  suc-
cessful,        some  failed,   but  the  grand  work  of  this  Society  filled  a
large  field  and gave its  greatest  lessons  to coming generations .
CITIZEN'S  ALLIANCE
On June 3,       1923,     The Women's Committee of  One Hundred of
the Weymouth Branch of the  Citizen's  Alliance  of  Massachusetts
met and organized a working body which had for its purposes
First.    -To  prevent  the  raising  of  money for  any  purposes  by
lotteries  and to bring all  the organizations  in Weymouth.    to  follow
the lead of the Vice- Commander of the American Legion in refusing
to collect  money in this manner.
Second.   -The Alliance  has  in  view the education  of the  public
to  a  knowledge  of  what  the  law  actually  provides,    and  to  the
great need and benefits  of its  enforcement.
Third.                                          To  secure  obedience  to  the law,   adopted by the Town
of  Weymouth,      which  prohibits  and  provides  a severe  penalty  for
the taking of money at any of the Sunday games or  sports,     either
as  a direct  charge or by collections.
Fourth.  -To undertake the obligation of securing obedience to all
laws,     both  by individuals  and organizations,    in order  that the chil-
dren of the town might have a fair chance for the right kind of living.
J.   F.  Robinson of South Weymouth was selected  as  President  of
the Alliance,      and in  opening his  address  spoke strongly  in  favor of
carrying  out  the  letter  of  the  law  in  relation  to  the  Eighteenth
Amendment.              It was pointed out that if  it should not be thoroughly
upheld  there will surely follow " a contempt for the law which will
undermine our very foundations. "
 - 223 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            701
The Alliance  proposes  to  educate  the  people  in  matters  which
law-abiding   citizens   wish  to   know,      showing  them  the  benefits
closely  following in the wake of good government.          The State  law
against  lotteries,     raffles,     chances  and prizes  was  referred  to  in  the
address.                  At  the  Sunday  games  and  concerts,       in  many  cases,
collections   are   taken,       a  custom  which  should  not  receive   any
support.
Mrs.   Florence   Burgoyne  of   East  Weymouth  was  appointed
chairman,       and  Mrs.  Junie  B.  Morrill  of  South  Weymouth,       Miss
Louisa  Humphrey  of  North  Weymouth,      Mrs.  T.  S.   Sampson  of
Weymouth and Miss Janet Harlow of  East Weymouth were elected
members of the Executive Committee of the Alliance.
ORPHANS  HOPE  LODGE,    A.  F.  AND A.  М.
(Abrief history from formation to Nov. 20,     1920)
Orphans  Hope Lodge,    A.  F.  and A.  M. was constituted  June 8,
1825,       by virtue of a charter by the M. W. Grand Lodge of Massa-
chusetts,     signed by the following- named Grand Officers :
John Abbott,   Grand Master.
Caleb Butler,     Deputy Grand Master.
Samuel Thaxter,  Senior Grand Warden.
John Veryes,     Junior Grand Warden.

Judah Loring.
John Dalrymple.
David Welsh.
1                         Ezra W. Sampson.
Levi Bates.

Solomon Ager.
The meetings were held in an upper room in the brick building
at  Weymouth Landing,    now occupied  by the  Cowing family,     the.
remainder of the house being used as a dwelling,   until 1827 or  1828,
when the meetings were held at North Weymouth.
During  the  anti- Masonic  period  the  meetings  were  discontin-
ued (about  1830)  and the charter,    etc.,   was returned to  the Grand
Lodge.         Unfortunately  the  records  from  1825  to  the  discontin-
uance  of  holding  meetings  cannot  be  located,     but  from  a  return
made to  the Grand Lodge Oct.  21,     1828,    it  appears that  the Lodge
had  made  gratifying  progress  and  growth.          In  that  return  the
following  organization was reported :

The fees  for the Degrees were fixed at $5 for each degree;      annual

Early  in   1860  the  question  of  securing  a  location  for  holding
meetings   under  direct  Masonic  supervision  was  discussed  and  a
committee appointed  to arrange the same.
On Feb.  21,      1860,     Masonic Hall over  Loud's  store  (so  called),
now the  Ford Furniture Company,    was dedicated by M.  W. Wins-
low  Lewis,      Grand  Master  of  Masons  in  Massachusetts,       assisted
by the  officers  of  the  Grand Lodge,    and the meetings  were  held at
this hall until 1884.
On Nov.  22,       1882,     the  subject  of  erecting  a Masonic  Building

was appointed consisting  of

to $10,000.

Abraham  Hathaway  Howland,      Jr. ,       Grand  Master  of  Masons  in

Reviewing  a  story  of  so  much interest,    the compiler is  tempted
to  note  so  many items  and  incidents  in  connection,    especially  if
a participant,    that it  might  become tiresome;       however,      it  would
seem pertinent if  a few of these incidents were touched upon.
On June  23,     1869,      twenty- three  members  received  demits  for
the purpose of affiliating  with  Delta  Lodge at Weymouth Landing,
Orphans Hope Lodge having previously recommended to the Grand
Lodge granting  a dispensation  for  a new Lodge to  be  located  in
that part of  the town.
On  Nov.   11,          1920,        a  like   request  from   Master  Masons  in
South  Weymouth  was  granted  and  a  request   for   dispensation
approved.
In  1875  the  semi-centennial  of  the  Lodge  was  observed  by  an
appropriate program at the Weymouth Town Hall,    which included
an  excellent  address  by  R.  W.  Brother  Edward Avery,       a  former
member of  Orphans  Hope Lodge,     a  Past  Master of  Delta  Lodge
and Past  D.  D.  Grand Master.
A comparison  of  the  roster  of  Reynolds  Post  No.  58  G.  A.  R.,
with the  list  of  members of  Orphans Hope Lodge,   shows  that  ap-
proximately 33 members served in the Civil War.
The number of members who served  during the World War was
approximately  42.     Five  Past  Masters  were  appointed   District
Deputy Grand Master by respective Grand Masters,    viz.:
Zechariah L.  Bicknell.
John P.  Lovell.
Leavitt Bates.
Franklin  D.  Thayer.
Gardner R. P.  Barker.

A notable  feature  in  connection  with  this  review  of  Orphans
Hope Lodge is  the long terms of service of several officers,     viz.:
James Torrey,    Treasurer,    1856-86,    31 years.
Charles Henry Pratt,    Secretary,    1856-73   18 years.
T. John Evans,    Secretary,    1874-98 ;      1902-20,    45 years .
Alvah Raymond,    Chaplain,   1866-82,     17 years.
Martin E.  Hawes,   Chaplain,    1883-88;      1892-1920,    35 years.
Henry B.  Raymond,   Tyler,    1868-1906,    39 years .
The total  number of  Master Masons who have been or  are  now
affiliated  with Orphans Hope Lodge is 679.    Death or other  causes
have  decreased   the   number  344.     The  present  membership  is
335.
For nearly a century Orphans Hope Lodge has been an important
factor  in  connection with the town of  Weymouth.         It  has  always
pursued a quiet  conservative course,    but the influence  has  always
been for the progress and welfare of the town.         Many of the prom-
inent  citizens   have  been  and  are  members.           It  is   now  passing
through  a  most  prosperous
rous  period,   and when its  centennial  is
observed,     as  no doubt it  should  and will  be,    the history  then will
show that  Orphans  Hope Lodge,    the  oldest  organized  body  in  the
town,     has a record worthy of emulation and commanding universal
commendation.
FREE  MASONS
The Order  of  Masonry dates back to  a time of which  we have
no  authentic  records.           The  Middle Ages gave  immense incentive
to  organizations  of this  character,     for  it  was then  that  the  great
cathedrals  were  built,     and  church  and  ecclesiastical  architecture
flourished  throughout  Europe,   and members of  these  guilds  trav-
eled  with  especial  patronage of  the church.           They were specially
endowed  by certain  privileges  not  granted  to  masons  who were
not  builders,     hence the term  " Free  Masons. "     Later we find  these
different   guilds  combining  and  probably  establishing  lodges  and
fraternal societies which easily fostered the Lodge of Masons.
Orphans  Hope Lodge was instituted  on June 8,     1825,     at  Wey-
mouth  Landing,    the  charter  being  granted  to  "John  Edson  and
others. "    John Edson was  the  first  Worshipful  Master  and Tim-
othy Gordon the first  Secretary.         During the Anti-Masonic excite-
ment  the  charter  of  the  Lodge  was  surrendered  in  1830,     but  on
Sept.  10,     1856,    it  was restored  to the Lodge.
Regular  meetings  of  this   Lodge  are   now  held  on  the  second
Thursday evenings of each month.     A fine  new temple has recently
been erected at East  Weymouth for the use of the  Masonic  bodies
of Weymouth.

PENTALPHA  CHAPTER,       ROYAL ARCH  MASONS
Of the  higher  degrees,      Pentalpha  Royal  Arch  Chapter  held  its
first   meeting  June  14,      1870,     Stephen  S.   Bradford,       High  Priest,
William  Humphrey,    King,      A.  A.   Hitchcock,      Scribe,      Samuel  A.
Bates,      Secretary.
The beginning of what finally  came to  be  Pentalpha Royal Arch
Chapter was a meeting of several  Companions in Washington Hall,
Weymouth,       May 9,      1870.    It  was  voted  to  apply for  a  charter  to
organize  a  chapter.          Other  meetings  were  held  in  Delta  Lodge
room,      in  the  vicinity  of Bates  Opera  House.       At the first  meeting
Stephen S.  Bradford,    who had previously been elected  High Priest,
was  appointed  to  present  a  petition  to  have  a  new  Chapter  to
Pilgrim  Royal Arch  Chapter of Abington,    which held jurisdiction
over Weymouth.
On May 30,        1870,     the  new  Chapter  decided  to  bear  the  name
Pentalpha,      and the petition was granted by the Abington Chapter,
which was  in  turn followed  by the  dispensation  from  the  Grand
High   Priest,             Henry   Pickering,      and  fifty-nine   Companions   or-
ganized  a  Chapter  and  afterwards  became  the  Charter  members .
Under  this  dispensation  the  first   meeting  was  held  on June  14,
1870,     and officers  were elected  as follows :
Stephen  S.  Bradford,    High Priest.
William Humphrey,     King.
A. A. Holbrook,      Scribe.
Amos D. White,    Treasurer.
George W.  Locke,    Captain of the Host.
Alden W.  Nash,      Principal Sojourner.
William S.  Wallace,    Royal Arch Captain.
Reuben Tirrell,     Master of Third Veil.
Alvah  Raymond,     Master of  Second Veil.
Augustus Vining,    Master of First Veil.
John W. Walsh,   Tyler.
At this  meeting  20  applications  for  the  degrees  were  received.
Work in conferring  the  degrees  proceeded  immediately,    meetings
being  held  every  two weeks  until Jan.  24,    1871,     when the  charter
was  constituted,      consecrated  and  recorded  by the  Chapter.           The
first  year saw an addition  of 41 members accepted.            The following
years  were taken  up by routine  work.         Much work and attention
was  required  to  preserve  the  Chapter during  the years  of  1879  to
1889,      St.  Stephens Chapter of Quincy gathering in many candidates
otherwise under the  Pentalpha Jurisdiction.
In  March,       1890,     in  answer  to  a  communication,    the  trustees  of
the  Masonic  Hall  Association,       East  Weymouth,       made  arrange-
ments so  that  the  Chapter should  have a Lodge Home in the new
building,    and they first  met in this hall April 8,     1890.
The  progression  in  members  and  interest   has  steadily  grown,
and in  1921  the  Chapter has  a  membership of  about 400.

DELTA  LODGE A.  F.  AND A. M.
Delta  Lodge  A.  F.  and A.  M.  was instituted  on June 6,      1868,
when a dispensation  was granted by Most Worshipful  Charles  C.
Dame,     Grand  Master  of  the  Grand Lodge  of  Masons  of  Massa-
chusetts,     to Edward Avery and others for a new lodge in Weymouth
to  be  called  " Delta, "  and  three  days  later  on June  9,      1868,       the
Lodge  held  its  first  regular  communication,    and on July 4 of the
same  year  made its   first  public  appearance when it joined  with
Orphans  Hope  Lodge  in  dedicating  the  Soldiers'        Monument  at
Weymouth.                This  was during  the days  when Zechariah  L.  Bick-
nell  was  District  Deputy Grand Master for  the district,     and upon
his  recommendation the Grand Lodge voted on June 9,     1869,     that
a charter  be granted  the  thirty  petitioners.         On July  2,       1869,      the
Grand Lodge came out from Boston for the purpose of constituting
and  consecrating  the  new  Lodge  and  installing  the  new  officers.
This  service was performed in a most impressive manner by Most
Worshipful  William  Sewall  Gardner,      Grand  Master,      assisted  by
other  Officers  of the Grand Lodge.
Hon.        Edward Avery was the first  master of the Lodge and was
very  largely  instrumental  in  promoting  the  new  Lodge.              Of  the
thirty  charter  members,     typical  and  representative  of  the  South
Shore citizenry  of a half century ago,    twenty- three were  members
of  Orphans  Hope Lodge,     one  of  Rural,   one of John Cutler,     one  of
Old Colony,     one of St.  Pauls,     one of Adelphi,    one of St.  Johns  No.
1 of New York City and one of Solomons Lodge No.  1  of  Charles-
ton,         S.   C.    Two of  these  charter  members  are  still   living,      while
all  the  others  who subscribed  their  names  with the firm  hand and
enthusiastic  purpose  of  a  vigorous   manhood  have  crumbled  to
dust and long since joined  their fathers .
The first  meeting place of the lodge was in Good Templars Hall,
Weymouth Landing,    in the building  now standing at  the southeast
corner  of Washington and Front Streets,    but it  was not long before
the  increased  membership  and  social  ambitions  of  its   members
 - 230 - 
708                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
necessitated  larger  and  better  quarters,     and  in  1870  a  lease  was
taken  of  a  large  two-story  ell  attached  to  the  residence  of  Elias
Richards  in  Washington  Square.            This  building  was  astride  the
line  between  the  two  towns  and therefore  one part  of the  Lodge
room  was  in  Weymouth  and  the  other  part  in  Braintree.       The
Lodge  remodeled  the  interior  of  the  property  for  its  purposes  in
a most tasteful manner and fitted  it out with dignified  and costly
furniture.                      As  a  credit  to  the  makers  of  those  days  it  may be
stated  that  much of  the  furniture  in  use by the  Lodge to-day is
that which was installed at this  time.        In 1890 the Lodge removed
to  Pythian  Hall,    located  in a building  on Washington Street  near
its  first  meeting  place,     and  remained  there  until  its   removal  to
Braintree  where  its   meetings  were  first  held  in  Pythian  Hall  in
that town.             Pythian Hall occupied  the upper  part  of the  Lyceum
Building   (so-called) ,       located   in  Storr's   Square,        and  which  has
since  been destroyed  by fire.         The Lodge occupied  these  quarters
until  December,    1907,    when the  present  Temple on  Washington
Street  in  Braintree was dedicated.
The  Lodge  enjoyed  years  of  great  social   prosperity  when  its
fame was  spread  far  and wide in the country  side.        When Delta
was entertaining  all  roads  led  to  the  Landing,    they came in  their
carriages  and  barges  for  a radius  of  twenty miles or more around,
for  they knew from experience that the cooking of  the good house-
wives of Weymouth was of a high  order and that the  turkeys  and
other  good things  which were to  be  served  to  them that  evening
would  be  done  to  a  turn.                The  early  records  of  the  Lodge  are
filled  with  references to  the many occasions of this kind.
On June 17,    1874,    on invitation of the Masons resident in Brain-
tree and under escort of the Old Colony Commandery of Abington
and  South  Shore  Commandery of  East  Weymouth,    the  Lodge as-
sisted  in  the  dedication  of  the  Soldiers'       Monument in  Braintree,
and on July 4 of  the same year it  participated  in the celebration
of  the  250th  anniversary  of  the  town  of  Weymouth.                On  the
afternoon  of  Sept.  26,    1881,    the  Lodge held  a special  communica-
tion  for  the purpose of attending  memorial  exercises  in  the Union
Congregational  Church  in  honor  of  James  A.  Garfield,     deceased
President  of  the  United States,    who was a distinguished  member
of the fraternity.       Aug. 1,   1889,   the Lodge attended the dedication
of   Pilgrim   Monument  at   Plymouth.            The  occasion   was  sadly
marred by drenching  rain  at the time the exercises  were held.          As
stated  before,    the Lodge moved to  the town of  Braintree  in  1900
as  the  result  of changing conditions  at  the  Landing and has  pros-
pered  exceedingly  in the  interval,     having  at  the  present  time  a
membership  of  over  500.    The  present  Temple was dedicated  on
Dec.   7,          1907,         by  Most  Worshipful  John  Albert   Blake,         Grand
Master  of  the  Grand  Lodge,     assisted  by various  Officers   of  the
Grand Lodge.
