The Lodge  observed the  fiftieth  anniversary  of  its  constitution
by a three days'     celebration on June 1,  2 and 3,    1919.    On Sunday,
June  1,      the  Lodge with  its  invited  guests  marched  in  procession
to  the  First  Congregational  Church and enjoyed a varied  musical
program and an eloquent discourse by the Rev. Edward A.  Horton,
D.D.,      Senior  Grand  Chaplain  of  the  Grand  Lodge,     the  occasion
being one of great dignity and impressiveness.       On Monday,    June 2,
Most  Worshipful  Leon  M.  Abbott,     Grand  Master  of  Masons  in
Massachusetts,      M.  W.  Melvin  M.  Johnson,      Past  Grand  Master,
and a large suite of Masonic dignitaries  were received and escorted
to  the  Town Hall where an elaborate dinner was served  to  nearly
400.    After  being  welcomed by the  Master of  the  Lodge,       Henry
D.  Higgins,       a  wonderful  oration  was delivered  by Grand Master
Abbott,       a  delightful   and  witty  speech  by  Past  Grand  Master
Johnson,    and the historical  address  by Walter J.  Harrison  a  past
Master of the  Lodge.        Tuesday evening was devoted to the ladies ,
when an elaborate  entertainment was provided in the Town Hall,
followed by refreshments of a varied nature,    and dancing.
Appended to  the historical  address  delivered  by  W. M.  Walter
J.   Harrison was a short  biographical  sketch of each of the  thirty
charter members,    and as  practically  all  of these  men were promi-
nent  or well-known in  Weymouth we believe  the same will  be of
interest  to  many readers  of  this  history  and so  we are  publishing
them in full.
EDWARD AVERY was born in  Marblehead,     Mass.,    March 12,     1828,     the  son  of
Gen.  Samuel  and  Mary  (Candler)   Avery.         After  pursuing  his  studies  in  his
native  town and at the classical  school  of  Mr.  Brooks  in  Boston,    he chose the
profession of law and studied in the office  of F.  W. Choate,    Esq.,   in  Boston and
also  at  the  Harvard  Law School.         He was  admitted to  the  bar in April,      1849,
and began the  practice  of his  profession  at  Barre,    Mass.           In  1850 he removed
to Boston  and  opened  a law office  with Geo.     M. Hobbs as  partner.          The laws
of bankruptcy and insolvency  received his  early attention and secured for  him
an extensive  practice  and  a  leading  position  at  the  bar,    which he  maintained
until the time of his decease.         In 1852 he married Susan Caroline Stetson,   daughter
of  Caleb  Stetson,    and  took  up his  residence  in  Braintree  in  1853.    He was  a
member of the lower branch of the legislature  from  Braintree in  1866 and of the
 - 232 - 
710                                LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
State  Senate in  1867.    In the latter year he was a candidate for both the House
of Representatives and State Senate and was elected to both branches,    defeating
the  famous  " Citizen "  Hobart  for  the  Senate  and took his  seat  in that body.
He was a member of  several  state  and national conventions of his party,     was a
candidate  for  Secretary  of  the  State  and  was  several  times  candidate  for  the
national  Congress.       He was the first  Master of the Lodge and held that position
for  the  years  1868  to  1870;         was  District  Deputy Grand  Master  of  the  16th
Masonic District  from 1871  to  1874 and again  in  1880;     and in June,      1877,      was
elected  Junior  Grand Warden of  the  Grand Lodge,    being  the only  member  of
Delta  Lodge who has been honored with a permanent membership in the Grand
Lodge.            He died at his residence in Boston Dec. 29,    1896,   and was buried from
Emmanuel  Church  December 31.    The services  were in  charge  of  the  M.  W.
Grand Lodge with  M.  W.  Chas.      C.  Hutchinson,     officiating  with  the assistance
of  the  Rev.  Brother  Edw.      A.  Horton,    and the  offices  of  the  church  were  per-
formed by the  Rev. Leighton Parks and the Rev. Wm.     Hyde.        Delta Lodge held
a special  communication which convened  at  the  Masonic Temple in Boston for
the purpose of attending  the  funeral.          So  passed  away one whom we have no
hesitation in denominating the " Father of Delta  Lodge, "  for it  was owing to his
initiative,       powers  of  attracting  others  to  himself  and constructive  ability  that
Delta Lodge came into being,   and then through his generosity and influence that
the Lodge attained its  high  standing in its  earlier  years.         Up to the present  time
he is  the  greatest  figure  in the history  of  the  Lodge and although  none  of us
know what the future may produce it  would seem as  though  he  might  remain
so  for  all  time.
NATHANIEL  FREDERIC THAYER HUNT was born in  Weymouth June 30,    1835,
the son of Maj.      Elias  and Eliza  Maria Theresa  (Soper)   Hunt.        He attended the
schools  of  his  native town and then engaged in the  fancy goods  business  as  a
traveling   salesman,       being   particularly   successful  as  such  until  failing   health
compelled him to  retire.          He was raised  in St.  John's Lodge No.  1 of New York
City,     was the first  Senior Warden of  Delta Lodge and a very enthusiastic member
for the  first  few years  following the founding of the  Lodge.     He died at Scituate
Harbor,      Mass. ,    Aug.  29,   1921 .
ELISHA  WATSON ARNOLD was  born  in  Braintree  March  25,      1837,      raised  in
Orphans  Hope Lodge June 3,     1863,   and was the  first  Junior Warden of Delta.
He demitted Sept. 30,    1879.    He was town clerk of Braintree from 1864 to 1868,
inclusive,    and represented  Braintree in the lower house in  1868.    For a number
of years he conducted a general store in what was then known as the " Lyceum "
on  Storrs '       Square,    Braintree,   later selling  it out and founding the provision  firm
of Skinner & Arnold on Dock Square in Boston.        He died while taking the baths
at Hot Springs,   Va.  ,    May 21,     1899.
AMOS STONE WHITE was born in Ashburnham,      Mass. ,   April 6,   1816,     the son
of Josiah  and Matilda  (Stone)  White.        He was raised  in  Orphans  Hope Lodge
July  25,     1860,     and  upon the  founding  of  Delta  became its  first   Treasurer,        a
position  which he held  for  fourteen  years  and upon  then resigning  received  a
rising  vote  of  thanks  from the  Lodge.          Being treasurer  of the  lodge  in  those
days  apparently  embraced  duties  not  conceded  by our  present-day  treasurers
even if they are  connected with large and influential  financial  institutions,       for
we learn  from the  records  that  all  bills  were  paid  upon presentation  whether
there  was any money in  the  treasury  or  not.              He conducted  a drug  store  in
Washington  Square,       Weymouth,      was  for  thirty- four  years  treasurer  of  the
Weymouth Savings  Bank,    Trustee  of Tufts'       Library,     and occupied other  posi-
tions  of  trust  and  responsibility  in  Weymouth  affairs.        He demitted Feb.  13,
1886,    and died in Weymouth March 27,     1891.
CHARLES GILMAN THOMPSON was born in Weymouth Oct. 20,    1837,    the son of
Gilman and Lucinda Thompson.         He was raised in Adelphi Lodge April 5,    1866,
and was  the  first  Secretary  of Delta.          Like the  Treasurer,     Amos S.  White,     he
served  the  Lodge for fourteen years,    resigned at the  same time and participated
with him in the rising  vote of  thanks accorded them by the  Lodge.          He was a
man  of  marked  social  characteristics,     deeply  interested  in  the  welfare  of  the
Lodge and an officer  of exceptional ability.       In the records  of the Lodge as com-
piled by him,    he has left the Lodge a legacy which is  the admiration of all  and
 - 233 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           711
at once the envy and despair of all succeeding secretaries,   for his beautiful pen-
manship  resembles  more the copy plate  of  the  steel  engraver  than  the  chirog-
raphy  of the penman,   with the names of candidates  and other  items  of impor-
tance in the records  thrown up in  large  script  and heavily  shaded.          For many
years he was connected with  the old  firm  of J.   D.  & M. Williams,      State  Street,
Boston,      and later  succeeded them under the name of Thompson & Leavitt.          He
died at his residence in Braintree Feb. 4,   1904.
ALVERDO MAson was born in  Swansea,    Mass. ,    Feb.  25,    1821.    He was raised
in  St.  Paul's Lodge Nov. 3,  1863,    was Secretary of the petitioners for a dispensa-
tion for  Delta,   served as the  first  Senior  Deacon of the Lodge and was Junior
Warden in  1872.   After his  graduation  from  Oberlin  College  of Oberlin,      Ohio,
he served for  many years  as  teacher in the schools  of Braintree and during  that
time compiled a copy of the  first  book of records  of his  native town where his
ancestors  had lived for  more than two hundred years and which he published at
his own expense.       In later life he was postmaster at East Braintree for eight years.
He died at Braintree May 13,      1892.
ALDEN WILDER NASH was born in Weymouth Jan.  10,    1835,   the son of George
and  Nancy  (Burrell)   Nash.           He was  raised  in  Orphans  Hope Lodge Aug.  15,
1866.   He was a man of most agreeable manners and conversation and in business
was a boot  manufacturer,     conducting  a large  and profitable  business.        Upon
the founding
ing of the Lodge,  he became its first Junior Deacon, was Senior Deacon
from  1869 to  1871,    Senior  Warden in  1872 and 1873 and died in  office  April  6,
1873.
ELBRIDGE  THOMAS RICHARDS was born in  Weymouth Feb.  15,    1837,      the  son
of Thomas and Lydia (Shaw)  Richards.         He was raised  in Orphans Hope Lodge
March 4,    1868.    He was the  first  Senior Steward of the Lodge,  Junior Deacon in
1869 and Sentinel in  1885 and  1886.    Owing to  failing  health he demitted May
22,      1888,      and went to  Riverside,     Cal. ,     but upon his return in 1891  he rejoined
the Lodge.          He was identified  with  the manufacturing  boot and shoe industry
of the town and in his later years conducted a retail shoe store in Lincoln Square.
He died in Weymouth Oct.  14,    1917.
REUBEN TIRRELL was born in Weymouth May 2,    1845,    the son of Elbridge
Gerry and Sophia Tirrell.           He was raised  in  Orphans Hope Lodge Dec. 11,    1867,
and upon the founding  of  Delta he became its  first  Junior Steward,   serving  in
that capacity for  four  years,     then as Tyler from  1877 to  1882,    inclusive,    then
as Sentinel from  1891 to  1895,    and again  from  1897 to  1899,    inclusive.        During
all  his life  he has been identified with the general store business in Lincoln Square
founded by his  father,    and in  Lodge matters  both in  office  and out  of office  he
has set an example for interest  in  the affairs  of the Lodge and attendance  upon
the meetings  that all  might  follow  with  advantage  and  credit  to  themselves.
He is  one of the two surviving charter members.
WILLIAM SPRAGUE  WALLACE was born  in  East  Braintree  Oct.  11,      1838,     the
son of William Vinson and Maria (Keen)  Wallace.          He was raised  in  Orphans
Hope Lodge  Dec.  27,       1865,     and  became the  first   Chaplain  of  Delta  upon its
institution  and served  in that  capacity  for  two years.           Then in  succession  he
held the positions of Junior Deacon 1870 and 1871,   Senior Deacon 1872 and 1873,
Senior  Warden 1874,    and was  elected  the  fourth  Master  of  the  Lodge  in  1875,
being  honored with  a three years'    term by the  members of  the  Lodge.         During
his administration,   the Lodge was exceedingly prosperous and reached a numerical
strength  of 109,    which was destined to  be high-water mark for twenty-six  years
or until  1902.    The  officers  of  the  lodge  by painstaking  work  and  under  the
efficient  leadership  of the  Master  achieved a perfection  of ritual  and work that
was the  envy  of  neighboring  Lodges  and  several  times  called  for  the  special
commendation of the  Grand Master and other  officers  of the Grand Lodge.          His
interest  in the affairs  of the  Lodge  has  never  abated,    and the  Masonic  Ritual
is  as clear and fresh  in  his  mind as  it  was in  the days when he sat  in  the East.
For many years  he operated  a boot- fitting  shop  which was an auxiliary to  the
boot manufacturing  business,     and  in  1876 represented  Weymouth in  the  lower
house.          He is  the oldest  Past  Master of the  Lodge and is  the  other  of the  two
surviving charter members.
RICHARD AMORY  HUNT  was  born  in  Weymouth  Sept.   2,       1818.     He  was

a man of unusual musical ability,    possessed an excellent voice,     was a performer

many Hall, "  presumably  because  the  slates  there made up were never broken.
He died in Weymouth July 23,     1898.
EBENEZER  ÁTHERTON  HUNT was born in Weymouth Jan.  2,   1826,    the son of
Atherton  Nash Hunt and his  wife  Susannah  Curtis  (Hobart)   Hunt.           He was
raised in Orphans Hope Lodge March 14,  1860,  and was Junior Warden of the
Lodge in 1867.    In 1869 he was elected Junior Warden of Delta,   in  1871 he was
Senior  Warden and on December  12  of the  same year he  was installed  as  the
third  Master  of the Lodge,    a position which he held for  three successive years.
Upon the founding of South Shore  Commandery he was offered the position of
Captain General,   which he declined with  the  statement that as a Commandery
was semi-military  in character one of short  stature had no business to accept an
office in it.       He was one of the boot  manufacturers of the town and like his uncle
Richard was one of the political  leaders  of his  district.        He served  his  town in
various  capacities,    including  that of chief of the fire  department,   selectman  for
a number of terms and Representative in the lower house in 1873.    In 1875 and
1876 he  served in  the State  Senate.           He was a member of the Union Congre-
gational  Church,     a trustee  of the  Weymouth Savings  Bank from 1875 to  1881,
and by his  contemporaries  was considered one of the solid and able men of the
town.            He passed away March 17,   1891.
FRANCIS  AMBLER was  born  in  Weymouth June 3,    1833,     and was raised  in
Orphans  Hope Lodge  May 21,      1862.    While he held no official  position  in the
Lodge,     he was active in  town affairs.         He was selectman in  1875 and  1876 and
was town clerk  from  1861  to  1878,      inclusive,     with  the  exception  of  1869 and
1870.    The two years that he failed of election were those when the  " Crispins, "
so called,     were in power.        The older ones will remember the " Crispins "  as being
a boot  and shoe  workers'      organization  which  was at  that  time  very  powerful
politically and turned out every one who was in any way identified with the old
order of things.        He was a druggist  for  many years  in Washington Square and
in later  life  conducted  a hay and grain  business  on  Shaw Street.          He died  in
Weymouth Dec. 8,      1898.
EBENEZER WILLIAM  HUNT was born  in Weymouth Dec.  4,     1823,    the son of
Maj.     Elias  and Eliza  M.  T.  (Soper)   Hunt.        He was raised in  Old Colony Lodge
Nov.  28,      1854,     joined  Orphans  Hope in  1856,    and  became one of  the  charter
members  of  Delta in  1868.    He was  engaged  in  the  wholesale  boot  and  shoe
business in Boston for  a number of years,    then conducted an insurance business
in  Weymouth.        On May 22,    1877,    he demitted from the Lodge and removed to
Orlando,    Fla. ,    where he died Dec. 27,   1909.
EDWIN P.  WOrster was born in Weymouth Aug. 24,    1826,    the son  of Ezekiel
Worster,     and was raised in Orphans Hope Lodge June 7,  1865.   In 1849 he joined
the army of gold seekers  which went to  California  taking passage in the barque
"Lanark" and consuming two hundred and fourteen days in the passage around
the  Horn.              Upon his  return  and for  nearly  thirty  years  afterwards  he was a
well-known figure  on State Street  in  Boston where  he was a specie  broker,    spe-
cializing in foreign  exchange;    and in 1869 was president  of the "Gold Board. "
The "Gold Board" was an association  of those who dealt  in specie and to which
banks and merchants  went when in need of gold to  meet domestic and foreign
obligations.             He was vice-president  of the Union  National  Bank of  Weymouth
from  1881 to the time of his death,   which occurred on July 25,  1900.

was  raised  in   Orphans  Hope  Lodge  Oct.  31,       1860.     He served  the  Lodge  as
trustee from 1869 to 1873,    inclusive,    and also in 1879 and 1880.    For many years
he was in  the  lumber business  in  Weymouth under the  firm name of  Loud &

ERASTUS  NASH was born  in  Weymouth  Dec.  16,     1827,     the  son  of  Deacon
John P.  and Rachel Nash.        He was raised in  Orphans Hope Lodge Oct.  5,    1864.
For many years he was engaged in the manufacture of boots under the firm name
of S.  W. & E. Nash,   and erected one of the finest residences in  the town.         He was
also  vice- president  of  the  Weymouth Agricultural  Society,   but  took  no active
part in town or  Lodge affairs.          He ceased  to  be a member of the  Lodge  in  1895
and passed away in Weymouth Jan.  28,   1905.
MILTON HEYWOOD READ was born in Orono,     Me. ,    Oct.  1,     1822,    the son  of
John and Mary Reed.    He was raised  in  Orphans
Orp        Hope Lodge May 18,      1864,
and although  he became one  of the  charter  members  of  Delta  he  never  took
any active  part  in the affairs  of the  Lodge nor of the town.       He conducted a
retail  clothing  store  on Washington  Square  in Weymouth,   demitted  from the
Lodge May 18,   1880,   and died in Weymouth Aug. 10,   1899.
GEORGE WILLIAM  WARREN was born  in Hopkinton,    Mass.,     April  20,      1840,
and was raised in Solomon's Lodge No.  1 of Charleston,   S.  C.,     on Sunday after-
noon Feb.  10,    1867,    under special dispensation from the Grand Lodge.         He served
in the Civil War as a member of D Company,   Third Battalion of Infantry,   then
in E Company,    51st  Massachusetts  Infantry,    and finally  as  a member of  the
6th  Unattached  Company  of  Massachusetts  Infantry,       of  which  company  he
was orderly sergeant.       After the war he was a clerk in the employ of Milton H.
Read in  Washington  Square,      Weymouth,    then  with  Richards  & Co.,     clothiers
in  Dock Square,     Boston,    and later  was  connected with the  Boston  district  of
the Internal  Revenue Department as inspector and gauger for  thirty years.            He
demitted from the Lodge April 12,  1881,  and passed away at the Soldiers'       Home
in Chelsea June 21,   1921.
JOHN METZLER WALSH was born in Halifax,     N. S.,    July 19,    1822,     the son of
James and Mary (Mearler)   Walsh,    and while still young came to South Brain-
tree,   removing in  1852 to  Weymouth.       He was raised in Orphans Hope Lodge
June 15,    1857.    He served Delta as Senior Steward from 1869 to  1871,    as Junior
Deacon in  1872  and  1873,       Senior  Deacon in  1874,      Senior  Warden from  1875
to  1877,    and became the  fifth  Master of the Lodge,    serving  from 1878 to  1880.
His contemporaries  speak of him as a man of unusual geniality and as one to
whom the professions  and ideals  of Freemasonry meant something more than
printed ritual.      He was an excellent officer  and, pos
and,   possessing considerable dramatic
ability,    the  work of the  Lodge under his leadership  was of  a very high  order,
and a standard for excellence  was set  which has never been  exceeded.       He was
engaged in the carriage painting business and also conducted the leading harness
business of the town for  many years.        He died in Weymouth Jan.  16,     1898.
FRANCIS FLINT Forsaith was born in  Deering,    N.  H.,     May 8,     1824.     He was
a charter member of John Cutler  Lodge of Abington in  1860,  and demitted from
that  Lodge when Delta was founded as he had removed to Weymouth in  1861 .
He was a deacon of the  Union  Congregational  Church  and in  his  chosen  pro-
fession  of physician  he endeared himself to  a large circle  of friends  not only as
a kind and sympathetic  physician  but  also  as  a true  gentleman and a useful
citizen.        He died in Weymouth,   March 11,   1894.
GEORGE ADONIRAM GUSTIN was born in Troy,    Me. ,   June 24,    1840.    He en-
listed  June 17,    1861,    and served in the band of the 9th  Massachusetts  Infantry
until Aug.  10,   1862,    when all regimental bands were disbanded.       He was  raised
in Orphans Hope Lodge Jan. 18,   1865,   and upon the founding of Delta he became
its  first  Marshal,    serving for  the year  1868.    He was engaged in the manufacture
of boots in  early life  and later  became a band musician again.        He dimitted from
the LodgeMay 28,    1907,    became a member of Humboldt Lodge No. 79 of Eureka,
Cal. ,    to which place  he removed and died June 11,   1922.
CHARLES STEWART WILLIAMS was born in  Weymouth June 1,  1844,  the son of
Henry and Caroline  (Stewart)   Williams.        He was raised  in  Orphans Hope Lodge
Oct.  4,    1865.    In the  Civil  War he was a  member of  Company A,     42d  Massa-
chusetts  Infantry,    and  was  captured  at  Galveston,      Texas,       together  with  the
colonel  and several companies of the regiment.       After spending a year in  rebel

WATERMAN THOMAS BURRELL was born in  Hingham May 12,    1832,    the  son of
Martin H.  and Mary W. Burrell.          He was raised  in  Orphans  Hope Lodge April
21,     1858,     and served  Delta as its  first Tyler  1868 and 1869 and as Junior Warden
in 1870 and 1871.    For many years he was the leading house painter of the town.
He demitted from the Lodge Dec.  15,     1885 and died in Weymouth  Dec. 9,     1903.
SOLON  WALTER  PRATT  was  born  in  Waterbury,       Vt. ,        March  27,      1828,           the
son of John Y.  and Sarah  Pratt.          He was initiated  in  Rural Lodge Aug.  2,     1855,
and joined Orphan's Hope in  1857.   He conducted a hardware business  in Wash-
ington Square under the firm name of S.  W. & L.  W. Pratt .             He demitted from
the  Lodge April  17,      1900,     and died in  Weymouth April 6,     1903.
CHARLES GORHAM  EASTERBROOK was  born  in Hingham Aug.  13,     1825,       and
was raised in  Old Colony Lodge March 27,    1855.    He was the founder and pub-
lisher  of  the  " Weymouth  Gazette, "  a  paper  which  for  many years  wielded  a
great influence  in the South Shore.       His intimates of those days refer  to  him as
a true and faithful  Mason,    having always at  heart the welfare of the  fraternity
and as  an  upright  and loyal  citizen  who cared  more for  the good of state  than
for  personal  emolument.         He conducted his business with sterling integrity  and
possessed  social  qualities to a high degree,    promoting with his genial disposition
the pleasure of all.          He died in Weymouth Sept.
Sept.  3,    1893.
FRANCIS ALLEN HOBART was born in Braintree Sept.  18,    1833,    and was raised
in  Orphans Hope Lodge July 25,    1860.   In early life he was a boot manufacturer,
but having a natural  taste  for  politics  that  occupation  gradually  absorbed  his
time to  the  exclusion  of  all  else,    and under the sobriquet  of  " Citizen  Hobart "
he  was  without  doubt  the  most  widely  known  man that  Norfolk  County  has
produced  since  colonial  times.        He represented  Braintree in the lower  house in
1860 and 1861 and was State Senator in  1865,    1869 and 1870.    He demitted from
the Lodge May 26,     1885,    and died in Braintree Oct.  14,   1903.
ASA FRENCH was born in  Braintree  Oct.  21,    1829,    was raised  in Rural  Lodge
in 1860 and admitted to  membership in that Lodge August 30 of the same year.
He was a distinguished lawyer of his time and was district  attorney  for  Norfolk
and Plymouth counties from 1870 to  1882.    In 1882 he was appointed by Presi-
dent Arthur judge  of the  Court  of  Commissioners of  Alabama Claims  at  Wash-
ington,         D.  C.,     and  served  as  such  from  1882  to  1886,      inclusive.          He was  a
close   friend   of  Brig.    Gen.  Sylvanus  Thayer,       a  native  of  Braintree,      who was
commandant  of the  United  States  Military Academy for  sixteen  years  and  fa-
miliarly  known as  the  " Father  of  West  Point. "    Asa  French  drew the  will  of
General Thayer by which he left  in  trust the sum of $270,000 for  higher  educa-
tional  purposes in the town of old  Braintree and which resulted  in the founda-
tion  of  Thayer Academy.          He also  drew the  will  of  Mrs.  Sarah  W.  Glover,       by
which in  1894 $194,000  more reverted to  Thayer Academy.          Thus he was largely
instrumental  in  providing  the  towns of  Braintree,      Quincy,     Holbrook and Ran-
dolph,    which  were  included  in  old  Braintree,     with  an  educational  institution
which for  many years  has  maintained a high standard of excellence.        He repre-
sented Braintree in the Great and General Court in  1866.    He demitted from the
Lodge Sept.  11,     1883,     when he took  up his  residence  in  Washington,       and died
in Braintree June 23,     1903.
EDMOND  STEPHEN  Soper  HUNT was  born  in  Weymouth July  19,     1827,       the
third son of  Maj .    Elias  and Eliza  M. T.  (Soper)   Hunt to  subscribe  his  name as
a charter  member of Delta Lodge.        He was raised in  Old Colony Lodge Feb. 23 ,
1855,         joined  Orphans  Hope in  1856,     and was a trustee of  Delta in  1869.    At one
time he was a fan  manufacturer,    but his real life  work was that  of pyrotechnist,
in which he achieved great  prominence  and success  and amassed a fortune.            He
was the inventor of the Hunt Life-saving Gun,   which he finally  sold to the John
P.  Lovell  Arms  Company after  failing  to  dispose  of it  to  the  United States  or
British  governments.         Besides  being  passionately  fond  of music,    he was a man
of great  originality  and in later  life  wrote  a  book for  private  distribution,      en-
titled  " Weymouth Ways and Weymouth People,"  in  which he related  his  per

sonal  impressions of those he had known in Weymouth,    calling  a spade a spade
and sparing neither relative,   friend  nor enemy to the great delight  of those who
were fortunate  enough to be favored with a copy by the author.          He ceased  to
be a member of the Lodge in 1876 and died in Weymouth Aug. 21,    1909.
GEORGE WASHINGTON WHITE,    Jr.,    the last  signer  of the  petition,     was born in
Weymouth Jan. 18,    1819,   the son of Capt.    George W. and Betsey (Burrell)  White.
He was raised  in Orphan's Hope Lodge June 1,   1859,     and was trustee of  Delta
in 1873 and 1874.   He was deputy sheriff  of Norfolk County for years without
number and was one of the prominent  figures  of his time.       In his later  years  he
was  postmaster  of  Weymouth for  eight  years.           He demitted  from  the  Lodge
Feb. 4,    1890,    and died in Weymouth March 8,    1899.
WESSAGUSSET LODGE,    A.  F.  AND A.  М.
On Oct.  12,      1920,    ten  Master Masons,    residents  of South Wey-
mouth,     seeing the need and realizing the possibilities  of a Masonic
Lodge in  the south part of Weymouth,    met at the home of Josiah
B. Reed to discuss and arrange to present the matter to  the officers
and members of Orphan's Hope Lodge at East Weymouth.          There
were present at that meeting
Frederic G. Bauer.
Josiah  B.  Reed.
Nathaniel A. Shaw.
William J.  Holbrook.
Charles H. Locke.
Walter V.  Reed.
William F.  Barnard.
Jacob S.  Wichert.
Carl W. Gridley.
George Reed.
From  those  present  a delegation  was  appointed  to  attend  a
meeting  of  Orphan's  Hope Lodge held  on Oct.  14,     1920,       when  a
full  consideration was given the project and it was the unanimous
opinion  of all  present that it  was an opportune time for the insti-
tution of another lodge in Weymouth,   and the mother lodge gave
every  assurance of her hearty  support and assistance.
A committee  was  chosen  to  secure  the  necessary  dispensation
from  the  Most Worshipful  Grand  Lodge  of  Massachusetts,        said
committee being the following gentlemen :
Frederic G. Bauer.
Elmir Millet.
William J.  Holbrook.
Charles H. Locke.
Jacob S.  Wichert.
Matthew C.  Sproul.
William F.  Barnard.
The dispensation was granted  and on  Nov.  23,      1920,     the  Lodge
was instituted  under the name of  " Wessagusset"  Lodge (a name
well known in  Weymouth history),  with  a charter  members'      list
of  seventy,       to  which  there  have been  generous  additions  and  a
steady growth is predicted.
On Oct.   14,         1921,       Most  Worshipful  Arthur  D.  Prince,     Grand
Master,       and the  Officers  of the Most Worshipful  Grand  Lodge  of
Massachusetts   made  an  official   visit   to  South  Weymouth  and
Wessagusset  Lodge  was  constituted  and  its   officers   installed   in

TEMPLE  COUNCIL,       ROYAL  AND  SELECT  MASTERS
Although Weymouth had had its  own Chapter and Commandery
since  1870,       the  Cryptic  Degrees  of  Masonry were not  established
here  until  1913,    until  which date  it  was  necessary  for  Masons  to
journey  to  Abington  to  receive  the  degrees  of  Royal,    Select,       and
Super  Excellent   Master.           This  was  so  inconvenient  that  when
Temple  Council  was  started  there  could  be found  in  the  entire
South  Shore  District  only fifteen  persons  who had received  these
degrees  and  many of  these  had  taken  the  degrees  while  living
elsewhere.
The first  definite  step  toward forming  a  Council  in  Weymouth
was taken  at  a meeting  of  Pentalpha  Chapter,    held  in  Braintree
on April  3,       1913,     when  several  Council  Masons  present  decided
that the time was ripe for action,     and accordingly called a meeting
on April  8,        1913,     at  the  residence  of  Col.  (then  lieutenant)   Fred-
eric  Gilbert  Bauer  in  South  Weymouth,     at  which  the  following
were  present:            Gardner   R.   P.   Barker,        Henry  P.   Tilden,        John
Taylor,         Arthur  W.  Burr,       Marshall  P.  Sprague  and  Frederic Gil-
bert  Bauer.              Those  present  unanimously decided  to  petition  the
Grand  Council  of   Massachusetts   to   issue   a  dispensation  for  a
Council to be held in Weymouth,     and made the necessary  arrange-
ments  to  start  the  organization.            The name Temple Council  was
selected  not  only for  its  Masonic significance,    but also  in  allusion
to  the  new Weymouth Masonic Temple,    for which plans  had just
been completed.
The officers,      elected  and appointed,     under the  dispensation  were
as follows:
 - 239 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            717
Thrice Illustrious  Master,    Gardner R.  P.  Barker.
Deputy Master,    Frederic Gilbert  Bauer.
Principal  Conductor of the Work,    Henry P.  Tilden.
Treasurer,     John Taylor.
Recorder,     Arthur W. Burr.
Chaplain,    Joseph Ellis Gardner.
Master of Ceremonies,   Winthrop J.  Cushing.
Captain of the Guard,   W. Edward Gutterson.
Conductor of the Council,   Ralph C. Stoddard.
Steward,     Marshall P. Sprague.
Sentinel,    Fred W. Baldwin.
The petitioners  for  the  dispensation  in addition  to  the foregoing
were  Fred  L.  Bailey,    Russell H. Whiting,    Charles  H.  Ramsay and
Oliver   Cushing.        Companions  Gardner  and  Bailey   were   Past
Masters  of  Abington  Council.
The dispensation for  the  Council was issued  May 28,    1913,      and
at  the  first  meeting,   held  at  Odd Fellows  Hall,     East  Weymouth,
June  6,         1913,        twenty-seven   applications   for   the  degrees   were
received.              On  March  5,      1914,     the  Council  was duly  constituted
by Most Illustrious  Edgar W. Evans and the Officers  of the Grand
Council   of   Massachusetts,          Right  Illustrious   Miah  G.   Kenney,
Past  Deputy  Grand  Master,     presenting  the  Council  a handsome
stand  of  the  national  colors  on that  occasion.
Temple  Council  held  the  first  meeting  of any kind  in the  new
Masonic Temple on Nov. 28,     1913,      and Companion Joseph Chase,
Jr. ,       who  received  the  degree  of  Royal  Master  on that  occasion,
was the first  candidate to  receive a Masonic degree  in the building.
Other  notable occasions  in  the history  of Temple Council  have
been as follows :
On Feb.  18,       1915,       at  a military  night,    believed  to  be  the  first
held  by  any  Council  in  Massachusetts,       Lieut.        E.  W.  Raymond,
Coast  Artillery  Corps,       M.  V.   M.,       received  the  degree  of   Royal
Master,       the  chairs  being  occupied  by prominent military  men.
On June 21,     1915,    the new ritual for the degree of Super Excellent
Master,         adopted  by  the  General  Grand  Council  of  the  United
States,     was worked for the first  time in  Massachusetts by Temple
Council  in  the  presence  of   Most  Puissant  John  Albert   Blake,
General Grand Master of  the General Grand Council of the United
States,       Most  Illustrious   William  H.  L.   Odell,       Grand  Master  of
the Grand Council  of  Massachusetts,   and officers  and members  of
the  Grand  Council  of  Massachusetts  from  various  parts  of  the
State.               On  Dec.  6,      1915,       Temple  Council  repeated  the  work  of
this  new  ritual  at  the  annual  meeting  of  the  Grand  Council  of
Massachusetts  in  Boston.       On Dec.  6,     1917,      a collection  of  relics
from  the  Verdun battlefields  was  exhibited.           On Jan.  4,      1923,      the
degree of Super Excellent  Master was exemplified by the  Council in
the presence of the Most Illustrious Dean K. Webster,    Grand Master
of  the Grand Council of Massachusetts,    and a distinguished  suite.
Temple  Council  had  six  of its  members in  the  military  service
of the United States during  the  World War.

718                                LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
The following  persons  have filled  the office  of Thrice Illustrious
Master,       serving,   except  where  otherwise  indicated,    from  October
of the year named to  October of the year following :
Gardner R.  P.  Barker,    May,    1913,    to October,    1914.
Frederic Gilbert Bauer,   1914.
Henry P.  Tilden,    1915.
W. Edward Gutterson,  1916.
Charles  H. Chubbuck,    1917.
Sydney G. Dunbar,     1918.
Cranston F. Godfrey,    1919.
Fred B.  Lawrence,    1920.
William J.  Holbrook,     1921 .
F. Wayland Preston,    1922.
Two members of  the  Council  have been honored  with  office  in
the  Grand  Council  of  Massachusetts,    -   Gardner  R.   P.   Barker
being  Grand  Principal  Conductor of  the Work for  the year  1916,
and  Frederic Gilbert  Bauer,   Grand Conductor of  the  Council  for
the year  1923.
The  Council  of  Royal  and  Select   Masters  occupies  a  unique
position  in  Masonry in  that its  degrees  are not a requisite  for ad-
mission  into  any  higher  body.         The  result  is   that  Councils  are
usually  comparatively  small  bodies   composed  of   those  Masons
most deeply  interested  in  the mysteries  of  the craft,      and have a
more  intimate  social  character  than  is  possible  in  larger  bodies.
Temple  Council  is  no exception  to  this  rule.         In its  ten  years  of
existence  it  has  grown steadily  until it  now (February,     1923)   has
152  members,     and  a total  of 160 have signed  its  by-laws  since  its
organization.           All  its  original  members  are  living  except  Arthur
W.  Burr,     who filled  the  office  of  Recorder  from  the  organization
of  the  Council  till  his  death in  1922,    and all  its  Past Masters are
living  except  Cranston  F.  Godfrey,    who died  in  February,       1923.
Temple Council has grown steadily in prosperity,  and its  meetings
are  unusually  well  attended.         In its  ritualistic  work and  in  the
impressive  manner  and  elaboration  of  detail  with  which  it   pre-
sents  the  degrees,    it  has  attained  an enviable position  among the
Councils  of  the  State.        Its  relations  with  the  parent  Council  at
Abington  have  always  been  most  cordial.             On  Dec.  17,      1914,      a
delegation   from  Abington  Council  visited  Temple  Council  and
presented  it  a silver  and gold cup for  use in the ceremonies.           On
June  21,      1920,    for  the  only  time  in  its  history,    Temple  Council
sent  its  entire class  of candidates  to  Abington to  participate  in  a
special  presentation  of  the  Super  Excellent  Degree by the  older
Council.       May the  future  of  Temple  Council  fulfill  the  promise
held out by its  ten years of life .
SOUTH  SHORE  COMMANDERY  No.  31,       KNIGHTS  TEMPLARS
Previous   to   1870  Old   Colony  Commandery  of  Abington  had
Templar jurisdiction  over  Weymouth;     therefore,      when the  South
Shore  Commandery wished  to  receive  its  Orders,     it  was given  to
 - 241 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           719
them from the  Old Colony Commandery.         In  1870 transportation
was by horse and carriage or by barges,    and,   having such a distance
to travel,     a late  Conclave returned the "Knights " home just  about
time to go to  work.         Therefore,    under these conditions  43 Knights
agreed  to  petition the Grand Commandery of  Massachusetts  and
Rhode Island  for  a  Dispensation  to form a  Commandery in Wey-
mouth.               The Old Colony Lodge giving their  approval,    on June 22,
1870,     a Dispensation was granted to open a Commandery of Knights
Templars in  Weymouth,    to be known as South Shore Commandery,
and the following Brothers formed the Lodge :

The Triennial  Conclave  of  the  Grand  Encampment which  was
held  in  Boston in  1895  stands  for  a  red  letter  week for  our  Com-
mandery  as  well  as  one of  the  most  successful  Triennials  in  the
history of the Grand Encampment.          While the financial  assistance
was most generous,     our guests  were most appreciative.      The days
of  outing  were  enjoyed  and two  Commanderies were entertained,
Killington of  Burlington,    Vt. ,    and Forest  City  of  Cleveland,     Ohio.
The prosperity  of  South  Shore  Commandery is  beyond question,
and is  a  loved,     honored  and respected  Lodge.       May it  be  forever
blessed  with  continued  prosperity  and  maintain  its  high  station
as one of the brightest stars in the galaxy of Knights Templars.
MAYFLOWER  CHAPTER,       O.  E.  S.
Mayflower  Chapter,        O.   E.   S.,       was  organized  in  Weymouth,
Dec.  5,       1898,      by thirty-four faithful  men and women.              The name
Mayflower being  suggested  by Mr.  Walter C.  Gutterson,    it  was at
once accepted as being especially fitting  to  a Chapter in  this  place.
The ship  Mayflower is  also  its  seal .
 - 243 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           721
On Dec.  17,      1898,    the first  regular meeting was held  in  Pythian
Hall,       Weymouth  Landing,     Mrs.  Olive  F.   Wellcome,    Worthy  Ma-
tron,      and  Mr. Joseph  E.  Gardner,     Worthy Patron .
Highland  Chapter  of  Somerville  exemplified  the  initiation  and
Mayflower Chapter No. 65 was duly instituted.        After  six months
of hard and good work they received.   from the Grand Chapter their
Charter  in   September,      1899.     These  loyal  people  met  twice  a
month in  Pythian  Hall,    and in January,     1900,    had a membership
offifty.
The present  Chapter looks  back with pride to its founders,     and
those  few  charter  members still  with  us  must be justly  proud  of
their  achievement.        Its  teachings  are  an  inspiration  to  all  who
hear them.
During the first  ten years its  growth showed a decided  interest,
the  social  life  being  emphasized  by its  members,     teas,     whist  and
musicales  being  prominent  in  its  program.         In this  way a  closer
fraternal  relationship was formed.
In  1907  the  Chapter  was  honored  by  having  P.  M.  Annie  E.
Jordan appointed a Deputy.        She asked  P.  M. Flora  S.  Matthew-
son of Keystone Chapter,    and an honorary member of this  Chapter,
to  be  her  Marshal,     and  a  reception  was  given  them  in  October,
1907 .
Until  1916  Pythian  Hall was large enough for the meetings,    but
the membership increased  and  larger  quarters  were  needed  and  it
was decided to move to Masonic Temple,    East Weymouth,     and in
November,       1916,     the  first  meeting was held  at that  place.           Since
that time a rapid growth in numbers has been noticed.
In 1918,     the year of the World War with all the " less "  days,     the
Chapter held its  own,     and also  was active through its  members in
all  relief societies .
The year  1920 was a wonderful year for  this  Chapter.        In Jan-
uary  they occupied for the first  time the beautiful  Masonic apart-
ments.             The glory  and inspiration  this  room gives  one  is  beyond
the power of tongue to  tell.         Every one feels  it  the moment they
enter,     and now,    with the  new organ,     leaves  nothing to be desired.
In  1920 also the Chapter again was honored by the Grand Chap-
ter,        P.   M.  Elizabeth  L.   Peyton  being  appointed  Deputy Grand
Matron,        and  with  her  Marshal,     Annie  P.   Beck,     was  tendered  a
reception in October,   1920.    P.  M. Helen J.  Murray was also invited
to  be an Assistant  Grand Warden,    and in  1922  P.  M.  Evelyn  G.
Brown was a Page at Grand Chapter  Sessions.           In 1922  Mary A.
Lewis,     who has been Chaplain since  1901 ,     was made a  life  member
to the great joy of all.      Later P.  M. Nellie L. Denbroeder,    a Charter
Member and an officer  since  1899,    was also made a life  member.
As is  usual  with all  fraternal  organizations,    its  growth after  the
war was phenomenal,    and its  membership is  now 250.
Of the original  membership only  five  are  still  with  us,     and we
rejoice  to  say  they  show the  same interest  they  did  twenty- five
years  ago.             The remaining  five  are  Mr.  Joseph  E.  Gardner,      first

Patron,        Mrs.  Flavilla   B.  Gardner,       Mrs.  Ellen   E.   Kidder,     Mrs.
Nellie  L.  Denbroeder,    Mr.  William  B.  Denbroeder.
The present  Matron,     Mrs.  Edith G.  Bicknell,     and Patron A.  E.
Hunt are  carrying  on the good work of  their predecessors  and feel
sure Mayflower Chapter is  a credit  to the town.

CRESCENT  LODGE  No. 82 ,       I.   O.  O.  F.
Crescent  Lodge No. 82,     I.   O.  O.  F.,    was instituted in  East Wey-
mouth Aug.  22,     1845.    Their first  meeting place being in the "Old
Green Shop"  on the corner of Broad and Middle Streets,    Weymouth
Center.                 There  were  six  signatures  to  the  charter,     viz.:      Warren
W. Barker,       E.  W. Coffin,   John P.  Lovell,   James Hawes,    Jr. ,     Josiah
E.  Rice  and Z.  L.  Bicknell,   the latter being a member for  fifty- four
years,        until  his  death  in  1899.
Meetings  were  held  for  three  years  in  the  " Old  Green  Shop, "
when in  1848,      a  new lodge  room was dedicated,      the  Lodge  now
numbering  about 90 members .
In  1865  new  quarters  were  obtained  over  Bicknell's  store  and
here,      in   1870,     was  observed  the  twenty- fifth  anniversary.             Grand
officers   were  present  and  witnessed  the  degree  staff   confer  the
initiatory  degree on a large class  of candidates.
In 1871 Crescent Lodge took part at the laying of the corner stone
of Odd Fellows Hall,    Tremont Street,    Boston,    at which representa-
tives  from all over the State were present .
In  1875  when  the  Lodge at  South  Weymouth was  instituted,
Crescent  Lodge gave withdrawal cards  to  nineteen members,     who
joined  Wildey Lodge,   thus  giving  the  new Lodge a good healthy
start.               This left  a membership in 1876 of  141  active members.
Twelve years  later,    in  1888,    the question of better  quarters  and
a larger  building was considered,    and in  1889  action  was taken to
build  the present  Odd Fellows  Hall,    on the  corner  of  Commercial
and  Cottage Streets,    and the corner stone was laid  the same year
and the building dedicated in 1890 to the use of all branches of the
Order.
In  1895 the fiftieth  anniversary of the Lodge was held here and
was well  attended by the Grand Lodge.
The Lodge has  also  passed  its  seventy-fifth  anniversary,      which
was  celebrated  by  the  members  in   a  most  successful  manner.
Aug.  19  to  22,      1920,     were the red-letter  days of its  history  and an
occasion  always  to  be remembered.        A committee of nine,    with the
first  officers  of  the Lodge,    made arrangements  and the  most com-
plete  details   were  carried   out.               There  were  present  the   repre-
sentatives  of  the  Grand  Lodge,    from  the  Encampment,      from  the
Rebekah branch and from surrounding  Lodges .
Alfred  S.   Pinkerton,   Past Grand Sire,     who was present,     had the
honor  of   attending   the   fiftieth    anniversary   twenty- five   years
before,     as  also  had the  following  Past Grand  Masters  and Patri-
archs.

WILDEY LODGE  No.  21,     I.  O.  O.  F.
Wildey  Lodge  of   South  Weymouth  was  instituted   March  9,
1875,    with  18  charter  members.         Its  growth has been steady and
it  stands second to  none in sustaining the object of its  organization.
It has a fine  building  erected  by its  members,   which with its  fur-
nishings  has  cost  $15,000.           This  building  contains  a  hall  for  the
use of  the Lodge,     a recreation hall for  the use of the members and
two banquet rooms.
The twenty-fifth  anniversary was celebrated  March 9,     1900,     the
reception  committee  consisting  of  P.  G.  M.  Louis  A.  Cook,     P.  G.
George L.  Wentworth,    P.  G.  Gordon Willis,      P.  G. J.  Burton Reed,
P. G.  Frank H.  Richards,    P. G.  Francis  F. Bullock and V. G. Karle
H. Granger.
History,      when the lapse of time makes the celebration  of  some
important  event worthy of  much interest,   clings  about the details
connected with its  origin as well as the more prominent occurrences
of its  subsequent history.
The following  brief  statement  gives  some account  of  the  origin
and later  history  of  Wildey  Lodge  No.  21 ,       I.   O.  O.  F.,      the  only
Lodge in  the Commonwealth named after the founder of the Order,
Thomas Wildey.
The  first    recorded  meeting  looking  toward  the  formation  of
an Odd Fellows'     Lodge in  South Weymouth was held at the resi-
dence  of  J.   Leonard  Curtis,     where  the  members  of  the  Order,
mostly  belonging  to  Crescent  Lodge of  East Weymouth,    gathered
on  the  evening  of  Dec.  12,       1874.     The  meeting  organized  with
Brother Wm.      H. Sargent as chairman and Brother John H. Stetson
as   secretary.           At this  time  the  members  voted  to  petition  for  a
charter  and to  insert  the  name of  " Wildey"  in  the  petition  as  a
proposed name.         Other meetings were held on December 19 and 26,
and at the latter  an entire  list  of officers  was elected.
 - 247 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           725
The committee on petitions  met the petitioners  at Tuck's  Hall,
December 29,   and to this  committee their claims for a charter were
presented.             Jan.  21,     1875,       Brothers  Wm.      H.  Sargent  and  D.  F.
Reed were appointed  a  committee  to  meet the committee on peti-
tions  at  the  Grand Lodge office,     Saturday,    Jan.  9,     1875.   At this
meeting it  was voted that the regular meetings  should  be held  on
Monday nights and that has always been the meeting night of this
Lodge.            On the  evening of January 18  the  by-laws were adopted,
and on  February 1 it  was voted to  lease Tuck's Hall for  a term of
six years.
On Tuesday  afternoon,       March  9,       1875,      the  Lodge  was  insti-
tuted,    the  following Grand Officers  officiating :
Julius Q.  Clark,    G. M.
Samuel B. Krogman,  Grand Instructor,   Acting D. G. M.
Henry W. Clark,    G. C.

On the evening  of April  26,     1878,      in  connection  with  the  cele-
bration of the anniversary of the Order,   the Lodge was the recipient
at the hands  of the ladies  of  a beautiful  silk  banner,     bearing the
likeness  of  the founder of  the Order,    the Three Links  and suitable
inscription .               This was a gala night in the history of the Lodge.
On May 20,     1878,    the members enjoyed  a notable occasion,     the
event being  the official  visitation by the  Board  of  Grand Officers,
John U.  Perkins,   G. M.  In later years the  Lodge has been honored
by numerous visits  of the Grand Officers .
During  the  spring  and  summer  of  1880  a  controversy  arose
between  the  Lodge and the  lessee  of  the  building  then  occupied
for  Lodge purposes  as  to  whether the rent should be $100  or  $200
per  year.                  The parties  being  unable  to  agree,      a  committee  was
appointed  to  see  what sum of  money could  be  raised  among the
Brothers  for  the purchase of land and the erection  of  a new hall.
The outcome was the laying  of the corner stone  of  a new building
in Independence Square,   Aug.  18,     1881,    by G. M. Henry W. Clark
and his  suite.       The building was duly completed and was occupied
for  the  first   time  Feb.  6,       1882.     The  dedicatory  exercises   took
place on February 16,   at 4 o'clock,    P.M.,    lasting through the evening,

and it  is  recorded that the celebration was one long to be remem-
bered by the participants.

MECHANICS  TEMPLE  OF  HONOR AND  TEMPERANCE
Mechanic Temple of  Honor and Temperance No. 25 was organ-
ized  in  East Weymouth March 8,    1867,    by men who felt  that there
was a need of an organization for the promotion of  total  abstinence
and  the  prohibition  of  the  liquor  traffic.         The growth  was great,
the  first  year  many of the business  men and  most of  the manu-
facturers  joining,   and its  influence in town affairs  was legion.          The
wives  of  the  members  organized  a Women's  Temperance Society
and its  success  was so  great that it  became nationally  known,    and
women came from the West to size up its  work and went back and
reported  to  the women of  Ohio,    and that magnificent organization,
the  Women's  Christian  Temperance  Society,    was  formed  which
to- day belts  the world and gives us in America that for which Me-
chanics  Temple  was  formed.        Each  member  took  the  following
pledge:        We will  not  make,     buy,     sell  or  use  as  a  beverage  any
spirituous  or  malt  liquors,    wine  or cider,     nor  any other  alcoholic
beverages  whether  enumerated  or  not,    but will  use all  honorable
 - 251 - 
LODGES  AND SOCIETIES                           729
means  to  prevent  their  manufacture or  use,     or  the traffic  therein ;
and this  pledge,   we will  keep and maintain inviolate till  the end of
life.        And among the number living  to-day,    June  20,    1923,      whose
names are  on the  charter  list ,     are  Willard  Dunbar,     Waldo Turner,
Ezra  B.   Tirrell,    Joseph  P.   Ford  and  many others  who joined  in
the early seventies.
They met  for  a  few  years  on  the  northeast  corner  of  Jackson
Square  in  a block which contained stores on the lower floors,   where
liquors  stronger than water were sold by the owner of the old build-
ing,      who always  closed  up his  business  in  smoke.           So  after  being
burnt out they purchased the land on the opposite corner,     formed
a stock company,
any,  sold shares at $25 par and built  Temple of Honor
Hall,      at  that  time one of  the finest Lodge rooms in New England.
It  was  dedicated with  bands,   torchlight  parade and  flag  presenta-
tion by the  ladies.          This was a large silk American flag,      and when
constitutional  prohibition  became a law fifty- two  years  afterward
it  was hoisted to the mast head,    and shook itself to pieces rejoicing
over the victory.
For many years the Temple met in this  Hall each week,     having
its  Council  meetings for working the advance degrees of the Order.
Its   Cadets  of  Honor,     for  the young men,     many of  whom to-day
belong to  the  Masonic and Odd Fellows  bodies,   can look  back to
the early  training they got in the Temple of Honor.        Its  influence
was felt  in all the surrounding towns,    many men joining from them.
As other organizations began to form in Weymouth and the churches
formed young peoples  societies  and took up the Temperance work,
the  Temple fell  away from  a  membership  of  several  hundred  to
about  twenty- five,    most of whom belonged in Hingham,    and after
the  death  of  Leonard  Thompson,    who had  purchased  the  bonds
and owned the building,   the Temple closed  up its  affairs  in  East
Weymouth in  1912  and moved to  Hingham,   where  it  continues  to
do the  work so  well  planned by the early  builders.        The Temple
paid sick  and death benefits,    and has  a  permanent watch fund of
which  Mr.  B.  B.  Sylvester is  trustee.        Several of its  members are
internationally  known  for  the  work  they  have  accomplished  for
prohibition.              And surely it  is  the  one organization  of  Weymouth
that can crow over what it  has  done,   - placed  Weymouth on the
map.
KNIGHTS  OF  PYTHIAS
On Nov.  30,       1869,     a few young men gathered in the shoe shop
of  the  late  John  W.  Hart for  the  purpose of forming  a Lodge  of
Knights of  Pythias and to apply for a charter for the same.         Nelson
M. Hubert was chosen chairman and Darius Smith,   secretary,    who,
with Reuben Tirrell,   James T. Pease,    Augustus T. Cushing,    Franklin
A.   Nash,        Benjamin  F.  Robinson,      P.  Henry  Linton,     Christopher
T.  Bailey,     Geo.    P.  Lyon,    Charles A.  Radcliffe,   Augustus A. Linton,
John W. Hunt,   Elbridge T.  Richards  and Dominick A.  Hart were
 - 252 - 
730                               LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
granted  a charter  and  Delphi  Lodge was instituted  in  St.  Johns
Hall,       Boston,   Dec. 17,   1869.
After  fifty  years  of  existence  only three of the above members
were living  in  1921,   -Darius Smith,   James T.  Pease and Reuben
Tirrell,      who were present at its  fiftieth  anniversary Dec.  18,     1919.
The first  officers  of the Lodge were as follows :
W. C.,    Nelson M. Hubert.
W. V.  C.,     John W. Hart.
W. P. ,      P.  Henry Linton.
W. R.  S. ,        Darius  Smith.
W. B.,      Reuben Tirrell.
N. G.,   Augustus Linton.
I.   S. ,     Benjamin F.  Robinson.
O. S. ,   Augustus S.  Cushing.
James T.  Pease,     Darius  Smith,    George  P.  Lyons  and Benjamin
F.  Robinson were appointed  Past  Chancellors  and helped  to  insti-
tute  the  Lodge Dec.  17,    1869.    Their  first  meetings  were held  in
Binney's,         Lincoln  Square,    which  was  destroyed  by  fire  Sept.  15,
1870,        when  Delphi  Lodge  lost   everything,     but  with  dauntless
courage they started again with an assessment of $3 on each member
to  replace  and continue their  work,     and with  the assistance  of St.
Paul  Lodge  of  Quincy,    who loaned  the  paraphernalia  to  do  the
Degree work.
These meetings were held in  William's  Hall,   over the store  now
occupied  by Kempel's  Drug Store,   until June 11,   1872,      when the
Lodge moved to the hall  over the store  of  M.  H.  Read on Wash-
ington  Street,    which  was later  moved to  Commercial Street,     and
occupied  by  the  Gazette  and  Transcript  Publishing   Company.
This  hall was occupied  until Aug. 3,    1874,    when Washington Hall
was rented,    where meetings were held until  1883,   when they moved
to the hall in a new building erected by Dr. A. G. Nye,    which was
dedicated by the Grand Lodge,      K.  of  P.,   and is  still  occupied by
Delphi  Lodge.
The  Lodge  has  had  several   branches  attached  to  it during  its
existence:         the   Endowment  Rank,       organized   in   March,          1879;
Arbutus  Assembly,    Pythian  Sisterhood,    organized  April  27,       1891,
and not receiving  recognition by the Supreme  Lodge;     and later  a
Temple of  Pythian  Sisters  was instituted  March,     1907,     and  is  in
existence to-day.       In June,    1904,    Delphi Lodge No. 10,    U.  R. K. P. ,
was  formed,         also   several   minor  branches  which  were  of  short
duration.
The present officers,    1920,   are -
C. C.,    Winifred A.  Brown.
V. C.,   Herbert F. Johnson.
P.,    Victor H. Hall.
M. of W.,    Grant B. Chase.
M. A. ,      Lawrence E.  Pray.
K. R.  S. ,    Arthur E. Bicknell.
M. of F. ,      Franklin P. Whitten.
M. E.,      Francis M. Drown.
I.  G.,    Elmer H. Goodspeed.
O. G.,    Sylvanus B.  Blanchard.
The present membership is  (1929)  188.
The Lodge meets in  Pythian  Hall  every  Thursday evening.
Eight members of the  Lodge served in  the  World War.

Many honors have been conferred on the Lodge.       In 1870 Nelson
M. Hubert was appointed a P.  G. C.,    and a member of the Supreme
Lodge.          In  1895  Hon.     J.   H.  Flint  was  elected  Grand  Chancellor
of  the  Grand  Lodge.          Numerous  Deputies  have been  appointed,
and several notable events appear on its  pages of history :
October,     1894,    Boston parade on silver anniversary of Grand Lodge.
Dec. 19,    1894,    own silver  anniversary celebrated.
June 17,    1894,   reception to G. C. James H. Flint at Weymouth.
Oct.  5,       1912,     grand parade at Weymouth.
Dec. 18,   19,    1919,    fiftieth  anniversary of Delphi Lodge.
During its  existence of fifty years it has had its " Season of Joy
and its  Hours of Sorrow, " but it is still  flourishing,  working for  the
uplifting  of  humanity  and  the  carrying  out  of  its   principles   of
" Friendship,       Charity  and  Benevolence."
DELPHI  TEMPLE  NO.     59,       PYTHIAN  SISTERS
(Auxiliary to the Knights of Pythias)
On March 25,     1907,    there  was a meeting held  in  Pythian  Hall,
Weymouth,     by the State organizer,    Fannie W. Eaton of Brockton,
for  the purpose of forming a Temple in  Weymouth,    and  on Mon-
day afternoon  and evening,    April  8,     1907,     Delphi  Temple No.  59
was instituted  by the State organizer,   the following being the  first
officers  elected :
Secretary,    pro tem,   Annie E. Jordan.
Past Chief,   Lydia W. Richards.
Most Excellent Chief,   Annie E. Jordan.
Excellent Senior,    Elvira P.  Smith.
Excellent  Junior,   Jeannette Dexheimer.
Manager of Temple,    Edith Inkley.
Mistress of Records and Correspondence, Tina H. Hyland.
Mistress of Finance,    Elizabeth S.  Hall.
Protector of Temple,   Fanny A. Walsh.
Guard of Outer Temple,   J.  Gertrude Newcomb.
Pianist,     Florence C. Richards.
The Temple was organized  with  the sincere desire  of promoting
the moral,     mental,     social  and  physical  elevation  of  its  members,
cultivating  a spirit  of fraternal love which shall permeate and con-
trol  their  daily  lives,    ministering  in  all  ways to  the  wants  of the
sick,       distressed  or  needy,     watching  at  the  bedside  of  the  dying,
paying the last  tribute  of love  and respect  to the dead,    comforting
and providing for the widow in her afflictions  and daily exemplify-
ing in every possible way the Golden Rule.
On Jan.  7,     1920,     the  Past  Chiefs'     Club was formed with a mem-
bership  of eleven,   which meets bi- monthly.         This  Club  has  taken
up charitable work along with its  social  efforts .

WEYMOUTH CIRCLE NO.     189,     DAUGHTERS OF  ISABELLA
Weymouth Circle  No.  189,    Daughters of  Isabella,   was organized
by State Regent Carolyn B. Manning of New Bedford at a meeting
held  in  Knights  of  Columbus  Hall  on  November 16,     1921.    Two
hundred  and forty- five  women were  present  and  became  charter
members,        the  majority  of  whom had  belonged  to  the  Catholic
Daughters of America,   which disbanded at a meeting in Knights of
Columbus Hall on Nov. 1,    1921.
The  Circle  composed  members  from  Hingham,     Braintree,       East
Braintree,      Quincy  Point  and the  Weymouths.           The object  of  the
Circle is  to render charity where it  is  needed,   whether in the  terri-
tory  covered  by the  membership  or  elsewhere,      and  to  promote
social  and intellectual  intercourse among its  members.
The meetings comprise one business  and one social a month,   held
in  Knights  of  Columbus  Hall.         The benefits  derived  by members
consist  of  a remembrance of flowers,    fruit  or books during  illness,
under the supervision  of  Susan G.  Sheehan,     chairman,    also  a mor-
tuary benefit.

In  December,       1921,     a charitable  committee was appointed by
Regent Helen L.  Griffin,    consisting of  two members from each part
of  the  town,   with  Annie  S.  Lynch,     chairman.         The duty of  the
members of said committee was to notify the chairman of any needy
case reported.         Upon investigation,   the case was immediately cared
for  regardless of nationality or creed,   and provisions,   fuel and cloth-
ing were supplied as  the case  required.         During the  first  year  849
garments  were  distributed   throughout  Weymouth  and  vicinity.
The demand for  clothing  was so  great,    it  became necessary  for  a
sewing  circle.         Margaret  E.  Coyne was appointed  chairman,     and
twelve members met an afternoon a week at their respective homes,
and  supplied  the  charitable  committee  with  an  average  of  forty
garments a month,    mostly clothes for children .
In  December,      1922,      a  Dramatic  Club  was formed through  the
efforts  of  Regent  Helen  L.  Griffin.              Twenty members  completed
the  State  University  Extension  Course  of  twelve  assignments  in
Oral  English  and  Public  Speaking  and  received  diplomas.            Miss
Julia  Reilly  of  Boston  supervised  the class  and at the conclusion
the  class  gave their  first  dramatic production  to  a crowded house.
In  February,      1922,      a  by-law committee  was  appointed,     as  fol-
lows:      Katherine  Cleary,    chairman;      Sara Cross,     Mary McCluskey,
Elizabeth   McCarthy,      Catherine  Melville,    Anna  Egan  and Annie
Knox.
The members have greatly  enjoyed  the social  meetings,    among
which were costume parties,     whists,    Halloween  party  with  Dutch
suppers,      musicales,    Christmas  parties  and summer outings.             The
music for all  entertainments was under the direction of the pianist,
Mrs. Alice Fitzsimmons.
The Circle  has also  held many public affairs  which have proved
successful ,      such as dancing parties,    whists,    gentlemen's night,    Chil-
dren's  Christmas  tree,     Pop  Concerts,     and  Charity  Bazaar during
the winter months and a field day during the summer.
The proceeds  from all  public affairs  help  the  Circle  to  carry  on
the extensive charity work,    which is  the greatest  aim of the mem-
bers.            The membership of the  Circle  has increased  from 245 mem-
bers  to 350 in eighteen months.
The Daughters of Isabella are a sister organization to the Knights
of Columbus and through combined efforts aim to be a credit to the
town of Weymouth.
ANCIENT  ORDER  OF  HIBERNIANS
The Ancient Order of Hibernians,    the oldest of all  Irish  fraternal
organizations,    was founded  in  Ireland  during the latter  part of  the
seventeenth century to defend the rights  and to  promote the prog-
ress  of the  Irish  race.           The American branch,    or the Ancient Order
of  Hibernians in America,   was  established  in this  country in  1836,
but it  was forty years later,   on May 16,    1876,   that the first  Division
of the Order,     No. 9 of East Weymouth,   was organized in Weymouth

GUISSEPPI  VERDE NO.     278,     SONS  OF  ITALY OF  AMERICA
A Lodge of  this  Order was organized in East Weymouth on Sept.
13,       1913,     and was named Guisseppi Verde No. 278.
Meetings  are held the second Friday of each month in  G.  A.  R.
Hall.
The charter  members  were  Euginio  Gatto,    Antonio Denti  and
Antonio Petrucci.
The purposes  of the Order are to  unite all  Italians  also  those of
Italian  descent throughout the United States  to use its  strength  to
protect  each  member,     to  teach  the  American language,    and to  re-
spect and love the country;       to  prepare and assist  all  those who are
capable  to  become citizens,    to  help  them and their  families  finan-
cially when in  need;     to care for orphans  of deceased members.
The motto of the Order is  " Liberty,    Equality,     Fraternity. "

L.   O.  O.  М.
The  Brotherhood  of  L.  O.  O.  M. is  founded  upon the splendid
principles  of  Purity,    Aid  and  Progress,     and is  designed  to  bind
civilized mankind closer  together with bonds of fraternal  love,     and
to  teach  the great Truths which have for  their  purpose  the  eleva-
tion of society.       The aims and purposes  of  the  L.  O.  O.  M. are  to
inspire  lofty statements relative to humanity's welfare.         All religious
and  political  rights  are  fully  recognized  by the  teachings  of  the
Order and questions  or references  of a political  or sectarian  nature
find no place for discussion within its  portals .
It  requires  fifty  male persons,   each over twenty-one years of age,
to  ask for  a charter,    and it  has  a clause by which medical aid  is
furnished  at  somewhat  reduced  rates,     thus  it  is  partly  beneficial
and partly  social,    having  a women's  branch  called  Moose Ladies,
who attend to the welfare of the members at their social gatherings.
The meeting place for both Lodges is in East Weymouth,    Temple
of Honor Hall.
ROYAL SOCIETY  OF  GOOD  FELLOws
It is  an endowment society  which had its  origin in the  state  of
Rhode  Island   about  1880   and   several   Lodges  were  instituted
throughout  the  State  of  Massachusetts.        A charter  was  obtained
for  a Lodge in East Weymouth,   which held regular meetings in  the
old  G.  A.  R.  Hall on Broad Street.      Its  tenets  were expressed by
the words " to promote benevolence,   morality,   science and industry."
There was  a Supreme Assembly,     a Grand Assembly,     and Subor-
dinate Assemblies,   the latter  being presided over by a Ruler  as  its
chief officer.
Each member paid  dues  ranging from $4.50 to  $7  monthly for
a life  insurance policy of $3,000.
The Lodge went out of existence in Weymouth about 1898.
KNIGHTS  OF  ST.       CRISPIN
Weymouth has been from early days a shoe  town and although
formerly  the  "factories "   were  very  primitive,     there  was  still   the
ever-jealous  care exhibited for the job held by the workman ;        and
as  time  changed  the  customs,    this  jealous  care  was  extended  to
 - 264 - 
742                               LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
help the brother workman,   and there followed the banding or union-
izing   of  the  operators.                This  gave  them  a sort  of  brotherhood,
primarily  formed  to  protect  themselves,     finally  grew into  a band
which attempted to coerce their employers.
One of the earliest " labor unions,"  perhaps the very earliest,     was
known by the name of "Knights of St.  Crispin,"  from the legend
that a religious fanatic fled  from the persecutions of the  Christians
from Rome to Gaul,   where he worked as  a shoemaker at Soissons .
He worked in  the cause of  Christianity  and was very charitable;
according  to  the legend his  benevolence was so great that he even
stole leather to make shoes for the poor.           In the year 287 he suffered
martyrdom.           Preaching by day and making shoes by night,    he made
a precarious  living,   but the governor learned  his  religion,     tortured
him and ordered him beheaded.      Crispin was afterwards  canonized
and thereafter was recognized as the patron saint of shoemakers.
All parts of Weymouth had its  members and very active societies
were  formed.             In the  south  part  of the town meetings  were held
over  " Pitcher's  store. "    They had signs,   passwords  and grips,      but
the  order  was  short- lived,    surviving  only  about  two  years.         Its
primary object was to prevent the bosses from "docking "  the help.
They wished to protect  themselves,    and  in event of dissatisfaction
they would strike.      Acommittee would then be appointed and they
called on the bosses to talk over grievances.        All shops in Weymouth
combined.
One,    Gilman Shaw,   worked for C. & P. H. Tirrell,   who had a large
California   trade.       Mr.  Bates,   one of  the  bosses,   hired  a man to
take  Mr.  Shaw's  place,     because  the  latter,     a member  of  the  St.
Crispin's,    would not stand a "dock. "    The whole shop crew stopped
and walked out in sympathy.        At last  they were called back,     all
the help went to work,    Mr. Shaw retained his  job and received  his
old pay.
Edwin  R.  Clark,      Pond Street,    was Treasurer;     Stephen  McGill
was always an active member.        The tenets were very strong  on all
points,      so  much  so  that  several  gave  up their  membership,     one
member joining at one meeting and resigning  the next.
In all probability there originated in Weymouth the spirit of com-
bination calculated to  unionize the efforts  of workmen,   and to  this
day it  is  a recognized  principle governing  much of the  industrial
life  of  the  nation.          Then followed  probably  the  first  " strike "  as
above recorded.
One of  the peculiarities  of  the  Order was that they were averse
to giving young men any instructions  in  the shoemaking  industry.
KNIGHTS  OF  LABOR
Following the disbanding of the Knights of St.  Crispin there was
formed an association  known as the Knights  of  Labor.             This  was
an  organization  founded  by  Uriah  S.   Stevens  in  Philadelphia  in
1869,     organized as  a national body in  1871,    and not until  1881 was
 - 265 - 
LODGES  AND SOCIETIES                            743
the name of the order made public.        It was primarily a secret order
of working men broader than the Crispins,    for  all trades  were  rep-
resented and governed by a general  executive board,    presided  over
by a general  master workman who had power to  order  strikes  and
boycotts.              The object of the order was the amelioration of the con-
dition  of workmen.
The society met in Tuck's Hall,    South Weymouth,     D. S.  Murray
being elected  Grand Knight,     Jacob  Baker,     Statistician,    and a Mr.
Stetson,     Grievance  Committee.
At this  time shoe machinery was just  coming in  to  use  and the
tendency was to  keep it  out and still  make the  shoes by hand.           In
Josiah  Reed's shop the union was very strong and kept the men at
odds  with their  bosses  and the members of the  firm.         Such differ-
ences were handled by committees appointed by the  Knights  and
mostly met with the Grand Knight,     D. S.  Murray,   at his  store.
SOUTH  WEYMOUTH  GRANGE
Through  the  efforts   of  a  deputy  of  the   Massachusetts  State
Grange,    who had been invited by a few citizens,    South Weymouth
Grange  No.  270  of  the  Patrons  of  Husbandry was  organized  in
December,      1907.
This  order  exists  not only  for  the encouragement  of agriculture
in  all  its  phases and interests,    but also  for the upbuilding of char-
acter  and intelligence,    the protection  and enrichment of the home,
the wise training  and education of children,   respect  and toleration
for  religious  belief,    the development of community service,     and for
a more lively interest  in public affairs  and a firmer  loyalty  to  our
country.
Although  there  seemed  to  be  a very general  desire  to  promote
the objects of the Order,    yet when the time came to undertake the
organization,     only forty-three  out  of  over a hundred who favored
the movement by word of mouth were willing  to devote themselves
to active effort  and the real work of the Order.      This  outcome was
probably due,     in part,    to  the fact  that  many other  organizations
were  already devoted  in  a  special  or  limited  way to  some  of  the
purposes  of the Grange and their members would not enter  into  a
broader,     more inclusive  plan  lest  it  overtax  them,    or  possibly  de-
tract  from  their special  interests.           The evening of the organization
was  very  stormy  and  some  could  not  attend.        Nevertheless,       25
members of  Braintree Grange came and rendered  necessary  assist-
ance  in  the  installation  of  officers.          One of  the  most  important
officers- elect was ill  and could not be installed and the duties of the
position  had  to  be  performed  throughout the year by temporary
appointees.                This  was  a  serious  disadvantage  and it  was  not  the
only one.          The  new Grange  seemed  to  be destined  to  experience
all manner of drawbacks and  unfortunate  occurrences  throughout
its  existence.            Without  attempting  to  recite  these,     it  remains  to
state  the  few  good things  undertaken  and  successfully  promoted;
 - 266 - 
744                             LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
the  membership  gradually  increased  to  nearly  60,    but  never  ex-
ceeded  that  number at  any  one  time,   although  about twice  that
number  of  persons  were  eventually  initiated.           Many interesting
and  profitable  meetings  were  held  in  which  members  who  were
entirely  unaccustomed to take part in public meetings,    or  to  study
and  prepare  papers  upon subjects  in  which  they were  personally
interested,      were  encouraged  and  helped  to  take  an  active  part.
Influence was exerted  to  promote exhibits  at the annual fair  of the
Agricultural  and  Industrial  Society,    and in co-operation with  that
society  quite  a number of Farmers'     Institutes were held  at which
excellent instruction was given by expert specialists and by profes-
sors  from  the  State  Agricultural  College.        Public  meetings  were
held  at  which  the  principles  and benefits  of  the  Order  were  ex-
plained  by  officers   of  the  State Grange.       Many visitations  were
exchanged  with  neighboring  Granges  and  a  wider  acquaintance
made with  people  of  other  communities,    especially  of  the  towns
bordering  upon Weymouth and of  those south  and east  as  far  as
Kingston.               Through the  activity  of  the  South Weymouth Grange
a new Pomona or  District Grange was organized  in  1908.    It  was
named  Mayflower  Pomona Grange and in its  district  there  were,
at  first,     5 subordinate Granges.        The number has now increased  to
14 or  15 Granges and its  influence  is  felt  throughout  the  district
and indeed throughout the State.          It is  a matter for regret that the
local  Grange had to  contend with  many untoward  circumstances
that hindered  its  increase  in influence  and in numbers and eventu-
ally made it  seem wise to surrender its  charter,    when all  about this
region,      as  well as  through the State and Nation,    the Order is  pros-
pering  and promoting the welfare not only of its  own membership
but also  of the communities where it  exists.       After an existence  of
nearly  twelve years of varying encouragement and discouragement,
it  was decided to close the accounts and surrender the charter.        Yet
the  hope was  cherished  that  the time might soon come when the
rising  sun of democracy,    with its  awakening interest in the culture
of the soil,     the protection of the home,   the education of youth,    the
welfare of the community and the elevation of manhood and woman-
hood,    would bring a new day and a new life  to  the Order of  Patrons
of Husbandry in the good old  town of  Weymouth and so link  her
more closely  with the  uplifting  spirit  and organized  forces  of  the
20th century.            The Grange was closed in the summer of  1919.
THE  WEYMouth AGRICULTURAL  AND  INDUSTRIAL  SOCIETY
In  1863  Mr.  George  H.  Bates  of  South Weymouth obtained  an
option on a tract of land bordering on Old Swamp River and a  new
road  from  the  village  to  Mosquito  Plain,    afterward  named  Park
Street,      purposing to build  a race course for his own use.        Asugges-
tion  was  offered  that  the  track  be made a public  one,     and then
came  the  idea  of  organizing  an  agricultural  society  with  a  race
 - 267 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            745
track.            Mr.  William H.  Reed was authorized to test the sentiment
of the people by offering stock at $10 per share.       He soon reported
that something  over  $2,000  had been  subscribed,    and on Oct.  12,
1864,       the following warrant for a meeting was issued :
TO QUINCY  L.   REED,    Justice of the Peacefor the County of Norfolk.
GREETING:
We,      the  subscribers  by this  agreement,     for  the  purpose  of  improving  and
encouraging the science and practice of Agriculture and Horticulture,    and stimu-
lating  competition  in  the different  departments  of  Industry,     do  hereby  asso-
ciate  ourselves  together  under  the  name  of  the  Weymouth  Agricultural  &
Industrial  Society,     to  be located  in that  part  of  Weymouth  known as  South
Weymouth,       in  the  County of  Norfolk,    Commonwealth  of  Massachusetts,      and
claiming all  privileges  provided by the General  Statutes,   hereby  request  you
to call  a meeting of said members for the purpose of perfecting  an organization
of said Society,   as by law in such cases made and provided.      Said meeting to be
held at  Chapel Vestry,   on Monday evening,   October 31,    1864,    at seven P.M.
(Signed)           GEO.       H.  BATES.

DAN.       W.  BARROWS.

by Quincy L.  Reed.            At a director's  meeting,   June 2,   1865,     it  was
