The first  fair was held Sept. 20 and 21,  1865,   the exhibition being
in a tent  185 by 85 feet.             Complimentary tickets  were issued  to  all
the clergymen of the town.            The affair  was a grand  success.
prediction  of  the most sanguine being  verified.    John  W. Thomas
was  chief  marshal  of  the  show.          The Weymouth  Band furnished

On May 1,      1866,      a  race  was  conducted  at the  grounds,     which
netted $215.                 On July 4,   1866,   a horse trot netted $462.             The second
annual fair  of the Society,    opened Sept.  19,    1866.    A drizzling  rain
interfered   with  all   arrangements.         The  drawing,      spading   and
ploughing matches were  held,   and have never been excelled  in  the
history  of  the  Society,    but the  racing  for  the  afternoon was post-
poned  until  Thursday,     which  proved  stormier  yet.              Still,       as  the
records  say,    " the best  of feeling prevailed,    and general  good  spirit
and cheerful acquiescence to  the will of Him who sendeth alike  the
rain  and  the  sunshine. "    At 10 o'clock,    John S.  Fogg,      President
of the  Society,    called  those in the tent  to  order.          The Rev. James
P.  Terry invoked the divine blessing.     Still it rained on the just and
on the unjust.           The Hon.    Marshall P.  Wilder delivered the address,
and he was followed by the  Rev.  H.  D.  Walker of  East Abington,
with  a humorous  poem.             The fair  was  continued  through  until
Friday,      which  proved  more  propitious,       and  there  was  a  match
game of baseball which attracted a large  attendance.            The receipts
were $ 1,401.12.
On  October  1   at  a  directors'     meeting  it  was  voted  to  borrow
$1,000,       and hold a horse fair for  two days.          This  netted  $100.            At
a directors'         meeting,   Aug.  25,     1868,    it  was  voted  to  change  the
main entrance from Park Street to Park Avenue,  and that the build-
ing committee proceed  at  once in  the erection of a building  100 by
40 feet.
Governor  Claflin  was  a guest of the Society at the fair  in  1870.
In later  years  Governor  Butler  favored  us with his  presence,     and
also  Governor  Russell.           Complimentary  tickets  were issued  to  all
clergymen in town as late  as  1870.    The increased  receipts  of  1871
and 1872 probably are accounted for by the withdrawal of this privi-
lege  from the clergy.
During the early years of the Society's  existence many rules  and
regulations  appear  regarding  the use  of the  grounds.       The gates
were kept locked,    keys were sold,    and as these keys were sometimes
loaned  it  was necessary  to  have restrictions  on their use.          At one
directors'           meeting,       two   members   acknowledged   entering   the

grounds  on  the  Sabbath,     but  legal  action  was  deferred  on  their
promise to desist.
In  1870  an  exhibition  of  fireworks  by  Edmund  S.   Hunt  was
given on the evening  of the 4th  of July,   in addition  to  the horse
race,     and  this  custom was continued  for  a number of years.             On
Tuesday  afternoon  and  evening,   Aug.  24,      1875,     a  grand  reunion
of  the  stockholders  and friends of the Agricultural Society was held
at  Agricultural  Hall.            The  Weymouth  Band  volunteered   their
services .            Refreshments  were  served  during the evening,     dancing
ensued,      and  a very  enjoyable  reunion  was  recorded.            These  re-
unions  were  continued  in  after  years.         During  1875  additional
room was provided  by more horse  sheds,    at  an expense  exceeding
$1,000.
On Aug.  26,       1878,     it  was voted  to  have  a firemen's  muster  on
the first  day of the fair.           The King  Philip  machine  of  Rockland
captured  the  first   prize.           In  1879  a  firemen's  muster  was  held,
$700 being  offered  in premiums,   the first  prize of $300 going  to  the
Conqueror.          On Jan.  21,   1881,    it  was voted to hold the fair  Friday
and Saturday,    September 30 and October  1 ,    and that the grounds
be kept quiet for  the Sunday following.        On Nov. 7,   1882,     it  was
voted  to hold  a harvest festival  in December.        On Jan.  16,    1883,
arrangements  were made to  have  a musical  festival  at  the  Town
Hall.          The Arion-Cecelia  Club was engaged,  the Weymouth Band
furnished  music,    supper  was  served  in  the  upper  hall,     free  car-
riages  ran from all parts of the town to the hall .
During  the  early  years  a good  deal  of  attention  was given  to
horse   racing.          Almost  every  evening  large   numbers  of  people
resorted  to  the track where the horses of Weymouth and adjoining
towns were exercised.        It was always  a custom to  hold entertain-
ments on the 4th  of July.     Popular  sports  have always  been  en-
couraged during the years  of the existence  of  our Society,    and all
the fashionable games have held forth at the fair,   such as baseball,
polo,      lacrosse,     clay  pigeon  shoots,      Indians,     football,      glass   ball
shoot,     bicycle,    foot race,    hurdle race,   dog circus,    etc.,   etc.
The  first   coaching  and  trades  parade  of  the  Society  was  given
in  1903,     taking the place of the grand cavalcade of early days.

SOUTH  WEYMOUTH  IMPROVEMENT  ASSOCIATION
In the year 1881 the citizens  of South Weymouth formed a very
important  society,     which  had  for  its   object  the  beautifying  and
rendering more prosperous the southern section of the town,   known
as  the  South Weymouth Improvement Association.          It  had a most
substantial membership and exerted a powerful influence in the ac-
tivities  of the town.       A call  for a meeting was drawn up under the
name of  the Village  Improvement Association  on April  27,       1881,
signed by seventy-six of the citizens,    and the first meeting was held
in Music Hall on the above evening,    at which the Rev.  George N.
Marden was chosen President.
The call for this meeting set forth as its  object the following well-
chosen and most laudable purposes :
The object of the Association is to awaken and encourage in the community
a sentiment and a spirit  which will act for the common interest;    to  create  and
stimulate in the individual  a regard for  the elevation  and improvement  of  the
community,    thereby securing better hygienic conditions  in our homes and sur-
roundings;        an improvement of our streets  and public grounds ;        a protection  of
natural  scenery and the building  up and beautifying  of South Weymouth and
so enhancing the value of its property and rendering it a still more inviting place
of residence.
On May 18,       1881,     a meeting was held  and a constitution  was
adopted which asserted  its  purpose to "promote the prosperity  of
the village  of South Weymouth and to do such things as  shall tend
to make the village more prosperous and beautiful or shall  tend  to
afford  greater facilities  of all  kinds for  its  inhabitants. "
The membership  comprised  all  of  the  public-spirited  business
men,      including  all  the  progressive  element  of  South  Weymouth
without  exception,     those whose best wishes  and best  efforts  were
for  the interest of that section of the town.
On May 28,    1881,   the constitution had been signed by sixty active
members and Dr.  C.  C. Tower was chosen President.
Ten days  thereafter,    on June 7,   the first  real work of the society
was performed in cleaning up the grounds of  the Second Congrega-
tional  Church.
Thirty  persons  on  that  date,     with  horses,      carts,       and  wheelbarrows,        began
grading,    cutting out the driveways and sidewalks,   and pruning the trees.       Among
thebusy
busy ones could be seen the  pastor nimbly using a rak
rake,    while Mrs.  Stanton
seemed to be equally energetic in supplying cool lemonade.
The by-laws  provided  for  a  president,     six  vice-presidents  and
twenty- four  directors,    and in  addition  several  subcommittees who
gave  special  attention  to  the  seven departments,     as  follows :         trees,
railroads,      sanitation,   public grounds,    library,   finance and entertain-
ment.           These committees were selected with special care and duties
appropriate  to  their  efforts  which  seemed fitted  to  them,   and the
 - 271 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           749
varied  projects  fostered  by them  included  a  very  wide  range  of
subjects.
In order  to  bring more vividly before you these duties  and  their
results,        a  partial  list  of subjects has been included which serves  to
show a most comprehensive field  of activity :       conferences,     proposi-
tions,       recommendations  and  investigations  were  undertaken;       de-
bates covered the Weymouth water supply and its  system,    the care
of the town clock and later with a substantial help of $300 for  a new
one;      electric road location,   annual fairs for the Fogg Library,    mem-
bership for  the Association and annual supper,   free  postal delivery
agitated in  1899,    committee appointed for beautifying schoolrooms,
institution of manual training,  street watering,   care of the greens
and squares,     spraying trees,    fighting  elm tree beetles  and Leopard
moths,        fixing  telephone  rates  and  installing  telephone  at  depot;
flagstaff  in  Columbian Square declared unsafe and replaced in 1903
by a new one costing  $220,    furnishing  several  flags;     better  train
service,    debate on trolley express,    concrete walks,   Great Pond water
investigation,       Fourth  of  July  celebration,    playgrounds,      drinking
fountains,      removal of burned buildings from square,   favoring water
meters,    erecting and maintaining street  lamps,   -such a variety of
important  matters,     each  receiving  the  attention  of  a  competent
committee and reporting all progress and results  to  the Association
with any further  recommendations.
In this manner intense interest was always  manifest and the best
results  obtained.         Fairs were held  to aid  the  Fogg  Library,    - one
in  1900,      on  February 22,    netted  $1,316.95,    which was paid  to  the
trustees.           Other fairs  were very successful in raising money for the
same cause,     that of 1902 netting $887.70.
On Jan.  23,       1903,    a meeting held in the  Fogg Opera  House was
addressed by Booker T. Washington,   a resident of South Weymouth,
and whose welcome by the society was most cordial.             His  address
gave the scope of work done by him at Tuskegee,    and his  aspira-
tions  for  its  future,    with the hope that the efforts  centered  on the
school  will  bear fruits  not only for  the welfare of his race,    but for
the broader  field  of  national helpfulness.         He was followed by the
Hon.       James  J.  Meyers,      speaker  of  the  House of  Representatives,
and also by Senator Harvell of  Rockland.
The  work  accomplished  by  this  Association  still   endures,       the
memorials  show  on  all   sides,        our  streets,        squares,       shade  trees ,
lawns and buildings  bear testimony.       South Weymouth is  a beauty
spot and to  the South Weymouth Improvement Association is  due
the honor and credit  of  an unbounded daily appreciation.
NORTH WEYMOUTH  IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION
In North Weymouth was posted during the week of July 15,   1884,
a call  for  a meeting to be held July 21,   1884,    in the Engine House,
Ward 1.     A good attendance showed the interest  in  the  new Asso-
ciation,      and a committee was appointed to draft preamble and by
 - 272 - 
750                                  LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
laws which were prepared and reported upon by them July 28,     1884,
when a body of officers  was nominated,     elected and installed,    with
Elias  S.  Beals  as  President.
The objects  of the Association  as  set  forth  in  the by- laws  were
" to improve and ornament the streets and public grounds of North
Weymouth by planting and cultivating  trees,   clearing  and repair-
ing  sidewalks  and doing such other  acts  as  shall  tend to  improve
this  section of the Town. "
On Aug. 5,      1884,    the following list  of officers  was chosen :
E. S.  Beals,        President.
F. A. Bicknell,    Vice- President.
John W. Bartlett,    Vice-President.
B. F.  Thomas,     Secretary.
Thomas F.  Cleverly,   Treasurer.
An executive committee of twenty- five members were appointed
and  later   apportioned  to  the  five  following  committees :             trees,
lighting,    streets  and sidewalks,    public parks  and greens,     and sani-
tation.
There was a first  membership of 30 active members,   increased  to
74 in one year.          The ladies  took active  part and were appointed to
the committees,   one in  particular where their efforts  netted $168.70,
which was expended for  the drinking  fountain  at  the  junction  of
Bridge  and Sea Streets .
The ladies  were  welcomed at the annual  suppers  and furnished
entertainments  to  raise  the funds  needed  in carrying  on the work
of  the Association.
At later  dates  there were added committees for  railroads,    beach,
gas,       clock,       membership,     mail  service,      bridges,     appropriations,      en-
tertainments,       telephone  and publicity,    the last  of which  included
the printing  in  the  "Weymouth Gazette"  articles  of  North Wey-
mouth interest  from the pens  of  the  committees.
Of all  these,     the  street  railway  committee was the  most active.
It must have been also  the  most aggressive  for  they  were  always
doing  something with  the Bay State  and  their  reports  often  filled
an entire  evening.
In  1909 there was a membership of 120.
The range of  work reported  on and  taken  up related  to  many
varied  transactions  and  shows  the  range  of  activities  which  came
under  their  inspection,      embracing  the  condition  of  the  Athens
School  yard  and buildings;     speeding  up the work on the  two big

POND  PLAIN  IMPROVEMENT  ASSOCIATION
This  Association  was organized July 28,      1908,    and incorporated
July 1,      1912.    The first  officers ,    elected in  1908,    were as follows :
W. L.  Swan,      President.
Charles E. Johl,   Vice- President.
J.  B.  Denbroeder,    Secretary.
Gilbert  Shaw,     Treasurer.
Its  purpose  is  to  further  the interests  of that part of the  town
known as  Pond Plain,    to make it  more suitable for residential pur-
poses and to beautify and protect the land and streets  and houses of
that section.            It has been most active in operation  and most com-
plete  in  success.            One hundred  and  fifty  shade  trees  have  been
planted,    three squares planned,   laid out and cared for,    a fire  depart-
ment organized and a chemical engine purchased,    streets  and side-
walks  received  attention  and a spirit  of civic pride was evidenced
by the absolute unanimity of the workers and the wonderful results
obtained.
The schoolhouse  on Pond Street  furnished  a meeting place  and
entertainments  were given  and  soon  a  building  fund  was  estab-
lished,     and on  March 28,     1911,     $250  was appropriated  and  made
a nucleus  for  the  purpose  of  building  more commodious  quarters
for  the meetings  of  the Association.           The building  committee was
appointed  Jan.  23,    1912,    and the  following August the site  of  the
new building was purchased.
During  1913 there was nothing  tangible to report and the Ladies'
Auxiliary,       seeing  the  need  of  a helping  hand,   formed  themselves
into  an organization,     and  in  the  latter  part  of  1913  the  Ladies '
Eureka  Club  organized  with  Mrs.  William  Fottler  as  President
and 35 names were affixed  to  the charter,    thereby forming a most
valuable  aid  to  the  Pond  Plain  Association.         They hold  monthly
meetings  and  supply  talent  and  committees  for  entertainments
which form the life  and interest  of all  such  organizations .
On Saturday,     March 17,    1923,    a large hall,   60 by 40 feet,    bunga-
low pattern,     was dedicated with appropriate ceremonies to  the use
of  the  Pond Plain  Improvement Association.

752                                LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
LOVELL'S  Corner  IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION
On the  evening  of  Oct.  12,       1910,       Mr.  Frank  Blanchard,       after
gathering   together   the  people  of   Lovell's   Corner,      explained   to
them the purpose of the meeting and what should be done in  the
way of  improvements,     such  as  better  streets  and  sidewalks,        im-
proving   property,       more  and  better   lights,      better   car   service,
cheaper  fares  to  points  where we should have them,   better  things
in  the educational line,    such as  lectures,    speakers,     and to  improve
sociability   among  our  neighbors.          From  this  time  on  meetings
were  held  in  Pratt's  Hall  and  Mr.  Blanchard  was  elected   first
President and Russell  Poole,   Secretary.          The dues were $1  a year.
The first  money spent  was for  an American flag,   to  be displayed
from  the  Hall window.        Interest  in the ground of the New Pratt
School  was displayed and money appropriated  to  take care of  the
same,       also   swings  and  teeter  boards  were  installed  in  the  yard.
Fifty  to  100 trees have been set out on street  or in yards bordering
the  same.               Through  the  influence  of  the  Association,         sidewalks
have been built,     drains  have been  established,    streets  have been
widened,        obstructions  have  been  taken  down  and  removed  and
curbing on four  sides  of Lovell's  Corner has been set.      Lights have
been installed and a playground has been purchased and equipped.
By the  generosity  of  the townspeople  a  Community Building  has
been procured.
A boy scout  troop was formed by Francis  W. Rea and backed
by the Improvement Society.        There is  also a group of Camp Fire
Girls under the auspices of the Association.
Poultry  and vegetable shows have been held from time to time.
Each year on the 4th of July has been held the annual field day,
which has  been popular and  the  community spirit  has been good.
In  fact,      Lovell's  Corner has been very much in evidence since the
Improvement Association  was instituted .
The following  Presidents  have
Frank N. Blanchard,   1910-12.
Fred Sampson,     1913-14.
Francis  W.  Rea,    1915-16.
Walter W.  Pratt,    1917-18.
served :
James B. B.  Smith,    1919-20.
James Stever,     1921-22.
Francis  W.  Rea,    1923.
Mrs. Mary Hayden,    Secretary.
Mrs. Florence White,    Treasurer.
THE  WEYMOUTH  BOARD  OF  TRADE
Ameeting was held  in  Masonic Hall,     East  Weymouth,    Jan.  30,
1908,      for  the purpose of forming a Board of Trade and for  the pro-
motion of  the  business  interests  of  our  town.          This  meeting  was
called  by  and  presided  over  by  Mr.  Frank  Humphrey  of  East
Weymouth,       who had  been  fortunate  in  selecting  a  speaker  and
worker in  similar  organizations,     Mr. Alfred  Donovan of  Rockland,
 - 275 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            753
to  address  the meeting,    explaining its  objects  and suggesting  plans
of  action and necessary steps in forming the Board.          At this meet-
ing a vote was taken and it  was resolved to form a Board of Trade.
A paper  declaring  this  intention  was  drawn  up  and  signed  by
forty-seven  men ready to join and carry out the work of  the Asso-
ciation.             Constitution and by-laws  were adopted,   committees were
appointed,      and  activities  were  at  once  started  for  successful  and
prosperous   efforts.           There  were  ten   principal   committees   ap-
pointed,   as follows :             transportation,   telegraph,   telephone and street
lighting,     town affairs  and  taxation,   membership,    insurance,      home
trade,      village   improvement,    press   committee,       new  enterprises,
publicity.
On February 6 the following officers  were elected :
President,     W. P.  Denbroeder.
Vice-President,   George A.  Walker.
Secretary,     W. M. Tirrell.
Treasurer,     Minot P. Garey.
Executive Committee:      Frederick Humphrey,   Henry E.  Hanley,   A.  P.  Worthen,
H. H. Longfellow and Frank H. Torrey.
Many and  varied  subjects  received   attention:       first   and  fore-
most always  the town warrant,    electric  express,    encouragement  of
new shoe factory -Geo.     E.  Keith's      playgrounds,       water supply,
conditions   around   Weymouth  Great   Pond,        administration   of
Water Board and installation  of meters,   filter  bed at Great  Pond
advised,         improvement  of  high  school  grounds,    combination  fire
truck,      dredging  Weymouth  Back  River,    insuring  town  buildings,
representation at Weymouth,    Eng. ,  sponsoring  $300,000  Memorial
Building,     fuel problem,   and other town matters.
After many years of prosperity the interest  flagged and no meet-
ings  were held  in  1921  or  1922.    The last  meeting,   held  Feb.  23,
1923,        at  the  Clapp Memorial,    was  attended by six  members and
one guest,     and it  was voted to  discontinue the Board of  Trade and
donate the balance of its  funds to  the Weymouth Hospital.
CITIZENS'      ASSOCIATION  OF  PRECINCT  FOUR
On the evening  of Feb. 21,    1922,     the  town meeting members of
Precinct 4 held an open meeting in the hall of the old Hose House,
Front  Street,      Nash's  Corner,     as  had been  their  custom  after  the
issuance of the town warrant,    that they might ascertain the general
attitude of the precinct in relation  to the articles  appearing therein.
The Hose House property having been "a bone of contention "
for a year past,   the presiding officer,   Mr. John F.  Robinson,     brought
to the attention of the gathering the imminent necessity of forming
some sort  of  an organization  that  would be able  to  take  upon its
shoulders  the  maintenance and upkeep of this  building,    otherwise
there seemed to be very grave danger of its  being auctioned off  and
Nash's  Corner being  left  with no public place  adequate  in  which
they could assemble if  they wished  to.
 - 276 - 
754                               LODGES  AND SOCIETIES
With this  thought in mind,   a committee of citizens were appointed
to  further  the  cause.              This   committee  was  as  follows :       As tem-
porary  President  and Secretary,     Mr.  John  F.  Robinson  and  Mrs.
Gertrude  C.  Andrews,    respectively;        Mr.  Richard  Halloran,     chair-
man;      Mr.  Theron Tirrell,     Miss Susie  Loud,       Mr.  Clarence Fearing,
Mr.  Alfred  Tirrell,      Mr.  Chas.      DeRusha,     Mr.  Samuel  French  and
Mr.  Sanford  Hollis .
This  committee agreed  to  meet the following  day,      February  22,
to  draw  up  the  customary  papers  incident  to  the  granting  of  a
charter  and to  transact  all  business  so  that  the proposed  associa-
tion might become a reality  without delay.
Mr.  Halloran  called  his  committee together  at  1  o'clock  on the
afternoon  of Washington's Birthday -a most auspicious time in-
deed,    if  one believes in that sort of thing -    at the residence of Mr.
Samuel  French,     Liberty  Square (another omen of good luck).         By
a unanimous vote,   the name Citizens'    Association of Precinct Four
was adopted.          A modest set of by-laws of six  articles was drawn up,
the gist of which is  as follows :
Object.                     To promote  the  public welfare  of  Precinct  4 and the  town  of  Wey-
mouth.
Active  membership  includes  the  registered  voters  of  Precinct  4;     other  resi-
dents  over sixteen  years  shall  be associate  members.       Only active  members
to hold office  or to have the right to vote.
Officers.                 President,   vice-president,  secretary and treasurer.       These officers  and
five others  duly elected to constitute a board of directors.
Annual meeting shall be held in the month of April.
These officers  were elected :
President,    John F.  Robinson.
Vice-President,    Clarence W. Fearing .
Treasurer,      Chas.      H.  DeRusha.
Secretary,  Gertrude C. Andrews.
Board  of  Directors :            Richard  Halloran,       Theron  L.   Tirrell,       Alfred  S.   Tirrell,
Sanford W. Hollis  and Samuel S.  French .
The charter was granted on the ninth day of March,    1922.
Thus  the  origin  of  a small  but  industrious  and  public- spirited
community center,    which  has  at  the  close  of  its  first  year,   April ,
1923,       created  a fine  feeling  of  fellowship  and  friendliness,    helped
itself  and  helped  others.          In  fact,     from  nothing   to   reasonable
affluence  has  been  accomplished in eight  months,   as  the Associa-
tion's  first  effort  was a little  baked bean  supper undertaken with
many  handicaps  indeed  when  each  waiter  was  forced  to  bring
sufficient  dishes  for  her own table,    chairs had to be borrowed  and
food  solicited  and eight tables  built,     but there were sixteen  grati-
fied  even  if  tired  women who were able  to  hand to  the Treasurer
forty  odd dollars .
Indeed  there  is  no tonic like  success.           Ambition was stimulated
and in August a Carnival and Block Party was staged on the green
 - 277 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            755
at  Nash's  Corner that  rivaled  the Weymouth Fair.          The Carnival
made money.         It paid for bracing the floor  of the hall,      which was
necessary  for  dancing  to  be  held  there;       it  bought  chairs,     dishes,
silver,       a  gas  stove and other essentials.          As a get-to-gether for  this
part of the town it was unprecedented.
With the coming of the fall months,   suppers,    concerts and dances
followed,      each netting running expenses plus.          Under the direction
of   Miss  Beatrice  Burr,      home  demonstration  agent  for   Norfolk
County,     an opportunity was given the women of  Precinct 4 to take
up home economics.         Miss  Burr has  been coming to us one after-
noon  each  month  with  helpful  suggestions  and  has  been  appre-
ciated.        A class  in  millinery  was  formed  in  February  with  Miss
Beatrice  Flower of  the  Norfolk  County School as  supervisor.            As
yet  the Association  has  had  nothing  special  to  offer  its  men,     but
they seem to have been content with the social  side and have had
sessions  of  their  own in  mechanical  arts  adjusting,     arranging  and
transforming  conditions in the building for the comfort and work-
ability of the members.           In fact they should hereby receive  credit
for   each  alternate   supper  as  they  have  planned  it,      cooked  it,
served  it   and  cleaned  up,    which  only demonstrates  more  clearly
the good fellowship which exists  in this  particular  association.
At the annual town meeting,   the month of March,   1923,    an article
in the warrant asking that the building at Nash's Corner,    known as
the  Hose House,    be given  to  the  Citizens'     Association of  Precinct
Four for  a suitable sum and other considerations,   the town reserv-
ing  the use of the building  for  election  or other  town  purposes  at
no cost  to  the town,     received the unanimous vote of the town meet-
ing members and the matter was turned over to the selectmen  and
the town council.
Thus  the  Citizens'    Association  of  Precinct  Four has  secured  its
desired building.

BUSINESS  ASSOCIATION  OF  WEYMOUTH AND  EAST  BRAINTREE
This  organization  of  the business  men of  Weymouth and  East
Braintree  was formed  March 19,    1923.    A committee was chosen
at this  meeting to draft by- laws  and to nominate officers,     and the
name given  to  the  organization  was  proposed  as   " The  Business
Association  of  Weymouth  and  East  Braintree. "     The  business
men of  these  adjoining  districts,   wishing  to  further  the  interest
and welfare  of the  section,  will  welcome  to  membership any one
who will pledge himself to the support of the organization.          Meet-
ings  are proposed to be regularly held the second Monday of each
month,    holding the annual meeting in April.
The objects  of the organization  shall be " the promotion of the
welfare  and interests  of  Weymouth Landing  and East  Braintree. "
When the  initial  membership  roll  was  closed,     May  15,          1923,
there were ninety names subscribed.

OLD  COLONY DRIVING  Club
While  not   strictly   a  Weymouth  institution,    the   Weymouth
Driving  Club is  one of the events of this  section,   partly  from  the
fact that the Club leases the Weymouth Fair Grounds,   making that
track their  racing course,   as well as the fact that the improvement
of  the  horse stables ,    grand stand,   judges'    stand  and the track has
called for  expenditures  of much money in  preparation.
The  Old  Colony  Driving  Club  started  with  a membership  of
five,     -Harry  C.   Thayer,        H.   P.   Hobart,       W.  H.   Foss,       George
French  and  B.  C.  Wilder,                   whose efforts  soon  brought  together
the  horse  owners  of the various  South Shore  towns,    and  on Jan.
 - 279 - 
LODGES  AND SOCIETIES                            757
24,      1908,       these promoters had the satisfaction  of a real demonstra-
tion of  interest,     so  great  that the first  meeting was adjourned  to
the  Odd  Fellows  Hall,       Braintree,     and  on January  31,      with  fifty
horse  owners  present,    the  organization  of  the  Club  was  effected
with  sixty- two  names subscribed  to  the  charter and the  following
officers  were elected :
President,    A. C. Drinkwater.
Vice- President,   Lot Lohnes.
Secretary and Treasurer,   Theron L.  Tirrell.
The Club has grown to be one of the largest and most enthusi-
astic  as  well  as  prosperous  clubs  in  New England  and  boasts  a
racing  track without equal in this section,  and the generous outlay
on it  has kept it  in the finest condition.         There are well-appointed
quarters  for sixty- two horses .
The race  committee meets weekly,    and the rules  in force  have
brought  the  sport  to  a high  level,   and the confidence  of  the  race-
goers  has  been  won and their  interest  in  a clean  sport  has  been
retained.
During 1910 there were 234 races;   in  1911,   234;     1912,   195;     1913,
194;     1914,     620.

ose  of organizing  a Lyceum.         Ather-

PREAMBLE
Desirous  of promoting  our  own intellectual  improvement and of awakening
in the  Community a spirit  of inquiry and a desire  for  the acquisition  of useful
knowledge,    and thinking that these objects may be best promoted by associating
ourselves  together  for  mutual debate  and public  lectures,     we do hereby  unite
ourselves  for  the purposes aforesaid.
This  was  followed  by a constitution,    the  first  article  of  which
declared that this  society shall be called  the Weymouth and Brain-
tree  Union  Lyceum and weekly meetings were provided  for .

After the adoption of the constitution  and by-laws  the following

Directors:        Elias   Richards,     John  W.  Loud,    Nathaniel  Blanchard,      Whitcomb
Porter and Asa B. Wales.
The first  subject  for  discussion  was  " Are  Capital  Punishments
Right  and Beneficial  to  the  Community?"
At the  meeting  held  in the  Washingtonian  Reading  Room  on
Oct.  24,      1842,    Jacob Allen opened the discussion  of this  question
in  the negative,     in  " a very  elaborate  and eloquent manner "  and
was followed by Silas  Binney,   Jr.,    in the affirmative.      After a very
spirited  and  interesting  debate  by  Messrs.       Pratt,      Nash,       Wales,
Porter,       Loud and Richards in the affirmative and Messrs.    Peterson,
Richards,        Spear,      Shaw,      Blanchard  and  Humphrey  in  the  nega-
tive,       it  was voted to  lay  the question on the table  for  one week.
This question was discussed at the next two meetings when it  was
finally laid on the table without settlement,   this being the disposi-
tion of every one of the questions discussed by this society.
As evidence of the varied  nature of  the  subjects  discussed,    and
also  showing the spirit of the times in 1842,    a few questions debated
have been copied from the records.
Ought Ministers of the Gospel to preach their Particular Views on Politics  on
the Sabbath Days?
Do Persons  who pray vocally practice Judaism,    and violate the Teachings  of
Christ?
Is  Charles  T.  Torrey  (supposing he has aided slaves  to  escape from bondage)
Guilty of any Crime against the Laws of God or Man?
Would the Prosecution of the Unlicensed Liquor Seller be productive of  more
Good than Evil?
Are Laymen Competent to discuss  and decide for themselves •Disputed  Points
onTheology?
Ought a Man trading with the South to take Slaves in Payment of Debts?
Is  it   Consistent for  an  Individual to claim to be a Christian  who admits  the

Does an Increase of Knowledge promote an Increase of Happiness?
Are Lawyers,      Doctors and Ministers Beneficial  to  the Community?
ArePromises in All Cases binding?
Are Labor- Saving Machines Desirable and Beneficial in the Community?
Is the Influence exerted by Females in Society greater than that of Males?
Which has the Greatest Influence on Man    the Hope of Reward or the Dread
ofPunishment?
Is  it  a More Just and Equal Mode of Raising a Revenue Sufficient to carry on
the  Government of the  United  States  by Duties  on  Imports  than  by  Direct
Taxation?
Does the Bible teach the Doctrine of Endless Suffering for Any Portion of the
Human Family for the Sins of this  Life?
Is it  right to follow the Dictates of  Conscience under All Circumstances?
Has Knowledge a Greater Influence than Wealth?
Is there Any Such Thing as an Ultimate Evil in either the Works of God or Man?
Is the Use of Tobacco Useful to the Human System?

Would the Southern Slaves be justified  in Taking the  Lives  of their  Masters

Much interest was manifested in the debates and many of  them
were  decidedly  spirited.           The  following  subject  was  vigorously
debated  for   five   consecutive   meetings:          " Does  the  Bible   and
Reason teach  the  Doctrine of the  Final  Holiness of all  Mankind ? "
The wording of this question was not acceptable to  some of  the
members  and it  was voted  to  omit the words " and Reason"  from
the same.
Those who took prominent part in the debate were A.  B.  Wales,
E.  Shaw,       C.  C.  Jordan,    J.   M. Spear  and  E.  Richards,      who spoke
in  the  affirmative,    and Dr.  Richards,   A.  N. Hunt and J.  P.  Peter-
son,    who spoke in the negative.
At the second meeting of the discussion  Mr.  T.  B.  Porter,       Sec-
retary  pro  tem,      reported  that  Mr.  Puttilow  in the course  of  the
debate  spoke twice upon the  point of order  in debating  the ques-
tion,    very much to the progress of coming to a settlement of " this
very   vexatious   and   unprofitable   question.  "        This   statement
aroused much comment and Mr.  Asa  B.  Wales moved to expunge
from the  records that clause which declares  that  the question  now
before  the  meeting to be " a very vexatious and unprofitable  one.  "
After spending  five evenings  on this  subject  it  was voted  to  lay
the matter  on the table,    and that was the way every question  of
whatever  sort  was  disposed  of,      no  decision  was  ever  arrived  at,
every question was " laid on the  table. "
THE UNION  LITERARY  CIRCLE
The  Union  Literary  Circle  of  Weymouth  and  East  Braintree
was organized in  1844.    At first  it  was a branch of the New Eng-
land Reading  Club,    which had its  headquarters  in  Boston,     and it
followed the course of study mapped out by this Club.           After some
time it  became a branch for three years of the  Chautauqua Circle,
using  the books  as  prescribed  by that  association.       At the end of
that  period  it  became  an independent  association,     laying  out  its
own course  of  study.         During  its   existence  the  Union  Literary
Circle  took  up  about  everything  in  science,     literature,       history,
poetry,     music,     philosophy,    discovery,    invention and politics.
It was a most  interesting  and  instructive  society  and  of  great
benefit to  the social life  of the two villages .
On Wednesday evening,   Jan.  20,    1909,    the Circle  celebrated  its
silver  anniversary in the lecture  room of the Union Church.

decided  to  disband  and a closing  night was held  on October  8  at
the  residence  of  Mrs.  Harry C.  Newman.
WEDNESDAY  NIGHT  CLUB
The  following  preamble  stating  the  object  of  the  Wednesday
Night  Club is  worthy of consideration :
Whereas,         Every good citizen is  under obligation to fit  himself so far as  in  him
lies,     for  the fulfillment of every political and social duty,     and
Whereas,      We believe that the more intimate acquaintance of leading citizens
is  promotive both of the general and individual welfare,     and
Whereas,        We believe  that  this  acquaintance  may best be cultivated  around
the social  board and in friendly debate,
We,    the undersigned,    hereby form an organization to realize these objects.
The above was signed by the following-named persons :

The Club met,     at different times,   in Tuck's Hall,    in  the Reform
Club Rooms,    and in the coat room at the Opera House,    and many
pleasant  and  sharp debates  were held  and much enjoyment  and
knowledge gained in a sort  of running fire  of interspersed  remarks.
A fair  idea  of  the  subjects  debated  may be  obtained  from  the
following:
Dec. 6,    1882,    Woman's Suffrage.
Jan. 3,    1883,    The Influence of New England Character.
Feb. 14,    1883,    Our Libraries.
Mar.  14,     1883,   History of the Constitution of the United States .
April 30,    1884,   Our Common School System.
Oct. 15,    1884,   Government Policy in Treatment of Indians.
April  1 ,       1885,     Village Improvement.
Feb.  28,    1885,  the Club had as a visitor the Hon.  James Humphrey,   who made an
earnest appeal for National Aid for  Education in the South.
Later,    meetings were held at private residences and the regularity
was  suspended.            Concerts  and entertainments  were arranged  and
on one of the last  occasions the parts  were assigned for the  reading
of  Shakespeare's  " Merchant  of  Venice, "   and  it  was  held  at  the
home of Louis A. Cook on Union Street.            This was the last impor-
tant meeting which was sponsored by the Wednesday Night Club,
and after  an existence of thirty-four years it  ceased to exist.
Mention should be made of the  influence  of the Hon.      Louis A.
Cook,    whose name shines  through the entire history of the Wednes-
day Night  Club.        He was a charter  member,    an active  worker in
every  office  of the  Club,    a prominent debater,    skillful  in  repartee
and of  broad views and generous ideas.        His death,    occurring May
16,    1918,     removed the closest link with the Wednesday Night Club,
for  at his  bidding the Club was again and again brought together,
and  at  this  last  meeting  his  hospitality  gave welcome  and  royal
entertainment to the Club and to its  invited guests.
THE  CENTURY  CLUB
It  is   unfortunate  that  the  records  of  this  most  active   Club,
which had its  home in North Weymouth,   have been lost,    and the
most active members have passed to the great beyond so that  the
actual  facts  are difficult  to  obtain.         The first  meeting of  this  Club
was held  Jan.  10,    1890,   with Gilman C.  Fisher,   superintendent of
schools,       in  the chair.         As the  Club elected  its  presidents  to  serve
from  one  meeting  to  the  next,    there  were as  many presidents  as
there were members.           The Club was at  first  composed entirely  of
men,      but later  ladies  were admitted and the  regular debating  club
became more or less  a  social  one.            The annual supper was always
an important event and most heartily participated in.          Enthusiasm
in  the  entertainments  predominated and very enjoyable  occasions
resulted.          After  fifteen  years  of existence its  meetings  came to  an
end.          The funds remaining in  the treasury were spent in the pur-
chase of pictures which now adorn the walls of the Athens School.

OLD  COLONY  CLUB
The  Old  Colony  Club  of  South  Weymouth  was  organized  in
1897,        and  State  federated  in  the  same year.        Its  motto  is   " One
Mind,         One  Purpose,     and  One Successful  Result. "    The founders
were  Mrs.  Elizabeth   W.  Newell,     Mrs.  Mary  E.  Holbrook,        Mrs.
Annette S.  Wentworth.
The following  persons  have held  the  office  of  President  of  the
Club:
Mrs. Mary E.  Holbrook.
Mrs.  Elizabeth W. Newell.
Mrs. Olive  F.  Wellcome.
Mrs.  Lucinda A.  Cook.
Mrs. Mary C.  Reed.
Mrs. Grace W. Willis.
Mrs. Sarah S.  Howe.
Mrs.  Mary W. Bauer.
Mrs. Edith B. Sinnett.
Mrs. Alice R.  Wagner.
Mrs. Marion T. Cate.
Mrs. Mary E. Hanson.
Mrs. Mary C.  Granger.
Mrs. Rena F.  Gay.
Regular  meetings  are held  the  second  and fourth  Thursdays  of
each month from October to April.
The annual meeting is the fourth Thursday in April of each year.
Members  may invite  friends  to  any  meeting  of  the  Club  on
payment of an admission specially  charged.
Committees are appointed which deal with questions relating  to
educational  matters,    literature  and  arts,     civics,    home economics,
public  health  and  nursing  problems.           Hospitality  and  dramatic
committees  are  also  appointed.
The Club has  a membership of  300 and at its  meetings  a pro-
gram is provided consisting of lectures and musicales of the highest
order.            Current  events  are  discussed  and the  Club  also  enjoys  a
dramatic and guests'    night  each  year.
Arrangements  are made for  visiting  places  under special  condi-
tions,     the Art Museum in Boston being chosen in 1919.
The Club play is  an annual event eagerly looked forward to and
is  always an unqualified success,   the talent displayed by the mem-
bers  of the Club being of superior quality.
It is  a custom of the Club to present two of the members of the
high school class with complimentary tickets  in recognition of their
superior  scholarship.      The holders  of  the tickets  in  1923-24  were
Miriam Holbrook and Ruth Tirrell.
The object  of  the  Club  shall  be  to  secure  all  possible  literary
and social  advantages for its  members and to benefit the commun-
ity in which it has been organized.

THE  COMMUNITY ASSOCIATION  OF  SOUTH  WEYMOUTH
This Association was formed from the members of a  Community
Bible   Class  which  held  regular  meetings  at  the  Union  Church
Vestry,      but which from lack of  incentive began to lag in interest
and which became the  nucleus  of  a much more ambitious  scheme
which  should  embrace the  whole townspeople in  one  Community
Association,      to which each person of either sex and of all ages could
attend.
Its  purposes were -
To  promote  mutual  understanding  and  good  will   among  all
individuals  and organizations  in  the community.
To  foster   a  strong,      virile,      loyal    and  aggressive   community
spirit.
To co-ordinate as  much as  possible  and practicable  the  energies
of  all  organizations in the community.
To inaugurate  a practical  all-sided,    long-term  program  of  com-
munity activity  and development.
As soon as  is  practicable and as far as  is  possible to provide and
maintain a community center  as  a home of  community  life   and
activity,        open   to   individuals,       groups    and   organizations,        and
equipped  for  recreation,     social,     moral,    religious  or  other  good  civic
purposes.
A committee of seven  was appointed  to  draft  proposed  by-laws
and  to  attend  to  other  details.           This  committee  comprised  the
Rev.  Ora A.  Price,     the  Rev. J.  H. Peardon,   Arthur Taylor,    Herbert
Torrey,       John F.  Robinson,     Howard H.  Joy and Winfield S.  Baker.
A lyceum  course  of  six  entertainments  was  given  during  the
season of  1920-21 which was well  attended and very successful.
Further  work has  been added for  the  children  by way of  stere-
opticon lectures.
The former  Union Church building  has been splendidly adapted
to the use of the Association,     the auditorium being used for  lecture
purposes  and the other parts  of  the building  for  social  rooms  and
a gymnasium.
The Association  was  incorporated  under  the  laws  of  the  State
of Massachusetts.

ful  to  attend.          Programs  were  so  arranged that time was  always
devoted  to   a  paper  or  an  informal  talk  on the  composer's  life,
followed by vocal or instrumental selections by the active members,
and the lives  and works of  French,     Russian,    Polish,    Scandinavian,
Italian,       Danish,      Hungarian,     Bohemian  as  well  as  American  com-
posers  were studied.
At the close of  the  first  season  a " gentlemen's  night"  was held
at  the  home of  Mrs.  Helen Allen  Hunt.           Club  members  rendered
the cantata "St.  Mary Magdalene,"  by Vincent D'Indy,     and solos
were given by Mrs. Hunt.
During this  year one musicale was given at The Home for Aged
People in  Braintree.       Songs familiar and dear to  the  inmates  were
sung by Mrs. Avery,     Mrs.  Whitten and Mrs.  Worster.
The season  of  1915-16 opened with an " Organ Day"  in  charge
of Miss Ethel Raymond at  the Congregational  Church,      East Wey-
mouth,       followed  by ten  meetings  held  at  the  homes  as  the  year
previous.                The year  proved one full  of  musical  treats,      and  many
artists  from outside helped  on the different  programs.           The gentle-
man's  night  was held  with  the  President,    Mrs.  Putnam,    and  12
Club   members   rendered   the  cantata   entitled   " The   Sleighing
Frolic.  "     The words were written by our Weymouth poet,     Francis
Moses  Adlington,    and  the  music  was  composed  by  Fred  Field
Bullard  and Grace Mayhew Putnam.
There were 83  associate members this  year,    and in  order  to  ac-
commodate them all  another season it  seemed advisable to hold the
Club meetings during  1916-17  at  Cochato  Hall,     Braintree.
A mission  school  also was started  and  Club members gave  both
vocal  and instrumental lessons  to those worthy at a nominal price.
The  season  of  1916-17  afforded  many  very  pleasant  morning
 - 291 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            769
musicales  to  members  and guests  besides  one evening concert  for
the public and an open meeting at  Bates Opera House.
Mrs.  Robert Hoffman opened her home for gentleman's night and
Mr.  John  Orth  and  Mrs.  Emily  Selinger  entertained  with  music
and poetry.
As the demands of war became pressing and calls  for  relief  work
urgent,     all  dues  and  Club  money were  invested  in  a  $50  Liberty
Loan  bond  for  a  scholarship  fund  in  the  mission  school.             The
members  felt  it  their duty  to  devote  all  their  spare  time  to  the
great call  of the country and the musicales were discontinued until
some future time.        The Club  proved one of  great  enjoyment to  all
and helped  to  awaken  a keener  and deeper  interest  and  love  for
music old  and new.
WESSAGUSSET  CLUB
The present  Wessagusset  Club,  consisting  of about 88 members,
comprises  nearly all  the business  and prominent men in  the north
part of  the town and also  a number of nonresident  members,    for-
merly  citizens  of  Weymouth.             The  Club  rooms  are  situated  on
Bridge Street  and consist  of  a reception  room,    reading  room,     pool
room,       etc.     The Wessagusset  Club is  the outcome of  a consolida-
tion of  the old Ten Club,   organized  about  twenty- five  years  ago,
and the  Independent  Club,    formed  several  years  later.
An annual ladies'     night,   whist parties during the winter months,
various  tournaments,     etc.,    are a portion of its  social  features.

SOUTH  WEYMOUTH FISH  AND  GUN CLUB
This  organization  was founded in  1893  with  the special  object
in view to enjoy the sports of hunting and fishing,  and among the
first  activities  was the  establishment of a practice range for  shoot-
ing.            This  was  located  on land formerly  owned by James Tirrell,
Jr. ,       on  Main Street,     now owned by Alonzo  Newbert,     and known
as   " The  Indian  Village  Farm.  "     Here  many  tournaments  were
held,    prizes  awarded for best shooting and much interest was mani-
fested.             Many good contests  were carried  through  but later  from
a somewhat  indifferent  management  the  interest  flagged  in  some
measure so  that the  Club underwent reorganization  and was then
known as  the Hawk Island Gun Club .
There were six charter members and officers  of the newly organ-
ized  Club,      viz.:

WHALE  ISLAND  CLUB
Organized on June 17,    1901,   it was one of the most popular social
clubs on the South Shore and was noted for its  hospitality and good
fellowship.
It  was  originally  located  on Whale  Island,     Hockley  Bay,     Wey-
mouth  Back  River.            Later  the  government  survey for  the  Hing-
ham Ammunition Depot took this  part of  Weymouth,    causing  the
Club  to  vacate  the  Whale Island  site,      after  which  they  obtained
their  present  location  at  Burin Island  at North Weymouth on the
shore  of  Weymouth Fore River.           History says  that when the  Pil
 - 293 - 
LODGES  AND SOCIETIES                           771
grims  left  Plymouth on their  way to  Boston,  they camped at  this
island.
The Club is  situated  within a short distance of the birthplace of
Abigail  Smith,   who became the wife of President John Adams,     and
also within a stone's  throw of where King Philip had his  first  fight
with the earlier settlers .
During its  twenty- two years of existence it  has entertained many
men prominent in the affairs of town,  State and Nation.          The Club
has never made distinction because of race,    creed or sect.
The original  organization was as  follows :
Monarch,      Baron Peter W. French.
Chieftain,     Earl E. J.  Brown.

KING  COVE  BOAT  CLUB  ( INCORPORATED)
On June 28,      1911,    nine men met at  Culley's  Boat House to  form
a float club.             Mr.  L.  H.  Culley was elected  Chairman of  the meet-
ing  (this  was  an informal  meeting) .        At this  meeting  were  F.   I.
Prentiss ,          Chas.          E.   Pratt,       Oliver   H.   Beane,       Lester   H.   Culley,
Edward C.  Culley,    Joseph  H.  McEnroe,    Albert Bates,   John Wolfe
and  P.  W.  Wolfe.
On July 7,      1911,    the second meeting was held  at  Culley's  Boat
House.              Edward  C.  Culley  was  elected  President,     F.  I.   Prentiss
was  elected  Secretary  and  Treasurer.            It  was decided  to  call  the
club  The King  Cove  Boat  Club.      Six more members were  added
to  the Club,     making 15 members.
On July  17 the third meeting was held at the  same place with
21  members.             On Aug. 6,    1912,     they selected a Club pennant.             On
August  12  a  set  of  by- laws  was  adopted.            On Jan.  1,      1913,     the
Secretary  reported  31 members.        On Feb.  8,     1913,    with the  Club
increasing  in  membership,     and  the  prospects  of  it  being  a much
larger  Club,      it  was decided  to  have larger  quarters,     so  they  pur-
chased the Bowles Cottage,   and turned it  into a clubhouse.
On Aug.  13,      1914,    the Club was incorporated with John Wolfe,

President,        Lester  H.  Culley,    Vice- President,       Cyrus  C.  Howland,
Secretary  and  Treasurer.           The  first   annual  field  day  was  held
Aug.  17,       1914.
In the year 1915 the Club purchased 2 more lots of land.         In the
year  1921  they  outgrew  the  old  clubhouse  and built  the  present

DAVIS  BATES  CLAPP  MEMORIAL  ASSOCIATION
One of  the  finest  buildings  of its  kind  in  Massachusetts  is   the
Davis  Bates  Clapp Memorial,     erected on Middle Street,    East Wey-
mouth,     in the year 1903.
In setting forth the purpose for which this memorial was founded,
we know of  no better  way than to  quote directly  from  the  letter
of  Mr.  and  Mrs.  Edwin  Clapp  to  the  Board  of  Trustees,      which
accompanied their deed of gift.         In this letter  they say :
This building has been erected by us in memory of our only son,   Davis Bates
Clapp,    who died Sept. 5,  1901,   in the twenty-fourth year of his  age.          It  is  for the
purpose  of  perpetuating  his  influence  and of continuing the interest  he had in
young men and his work in their behalf,   that we have built this memorial.
It is  our very earnest desire that this building,   its  grounds and equipment,    shall
be used to promote good citizenship,    and straight,   clean,  manly living among the
young men of Weymouth and its  surrounding  towns.
We believe  that  young men require and should be provided  with  means  for
physical  exercise  and  social  recreation,     and the  Davis  Bates  Clapp  Memorial
Building has been carefully planned,   and fully equipped to serve those ends.
The erection of the building,  however,   is only the first step toward the results
which we hope  to  accomplish.         The building must be used.       It  was built  to be
used,   and we want it  to be used.         There must be a genuine atmosphere of fellow-
ship  and helpfulness,   of insight  and sympathy created  before  the  building  will
begin to accomplish the good which we hope it  will bring  to this community.
While  our  primary  purpose  in  erecting  the  Davis  Bates  Clapp  Memorial
Building was to help young men of this  community in a practical  way,    it  was
not,    and is not our purpose that the building should be used exclusively by young
men.          The boys should be welcomed,   and the girls,  and young women,    too,  so
long as their use of the building does not interfere or conflict with its  use by the
young men.
Neither do we deem it wise to limit the scope of the influence of the Memorial
Building  to the town of  Weymouth.        While designed primarily for  our  towns-
people,    we shall be glad to have the building  used by the neighboring  towns as
well.
It is our firm conviction that the controlling principle and the underlying motive
for  the accomplishment of this great purpose must be a Christian  motive if  that
purpose is  to be carried  steadily  and effectively  forward.
 - 295 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            773
To this end we believe that the  administration of the building  should be and
should  continue  absolutely  independent  of  any sectarian  or  denominational  in-
fluence.             Its  purposes  are  as  broad as human life,    and we desire to  see its  work
so  administered.
The building  has  a gymnasium of  convenient  size,    well  lighted
and fully  equipped for all-round physical culture.
Regular  classes   for  men,      senior  and  junior  boys,      women  and
girls,    are held each week during the fall,   winter and spring months.
Indoor sports  and games are  conducted  and there  are several  uni-
formed  basket  ball  teams  who play  throughout  a busy  winter's
schedule.
After games  in  the gymnasium,    the welcome  shower  baths  add
in  no  small  way to  the invigorating  and stimulating  effects  of  the
exercise.
There  are  two  bowling  alleys,      of  regular  size,    well  lighted  and
ventilated,       equally  good  for  both  day  and  evening  use,     while  a
fine  gallery  of elevated seats  behind the alleys  affords  an excellent
view of the games.
A spacious  reception  room,  with its  fireplaces,    easy  chairs,     and
comfortable settles ,    offers  a splendid place for social  intercourse ,
a place  where  the members  may drop in  for an hour's  reading,    a
pleasant chat  or a game of  pool,     billiards,     chess  or checkers .
There is   a  fine  auditorium  on the  second  floor,   seating  several
hundred people,   equipped with stage,  dressing rooms,    grand piano,
etc. ,     well adapted for plays,     lectures  and entertainments of various
sorts .
The  Association   is   especially   fortunate   in  its   athletic  field,
covering  about  6  acres,     immediately  adjoining  the  building.          A
hill,      rising  at  the left,    forms  a  natural  observation  stand,    and the
entire field  is  kept closely mowed throughout the season,   so that it  is
in excellent condition at all times for the different  sports  and events.
The  Davis  Bates  Clapp  Memorial  Association,     therefore,         fills
a unique place  in  the  community,    being  able,   on account of the
ample  endowment,      to  offer   its   members  every  opportunity  for
exercise  and  social  recreation  at  a  cost  so  slight  that  it  is  well
within  the reach  of all.
WEYMOUTH BAND
In  1843  the  Weymouth Band was organized  through  the  efforts
of Mr. Amos S.  White.          The first  members were
Amos S.  White.
Adoniram Bowditch.
Benj.   Leach.
Ebenezer A. Hunt.
Edmund S.  Hunt.
Silas Binney.
Lorenzo H. Loud.
Francis  H. Tilden.
Their  first   appearance  in  public  was  at  a  Sunday-school  picnic
in  Braintree,         July  4,     1843.    Later  they  played  at  musters  and
accompanied the Amazon Engine Company on all their  excursions.
 - 296 - 
774                              LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
After  five  years  its  real  organization  took  place,       Mr.  Amos  S.
White having  served  as  leader  only  until  some one would take his
place.            He was succeeded by Mr.  Robert Raymond who was leader
until  1848,      when  Mr.  C.  L.  Stetson of  South Weymouth was chosen
leader  and  Mr.  White clerk .
The  old  band  filled   quite  a  space  in  the  village  and when  the
members  gathered  in  the  old  Amazon  Hall  on  Monday nights  it
always   attracted   a  crowd  of   interested   ones   listening   to   the
music.
Organizations  had  in  former  times  been  formed  for  furnishing
music for  May trainings  and fall  musters,     and from  1800  to  1845
The Weymouth  Band,    1843
C.  L.  Stetson,    Frank  Holbrook,        E.  S.  Hunt,     F.   H.  Tilden,      Wm.      Bishop,  Amos  Merritt
Lorenzo Blanchard,  J.  Thayer,  A. Bowditch,  Amos White
such  musical companies served for  marching,    but in  1825  the  fore-
runner  of  the  Weymouth Band took shape.           This  earlier  organiza-
tion included members from  Braintree,    Quincy,     Randolph,     Stough-
ton  and Weymouth,     and this  band sufficed  for  its  purpose of  May
trainings  and  musters.            The  military  spirit  pervaded  these  gath-
erings  and  the  band was indispensable.
R.  A.  Hunt relates  of  one muster held on the west side  of Pleas-
ant   Street,        on  land  then  owned  by  John  Dyer:          " I    remember
going with  my father  up to  Lovell's  Corner,     where the  troops  met
and marched to the muster ground,     headed by the band. "
The  musters  about  1830  fell  rapidly  into  disrepute  and  finally
 - 297 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            775
became a parody on their former importance  and  soon  after  were
discontinued,       and with them this  early band became a memory.
However,      again  in  1838,       a small  band  was  started  in  South
Weymouth which was in existence  about ten years when most  of
the members joined the Weymouth Band.       At this  time also,     and
under  the  instruction  of  James  L.   Bates,       the  East  Weymouth
Band was organized  in  1840  and disbanded  in  1848,    its  members
also  joining  the real  Weymouth Band.           Therefore,     it  may be ob-
served  that the band formed in 1843 found the  most excellent  ma-
terial  from which to draw for its future life  and vitality.
Records  are wanting up to  1848 and then very incomplete.            In
1848 the members of the band had increased from eight  to  twelve,
as  follows :           R.   B.   Raymond,    Amos S.   White,       W.  W.  Raymond,
Frank  Holbrook,      Benj .      V.  Leach,     Jonathan  Thayer,       E.  S.  Hunt,
James  F.  Glover,    George  W.  Nash,    Wm.      Bishop,   A.  J.   Bowditch,
Abijah Allen.             On Oct. 10,    1848,   it was voted to admit Henry Ryan,
Amos Merritt  and  C.  L.  Stetson  as  members,     the  latter,     in  1849,
succeeding  R.   B.   Raymond  as  leader.         C.   Loring  Stetson  con-
tinued in that capacity up to November,    1883,    a period of  thirty-
four  years,       when he resigned.          Under  Mr.  Stetson  the  band  at-
tained a high degree of proficiency,    membership was increased  and
instrumentation  was  amplified.        The  history  of  the  band  is  in-
separable  from  that  of  C.  Loring  Stetson.            His  efforts,       crowned
with  success ,      made its  reputation known everywhere  as  the  finest
band in the country.        Its  services  were country-wide,    even beyond
New England.         The band traveled  several  times  to  Philadelphia.
In  1852,       in  Boston,   it  played at the  funeral  obsequies  of  Daniel
Webster,       also  those of  President Tyler in 1850.    In  1856 it  served
as  Regimental  Band  of  the  Fourth  Regiment  of  Massachusetts
Volunteer  Militia.               Several  members  enlisted  in  the  War of  the
Rebellion,       but  the  ranks  were  always  full  and there  was  never  a
break  in  the  organization,     and  in  1865  they were  in  the  highest
state  of  perfection.             On  Oct.   22,        1865,       in   Philadelphia,       ninety
bands  from  all  over  the  United  States  were  gathered,     and  com-
petent  judges  gave to  the Weymouth Band the highest praise  for
surpassing  all  the  other  bands  assembled.          They were  invited  in
1869  by  P.  S.  Gilmore to  assist  at the " Peace Jubilee "  and again
in  1872  at  the  World's  Peace Jubilee.
At the Town Hall the annual "Fast Night Concerts " weregiven
many  years   successively   with  the  best   talent   in  the  country
assisting.
In  1883  Mr.  Stetson  resigned  as  leader  and  also  withdrew  as  a
member  after  thirty-four  years  of  active  service,     filling  all  posi-
tions  with marked ability  and distinction.            He was a man of vast
musical  experience,    mature  and  sound  judgment,     upon whom a
dependence could be placed with confidence.
The fiftieth   anniversary  of  the  Band,    held  in  East  Weymouth,
Sept.   22,         1894,     included  a  reception,    dinner,   speeches,       historical
sketches,       fireworks  and  an open- air  concert  by the  Band.

SIMPSON  DRUM  CORPS
During  the  years  following  the  Civil  War there were formed  in
many communities organizations which tended to foster  the martial
spirit  and perpetuate  the military  habits  and training  so  recently
learned by their fathers while in the military service of the United
States.               Patriotism  was  a  watchword  and  some  outlet  must be
had for  the enthusiasm of youth.
In  1873,        in  South  Weymouth,    was formed  a very  noted  Drum
Corps,      known  as  the  Simpson  Drum Corps,     named  after  Daniel
Simpson,            a  distinguished  veteran  and  member  of   the  Ancient
and Honorable Artillery  Company.
This  organization  was known from  Maine  to  Virginia  and was
intimately  connected  with  the  Ancient  and  Honorable  Artillery
Company of  Boston and  also closely  allied with  the  Independent
Corps   of   Cadets.         For  many  years   the  Simpson  Drum  Corps
formed  an  integral  part  of  these  organizations  and  attended  all
their programs  in the capacity of official  drummers.
The original  roster  of  the  Corps  included  Herbert  Boynton,       a
most  efficient  drum  major,    five  drummers,      namely,     Andrew  J.
Simpson,      Walter  H.  Joy,     Fred  Bates,    Lloyd Andrews  and Henry
Poole;        four  fifers,        namely,    Quincy  Torrey,       John  A.   Coughlan,
Hobart  and  Randall  Gilbert;       also  George  Loud,     cymbals,
and  William  Read,     bass  drum.          Some time  later  four  additional
drummers  were  added,     namely,      Fred  Curtis,   Joe  Deane,       Warren
T.  Simpson,      Burton F.  Church.
The Ancient and Honorable Artillery  Company held drum-head
elections  for officers  each year in June on Boston  Common,    and an
annual meeting in October,    at which the  Drum Corps  was  always
present.
The Independent Corp of Cadets also depended on the Simpsons
for  music,    and in  October,     1881,     they  accompanied the  Cadets  to
Yorktown,            Va. ,    attending  the  centennial   anniversary  of   Corn-
wallis'        surrender to  the American  army.
The  President  of  the  United  States,       Chester  A.  Arthur,      with
several   representatives   from   France,       descendants   of   Lafayette,
John  D.  Long,     Governor  of  Massachusetts,    and  many American
statesmen were present at this one hundredth anniversary.          Colonel
Edmands of  the  Cadets  was very  precise  in  all  his  arrangements ,
preparing each evolution in a military manner,   and the Corps met
the  President  at  the  landing  and  marched  to  the  headquarters
assigned   to   him  and  remained  on  parade  during  the  exercises.
Governor  Long was at this  time accompanied by the  Cadet  Corps
as  his  body guard.
The uniform was very  showy and with the care bestowed upon
it   they  always  presented  a  most  attractive  appearance.           Spotless
white  waistcoat,     cutaway  dress  suit  style  of  coats,      crossed  with
gold  braid,        gilded  epaulets,      trousers  of  officers   blue,     and  Cadet
 - 300 - 
778                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
caps with pom- poms gave an imposing effect.           Drum Major Boyn-
ton wore a high beaver Busby and a uniform similar to the players.
It  was related  of  the  Drum Corps  when they began to  play  that
every man within hearing changed his  step to the beat of the drum,
even  if   a full  band was  marching  near  them the  step was in time
to  the drum beat.
The snare drums were made by Joe Treat of Boston,   at that time
costing  about $30 each.            A nickel- plated barrel on each drum gave
a most  attractive  effect  to  the  instrument.       The bass  drum  was
purchased from the old Germania Band of Boston,    and is  at present
being  cared  for  by Troup 5,       B.  S.  A.
The principal  fifer was Quincy Torrey,    who was one of the most
noted  members of  Stetson's  Band.          His  record  as  a dry wit was
also  notorious.           It  is  related  that while marching in a Republican
parade an apple was thrown and hit  Mr. Torrey,    who remarked that
he " wondered how the thrower knew he was the only  Democrat in
the parade and had plugged him with an apple.  "
The first  appearance of the  Drum Corps was with the Cadets of
Boston on June 17,   1872,   when "Jim Fiske "  attended a celebration
at  Charlestown with a South Carolina Regiment as visitors .
Later  programs,      besides  the  Yorktown  celebration,    included  a
Drummer's  Tournament  at  Springfield,     with  only drum corps  to
participate,     but when they arrived  at Springfield  it was found that
Colt's  Armory Band was present,    and the Simpson Drummers won
the  second  prize,     the  Band  taking  the  first.         At this  gathering
" Old  Warren Simpson "  was with them,     seventy  years  old  and  a
superexcellent  drummer,   who used  a drum which had seen service
in  the  Revolution.
The Butcher  Boy Fire Veterans always demanded their  services,
for  without  them  they  were  unlucky,    and if  they  were  there  the
hand tub generally won a prize.
At one of  the  Conqueror  Musters when no record  was made by
the  local  engine,      the  Corps  marched  up  Pleasant  Street  playing
" Oh,      dear !       What can the  matter be?"
The  Corps  was in  existence  about  ten  years  and  officiated  for
G.  A.  R.  celebrations,     presidential  elections  and  pretty  generally
for  all  organizations.
COLUMBIAN  FIFE  AND  DRUM  CORPS
On the first  day of July,   1896,    several of the young men of South
Weymouth  formed   themselves   into   a   company  of   musicians,
known as  the Columbian Fife and Drum Corps.
There was much interest  shown by these boys in their organiza-
tion  and also  by the  citizens  of  the  section  from which they came.
Contributions  from  the  townspeople  gave  the  necessary  funds  to
the  Corps with which to purchase a  bass drum,    which is  at present,
July 1,     1923,    in  the  possession  of  and  used  by Troop  5,       B.  S.  A.,
in their field days and for marching.        The cymbals used were handed

LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                           779
down from the former Simpson Fife and Drum Corps,    and the boys
bought  their  own  uniforms,    drums  and different  musical  instru-
ments.
The original  membership included the following young men:
Sumner P.  Bowker.
Fred T. Barnes .
Ernest E.  Belcher.
Louis P.  Curtis.
Fred I.   Cushing.
Leonard D. Deane.

through whose efforts  the Corps was properly drilled and instructed
A few years  later with the addition  of  Wm.     E.  McAuley,     bugle'
Frank  W.  McCormack,     piccolo,      Arthur  E.  Hawes,     trombone,      the
name was changed to the Columbian Fife,   Drum and Bugle Corps,
and with the addition of some hired talent the Corps  gave  several
engagements with full orchestra programs.
The original place of meeting was at Clapp's Hall,   but later  was
changed  to  outdoor rehearsals.
The  leader,        Frederick  I.   Cushing,  was  elected,    together with  a
Secretary,          W.  S.   Holbrook,      and  a  Treasurer,      Alvin  C.   Thayer.
The drum major was  Mr.  Charles  Gilbert,    whose graceful dignity
and  ability  with the baton won unexcelled  comments.
Their  first   appearance  was  with  the  Conqueror  Veterans  Fire
Association  at the  Fair Grounds,   September,   1896.    On this  occa-
sion they wore their new uniforms and presented a fine  appearance.
Avery elaborate uniform was in use during the latter years and the
Corps presented one of the  finest  appearances of any in  the State.
On Armistice Day,   Nov.  11,    1918,    the company gave an exhibition
which was in keeping with the occasion and since then the meetings
have been discontinued.
THE DEWEY CLUB
This  Club,     so  universally known under the  name of  the  Dewey
Club,    was first  organized under the name of the South Weymouth
Social  Club,      but having been founded in  1898,    about the  time of
Admiral  Dewey's  victory  at  Manila,     several  members  suggested
the change of name,   and while it  was never formally adopted,    the
name  Dewey  seemed  to  be  the  acknowledged designation  of  the
Club.          The original  purpose was principally  social,   having a read-
ing room with commodious quarters  at  184 Main Street,      in  which
the meetings were held and a club center established.       The roster
of  the original  Club  included  mostly younger men from  Ward  4
and several from Ward 5,  the Club numbering about thirty members.
The  Club  was  strictly   a  temperance  organization,     it  being  a
jealously  guarded principle  not to  allow  anything  suspicious  inside
the Club room,     so if  punch  happened to be the principal  refresh
 - 302 - 
780                                 LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES
ment,      it  was placed  on a stand just  outside the window where  it
could be easily  reached.
A genuine  ping-pong  table was made by some party  unknown,
by sawing  off  the  legs  of  a perfectly  good  pool  table  and taking
out the cushions.
Boxing glove tournaments furnished some excitement and taught
the manly art  of self-defence to several members.
One Fourth  of  July  the  special  officer  on  guard  was,     by acci-
dent (?) ,    locked in the refreshment room while the members outside
started  an illumination.
Magazines,       periodicals  and games served  to  furnish  amusement
to  the Club members.
In  the  later  years  of  its  existence  ( 1908,      1909  and  1910) ,      the
Club turned its  energies  to baseball,    and for three years was privi-
leged to encounter some of the best clubs  in  southeastern  Massa-
chusetts,       becoming  a  member of  a league  formed  of  clubs  from
Rockland,       Stoughton,      Randolph,     Brockton,     Taunton and Quincy.
Several   closely   contested  games  were  played  with  the  Norfolk
Club  of  South  Weymouth  at  the  Fair  Grounds,     but  the  home
grounds  were Garfield  Park,     Weymouth Landing.
The Club won the  pennant in the league during  the  season  of
1910.
Players  of higher abilities  were hired for the games and expenses
began to  exceed  the  receipts  and the interest  began to wane,    and
after  an  existence  of  ten  years  the  regular meetings  were discon-
tinued,      although  several  reunions  have  been  held  from  time  to
time.
THE  NORFOLK  CLUB
Common interest  in  the bicycle,     at  a time when the desire  to
own  a  " safety "   animated  most young  men,    frequently  brought
together  in  the  rear  of  the jewelry  store  of  Charles  H.  Tinkham
in  Music Hall  block,    South  Weymouth,    a young and enthusiastic
group.            Memory sets  the date  in  the year  1889,    and the names of
the regular members of this  little  band as Walter L.  Bates,     H. Wil-
bur Dyer,     Arthur C. Heald,    the brothers,   J.  Howard and Walter R.
Field,        Edward P.  MacBride and Charles H. Tinkham.
In the year 1890 the above- named group,    with additions  increas-
ing the number to twelve,   organized themselves on Memorial Day
as the Norfolk Cycle Club.
Quarters  were  established   in   the   Fogg  Building,       Columbian
Square,     in  the rear of  the middle room,    then occupied by the post-
office,       and as  interest  in  cycling  grew  with  the  perfection  of  the
pneumatic tire,    so did  the  Norfolk  Cycle  Club  grow.         Gradually
larger  quarters  were  obtained  in the  Fogg Building,    and bowling
alleys  some years  later  were  installed.
At about this  time two other clubs  had appeared in South Wey-
mouth,                     the  Hawthorne,    with  quarters  in  the  old  Savings  Bank
house on Main Street,    and the Lincoln,   whose members originally
 - 303 - 
LODGES  AND  SOCIETIES                            781
were boys,      shortly  to consider  themselves men.            In January,     1894,
these  two clubs  united with  the  Norfolk  Club and larger  quarters
were taken  in  the  Fogg  Building.        In  1898  the  Club  was  incor-
porated under the  name of the Norfolk Club of South Weymouth
and at that time the membership numbered eighty- five.
For  several  years,   as  it  had previously been,    the  Club remained
the  center  of  bicycling  interest  in  South Weymouth.           Road  races
had been and were of frequent  occurrence,     and rivalry.   with  other
towns  and villages  was keen.
The days of  the cycle  as  a sporting  implement for  the  amateur
came to an end,  and the Norfolk Club became purely a social club.
In  1913  the  Club  took  title  to the  Fogg  Opera  House Building,
which has for the last few years been managed through a committee
of  the  Club.       Membership hovers  around  the two hundred  mark,
the  limit  set  by the  Club by- laws,      and as  large  a membership  as
the  present  Club  quarters  can conveniently  contain.
The moving of the  two banks,    which will  occur  within  a year
from  the present  time,    will  give the  Club opportunity  to  broaden
its  scope to considerable  extent.
Hitherto,        the  Club has been  a convenient  meeting place in  the
center of things  in  South Weymouth;      its  quarters have been avail-
able  to  members  and  non-members  for  public  purposes,       and  its
members are always expected to do their share when there is  work
to  be done.                The Club has  carried  out the purpose of its  charter
"for  encouraging all  public exercises,    to  cultivate  a more intimate
knowledge of  all  events  affecting  the public welfare,     and  so  far  as
possible to use  its  influence for the public good,"  and  more;        and
so it  must do in the future.
