REPORT  OF  LOUIS  A.   COOK,        ESQ.
To the  Citizens  of Weymouth:
Herewith is  presented  a report  upon my recent mission to Wey-
mouth,    Eng. ,    to represent this town at the unveiling of the Endicott-
Clark Memorial,    recently erected  to  commemorate the virtues  and
achievements of John Endicott  and  Richard  Clark.         The program
and  addresses  following  will  sufficiently  set  forth  the  characteris-
tics  and  renown of  the men honored by the erection of the memo-
rial.             The inception  of my journey was founded on the receipt  of
the  following  letter :
DEC.     16,      1913.
SIR:   - I   am desired by the mayor of this town to write you under the follow-
ing circumstances.        History appears to  show that John Endicott,   the first Gov-
ernor of Massachusetts Bay,    and Clark sailed from Weymouth in the  ship "Ab-
igail"  in the year 1628,    and to mark this interesting fact a fund has been raised
and a memorial is  to  be erected on the quay adjacent from which these worthies
sailed.              It  is  proposed  to  unveil  this  memorial  in  the  first  week in  June,    and
efforts are being made to  obtain the services of the American ambassador for  the
occasion.
From the  best  inquiries  I  can make I  have ascertained  there  are two towns
bearing the name of "Weymouth"  in the United States,    one in Massachusetts
and the  other in  New Jersey,    and I am desirous  to  express  the earnest  hope of
our town that you will induce a representative from your town to visit  us on the
occasion  mentioned.
I need hardly say if you succeed in doing this  your representative will receive
a very hearty welcome and our Borough will consider it  a great honour.
Thanking you in  anticipation,       I  am,    sir ,
Your obedient servant,
The Mayor,    " Weymouth, "  Massachusetts,     U.  S.  A.
H.  A.  HUXTABLE,
Town Clerk.
At the  annual  town  meeting  held  March  9,      1914,       under  the
article  calling  for the appointment of committees,    I  was elected  to
serve  the  town on this  honorable  and  important mission.           Before
departing on my journey it occurred to me that it would be appro-
priate  and desirable to  take with me some specimens of the handi-
work for  which  our  own town had been celebrated  for  a hundred
years  or  more,    and in  furtherance  of  this  idea  I  invited  the  shoe
manufacturers to contribute towards this project.         This resulted in
the  special  manufacture  of  a  pair  of  men's  shoes  by  both  Edwin
Clapp & Son and the Stetson Shoe Company,   and the contribution
of a pair of ladies'    shoes by the Geo.    E. Keith Company.
On the 19th of  May,    a charmingly fine  morning,   accompanied by
Mrs.  Cook,       and with a party of well-wishers  present to  bid  us  bon
voyage,    we set sail  on the steamer " Arabic "  of the White Star Line,
bound for  the  port  of  Liverpool.

JUDGE  LOUIS A.  COOK  SAILS.     1
Given Royal Send- off Last Tuesday on Journey to  Weymouth,   Eng.
Amid cheers  and best wishes from a host of friends and associates,    Hon.    Louis
A.  Cook sailed  from  Charlestown last  Tuesday on the steamship "Arabic"  for
Liverpool,       Eng.         Judge  Cook is  to  represent  this  town at  the celebration,       the
first  week in June,   of the town of Weymouth,     Eng. ,    when the memorial to  the
first   Governor  of  Massachusetts  Bay  Colony,      John  Endicott,    who sailed  from
Weymouth,     Eng. ,    June,    1628,     will  be unveiled.
The town and the Board of Trade of Weymouth were represented at the dock
by A.  P.  Worthen,     D.  M. Easton,    M. Sheehy,    William C. Earle,    Louis A.  Cook,
Jr. ,       S.  R.  Cook and E.  W. Hunt.
Town Council  A.  P.  Worthen  presented  Mr.  Cook with his  credentials,       and
then  D.  M. Easton,    in his  own original  manner,    presented  the  tourist  with  an
elegant bouquet of choice flowers.
President E. W. Hunt of the Board of Trade extended best wishes to  Mr. Cook
and sent greetings and congratulations to the  mayor of Weymouth,   Eng.,   and all
his countrymen,    also  an invitation to attend our coming three hundredth anni-
versary celebration.
Mr. Cook was accompanied by Mrs. Cook.       After spending some time looking
up historical records in Weymouth,    Judge and Mrs.  Cook will return to London
and then go to Paris,  where their daughter,   Miss Florence Cook,  will  join them
from  Rome.      They will  return about August first .
Mr.  Cook takes  with  him the  following  credential  from  the  town  clerk  of
Weymouth and testimonial  from Governor Walsh which were prepared by Town
Counsel Albert P. Worthen:
To the Mayor of the Town of Weymouth,    Eng.
The people  of Weymouth,     in the county of Norfolk and Commonwealth  of
Massachusetts,   accept with great pleasure the invitation extended by the people
of Weymouth,    Eng. ,    to send a representative to visit  them upon the occasion of
the unveiling of a memorial marking the place from which the  first  Governor of
Massachusetts Bay and Richard  Clark sailed  in  1628.
In common with the  numerous  other  settlements  in  this  country which bear
the names of the places  in old England from which our  forefathers  came,    the
people  of Weymouth,     Mass. ,    cherish  sentiments  of sincere  esteem  and respect
for the more ancient  mother town of Weymouth,    Eng.
Moreover,      in  the words of John Endicott himself,    whose departure from your
shores  you  propose  to  fittingly  commemorate:      "God's  people  are  all  marked
with one and ye same marke,    and sealed  with  one and ye same seale,     and have
for ye maine,     one and ye same harte,    guided by one and same spirite of truth;
and where this  is  there can be no discorde,    nay,   here  must needs be sweet har-
monies."
In furtherance of this purpose and in token of their endorsement of the above
sentiments,    the people of Weymouth,   Mass., at a legal town meeting held March
11,   1914,     elected Judge  Louis  A.  Cook as their  duly  accredited  representative
from said town to attend the proposed celebration.
In testimony whereof I  hereunto set  my hand and affix  the seal  of said  town
this  eighteenth day of May in the year of our Lord one thousand nine,hundred
and fourteen.
(Seal.)
JOHN A.  RAYMOND,
To the Mayor and Inhabitants  of the  Town of Weymouth,    Eng.
Town Clerk.
Weymouth was  the  first   settlement  in  Massachusetts  Bay  Colony  of  which
John Endicott was the  first  Governor.        Just  as that colony has  developed  into
the  Commonwealth  of  Massachusetts,      so  in its  course of nearly  three  centuries
1 From the " Weymouth Gazette," May 22,   1914.

784                     REPORT  OF  LOUIS  A.   COOK,        ESQ.
has  that  first   settlement  become  one of the  largest  and most beautiful  of  the
many towns in which the Commonwealth takes pride.
We of New England can well understand why our fathers,    in many instances,
brought with them and bestowed upon the place of their new home a name "in
honor and love to  their  dear and native country.         Not only that,    but they also
brought  with  them  those  lofty  and sterling  principles  of  thought  and  action
which have contributed so much to our prosperity and secured for  us the mani-
fold blessings we now enjoy. "
As the present  Chief Executive of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts,      and
on behalf of all her people,    I send to the town across the sea of which our Wey-
mouth is  the namesake,   greetings and congratulations.
(Great Seal of the Commonwealth. )
DAVID  I.    WALSH,
Governor.
We arrived  in  Liverpool  Wednesday,     May 27,    at about 4 P.M.,
and went by a special  train  for  the  boat's  passengers,       across  the
verdant and luxuriant fields  of England to London.        After spending
two  or  three days  in  London,   we journeyed to  Weymouth,     some-
times called the Naples of England,   via Southampton,   and,    arriving
an hour or  more late,    we went to  the  Hotel  Burdon to which we
had  been  previously  assigned  by letter.            There  we found  H.  A.
Huxtable,      Esq. ,   town clerk  of Weymouth,   awaiting  us.     We were
cordially  received  and told  that  we were the  guests  of  the  town.
We were at  once invited  to call on him the next day at his  home
in  Dorchester,    which we did,    and we were very pleasantly  enter-
tained at tea and were given the opportunity of seeing his  attractive
gardens.
On  Monday,       in  an  auto  kindly  furnished  by  Mr.  Herbert  J.
Groves,       under  the  guidance  of  Colonel  Symes  and  his  wife,      we
were taken to  Sherborn to  inspect  the rare  old  abbey and a boys'
school  there  located.       Upon a wall were inscribed the names of the
Masters  of  the latter since A.D. 705 .
Other  places  of  interest  were  shown  us  on this  trip,     and  the
day was delightfully  spent.
The town  of  Weymouth is beautifully situated at the mouth of
the  Wey River,                       whence its  name,               and on  an  attractive  open
harbor,      while on one side of it  is  also  Portland  Harbor.           It  has  a
population  of  about 24,000  and has  long  been  a famous  summer
resort.              It  has  an esplanade  a mile  or  more long,     which  extends
along  the  beach,   and that  and " the  sands "  attract  local  as  well
as foreign patronage.       It also has its  parks and charming drives,     and
is  altogether  such  a mother- town  as  may command the pride  and
admiration  of her daughter on this  side of the water.
On  Tuesday  morning,   June  2,     the  day  of  the  celebration,      I
attended the opening of the Court of Assizes under the guidance of
Mr.  Huxtable,    and was there  introduced to  the  celebrated  author,
Thomas  Hardy.           The day happened to  be  Mr.  Hardy's  seventy-
fourth  birthday,    and he was  in  attendance  upon  the  court  as  a
grand  juror.               I  found  much  in  the  proceedings  of  the  court  to
interest  me.                The  great   event  which  brought  me  to   England
occurred  on the afternoon  of  this  day,   and although the forenoon
 - 307 - 
REPORT  OF  LOUIS  A.   COOK,        ESQ.                                                                                           785
had been stormy,   the weather cleared  so  that  it was  no drawback
or hindrance to the celebration.
I  took  occasion  to  examine  the  records  in  several  parishes   in
search  of  Weymouth (Mass. )   names.               In the recorded  statistics  of
three  hundred  years  ago,      at  St.   Mary's  Church,        Weymouth,        I
found  these  names:        Bartlett,      Cook,      Lovell,     King,      Pitt,      Rogers,
White,       Thompson,       Bayley,       Randall,       Whitcomb,       Reade,       Martin,
Hunt,     Sanders  and Willis,   -all  Weymouth  (Mass. )  names.
At the  Parish  Church of Wyke Regis  (Weymouth)   I  found the
following,      recorded  about  two hundred and twenty-five  years  ago :
Dyer,         Cook,         Pitt,      Rogers,       Ford,      Hunt,     White,      Dizer,      Thompson,
King,        Reed,      Bayley,    Bartlett,     Randall,     Humphrey,    Lovell,     White,
Raymond,          Martin,       Christopher   Webb,     John  Blanchard,         Dyer,
Bates,     Pratt  and John Barnes .
Knowing that the Thayers who settled  in  Braintree,   Weymouth
and Mendon,    came from Thornbury,     near  Bristol,    in  the western
part  of  England,   we made a journey to that place and found it  a
quaint old village with a large parish church and an interesting old
castle  adjoining.        Here  I  was  permitted  to  examine  the  parish
register  under the surveillance of the Vicar,   who kept  one eye  on
Mrs.  Cook,       lest  she  might be a suffragette.          I  also  found  many
familiar  names here.       I have long had an idea  that  some  others
besides  the Thayers  may have come to  this  vicinity from Thorn-
bury  which  is  in  the  county  of  Gloucestershire.           The  following
names,    many of  them frequently  repeated,    were found upon  the
Parish Register of three hundred and fifty years ago,    the aforesaid
register   being  in  a most  excellent  state  of  preservation :             Thos.
Holbrook,       Thos.    White,    Thos.     Dyer,    Thos.    Thayer,    John Thomas,
Jone Aldrich,     Jone Bicknell,    Ford,   Cook,     King,    Richards,    Thomp-
son,      Hunt,        Nash,      Wright,     Bayley,    Blanchett  (Blanchard) ,       Philips,
Neale,      Lovell,   Willis,    Long,    Edward Hunt,    Whitman,     Reed,     Webb,
Poole,      Baker and Derby.
It seems to me rather remarkable that so many of the above names
should  have appeared among the early  settlers  of  Weymouth and
vicinity,    unless  there were other immigrants than the  Thayers  that
came from that vicinity.
In London  I  spent about ten days in the British  Museum,     read-
ing manuscripts relating  to early New England history,    and while
there  I  took many notes  that I thought might have some bearing
on our Weymouth beginnings.     The following,    which I  have never
before seen,     seemed to be the most notable :
In 1623,  about 120 emigrants set out to plant in Delaware Bay,    but were forced,
by cross winds,   to land about 25 miles to the south of Massachusetts,      and there
they established  a colony,    which begins to thrive,    having increased to  about 500
people.
The above throws  additional light upon the permanency of  the
settlement   from  1623,     and  also  a  new  consideration  as  to   the
colony's being headed for  Delaware Bay,  -and being accidentally
 - 308 - 
786                       REPORT  OF  LOUIS  A.   COOK,        ESQ.
driven  into  Massachusetts  Bay,                     upon which statement  I  am as
yet  somewhat skeptical.
By special  arrangement  I  visited  the  Colonial  Offices  in  London
and inspected  the original  passenger  list,     which was discovered  in
the  year  1870,     of  the  Rev.  Thomas  Hull's  Company that  sailed
from Weymouth,     Eng. ,     March 20,      1635.
Leaving Weymouth June 8,    we went to the Isle of Wight,    crossed
the island  from  Cowes,     and came to  the beautiful  seaside town of
Ventnor,         where  we  presented  to   Mr.   and  Mrs.  John  Morgan
Richards   our  letter   of  introduction,      and  where  we  were  most
graciously  received  and  entertained  for  two  days  at  their  home,
Steep Hill  Castle.        Our host and hostess were both American born.
They were the parents of the well-known writer,     Mrs.  Pearl  (Rich-
ards)   Cragie,      now deceased,     who wrote under the nom de plume of
John Oliver  Hobbs .
Returning  to  London we were invited  to  attend  the opening  of
the  English  and  American  Historical   Rooms.           A luncheon  was
served,      and here we met former Ambassador Bryce,     who presided,
and our present  ambassador to  England,    Hon.    Walter Hines Page.
We received  an invitation  to attend,    at Trowbridge on June 17,
the  Centenary  Celebration  of the  Induction  of George  Crabb,     the
poet,    into  the  rectorship  of  the  Parish.          A public  luncheon  was
served  in  the  Town Hall.           Mr.  A.  M.  Broadley gave the historical
address  and I  was introduced,    among others,     to  speak.            The entire
afternoon  and evening were devoted  to  the  commemoration,     and
after   the  church  service  in  the  evening,    at  which  the  Dean  of
Salisbury  delivered  the  sermon,    we were asked by the rector,     Rev.
Percy A.  Nash and his  good lady,    to  dine at  the rectory with  the
dean.
On July 4,    we attended the reception given by Ambassador and
Mrs. Page to Americans in London,   which was very largely attended,
and  there  among others  we met some Americans  with  whom we
were acquainted.
Immediately upon our return  to  London we journeyed again  to
Bridport  in  the  south of  England,    where we were  entertained  for
four days  most pleasantly by Mr.  Broadley,   who had invited us in
order  that  we might  help  him  celebrate  his  birthday  which  oc-
curred Sunday,   July 19.    He placed his  large library of more than
30,000  volumes  at  my disposal,       and  while  there  I  learned  that
Henry Waltham,    an early settler in our Weymouth,    may have been
a former  mayor of  old  Weymouth,    as  there  was  a mayor by that
name in  1623 or thereabouts.            This Waltham was the owner of the
mill  property  in  East Weymouth.          Mr.  Broadley  is  anxious  that
Americans  should  know  more  and  see  more  of  the  picturesque
landscapes  in the south of England,   having a feeling that it  is  being
neglected  for  other  less  attractive  regions.        We found  his  house
full  of  pictures,      curios  and  interesting  objects.         He gave  me an
old chain  or fetter dug up on  the  Gorges  Land,   which he said we
could  hang  up in  our  Town  House.           Alas!      When I  returned  our
 - 309 - 
REPORT  OF  LOUIS  A.   COOK,        ESQ.                                                                                          787
Town House was no more.           I left with him our Historical Society's
publications  Nos.      II  and III ,     and when we were leaving  Bridport,
as the train passed Mr.  Broadley's house,    he and his  servants were
on top  of  the house just  pulling down,    as  our  train  went out  of
sight,     the Stars  and Stripes,   which had been flying during our stay
as  a matter of courtesy  to  us.             I  may add also  that on the day of
the  celebration  in  Weymouth,     while  the  British  flags  were  flying
everywhere,       I  noticed  that  at  the  Hotel  Burdon,    where  we were
being  entertained,      a large  United  States  flag  only  was displayed.
Again,    at Steep Hill  Castle,   Ventnor,   during our stay  " Old Glory "
was at the top of the high stone tower.
These marks  of  courtesy  touched  us,    and  I  may say  that  in  a
number of addresses that  I heard,   both from English and American
speakers  overseas,    the sentiment was almost sure  to  crop out that
after  a hundred years  of  peace  these  two  great English- speaking
peoples  ought never again to strive in war against  each other.
For a week before our departure black clouds of war were rising,
threatening  all  Europe  with  disaster,       and  on  the  very  day  we
sailed  away from Liverpool  (July 28)  war was declared by Austria
against Servia.         We returned,    as we went,   on the Steamer "Arabic, "
and when halfway over,    or a little  more,    the wireless  gave us  the
news  that  Germany and  England  were  involved,     and  then  arose
rumors  of  German  cruisers,     and  some  acts  of  precaution  ensued,
but  I  saw  nothing  on board  to  indicate  that  fear  pervaded  the
passenger  list.             On August 6 we were safely landed in Boston.and
received  many congratulations  from our friends.
And so  the mission of your representative from New Weymouth
to  Old Weymouth went into  history.
Respectfully submitted,
LOUIS  A.  Соок.

WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE
Compiled by BATES  TORREY
Considering  Folklore to mean the traditions,   beliefs  and customs
of  a people,       abundant  material  for  a  chapter  like  this  ought  to
have  accumulated  while  the  History  of   Weymouth  was  in  the
making;        and  if  reticence  in  many  directions   could  have  been
overcome,     what a  record  of  reminiscence our pleading would have
evoked.       Also,   if old residents had memories proportioned  to  their
generous  inclination  to  assist  in  this  compilation,    a much better
showing might have been made.
However,        acknowledgments  are  due  to   Helen  H.   B.   Hobart,
Eben  P.   Pratt,        Jason  B.   Orcutt  and  Herbert  A.   Newton,      who
responded  liberally;       and  to  many others  who helped  more  than
they realized .
No  special  order,     either  of  event  or  date,    has  been  suggested.
A Weymouth rustic,   taking a paper of peppermints from his pocket
and scattering  them on the table,    said " Come,     Sal. ,    let's  browse. "
Let  the  reader,     opening to  this  chapter,     do likewise.
Thomas  White  may have  come  with  the  Weston  Colony,         or
about  1624.    He was  a member of  the  First  Church  and  owned
about  75  acres  of  land.           He had four  sons  and a daughter ;        three
sons  were captains,   and the daughter married a captain.         Captain
Samuel  achieved  this  distinction,    that  when Sir  Edmund Andros
made  his   escape  from  the  Old  Castle,      Capt.     Samuel  White  of
Weymouth  received   a  warrant  from  Governor  Bradstreet   and
his  council  to  pursue Andros  and bring  him back,    which  he did
with his  troop of fifty- two men,    and for  which he received  £22 8d.
Deacon  Thomas White (third  generation)  had a son Nathaniel
who was the first  physician of the town.        A sister  of Dr.  Nathaniel
married in  Braintree,     and her daughter married a Shaw,     becoming
the  parents  of  Chief  Justice  Lemuel  Shaw,    whose decisions  are
often quoted at  the  present  time.
Samuel White of the fourth generation married Prudence,   daugh-
ter  of  Samuel  Williams,     Esq. ,     of Taunton,   and they lived  in  that
city.              Mr.  White was an eminent lawyer,    much in public,   a deacon
and  a colonel.          He was  of  fine  appearance,   great  sagacity,       irre-
proachable morals,     and an eloquent  speaker.         He was representa-
tive  or councillor from Taunton nearly every year from 1744 until
his  death  in  1769,    being  Speaker  of  the House in  1759,     1764 and
1765.    As  Speaker he  signed the letter from  Massachusetts  to  the
other  colonies  under  which  the  first   Colonial  Congress  was  held
 - 311 - 
WEYMOUTH FOLKLORE                         789
in  New  York,       October,      1765,     for  the  purpose  of  defeating  the
Stamp  Act.                  Thus  he  set  in  motion  the  organized  action  that
brought  about  the American Revolution.
Dr.  Nathaniel White had  a brother Thomas who married  Sarah
Loring  of  Hull,     and  from  her  father  who  owned  slaves  Thomas
White (fourth generation)   bought a negro girl  named Dinah.            The
bill of sale is  on record,    a document couched in the formal language
of  a legal  transaction  and giving  evidence  of  the ownership  of  a
slave in Weymouth.
This same Thomas White,   4th,   had a son Silas,    who was a soldier
of the Revolutionary War,    and he and his wife and the slave Dinah
joined the church in South Weymouth the same day.         Dinah had
to sit  in  an assigned place in the gallery.      She did the heavy work
of the household and took full charge of the dinner at Thanksgiving
time.             This was a large proposition,   as a very large family assembled,
and  Dinah  " Hoped the  Lord "  each  year,    she  was  so  tired,      " she
would  never  live  to  see  another  Thanksgiving! "     And finally  her
wish was realized .
When  the   British  threatened  to  land  at  Cohasset,       and  were
alarmed  by martial  music (the  tradition,    or  fact,     being  that  two
housewives,      one with a drum the  other with  a fife,    made pretense
of  a troop  of  soldiers  in  ambush and the  menacing  British  sailed
away)    Capt.        Silas  White was at church,     and a courier  thrust  his
head into  the open window and shouted that the British  were off
Cohasset.                     Thereupon   Captain   White  stalked   out  of   church,
assembled  his  company  and  hastened  to  that  town,       but  before
arriving  there he learned that the danger had been averted by the
brave  and  resourceful  Bates  ladies .
Dea.      Samuel Whitman,   who was born in 1673,   and died in 1778,
lived  one hundred and five years,     and the confirmation of that fact
is  this:    At the time of the  Revolution  there was a  rumor that the
British  were to invade this part of the country,    and to go through
Weymouth.                People  became  frightened   and  prepared   to   leave
town;    some of the  Lower End Whitman family started  for Abing-
ton,    and on  the way stopped  at  Dea.      Samuel Whitman's  whose
family  was  going  also.         The lady  who tells  the  story  was  one  of
the  party,       and  remembers  seeing  Deacon  Samuel,     then  over  one
hundred,       going  about  the  house  getting  valuable  documents  to-
gether  to  save them.
Sayings  and  " Sich." -   Caleb  Hawes,    when he  took  from  the
factory a case of boots  (to be " made" at home as the custom was),
if  they ran in sizes  from 6 to  10 he would always make up the 6's
first .               His  explanation was this :       " Wall,    ef I wuz to die,     the other
fellow  would hev to make the larger  sizes."
The daily stent would be two to  three pairs,  but if  Caleb was in
a care- free  mood he would decide upon " Two pairs  and a fox hunt
to-day,      and  four  pairs  to-morrow. "

Oran White (so long  town clerk)   and his father were working  in
the woods where there were many gunners,     and bullets  were flying
dangerously.                  Thomas  White  told  the  neighbors,      " Spat  went  a
ball right  where Oran stood,    and I  told  him to step so  I  could see if
he was shot. "
Esau Loud announced that he was going to take a pill,     and then
double  the  dose  every  day  for  a  year.              On such  rather  visionary
premises  Leonard Gardner figured  that the quantity of pills  would
more than  fill  Otis  Cushing's  big  white- top express  wagon that he
drove to  Boston every day.
Warren Thayer House
The Poole Tavern at the junction of the roads at  Pond Plain was
conducted by Warren  Poole,     and when the turnpike went through
he established  a toll-gate  at this  point.          This  must have been one
hundred and twenty years ago,    as he died in  1858 aged seventy- six.
The Warren  Thayer house  across  the  street  was  built  one hun-
dred  and seventy- five  years  ago,     and  had in it  laths  of split  cedar
about  twenty feet  long.
The  brick  house  formerly  owned  by  David  Shaw,      and  subse-
quently  by  Alden  White,      well  known  as   a  dance  violinist   and
prompter,     was  used  as  Hovey's  tavern  before  the  Revolutionary
War,      and  patronized  liberally  for  many years  after.

WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE                         791
Dea.            Jacob  Loud,    driving  through  the  village,    huddled  up  or
crouching  in  his  seat  as  was  his  wont,      gave  the  appearance  of
senility  and abstraction,    but the boys who tried  to  catch  on found
it   otherwise,    and  the  Deacon  himself  " allowed"  that  he saw  " a
great  deal  more than  they gave  him credit  for. "
Dr.  Appleton  Howe usually  had a melon  patch  at  the  west  of
his  house,       and quite  frequently  the  boys  timed  the  maturity  of
the melons just a little  earlier than the worthy doctor.          So one day
he opened  one  of  his  most attractive  melons  and inserted  therein
enough physic to make it  interesting  for the partaker,     and  it  was
not  long before  Dr.  Howe was summoned to  attend  a lad  afflicted
with  a  grievous  illness.            The  parents,       much  worried,       asked  the
doctor  if  he thought the boy would pull  through all  right.           " Yes, "
he replied,    " if  he keeps away from my melons.  "
In  the  old  School  District  days  Mr.  Lovell  Bicknell  of  East
Weymouth was  always  a dominant figure  in  the meetings  of  the
Third District.          It  is  related  that upon one occasion  the meeting
had organized  and acted upon two or three articles  of the warrant
before  Mr.  Bicknell  arrived.       He came blustering  in  and at  once
demanded  to  know what business  had  been  transacted,    and was
given  the  required   information  by  the  moderator.             Thereupon
Mr.  Bicknell  announced  in  his characteristic gruff way:        " I  move
that we reconsider all  that has been done in this meeting. "     Itis
hardly necessary to  state that the motion to  reconsider was carried
without debate.
On the  left-hand side  of  Front  Street,   going  north  toward  the
Landing,     and a short distance around the corner from Amos Mer-
ritt's  needle  shop,    stands  the old  Ezra Reed house,  said to contain
frame  timbers  gotten  out for  a church edifice  planned to be built
in  the  rear  of the James  Martin  residence  on  Park Avenue  now,
but then given to the parish by Capt.   John Vinson,   2d,    a cemetery
being  included in the gift.          This latter was never large,    and in  the
lapse  of years  only  a few  stones  have survived  that  or  vandalism
until the Historical Society began to give it  care.
Passing  close  by is  the  " Town Path,"  so  called,     probably  the
vestiges  of the Indian trail to  Plymouth Bay,   and the path used by
people  of  this   locality  to  go  to  the  First  Church  at  Weymouth
Heights   before  a  church  was  established   in   South  Weymouth.
This is  a continuation of the path which originally came via Union
Street  to  May's  Corner,     and then down the hill,    crossing  what is
now  Pleasant Street  near  the John S.  Cobb place,     thence  to  and
through  " Martin's  Plain, "  and on toward  Middle Street  by Hol-
brook's Meadows.
The Reed house was built in 1767,    the  project  of  building  the
church  by  the  cemetery  having  been  abandoned.            In  1723  the

792                                 WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE
Second  Church was  erected  near  Columbian  Square,    which site  it
still  maintains.
Leonard Gardner won wide fame by his computation of a Transit
of Venus,      the  second  calculation  (the  first  having been  burned)    of
which  is   deposited  with  the  Hingham  Historical  Society  in  Mr.
Gardner's  native  town.       He was largely  self-educated,    borrowing
enough French from books and linguistic friends to read the mathe-
matical  works which only that language could  supply,     and by la-
borious  methods  reaching  results  more accurate  than those of the
authorities   at  Washington,       where  Mr.  Gardner  went  and  was
entertained.
Before  making  the  Transit  of  Venus  calculation  Mr.  Gardner
had  figured  several  eclipses,     and  one year  he  predicted  the  moon
would  rise  on  a  certain  date  at  6.30  o'clock  partially  eclipsed,
though  it  was  not  so  indicated  in  the  almanac.          The  neighbors
laughed at him,   but upon the appointed day,   after eating his supper
as  usual,      Mr.  Gardner  went to  the  door,     watching  for  the moon
to  rise.              He noted  a  gathering  of  neighbors  at  the  next  house;
they  too  were  waiting,    but  making  rather  a jovial  time  of  it.
Pretty  soon  the moon appeared,   and sure enough,    it  was partially
obscured;     the almanac had certainly  omitted  something,      and  he
had  the  laugh  on  the  neighbors,      who “ acknowledged  the  corn, "
as the saying is .
Mr.  Gardner  never  studied  algebra  or  geometry,     but  he  used
LeVerrier's  Tables  of  Logarithms,    which had been awarded a gold
medal by the British Royal Astronomical Society,   and were supposed
to  be  perfect.         When calculating  the  Transit  he came to  a situa-
tion where he could not make it verify.         He retraced his  steps  care-
fully,    but it  would not come right,   though he found the place where
the difficulty lay.        He reconsidered  LeVerrier's Tables  and noted  a
figure  that he did not like  the looks of,     and he proceeded to  figure
out what the number should  be,    discovering  that  that  number of
the  famous Tables was wrong.        He subsequently found three other
errors  in  the logarithms,     four  in  all.         He then reviewed his  calcu-
lations  and achieved  a result  more accurate  than  any one  in  this
country had accomplished.
Incidentally  Mr.  Gardner went to  Cambridge to  see  a Harvard
professor  of  astronomy,    to  tell  him about his  home work.            The
professor  was  incredulous  when told  by  this  countrified  looking
individual
dividual  that  he had  with  him  the  calculation  of  a Tran
Transit  of
Venus,     and he questioned his  visitor  rather closely,   challenging  his
results.                In  proof  of  his  statements  Mr.  Gardner  produced  his
figures,        and  casually  remarked  that  he  had  found  errors  in  Le-
Verrier's  logarithms.         This  was almost too much for  the  professor
to  believe,      and he became interested  and asked that the particular
figures   be  shown.          Mr.  Gardner  pointed  out four  errors  he  had
found.              The professor made some calculations of his own,     admitted
that  Mr.  Gardner was right,   and said that he had " made a  real
 - 315 - 
WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE                         793
discovery "    which   explained   difficulties    that   American  mathe-
maticians  had been having with the Tables .
The Harvard man expressed himself as  pleased that the country
astronomer  had  called  upon  him,    and  promised  to  write   Prof.
Simon Newcomb,   the noted astronomer at  Washington,     calling  his
attention  to  these  errors.              This  he did,      and  Mr. Gardner received
a  nice  letter   from  Professor  Newcomb,      and  later  on  was  given
mathematical work to do for the Nautical Office of the government.
As  illustrating   Leonard  Gardner's   painstaking  methods,        one
logarithm  all  astronomers  use  is  that  representing  the  sun's  dis-
tance,     which is  made a sort of reference line for all  their work,    and
this   important  basis  was  carried  out  to  the  fourteenth  decimal
place.           Our townsman thought it would be more accurate if  carried
further,       and  he  figured  it   to  the  fifteenth  place,   the  labor  of  a
month.
The Old Arnold Tavern.                       Memorabilia of former days would be
incomplete  without mention of the Old Arnold Tavern,     so  called,
which was located at the bend of  the  post  or stagecoach road (the
Weymouth  River  road)    connecting  Boston  and  Plymouth,      later
known as  Commercial Street.
Here  at  the  edge  of  the  village  green  or  town  square  " mine
host, "  Samuel Arnold, conducted in the eighteenth century a pros-
perous  hostelry.          His  son  Samuel,    when  a growing  business  de-
manded more room,  built the hotel afterward known as the " Wales
Hotel, "   later   the  property  of  the  Sacred  Heart  Church.               This
same son in 1803 erected  the brick edifice  known as  the " Cowing
House, "  notable for its  beautiful old colonial  doorway and window.
The Cowing House and Wales Hotel were set on the opposite side
of the road from the Old Arnold Tavern .
It was the crowning  event  of the day when the stagecoach drew
up at  the Tavern,     the  driver  on his  high  seat  curbing  his  horses
when making a grand sweep toward the entrance.          Excitedly  the
darkey would come running out and reach for the mail bags ;      newly
arrived  guests  or hungry travelers  to  places  beyond would  hasten
into  the  Tavern for  refreshment;       topics  of the day would be dis-
cussed around the blazing fire;   the jaded horses would be fed by the
aforesaid darkey,   and then watered at the town pump.
Across  the  square sloped the rocky hill  with the beginning  of  a
roadway now designated as  Front Street,     and at present  bordered
by fine  estates  where country pastures  were of yore.        The willows
by the Weston Cottage were green near the meadow,   but the road
by the  river was more traveled  and pleasanter  to  traverse.           Sub-
sequently the new Turnpike was constructed,    in  more recent  times
named Washington Street.
It is  related that in the  Tavern convened the Town Committee
of  Correspondence,   consisting  of  Dr.  Cotton Tufts,     Major Lovell,
Major  Vining,       Capt.       Asa  White,        Josiah   Colson,       and  probably

WEYMOUTH FOLKLORE                         795
others,     their function being to arrange plans for uniting with neigh-
boring towns to defend the rights  of the people of that Revolution-
ary time.            March 9  (in  1774 or  1775)   they organized,    selecting  Dr.
Tufts  as  chairman and  Captain  White  as  secretary.           Here  in  the
Old  Arnold  Tavern,    with  patriotic  ardor,    they  agreed  to  furnish
men and powder,   and it  is  rumored that within the Tavern powder
and bullets  were stored  and arms stacked .
Picture the  earnestness  of these true men meeting there  in spite
of the danger.        Imagine the chairman with his gold cane and snuff-
box,      the  Captain with his  sword,    each in smallclothes  with colored
coats,      ruffled  fronts,    silken  hose  and buckled shoes.       Would that
Weymouth possessed  a painting  of the  historic  scene,      to  give  to
posterity  an abiding  realization  of  the courageous founding  of  our
country.
The Old  Arnold  Tavern  was  leveled,    it  may be  thoughtlessly,
for  business  progress  or improvement,    but of all  the  pre-Revolu-
tionary  buildings  in  Concord,     Lexington,    Salem  or  Quincy  none
were better preserved at the time of  this demolition,     or contained
more stout white oak timber than this  historic  edifice.
The  Smelt  Brook.  -Weymouth is  proud  of her  territory,       and
that  she  retains  all  her  original  bounds ;      so  much so  that  efforts
for  a division  of the town have always been futile,   in  spite of the
enormous  expense budgets for  roads  and schools,    and the alluring
advantages of a diminished geographical area.
At one period Weymouth Landing coveted a piece  of Braintree,
and at another  the  desire  and design  was to  combine Weymouth
Landing and East Braintree  so  as  to  make one town bordering  the
banks of  the Smelt Brook.     There was a plan,   too,    in South Wey-
mouth to divide the town by a line that would set off  that village
in company with Lovell's  Corner  (Porter)   and Nash's  Corner,      or
approximating that territory.
The Smelt  Brook is  still  a boundary,    as when the  early  settlers
defined  it,        and  this  limit  or  landmark  separated  the  Plymouth
Colony from the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,    and it  is  so  stated  in
the original  charters.        It might be fitting  to  set  up a tablet  giving
these  facts,       and saying  that  the  Pilgrims  settled  upon  the  Wey-
mouth side  and the  Puritans upon the Braintree side  of the Smelt
Brook.
A humorous touch is  given  by the  tradition  of the lad  who at-
tempted  to  collect  toll  at  the  Smelt  Brook,     which  at  one  period
was open  to  give opportunity for horses,     with or without vehicles ,
to pass through,  as they might many a roadside rivulet;      but pater-
familias  got wind of the enterprise,    and a vigorous  spanking  sub-
dued the commercial instinct.
The coal problem of  to-day ( 1922)  and the probable future  sup-
ply of coal  adds pertinency to the following :
The first coal brought into New England made a great change in

796                                WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE
domestic affairs.         About a hundred years ago a load of  that species
of fuel drawn through the streets  of Weymouth occasioned surprise
and some unfavorable comment.       One small boy picked up a lump
of  coal,      and  running home to his mother said,   "See,   mother,     they
say  this  black  stuff  will  burn. "    The stuff  was  placed  before  the
open  ( ? )   fire,      but the  result  was  not satisfactory,    and  the  verdict
was,      " Poor stuff;    we'd rather own a woodlot and burn good wood."
In  South Weymouth Josiah Copeland,   who lived  in rather primi-
tive  fashion  at the corner of Main and Winter Streets,    bought his
first  cook  stove,    and next morning a neighbor  saw  smoke issuing
from doors and windows.         Hurrying over to investigate,     the neigh-
bor  found  " Old  Cope,"  as  the  community called him,    in  trouble.
"The old  stove is  no good;     it  won't draw,"  he said.     Removal of
the  covers  disclosed  nothing in  the  fire  box,    for  he had made his
fire  in the oven.           Thus may education be prompted by experience.
Dea.      Jacob  Loud,    who was postmaster about 1838,   was capable
of a drollery now and then.      Driving to the Landing in early spring
he,     with  another,     passed  a swamp where the  frogs  were peeping.
The  Deacon says,    " I  have a sort  of  control  over  those  frogs  and
every  one will  stop  when I  speak  to  them. "     After  proceeding  a
little  farther  the  Deacon shouts,    "Stop!      Every one  of  you !   "  and
the  peeping  ceased  instanter,      greatly   to  the  amazement  of  the
Deacon's  companion.        Then  a  little  way beyond he said,       " Now
begin  again,  "  and the frogs piped up afresh.
William Reed,    who tells  this story of the Deacon,   was much puz-
zled  by the  happening,    and  the  strange  power over the  frogs  re-
mained a mystery until Deacon Loud confessed there was a certain
wooden bridge  across  the road,    and when the wagon hit the bridge
the  frogs  were  struck  dumb -until  the  rumble  on  the   boards
ended.
Right  near  Nash's  Corner  lived  Jason  Orcutt,      Sr.,      a  lover  of
music who played  the  ophicleide  in  the  South  Weymouth Band,
of which James L.  Bates was leader,    and later  on figured conspicu-
ously  in  the  community  vocalism  of  those  days  called   " Sings, "
which  were  at  first  held  at  neighborhood  residences,     and  then  in
the  schoolhouse just below the  corner.           William  B.  Cook officiated
as  conductor,       and  one  song  book  used  was  "Ancient  Harmony
Revised, "   and  another,      " Father  Kemp's  Collection. "     The  old
tunes  were set  for  a part  termed  " counter"  instead  of alto,   being
an  octave  above  the  ordinary  alto  part.             Elias  Hunt,      father  of
Edmund S.  Hunt,     was a  famous counter- tenor  singer,      notable be-
cause few voices would have the requisite compass.            Leonard Gard-
ner,        referred  to  elsewhere  as  the local  astronomer,    played a yellow
cello  at these  concerts.         Everybody was expected to  sing  " hard,"
and interest in the result was evidenced by the crowds that attended.
Of course  there were no  movies then,   and the staid  lecture  course
had not arrived.

Henry Stetson,   brother of  Charles  Loring Stetson who conducted
the  Weymouth  Band for  about  thirty  years,      was  rather  cynical
about a good many things.       He was interested  in music,    played a
valve  trombone in  the band,    a double-bass  for dancing,   and when
the number of instruments  required for  a dance orchestra  was re-
duced he was heard to say that it would not be a great while before
the dance band would consist of one man sitting  in a corner pound-
ing out the time on the floor  with  a cane.          After  having  an  " im-
pression"  taken by a dentist for some new teeth,  Henry remarked
that  he had just  been over to have his  mouth "lathed  and plas-
tered."
Acolored couple lived  on the borders of South Weymouth,     and
one day the husband was ill   and  Dr.  (Appleton)   Howe was  sent
for.               The doctor instructed  the wife to " put a mustard plaster  on
his  chest.  "     The next day he called,    but noting  no improvement,
asked the wife if  she had done as he directed.        " No,   Massa Docter,  "
she  replied,     " he din have no chist so  I  done put it  on his  trunk. "
This  same man when trimming his  trees  sat  on a limb  he was
cutting  off  and was  precipitated  to  the  ground,    breaking  his  leg.
When he died at a very advanced age his wife selected the hymn to
be sung at the funeral,  -" When blooming youth is snatched away. "
Ezra  Reed,     the elder,   who lived  in the  old  Reed house on the
road to the Landing (elsewhere referred to) ,   was a miller,    and stand-
ing  in  his  door and seeing  one of his  relatives  approach  he would
invariably exclaim:      " Well,    if  here aint Samanthy [for  instance]   -
sartin  as  '  tis  sartin. "    He always said just that.
Before  the  introduction  of the railroad  (about  1840)   nearly  all
freight  was  brought  into  Weymouth on board  the  packets  which
sailed  between Fore River and Boston – or  Back River,    and goods
were transported from the wharves in  all  directions  by ox teams.
Upon one occasion  an  ox  team got  stuck  on  " Major  Bayley's
Hill,"  so  called,   and this  load contained  nothing but rum,    giving
the  intimation  (novel  in  these  prohibition  times)  that  it  required
quite  a  quantity  of  liquor  to  supply  the  taverns  of  the  village,
there being at least  three at that time.
One of  these  public  houses  was  later  known as  the  Quincy  L.
Reed estate.           The walls were built very thick,   and the window cas-
ings  were constructed with  a cover  beneath  which the  liquor  was
stored.            A lot  of  sporty young fellows  were wont to  congregate  at
this place,     riding thither on horseback,    and it  is  stated that on one
occasion  they  proposed  to  race to  the hotel,   the one arriving  last
to  pay the  whole toll.           Of course  each was eager to  be first  at  the
finish,       and one was so  fearful  he would not win that  he spurred
his  horse to  such speed that he could not stop,  but galloped  right
through  the  doorway  and  into  the  taproom.        The marks  of  the
horse's  hoofs were visible  there for  a long  time.

Dea.        C.  A.  Wright,      the  well- known dry goods  dealer  of  Colum-

Probably  the  last   Indians  in  Weymouth  were  Aaron  and  his
squaw  Penelope who lived  on Hawk Island in Great  Pond.            Aaron
was of unreliable  character,     and was shot for  stealing hens.        Pene-
lope then went to live  with the Blanchard family that had a black-
smith's  shop on Pond Street not far  from Kelsey Grove.         She after-
wards  joined  with  the  Second  Congregational  Church,      the  record
being  still  extant,    reading  “ Penelope,    an  Indian, "  etc.
Hawk Island,  Weymouth Great Pond.         The last Indian in Weymouth,
" Old Aaron," was buried here
In the  early days there was a substantial deposit of iron ore  (bog
iron)   at  the  Great  Pond,     as  evidenced  by records  showing  the ap-
pointment of  persons  to  supervise the obtaining  and disposition  of
this  product.            It probably was picked up on the shore of the pond,
or dredged from the bottom in  some way.
Back of  the  Palmer Loud house  on  Pleasant Street,     near  where
the  river  crosses  the  road,     there  was  formerly  a dam and a small
pond with  a grist  mill ;       and also  there was some sort  of a smelting
process,      as  indicated by fragments of slag,    with charcoal  imbedded
therein,     found close  by.           It  is  possible,    too,    that some of this  iron
ore was utilized  by the Weymouth Iron  Company.

Parson  Smith  of  the  Old  First  Church  at  Weymouth had  two
daughters,       Mary and Abigail.         Being  attractive  maidens  they had
lovers  in  due time,    and  Mary  made  a  choice,      after  her  father's
own heart,     of a young man of substance  and standing  in the com-
munity.
Abigail,     however,    preferred John Adams,    a young lawyer of the
neighboring town of Braintree,    a choice not agreeable to her father.
At a subsequent Sunday service  the  worthy divine,    apparently
giving  voice  to  his  feelings,     delivered  an  interesting  sermon  from
this  text:         " Mary hath chosen that good part which shall  not be
taken from her,  "  which was surely solace to his  chagrin because of
Abigail's defection.
But another Sabbath he took the text:      " For John came neither
eating nor drinking,   and ye say He hath a devil, "  adopting the sub-
stance  of Luke 7:33.
Notwithstanding the eloquence and the opposition of the eminent
preacher the young lawyer won his  case,                   namely,       Abigail for  his
bride,           and  as  the wife  of  our second  President,   Abigail Adams
is  enshrined in the hearts of all  true Americans;     also as the mother
of a President.
Many are familiar with Trowbridge's poem about Darius  Green
and  his   flying   machine,      but  few  are  aware  that  a  Weymouth
boy  may  have  inspired   those  verses.             Turner  Torrey,       resident
upon  Torrey's   Lane  (now  Kensington  Road  in  Ward  3)    cher-
ished  an ambition  to  fly,   and fashioned a device for  the purpose.
One day he adjusted this winged machine to  his  person and soared
from the  barn roof ;         but,    alas!      he fell  ignominiously  to  the  earth,
to be the butt of his fellows for long after.       And yet he was a pioneer.
Quaint Sayings.    -"Haste makes jackets "  became a family by-
word after  the young son had enjoyed his  first  day in  school,     and
mother had asked the sum of his knowledge acquired,   which proved
to  be  a  familiar  quotation.             Even  the  boys  wore  calico  (print)
waists  in the olden time.
At the approach of the minister the boy would hasten home and
say,      " Mother,   wash my face,    Father Perkins is coming;   "   and upon
his  arrival  the girls  would curtsy with shy respect.
"You are eating your white bread now,"  was the common saying
to  the bride,     happy in the possession  of an attentive  husband  and
a new home.           But why the " slam"  conveyed by that  careless  re-
mark?     wasn't the future promising?

Some Natural  Phenomena.    —A reputed  Indian mill to be found
in a clump of woods off  Columbian Street,   on land owned by Mrs.
E.  B.  Nevin,     gives  a hint of primitive  methods of grinding  corn .
It  consists  of  a boulder hollowed  at  the  top,   with an  egg- shaped
stone lying upon it  about large enough to suggest manipulation for
a grinding process,   carrying out the mortar- and- pestle idea.          It  is  a
singular  fact  that  the  oval- shaped  stone  should  remain  with  the
nether millstone all  these years,    now covered with moss  and bear-
ing  unmistakable marks  of antiquity  -and  use.
Another boulder  called  " The Sphinx, "  showing the profile  of  the
late  Queen Victoria  quite strongly,    is  located  off  Essex Street,     and
at  one point in view of the highway.
The  " Millstone  Rock,"  just  across  by  a rude  footbridge  over
Big  River,       so  called,   might  be  reached from  Main Street  by  the
meadow path beginning near the former Edward Nolan place.           This
rock can also be reached by the path from West Street just beyond
the  Reuben Loud residence,   and has long been an object of interest
to  strollers   like   Bradford  Torrey,      the  naturalist,     who  made  the
"Millstone   Pasture"   his   questing  place  for   birds   and  nature
study.
In  the " Railroad  Pasture,"  farther  along West Street  near  Vin-
ing's  Crossing,    there is  a huge boulder of conglomerate  (pudding-
stone) ,     almost spherical  in  shape,    suggesting  an aerolite  poised  on
the side hill  almost in danger of rolling into the road.
It could not be said  of Mr.  Calvin  Packard that he exemplified
the  "Vaulting  ambition which o'erleaps  itself. "     He was  the  pro-
fessional  wood sawyer of  the village,   and wherever the day's  work
found  " Cal.  , "  there  with  stolid  patience  he fulfilled  his  mission.
One day at  the  noon hour he was  across  the  street  from a confla-
gration.              Mrs.  Lydia  Cushing's  residence  burned  to  the  ground.
Cal.       looked  upon  the  scene  of  excitement  and  then  remarked,
" Wall,         I   guess  I'll  finish  my dinner. "

An economical  trait  was  exhibited  by the   Mr.  Chandler  who
built  the  six-tenement  house  near  Independence  Square,       in  the
fact that he used to buy a skein (stick)  of candy just before dinner
time and eat it  so  as to spoil his  appetite.
In  the 60's  and 70's  Dea.    Jacob  Loud  of  South Weymouth had
come to  be a venerable and interesting figure riding about town on
the high seat of an open express wagon.          The Deacon was a quaint
character,      voicing  his opinions  in  local  church  and secular  affairs ,
with enough law at  his  command to  enable him to write wills  and
attend to many contractual  difficulties   in the community.         Some
of his  sayings  are remembered,    one being,   " When I  look's  tho'        I
know the least  I  know the  most;  "    and another as  a parting  shot
after  a domestic  tiff,     " Ef I  wuz to  live  my life  over  again  your
name wouldn't be ' Liza  Laoud !  "
Herring  Brook  Happenings.  -Much  water  has  run  down  the
Herring  Brook since colonial  days,    and many fish  withal.             Under
the autocratic rule of " Uncle"  Lovell Bicknell,    its  ablest  adminis-
trator,         100,000  alewives  were  often  taken  in  a day.         Lovell  Bick-
nell was a stout,   pudgy man with a shaven and florid  face,    and usu-
ally  wore two  pairs  of  spectacles,   the pair  not in use  pushed  far
back on his  forehead,    and carried a big bandanna handkerchief  in
his hat,    frequently mopping his face.          While somewhat of a despot
he did get  things done.
With him were associated James (Jim.)   Lovell and Samuel Orcutt,
all   being  Jacksonian  Democrats     genuine  "hunkers. "      " Uncle
Sam.  "  was little  and talkative,   his pet phrase being,   " Obey orders
if  you break owners.  "    He smoked Cuba (Short)  Sixes that retailed
two for a cent;     he would cut them in half,  and hold them to a finish
with a pin or straw.
In the 60's  and early 70's herring were in great demand;        citizens
or  taxpayers  of the town paid $1  for  400,    or  any part  thereof pro
rata;    outsiders paid 50 cents a hundred.         After  supper,    when her-
ring  were  " running,"  the  bridge  rail   would  be  decorated  with
spectators  gathered to  see the fun and make it.
The bins  or " weirs,"  as they were called,  were much larger than
the  accommodations  to-day,    and  men and  boys  crowded  around
with buckets and barrels  waiting for the word.        Above them stood
Mr.  Bicknell in his element,   and when he gave the signal  they were
like street gamins struggling for pennies.        Sometimes he would order
a count  as  the  fish  were picked  up,  just  according  to  his  mood.
There was a tradition that every family was entitled  to six herring.
This Mr. B.  stoutly denied,   though he would give them grudgingly.
As is  the case to-day,    citizens often complained that outside buyers
were unduly favored.
Now and then a boy would shy a herring into the crowd of loafers
on the bridge,   whence it  was  returned  whizzing  through  the  air,

likely  as  not hitting one of the triumvirate,    eliciting  a flow  of  lan-

" O.  L.  Dunn"  tells  of an incident back in the 70's when he was
salting  herring  for his  neighbors  and had to  scheme for  a  supply.
Smelts  arrived  before  the herring,    and dams of  stones  were built
across  the  brook by the smelters.      These obstructions  excited  the
wrath of Major-domo Bicknell,   and the mandate went forth,     " Every
man count his  herring.  "
O.  L.   Dunn and  another  boy went partners  on  the  catch  and
gathered  two barrels'     full.          Mr.  Bicknell came along as  they were
counting them on the grass,   and he asked whose they were and how
many.        He was told there were 800.    " Call it  1,000,"  he said;      " no,
make it   900,      but you are one of the fellows that fill  the river with
stones,     and you will have to pay 50 cents a hundred."   Now,    while
a citizen  could  be  charged double price for exceeding 400,   practi-
cally it  was a dead letter.          It was easy enough  to  ask  a friend  to
claim ownership,   and so by hook and crook or shrewd management
the  desired  quantity  and  price  were  achieved,     although  " Uncle
Lovell"  was a hard man to  deceive.           He was  a good deal  like  a
chestnut  burr,    - rough  outside but pretty good-hearted  after  all,
and  charitable  toward those in  need.
Mr.  Benjamin  Bates  of  East  Weymouth (1787-1862)  purported
to  be suffering  with rheumatism.           One day a friend meeting  Ben.
on the street  stopped  for  a  chat.            " Well,     Ben.,    how is  the rheu-
matiz  to-day? "     " Gets wuss  every day, "  was the reply;       " yister-
day I  could get my arm so high, "  raising  his  hand to  the shoulder
and dropping  it;     " terday, "  raising  it  to his  waist,   " I  can't  get  it
only so fur. "
Marshall  C.   Dizer  as   a  business  man and  pioneer  shoe  manu-
facturer  had  few  equals  and  no  superiors.         He was  long-headed
and shrewd,     and there was little  that  happened in his  factory that
escaped  his  attention.             Charles  R.  was  a  fellow  member of  the
Baptist  Church  and  a  treer  in  the  Dizer  factory.          He was  quite
familiarly  acquainted with  Mr.  Dizer,    and when the latter  would
come into  the  treeing  room  on  a  round  of  inspection,       " Charles "
would select  his  best  looking  piece of work and hand the boot  to
" M. C."  for  his  examination.          One day,   after  pretty close inspec-
tion of  a boot,      Mr.  Dizer  said,    " Well,      Charles,     do you think you
have another on your rack that looks as well  as  this  one?"    That
was  " Charles' "   finish   as   an  exhibitor,      because  his  fellow  treers
made his  life  a burden thereafter.
Acontemporary of  Mr.  Dizer was the maker of a shoe known as
a top- notcher all over the country which for years has led the trade
unexcelled.             No employee in  his  factory  knew better  how a first-
class  shoe  should  look  after  going  through  all  the  departments,
though  in  the  details  of  those  departments  it  is  fair  to  presume
that  the specialist  ought to have some skill.

One day this  manufacturer  criticized  one of his  oldest  hands,       a
man who had spent most of his life  treeing boots and shoes.           After
some faultfinding  the " boss "  said,     " Now I  will  show you how to
tree  a  shoe,  "   and  he did  so  and  passed  it  up with  the  remark,
" There,    that's the way I want a shoe treed. "   The workman waited
until the boss had passed along,   and placed the shoe in a conspicuous
place,     resuming his work.      After dinner  the boss walked  into  the
room  -and also into the trap.         Picking up the same shoe,  " Do you
call  that shoe treed? "     " No, "  was the reply,   " I don't,      but that  is
the shoe you treed  this  forenoon. "
It is  related of Col. Ben.    S.  Lovell  that when the Civil War began
he wanted very much to  enlist,   but being only seventeen years old
he was too young,    and more than that,    his father objected  to  his
going to war.           Ben.     at that time was driving a delivery wagon for
the local  grocer,   and one day drove his  team to  the depot,    hitched
the horse to  a convenient post,   boarded the railroad  train for Bos-
ton,      and there in some manner procured enlistment.        Then he re-
turned  home,   told his father and won reluctant consent to the ad-
venture.          Ben.     Lovell's  war experiences  constitute  another  story.
Suffice  it  here to state  that when he left  home his father  promised
Ben.       a  hundred dollars  if  he would  abstain  from  smoking  while
away.           In due course he safely returned,   and hailed his father with,
"Hello,     Father,   where's that $100?    I haven't smoked."
In  the 40's  the cost  of living  occupied  a very  moderate  scale,
quite in contrast with the " hard times"  after  the Civil  War,    when
flour  was  $20  a barrel,     and with  the  " H.  C.  L."  after  the  Great
War,     when coal  was $15  a ton and hard  to get at  that.           About
1840  a  New England  undertaker  presented  as  his  whole  bill  for
laying  out,     the coffin,  shroud and cravat,    the hearse,    one carriage
and interment,   $32.50;    and in South Weymouth Dea.     Josiah  Reed
at that same period went forth  with  $75 to buy his  housekeeping
outfit ;       bought all  he thought he needed and had a few dollars  left
in his pocket.
The Deacon was a friend  of  the  negro,    and it  was not generally
known  that  he  endowed  an  educational  institution  in  the  South ;
but  in  a time  of  religious  (not  exactly  intolerance,     but  perhaps)
severity he stopped an expressman from running his teams through
the village on Sunday.
Pursuing  his  vocation  the  Deacon stood with  Francis  S.  Torrey
at  adjacent  cutting- boards in the shoe factory,    when suddenly  the
Deacon  said,      " Francis,    let's we go into  the  business  of shoe mak-
ing. "    But Francis lacked confidence in  the wisdom of the under-
taking and declined the partnership.     Josiah  Reed,   however,     made
the venture,      which developed into  a considerable business,    making
him some money and  a  man of  importance  in  the  community.
When the subject of a town water system was first  suggested in  the
early 80's,     in meetings of the South Weymouth Improvement Asso

ciation  and  the  Wednesday  Night  Club,     Deacon  Reed  warmly

After  the  battle  of  Bull  Run the  12th  Mass.     Regiment,      a  part
of  which  was  Company  H of  this  town,     was  marching  through
Warrenton,       Va. ,      and  there  were  many children  by  the  roadside
watching  the  soldiers  as  they  passed.         At one place  there  was  a
little  girl  who,    to  show her  loyalty  to  the South,     waved a small
Confederate flag.
When the  colonel  of the regiment saw it  he ordered  a halt  and
demanded the flag.      The little girl  and her sister ran into a near-by
yard and refused  to give it up,  but finally  the officer  took it  away,
not before  the  little  girl  said,    defiantly,    " You can  take  the  flag
away from a little  girl,    but you can't take it from our soldiers,     and
if  I  had been in my own house,"  pointing  across  the  street,     " you
wouldn't get it  now. "
That night McClellan's army camped just outside the town,    and
the same evening a captain and his orderly rode to the house and
asked   if    the   little   girl   who  surrendered   the  flag   lived   there.
Terribly  frightened the child  and her mother came forward,     when
the  officer  said,      " Ladies,      I  witnessed  the  scene  from  across  the
street  this  morning,     and  was  so  mortified  that  I  have  come  to
bring a peace offering  and to ask if the little girl will make me a
flag.  "     He then  called  his  orderly,     and  giving  them packages  of
fruit  and candy,    said,   " I  will  call  for  the  flag  in  the  morning,"
which he did,   leaving a photograph,    upon the reverse of which was
written,        " To the pretty little girl who so kindly presented me with
a flag.           With good wishes,   Truly,    James L.  Bates.  "
The flag  made by the little  girl,   a beautiful  symbol of southern
loyalty,     is  now in the collection  in the Fogg Library,    and the inci-
dent lingers,      illustrative of the bond of humanity which eventually
was  to  unite  the  former  belligerents  of  the  North  and  South  in
lasting  peace.            The little girl  is dead,  but an older sister  survived,
and  since  the  war  correspondence  has  been  interchanged,      and  a
visit made by the daughter of General Bates.
Amemorable event in the annals of the town was the establish-
ment of the  Union  Church in  1810.    The edifice  was obtained  of
the  Hollis  Street  Society in  Boston,    and floated  upon a raft  down
the harbor and up the river,    to be set not far from the Smelt Brook
over the line in East Braintree.       It was a blessing to have a church
so  near a congregation that previously had to go to  the Old North,
to  the  First  Church in Braintree,    or two miles to the South Parish .
One evening the loungers  in  Joseph  Orcutt's  shoemaking  shop,
South  Weymouth,     conspired  to  smoke the  old  gentleman  out  by
an  extravagant  burning  of  the  " weed. "     When  the  atmosphere
had gotten  rather  murky and almost unbearable by all  concerned,
old  Joe  casually  remarked,    at the same time pulling  forth  a black

T.  D. ,        " Wall,    as long as you fellows  seem to be smoking  I  don't

The beautiful  stream known by its  Indian name of Monatiquot
all  through  the  early  settlement  and  Revolutionary  times  was  so
designated  as  far  as  Braintree  Great  Hill  (now  Hough's  Neck,
Quincy) ,      but  later,    when  government  surveys  and  charts  were
made,       the  lower  reaches  were  named  " Weymouth  Fore  River"
and " Quincy Bay. "
Here the  Indian in his frail  and swift canoe caught  smelts  and
herring  in  river  and  bay,     and  the  white  settler  soon  learned  to
provide himself with fish  and clams,   the tide being always  an  im-
portant  factor  in  salt-water plans.
Weymouth  of  the  olden  time  was  somewhat  engaged  in  ship-
building all  along the shore.          The Tilden shipyard on the meadow
was  successful  in launching  sloops  and  schooners ;        packets  plied
between  Boston and Weymouth wharves,     and often  sailed  as  far
as  Maine for lumber.        All the waterside activities brought business
to the town.
One notable  event  was  a  grand  patriotic  meeting  held  at  the
Union  Church in  1840,    when  President  John Quincy Adams was
the orator of the occasion.          The Whigs had elected William Henry
Harrison  over  the  Democratic  candidate.          In  a month  the  Presi-
dent had died,    and the Vice- President      a Democrat   - succeeded
to the office.           In those days the two candidates securing the greatest
number of votes were chosen,    irrespective of party.
President   Adams  spoke  of  this   sudden  change  of  front,        and
advocated  the  desirability  of  having  both  President  and  Vice-
president  of  the same political  family,   and supporters  of  the same
platform.          Before  a large  audience  our fourth  President  pictured
the great disappointment of the people.       In a high-pitched,   squeaky
voice  he  said,    " The people  thought  they  had  Rachel,     but  when
they  awoke     behold,    it  was  LE-AH!   "     This  telling  application
of Scripture elicited  great applause.
The  patriotic  anthems  and  resounding  cheers  of  that  meeting
are  vividly  recalled.         A stage  had been  erected  in  front  of  the
pulpit,    whereon sat all the dignitaries,   while the house was crowded
by an enthusiastic  audience  gathered  to  listen  to  the  " old  man
eloquent."    "Ode to  Science"  was sung with spirit,  -" Haughty
tyrants  we disdain,    and shout ' Long live America! '"
Before   another   presidential   election    the   system   had   been
changed,      and both  high  offices  were  filled  by incumbents  of  the
same  political  faith.            The  Union  Church  of  the  1920's  can  tell
another story to  succeeding generations.
The captain of the packet at Weymouth invited  a friend  to  sail
to  Boston,      together with his  three  sons,    and arriving  at  the  Hub
the  father  took  the  party  to  the  hotel  for  dinner.            Of  course,        a
 - 328 - 
806                                 WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE
treat  was  in  prospect,     and  one of  the  boys  said,     " Let's  have  a
rarity!"
After  a  prolonged  inspection   of   the  bill  of  fare  they  finally
settled  upon -  beefsteak.                  At home it  was the  custom  to  have a
" beef  critter"  hanging  in  the  shed,    and  sometimes  a  lamb  or  a
hunk  of  home- raised   pork,      so   that  the  idea  of  beefsteak  being
a  " rarity "  was productive  of mirth  in  the  home  circle,    and the
remark  " Let's  have a rarity"  persists  to this day.
The  Negro  Minstrel  Show.      -This  sort  of  entertainment  seems
to  bear  a  relation  to  the  period  of  the  Civil  War and the darkey
element  connected  therewith.        Shows of  this  character  were given
by white  people  in  black  face  (burnt  cork)   in  the  60's,      a  well-
remembered one being that in the cutting  room of the William A.
Shaw  shoe  factory  in South  Weymouth just after  the  war,     when
G.  M.  and  Theron  Hawes,     Jason  Orcutt  and J.  Emmons  Derby
sang  " Babylon  is  fallen,    Babylon  is  fallen,    and  we's  agwine  to
occupy   the   land. "      With   their   leveled   guns   (wooden)      and
threatening,         " Look  out  dar,   we's  agwine  to  shoot!  "   they  were
sufficiently  terrifying  to  the youthful auditor.
In  1869,     when the  first  Peace Jubilee was held in the mammoth
building  on the made land  in  Boston's Back Bay,   one of the side
shows  in  a tent was the  Morris  Brothers  Minstrels,    with the then
famous   " Little   Mack"   appurtenant   thereto.        Later   on   Dock-
stader   and  Primrose  & West  delighted   thousands,     and  in   the
country  town  the  amateur  minstrel  show  was  always  the  best
money getter in any local function.      The first money of consequence
earned by the  Norfolk Club,  which paid the rent for  a room,     was
by a minstrel  show.
Tradition  hath it  that the  last  survivor of  the  Indians  in  these
parts  had his  wigwam located  not far  from  the back door of  the
Thomas  Nash house  at  Nash's  Corner,      near  a  well-known  spring
of  water  and an almost  equally  famous  pear  tree.          This  wigwam
was often visited by the neighborhood  in  a friendly way,    and one
day  some  children  calling  upon this  good  Indian  were  invited  to
partake  of  eels  that  he was frying.      They ate  so  hungrily of  this
repast  that  none were  left  for  the  host,    who thereupon  grunted,
'Papoose  like   um  eels,      Ugh!        Eat  um  all.            No  eels ,    -black
snakes!  "       Which  unsavory  situation   rather   surprised   the   said
papooses  and  disgusted  and  angered  their  parents;      but  the  tale
is  told  in various ways,     and may have had some foundation of fact.
It  is  reasonable conjecture whether this  was one of the four Indians
said  to  have  lived  near  by,  their  names  being  Bylam  Bicknell,
Balaam Bates,    Butterworth Bolton and Bolum Birch.

There would seem to have been  a golden age of transportation
in  Weymouth,      preceded  by  the  time  of  no  railroads,       steam  or
electric,     and followed  by the  reaction  after  the  Great  War,     when
there was a peculiar period of lessened accommodation.
But in  the  very  olden  days the family  carriage  obtained,      then
the  " horse  ' n-buggy "   and  beach-wagon  stage,     succeeded  by  the
bicycle   and  electricity-driven   vehicles.        It   was  no  uncommon
thing  for  residents  to  drive  the  family  " horse  ' n  carriage "    into
Boston upon the presentation of the " Creation "  or the  " Messiah "
by the  Handel  and  Hayden  Society,     and  enthusiasts  have  been
known to walk the fifteen miles,   with such enjoyment as the goal.
Edmund  Thomas  has  written  of  a  Weymouth  town  meeting
(as contributed by Quincy L.  Reed) ,    somewhere between 1820 and
1830,       or  perhaps  a little  earlier,    for  Eliphalet  Loud died  in 1832,
and  Harvey  Reed removed  to  Bangor in  1833.    It is  obviously  a
good reproduction of doings a hundred years  ago.

Silence,   boys!     The great gun of North Weymouth,   the honorable
Christopher  Webb,    takes  the  floor.             Mr. Webb is  in his  manhood's
prime,     liberally  educated,  by profession  a lawyer,    and with the  air
and  manner of the polished  gentleman.           His  words  are  measured,
every  sentence  wrought  into  connecting  links,   with  elaborately
rounded  periods,    uttered  with  such earnestness  or  melting  pathos
as   to   command  the  undivided  attention  of  his   audience.             But
notwithstanding his  excellent chain of  reasoning and the seemingly
logical   treatment  of  the  subject  at  issue,     it   is   apparent  that  a
country squire  has discovered flaws in the argument.

the  portly   figure  of  Eliphalet  Loud,       Esq. ,     rises   to   address   the

While  Squire  Loud  speaks  all  eyes  are  riveted  upon  him,      and

pointed  illustrations ;      and when he resumes his  seat the impression
is   left   (with  the youngsters  at  least)   that  his  mental king's- arm,

Capt.       Elijah  Bates  of  South  Weymouth,   a citizen  of  diversified

To  draw  upon  the  fund  of  anecdotes  possessed  by Quincy A.
Torrey always  proved interesting  entertainment.           As a lad he,    like
many another boy,    was charmed by the music of the brass band,    of
which he later in life became a member.         May Training Day was a
festive  occasion  in  the  olden  time,  when the militia  in  gorgeous
uniforms,           accompanied   by  the   band,         marched   to    the   Town
House.
Everybody who could went also,    but,    alas,    Quincy's mother told
him he could  not go,   and it  was with  a heavy heart  that  he  saw
them leave the  square in South Weymouth and march down Sheep
Street.              However,    he got as  near the band as he could,    and thought-
lessly kept on with them,   so carried away with the music that they
had  reached   Lovell's   Corner  before  he  realized  his  wrongdoing,
with  the  Town House but  little  farther  on.                " Well, "  he  philoso-
phized,    " I  knew I  was in for a licking  when I got home,    and I  felt
that it wouldn't hurt any more if  I  went the whole way,    so I  kept on,
and when  I   reached  home took my punishment like  a man    but
it  was worth it."
William A.  Vining,    a native of Weymouth,    but later  residing  in
Hingham,      at  this  writing  (1920)   enjoyed  the distinction  of  being
one of  the  few men living  who were present  at  the  surrender  of
 - 331 - 
WEYMOUTH  FOLKLORE                         809
General  Lee,     April 9,  1865.    Mr. Vining well remembered the scene
at  the  historic  McLean house  on  that  memorable  occasion.                 He
was upon the piazza of the house,    and,    looking  through a window,
saw  General  Lee dressed  in  an immaculate  uniform  of  gray,       en-
tirely   new,       and  wearing  a  handsome  sword,      probably  the  one
presented him by the state  of Virginia.           In sharp contrast  to  him
was General Grant,    in the uniform of a private spattered with mud,
his  only  insignia  being  the straps  of  a lieutenant  general.             These
two sat at a table,    while near by stood Gen. Phil Sheridan and some
other  officers  of lesser  note.
Mr. Vining,     in reminiscences of life  in camp and field  said he did
not know just  how near he came to being captured by the Rebels,
but one dark night when on vedette duty the enemy surprised and
captured four  of  his  comrades only  a few hundred yards  from  his
post,   " and  two of them died in  Rebel prisons. "
"But I  want to tell  you about my drawing rations for  ten of our
men who had been detailed for  special duty.      We had a mess tent
of our own with a colored cook,   and I had to get a requisition from
the  commanding  officer  for  ten  days'      rations  for  ten  men every
time they were required.        Our allowance was carefully apportioned,
and sometimes we did not have any too much to eat;    but one day
some one made a mistake and added another cipher  to  the second
10,    so that it  read '10 days'   rations  for  100 men,'   and the  Commis-
sary  Department loaded up two mule teams for  me,    which  I   took
without saying  a word,   and when  I  drove up to  our  quarters  the
black cook came running to meet me,   his  eyes bulging with amaze-
ment,   and exclaiming,  ' for Gawd's sake,    Massa Billy,   what you gwine
to do with all  those rations?'         'You keep still,'    I  said,    ' we're going
to have enough to eat for once in our lives . '   "
When  President  Lincoln  made his  second  call  for  300,000  men
in  1862 our selectmen sought to  fill  Weymouth's quota in  various
ways,      among them the holding of war mass meetings at the Town
House,     with bands and special  speakers  aided by local  talent.
At one of  the  meetings  Elias  Beals,      a  North Weymouth spell-
binder,      urged  the boys to  enlist  by telling  them what a picnic  it
would be to  go  to  the front.     " The war can't  last  three  months, "
he  said,   " and our Yankee volunteers  will whip them out of their
boots  before  that  time.           Why,     all  you will  have to  do when you
meet the Confederates will be to tell them you're from Weymouth,
and they will run their legs  off  to get away.  "
The quota was supplied,   and 101  good men and true went into
camp for  a few days,    then leaving  Boston August 22 for  Washing-
ton.           Three weeks after  that,    on September 14,    they had their  first
encounter with the  Rebs at  South Mountain.       Following  an after-
noon of  skirmishing in the woods and fields  of  Turner's  Gap they
were suddenly attacked  about sundown,   and from behind a stone
wall they maintained a position,   battling until darkness put an end
to it.

During its  fiercest  stage,     and after  several had been killed,       and
Corporal  Pratt and others had been wounded and carried from the
field,         " Boss "   Richards  as  he  was  familiarly  called,    having  used
nearly  all   his  cartridges,        turned  to  a  comrade,       and,      rolling   his
quid to  the other side of his  mouth,   said,    " B'    Gawd!    Aint it  ' bout
time somebody told  them fellers  we came from Weymouth? "
Somebody must have told  them,  for  the  attack  ended  shortly
afterward,       and the enemy were not seen again until the following
Wednesday  at  Antietam,      where,      instead  of  running  away,      they
were  exceedingly  rude  and  ungentlemanly,     shooting  their  guns,
shouting vile  names,    and in every way belying the promises  made
at the war meetings.
Mr.  Herbert A.  Newton passes  along  this  anecdote  told  to  him
by his  grandmother,    who was a  South  Weymouth Orcutt,       and in
