SOME  REMINISCENCES  OF  WEYMOUTH
IRON  WORKS
By O.  L.   DUNN
Three  separate  lines  of manufactures  have served  to  put Wey-
mouth " on the map, " and through them our town may justly claim
to have contributed its  share of the necessities  and comforts of life:
first,       the  iron  works,     whose  nails  helped  to build  the houses  over
our  heads;        second,    the  shoe factories,   whose products keep men's
feet  from the ground;     third,   the phosphate works,   which help  to
grow the food for  our interiors .
The iron works have come and gone,   just as have the industries
of the neighboring  town of Hingham;    her rope walks,     bucket fac-
tories,      salt  works,   her big  fleet  of mackerel  schooners  (handliners)
all  crowded out by the march of progress .
Fifty  years  ago  the  iron  company was the biggest  industry  in
town,      and a strong,    if  not the  greatest,   factor  in building  up East
Weymouth.               To  the  older  natives  these  are  moving  landmarks
showing  plainly  the changes made by its  coming.         Let us  try  to
picture in our minds the Back River and Herring  Brook before its
coming.             Whitman's  Pond was then less  than one-half its  present
size,       and in  the spring  the spawning herring  ran directly  into  the
pond.             There was,    or  had been,    a  tack factory across  the private
way from the garage on Water Street,     and earlier still  a grist  mill
on what was called Herring Island.          Ever hear of it?    It is  the tri-
angular piece of land between the bridge on Pleasant Street at the
beginning of Iron Hill Street and the one opposite the junction with
Water Street,       the  two  streams  uniting  near  the garage  on Water
Street.              The  old  gambrel- roofed  house  and  the  old  Urban  Rice
house opposite  are  on Herring  Island.
Early in the forties  came the  " Company,"  as we will  henceforth
call it.          At that time,    except for the houses on Pleasant Street  (few
in  number)    and  a  part  of  Broad  Street  to  the  west  of  Jackson
Square,     all  west was pasture and meadow.            The outlet of the pond
found its  way down between the hills,     now partly dug away,     and
through the meadow to the salt marsh.             There was no railroad then,
and  the  fresh  and  salt  meadows  extended  from  the  rear  of  the
Peake's  building  to  Hockley Gut.           The Company had before  it  a
big  job,     for  those days,     at least.          First,    they had to  buy a strip  of
land from the pond to  Back River and land or flowage rights  about
the  pond.                The first  flowing did  not enter  Humphrey's Cove that
was bought and flowed some years  later.          Then the building of the
several  dams  and the  canal,   taking from the hillsides  the  material
 - 355 - 
SOME  REMINISCENCES  OF  WEYMOUTH  IRON  WORKS   833
for  that  purpose;      also  a  wharf,    as  the  transportation must be by
water.                Previous  to  this  time  there  was  a  little  wharf or  landing
farther  up the  stream,     east  of the  Keith  factory,    used mostly by
stone  sloops .             It  can be easily  located  to-day.           They also  built  a
canal  to  connect with Elias  Pond,     near  the cemetery with a flume
in the east corner.            One can trace the lines  of the canal now;        Ray-
mond Street  crosses  its  old bed.
The  reservoir  on  Commercial Street,     still  called  by that  name,
was separate from the canal,    the bank between the two having since
been washed away and connected by a flume in the north corner.
Probably  the  next  step  was  the  erection  of  the  many buildings
which we will describe as we remember them as early as 1855.   The
big car barn of to-day replaced their  first  building wholly of wood,
which was burned June 16,  1869,    always called " The Rolling  Mill "
or  just  plain  " Mill. "
Farther  down opposite the garage was the  Center  factory,       for-
merly  the  tack factory of  Dean Randall.           The Art  Leather  Com-
pany occupied it at the time it  was burned.        Opposite was the Old
Forge,      for  many years  used as  a  storehouse  and later  as  a  garage,
also  burned with  the  Center and the Town House.
In the mind of the writer is  a faint impression of an earlier period
when  this  forge  was  turning  out  anchors,      big  chains  or  similar
products.
At the wharf was the Lower factory,    now used as a wool-scouring
plant,     though it  constitutes but a small part of the present group of
buildings .          Between it  and the wharf was the slate  storehouse now
almost  hidden by surrounding buildings.           Between the canal and
Leavitt's   coal  yard,     facing  the  railroad,     was  the  Cooper  Shop,
where the nail  kegs were put together,    the hoops and staves  being
made  elsewhere.          The  Carpenter  Shop  was  about  the  center  of
Herring  Island.          On the  left  as  one entered the mill yard was  the
stone  office  (still  there) .          South of the office  and above it  was the
big barn and several tenements.        The Company owned some dozen
or  fifteen  tenements from the pond to the wharf.
On the right,       just  above the  mill,   was the boarding  house.       A
few  years  ago this  building was divided  in  the center  and moved
to  Riley  Avenue,     and rebuilt  into  tenements.       Each  nail  factory
had  its   own blacksmith  shop  and  was  limited  to  the  cutting  of
certain sizes,     mostly from hot plate.        The mill was the main thing.
In the west end were the nail  machines,   cutting the big  spikes,      20
and 40 penny and large board nails.        At the other end in the south-
east  corner,     close  to  Iron  Hill Street,    was the big  forty- foot  diam-
eter  overshot  water  wheel,    which  ran  the  rolls.           Later,     the  big
wheel  was  removed  and  turbines  substituted.       It  took  so  much
more water to run them that it  caused an annual shutdown for want
of water,     whereas before this  happened only in a dry season.            Once
under way the momentum of a big overshot was sufficient  to  carry
it  with  a comparatively  small  quantity  of  water.              Next  to  the
wheel were rolls  of various  sizes .
 - 356 - 
834     SOME  REMINISCENCES  OF  WEYMOUTH  IRON  WORKS
About the middle of the big building was a large upright engine of
one  hundred  and  fifty  or  more  horsepower.          This  engine  was  a
thing  of  beauty as  well as  of power,    handsomely painted,     its  brass
work polished to the limit,    enclosed in a big room as fine as was the
engine.              The contrast between the inside and outside of the engine
room was extreme,   to put it mildly.    In the early years a little Eng-
lishman by the  name of  Cort was  engineer.     He had  three  boys,
Sam,      Tom and Eddie.         They were English all  right,    regular  Cock-
neys,      and the way they left  out and added " h's "  was amusing  to
the  rest  of us boys.            Sam,    the oldest,    was a quiet,    serious fellow of
twelve,      and seemed to  us boys to  be able to run the  engine  about
as well as his father.      Eddie,   the youngest      "Eddie Two Thumbs, "
we called him     was the proud and envied possessor of two thumbs
on one hand,  side by side,    and not much larger  together than the
other.                  Later,       Charley  Bowen,     eldest  son  of  B.   W.  Bowen,      the
superintendent,    had charge of the engine until the finish .
Along the  front of the mill,  facing  the  yard,   were  the  furnaces,
and  between  them  and  the  nail  machines  was  the  trip  hammer,
squeezers  and shears.        On the other side of the yard were big piles
of  iron  ore,     pig  iron,    coal,     mostly  soft,     and  flint  or quartz.          And
"that  reminds  me"  of  a way the  boys  of sixty  years  ago  had of
earning  a dollar,   unknown to  the boys of to-day and to  most men
also.                  We used  to go to the different gravel  banks and gather  flint,
varying in size from that of a baseball to a football,   cart it  home in
a wheelbarrow,    for  which the  Company would pay a dollar  a ton
delivered  to their yard.         Unless  one had a relative  or friend owning
a horse  and  cart  one-half  would  go to  the  carter.             Those dollars
were certainly earned.      If a boy wheeled home fifty pounds at each
trip it would have taken forty trips to have accumulated a ton,   which,
if   carted  free,   would give him  21½ cents  a  trip.          How the  present
generation  of  boys  would  fall  over  each  other  hunting for  flint!
Whether the supply did not equal the demand or not is  uncertain,
but  a few  years  later  they  stopped  buying our  flint,      and bought
quartz by the carload.          It is  always so       if  one has a  " snap "  it  is
short- lived.               Probably  the  flint  or  quartz  aided  in  freeing  the  iron
of its  impurities.
Our  earliest   recollections   of  the  officials   were  Increase  (" Old
Man")    Robinson,    president;        Warren  W.  Barker,      treasurer ;      John
Washburn,       superintendent ;         Robert McIntosh,   clerk.           Some years
later  John  Washburn was succeeded by Benjamin W.  Bowen,     and
still  later David Tucker followed Warren Barker.          Robert McIntosh
was with them to  the  end,    and at the time of his  death  two years
ago was the last  of the old office  force.
It  was  interesting  to  see  the  various  processes  involved  in  the
manufacture  of  the  nails ;        the  furnaces,      whose  fires   were  seldom
raised  to  a  white  heat,      and  charged  with  iron  ore,    pig  iron,      and
" scrap."    Ask  " Mick"   Fogarty  and  " Nachie "   Lonergan  about
the  scrap iron.            They were " pilers ”  in  their young days,    piling  the
pieces  of scrap on boards  ready for  the furnaces.          Then the "pud
 - 357 - 
SOME  REMINISCENCES  OF  WEYMOUTH  IRON  WORKS   835
dlers "  and their  helpers,   -big brawny men stripped  to  the waist,
stood in  front of the roaring  furnaces,    and,     through holes  in  the
thick  iron  door,     with  long  bars,   " puddled"  or  mixed  the  melted
iron  until  it  formed  a  " heat, "  - a white- hot mass  free  from  its
dross.             Then the furnace door was opened and a man with a big
pair of tongs running on a pulley overhead thrust it into the furnace
and pulled out the heat and rushed it,   dripping a rain of sparks,      to
the squeezers,      and from that to the big trip hammer;   then to the
different  rolls,    where  it  was  flattened  into  lengths  of eight  or ten
feet,     some  fifteen  or  eighteen  inches  wide,    of  various  thicknesses,
according to the size of the nails  into which it was to be cut.
Then it  went to the shears,    where it was cut crosswise into strips
as wide as the nails were to be long.      At times a small low- wrought
iron  cart eight or ten inches deep was backed up to the furnace to
be filled with the dross,    or "slag,"  which poured from an opening
at the bottom of the furnace.           This  " slag,"  when cold,    would be
broken and dumped as filling  in vacant lots.       There must be thou-
sands of  tons beneath  the  surface of the lot  near Jackson Square,
near  the  billboards,     Water Street,     and  Commercial,     from  the  her-
ring  house  to  Wharf  Street,      known  as   " The  Black  Road,  "  kept
in repair by the  Company with slag  and ashes.       Excepting the nail
departments,    the mill started work at 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning.
Often  the  whole  village  was  lighted  with  the  columns  of  flame
streaming from the high smokestacks.          Their day ended soon after
noon.
The puddlers were the best paid hands employed,    except,   perhaps,
some  of  the  boss  nailers,     some of  whom controlled  a number  of
machines,        hiring  " second  hands "  to  " turn  plate "  for  the  extra
machines,     the  " boss " grinding the knives  and otherwise caring for
them.           Both boss and second hands were paid so much per hundred.
To turn plate  the  operator sat on a high stool in front of the ma-
chine,      handling  a rod about five feet  long,    its  near end supported
by a hook in which it  turned,    and the plate held in nippers on the
front end.         After learning to  time each motion with the movements
of the machine he pushed the plate squarely against  the bed knife
and turned it in time for the next movement so that the head of the
second nail was cut from the other side of the plate,   cutting perhaps
a hundred a minute.         Some boys  turned  plate  through  the vaca-
tion.              Not many,    however.          Sitting  all  day in  summer on a high
stool  did  not appeal to  many boys  then,    and would to  even fewer
now.         And who can blame them?    Boys and girls  need play as well
as  food.                A combination  of work and  play is  ideal  and practical,
too.            A boy of to-day can get fun and profit  from pig and poultry
clubs,     and farm and garden.
To  some  " grown-ups "   (a fortunate  few) ,      work  is   a  pleasure.
This  applies  to  authors,     artists,    inventors,     also  to  evangelists  and
missionaries.                 Happy  are  they,    and  " may their  tribe  increase. "
But this  is  supposed to be ancient history and not a modern essay.
So we will  " take up the thread  of our discourse, "  as  the old-fash
 - 358 - 
836     SOME  REMINISCENCES  OF  WEYMOUTH IRON  WORKS
ioned ministers  used to  say.         Good old men     they were " the salt
of  the earth. "   And those discourses  held  a message seldom given
out from the modern pulpit, -the Gospel the Good News of Sal-
vation  by Faith,    the great  need of this  poor distracted  old  world
to-day.          But the boss nailers,   most of them,   came with the Company
or  a few years  later.        Some of  them were John S.  Porter,      Thomas
and Simeon (" Sim " )   Bearce,    Ben River,    Thomas Harding,    William
Cummings,        Thomas  Nichols  and Joseph  Steven.         They  ran  the
" feeders " at the Center.        All a boy had to do was to replace a plate,
the machine did the rest.           Others were Pelham (" Pel")    Morin and
Dyke,    who had the big spike machines.        It was a man's job  to turn
that  plate,      and Thomas Orr's,      who is  still  living  on Middle Street
next to  the High School at ninety- three years of age.           Turning plate
is  doubtless one of the lost arts.         Probably the nail-cutting machines
now in use are self- feeding.
In the manufacture from the raw materials of so bulky a product
as  nails,      the  question  of  transportation  was of  much  importance.
There  being  no  railroad  the  Company made use  of  horses,      oxen,
sailing  vessels  and scows .         Besides  the wharf here they had one at
the mouth of Back River,   one- quarter of a mile above the phosphate
works on the same side of the river.        Little or nothing remains of it
to-day.             Here came  vessels  loaded with pig iron ore  and coal,    the
soft  coal  from  Pictou,      N.  S.     Their  cargoes  were  transferred   to
scows,     which were "poled "  up the river.
Two or four men started from the front or bow of the scow,    set
their  long  spikes  into  the bottom  with  the  other  end against  the
shoulder,        walked to  the  stern,   trailed  back to bow,    and repeated.
Another  steered with  a wide sweep.       Always planning  to  go with
the tide,     they made fair progress for  those days.          The scows  were
about forty feet by ten feet,     and about four feet  deep.            The Com-
pany built  them across from the wharf,   where is  now the gravel pit.
Dea.       Jairus  Sprague  and  Daniel  Bates were among the carpenters.
Mr.  Bates  was  killed  when the  present  building  was being  built.
Levi  Barker  of   Lovell's   Corner  later  was  head  carpenter.               The
sloop  " Gen.  Lovell "  was  named  for  Solomon  Lovell  of  Revolu-
tionary fame.           He owned King Oak Hill and built the fine old colo-
nial house at its  foot for his  daughter.
The " Gen.  Lovell "  was a  bluff- bowed craft of sixty  tons,     prob-
ably once a  stone- carrying  sloop,   slow and sure.            She  carried  nails
to  Boston and  brought back scrap  iron.           Her crew comprised the
skipper  and  three  men.          John  Pratt  was  skipper  at  the  time  of
which we write,     succeeded at his death in  1857 by Nathan Good-
speed.           A few years  later  the  " Gen.  Lovell"  was condemned  as
worn out  and replaced  by  " The  Hardscrabble, "   and  she  proved
true  to  her  name,     as  she  was sunk three times while in the  Com-
pany's service,    once at the mouth of Back River,     a great place for
flows  and  squalls,     and  twice  off  Fort  Independence,      now a  city
playground.               After  being  raised  and before  leaving  she  was  run
down and sent  again to the  bottom.            Later,    " The Hardscrabble "

was  owned  for   many  years   by  Joshua  Phillips   of  Weymouth
Landing.
The scows  were  unloaded  with  the  aid  of  a "donkey"  engine,
and their cargoes temporarily left on the wharf,    and later  removed
by teams  of  oxen  and  horses.          The  Company owned  some  fine
horses,      their  five  pair of grays,     with  B.  O.  Raymond of  Cottage
Street  for  driver,    were often seen on the pole of the  " Gen.  Bates "
engine.            Their oxen,   too,   of which they had several pairs  or  yokes,
were prize winners at the agricultural fair.          The oxen were shod at
the  Center blacksmith shop,   and were held up or slung up by broad
leather bands passing under their bodies.         Evidently unlike  horses
or dogs,    they couldn't stand on three legs.         These teams also carted
the nails  to  the wharf,    unloading  into  the  storehouse  or  direct  to
the sloop.             There was a track carrying a flat handcar from the lower
factory through the storehouse to  the edge of the wharf.
With  the  Company  came  many  workmen  and  their  families,
adding  hundreds  to  our  population,     heretofore  about  all  natives,
and  the  Company's tenements were not able to house them.         But
our housing problem was promptly solved by our original promoter,
a whole syndicate by himself,     Cyrus Washburn,     a far- sighted  car-
penter  and builder.         He saw his  opportunity and rose to  the occa-
sion.             Buying a  tract  of many acres,     mostly  pasture,       he  laid  out
what are  now Shawmut,      Washburn and Lake Streets  to  the  ball
field,        and  side  streets  from  them.          By 1855  he had built  many
houses on these  streets,    selling  some,   but probably owning at one
time from fifty  to one hundred dwellings  in  East Weymouth alone.
Most  of  these  were  of  second-hand  material  from  buildings  he
bought and tore down in  Boston.         Not all  his  houses  were of  the
" patchwork "  variety;    the two- story dwellings on the right side of
Shawmut Street,    and others in the village of that type,   were built
by him  in  earlier  years.         He made a fortune  in a few years  and
became the heaviest  taxpayer in town.        He also  held stock in  the
Company,     but got out before its  finish.

From 1850 to  1880 the  Company prospered,    then  the  competi-
tion of  the  Pennsylvania mills  began to  tell,     as  they had coal  at
their  doors  and pig  iron,   and was hundreds  of miles  nearer.
ten years it  fought a losing battle,   but there could be only one end-
ing,     and  together  with  the  Bridgewater,       Somerset,       Fall   River,
Wareham and similar mills,   they were forced  to close.
Most of  the Company's employees found work at other  trades,
many in the shoe factories,    and Weymouth is  still  a manufacturing
town.
Most of the newcomers became permanent citizens,   and many of
their descendants are prominent in business circles  and have served
the  town  in  various  offices.        Among  the  names  not  previously
mentioned  are  Connell,     Cullen,     Connors,      Carroll,     Daly,     Donahue,

Weymouth with  its  water  front  so  near  to  Boston offers  many
inducements  to  big  enterprises,     and  its  citizens  need  have  little
fear  for  its  future.     Perhaps  our new form of town government
may contribute  to its  growth.           Most of its  prosperity  in  the past
it  owes to  the rank and file  of its citizens.      We have had no family
or individual  to do for Weymouth what the  Drapers have done for
Hopedale,      the  Whitings for  Whitinsville  or  the Ames's for  North
Easton.
Perhaps it  is  just as well.        Self- reliance  is  as good for communi-
ties  as  for  individuals.            Benefactors  sometimes  become dictators.
Weymouth has had native and adopted sons of whom she has been
proud,  -men of influence,     a help  and a credit  to  the community,
but no political  or industrial  " boss"  dims  the record  of her  three
hundred years.
To know Weymouth's past is  to have faith in her future.

IS   WEYMOUTH  THE  ALMA  MATER  OF
BOSTON
From a paper read before the Weymouth Historical Society,    Oct.  27,    1897.
In a paper read before the Weymouth Historical Society Wednes-
day,     October 27,    the question was asked,   " Is Weymouth the Alma
Mater  of  Boston?"  and the  following  facts  were put  forward  as
substantiating such claim:
1.   William  Blackstone,    the  first   settler   of  Boston,       was  from
Weymouth.              This  is   practically  established  by  Charles  Francis
Adams,     president  of  the  Massachusetts  Historical  Society,      in  an
article  printed  in  the proceedings of that society,  Vol.      XXI.  ,     page
198,     A.D.  1878.
2.   The first  salaried  male singer  in  a Boston church  is  said  to
have  been  Maj.     Elias  Hunt,   a counter  tenor  vocalist  from Wey-
mouth.
3.  The founder of the Boston Public Library was Joshua Bates,
a native of Weymouth.
4.   William  Smith  Shaw,    who was a son of Rev. John Shaw of
Haverhill,    and his wife,   Elizabeth Smith,   a daughter of Rev. William
Smith,      pastor  of the  Old North  Church in  Weymouth,    was  pre-
eminently the chief  among the founders of  the Boston Athenaeum.
His  mother  Elizabeth  was a sister  of Abigail  Smith,    who married
the young Quincy lawyer,    John Adams,   afterward President of the
United States,    and she was not less  distinguished  than  her  sister
Abigail for  intellectual  power and literary  attainments.
It  is  not,     therefore,     presumption  made out  of whole cloth  to
claim  that  Weymouth is  the  Alma Mater of  Boston in  three  re-
spects,     which are certainly not in ignoble lines,    the mother country
of her first  settler,    her exemplar in music,   her benefactor and help
in  literature.             (See  History  of  Boston Athenaeum,   Metcalf & Co.,
1851.)
Our claims to the gratitude of Boston do not end here.        We might
refer  to  the Weymouth parentage of  Robert Treat Paine,     a signer
of  the  Declaration  of  Independence,    who was the  ancestor  of  the
public-spirited citizen of the same name,   who to-day gives  his  time
and strength  to  helping where help  is  most needed in  the city  of
his heart.
We might  speak of the able ministers  of the gospel  Weymouth
has  furnished  to  Boston,    beginning  with  Rev.  Thomas  Thacher,
whom we sent  to  occupy  the pulpit  of the  Old  South  Church  in
1670,        and his  grandson,    Rev.  Peter  Thacher,    who went from our
"Old North"  Church to  the North Church in  Boston,    in 1723.
 - 362 - 
840          IS   WEYMOUTH THE  ALMA  MATER  OF  BOSTON
We might add to  this  list  the  names of  Rev.  S.  H.  Hayes  and
Rev.   D.   W.  Waldron,      the  able  and  respected  city  missionary.
Among  the  physicians  the  name  of  Dr.  William  Fifield  can be
spoken with pride,   and no one can fail  to be familiar with the effi-
cient  lady of the Boston school committee,   Mrs. Emily Fifield,      his
wife and widow.
How large a list of choice teachers we have furnished to the Bos-
ton schools  I  am not prepared to say,  but Weymouth seems to have
been for  many years  a favorite training school for that market.
I cannot omit to mention my long-time friend,  the head of  the
Dorchester High School,   Charles Jarius Lincoln;     or John F. Dwight,
the efficient  master at  South  Boston,   who,   though not a native,    is
by  choice  a  resident   of  Weymouth,      and  worthily  sustains   the
musical reputation of the old  town as  an instructor  and conductor
of vocal classes;    or the gracious lady who has just been solicited  to
carry her mature scholarship and the results of her long training  in
our  North  High School  to  fill  a gap  in  the  educational  ranks  of
the city.
It would not be right,    however,    in  these  times,   when patriotic
history is  at such a premium,    not to remind Boston that our Gen.
Solomon  Lovell  was,     in  Revolutionary  times,    commander of  the
military division of which Boston was the center,   and protected and
defended  her,     with  the sound judgment which  was  acquired  and
trained  in  our service.
In closing,       I  might say that by mere attraction  of descent  and
name we might almost expect to find,    as we do find,   in command of
the  "warship  Boston "   a  grandson  of   Capt.       William  Wildes  of
Weymouth,      whose wife  was daughter  of  the  very Gen.  Solomon
Lovell just  referred  to.

PEREGRINE  WHITE
Hon.      George White contributes  the following valuable historical
paper,       referring  to  Peregrine  White,      born  on  the  " Mayflower,  "
whose alleged residence in Weymouth at one time has been asserted
by another contributor,    who has a will in his possession which was
witnessed  by  Peregrine  White,     who he  believes  was  the  original
Peregrine.            It  is possible that this  ancient worthy did reside in this
town for a time,   as his son Peregrine lived,   we are informed,    near the
David Richards  place,    at  the Landing,   and it  is  believed  that  his
father  at  times  took up his  abode at some periods  with his  son,
Weymouth being a livelier business place than Marshfield.
PEREGRINE  WHITE,      SR.
Peregrine  White,    Sr.,    son of  Wm.    White,   was born on board of
the  " Mayflower "  in the harbor of Cape Cod in 1620.    He married
Sarah Bassett in 1648,   daughter of Wm.    Bassett,    and died July 20,
1704.    His widow Sarah died Jan. 22,    1711 .
Peregrine  White,   Jr.,   son of Peregrine aforementioned,   was born
in 1660,    and by wife Susanna had son Benoni ("and others,   "  says
Davis  in  his  " Landmarks of  Plymouth ") .         Said Benoni was born
in  January,     1686.
The Historical  Society  has  an ancient deed dated  1686,    signed
by Gideon Tirrell  and witnessed by Peregrine White.
Hon.        Joseph  W.  Porter,     a high  authority in Weymouth annals,
says  that  Peregrine White lived in Weymouth in  1690,    and was  a
tithing man in the same town in  1695.
Mr.  Francis  Hunt of Weymouth has an old  memorandum book
kept by Ephraim Hunt,    containing an agreement signed  by Pere-
grine White,    wherein he stipulated to deliver 2,000 feet of two- inch
pine plank for  £7 by the first day of May,     1695-96.

WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
By JOHN HARRIS GUTTERSON
This is  by no means the  first  attempt at a record of Weymouth
musicians.              The late John Jay Loud of the Landing had the matter
very near  his heart during the last  active years  of his  life,    and he
wrote,     from time to time,    many a valuable criticism of the men and
women musicians of his day.          No town has ever had a better citizen
than  Mr.  Loud.        He loved  Weymouth's  location  and  her  tradi-
tions;      was  interested  in each  and every institution  and  proud  of
her musical supremacy,    deeply lamenting any lapses from the high
standard she had attained.    Some of us  now living  can remember
Mr.  Loud's  father,    the late John W. Loud,    his  commanding figure
and his  fine bass voice;     and as the mother was a Blanchard,    which
name means  music,    it  is  no wonder that  the  son  possessed  both
musical  temperament  and  the  fine,     strong,    baritone  voice  which
some,     even of this  generation,    very  clearly  remember.              Mr.  Loud
was my neighbor during the years of which I  speak,    and we often
talked over the possibility  of a record of the singers and players  of
Weymouth,      and from  Mr.  Loud  I   had  learned  the valuable  truth
which was later to become the dominant note of this chapter,    which
is   that  musical  inheritance  and  environment  are  more  valuable
than special  and  exotic  training  in music.       He believed  that  one
should  sing  as  one spoke,   -naturally  and without self-conscious-
ness,       letting   the  gray  matter  guide  the  tone.       His  own  singing
exemplified  the theory.
This  chapter  was begun with  great  pleasure.        It  was  good  to
think  that the time had at  last  arrived,    and that mine was to be
the pen.            The pleasure  has remained all  through,   but there  is  also
a deep  and  still  deepening regret,    first,     that  Mr.  Loud's  valuable
co-operation  is  no longer  possible,     and  second,    that  the  finished
product  is,     alas,     so  very,    very incomplete.
At this  time  I  would like  to  thank all  those who have so kindly
replied  to my request for names and dates;  also to remind the many
who will  find  these  pages  disappointing  that  meager details  and
even  errors  are  not  occurring  from  any lack of right  intention  or
endeavor on the part of the writer,   but because those who knew the
facts  failed  to impart them to him.
The Weymouth of fifty years ago,    many now living can remember
quite distinctly;     but the Weymouth of one hundred and fifty years
ago,     of two hundred,   and now,   in this year (1923) ,    of three hundred
years ago,    who now living can imagine,   much less  about it who can
write?
 - 365 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                843
The South Weymouth of  my childhood was a long distance from
Weymouth  Landing,    my home.         What possible  link  could  there
have been in  1723,     even,    when the South Parish was divided  from
the North?
And still   earlier,    when down on the  coast  was  Plymouth,      busy
with its  own struggles,    and busy in its own way (for the Pilgrims,
you  remember,   had spent  some pleasant,    profitable  and certainly
formative  years  in  Holland,    becoming  less  distinctively  English
than were the other settlers  on  Massachusetts  Bay) ,   with miles  of
trackless  forest  between  filled  with skulking  savages  and  howling
wolves ;      above,    on  the  north,    was  Boston,     aristocratic  and  more
English,      because  more  under  the  influence  and  protection  of  the
Crown,       Weymouth  between  them,      first   a trading  post,      then  an
attempt  at  a  settlement  by  Church  of  England  folk.              Calvinist
Puritans  north  of  them,     Pilgrims -Grim  Piles       south  of  them;
no  wonder  there  was  born  the  New England  conscience,  -  that
" state of mind"  which only those who inherit  it  can even partially
understand,      and whose workings no one can anticipate nor rightly
explain.             Certainly,    no musical help from either north  or  south of
them;     the  great  English  Puritan,     Cromwell,     you  remember,      had
delighted  in  destroying  church organs,    and the  Pilgrims  knew but
six  tunes  and cared to know no more.
66
How could  any one here sing  even the " Lord's songs "  in such a
strange  land" !        Besides,   Weymouth was poor.         There are no early
examples of fine dwellings such as  even now exist  in Hingham and
Cohasset.                It  was,    you know -
Hingham for beauty,   Cohasset for pride.
If it  hadn't been for herring,
Weymouth would ha'    died.
It was a fight for existence in which even the Smelt Brook played
a great  part.            Weymouth joined with  Plymouth to battle  in  com-
mon the  common  enemies,                  starvation  and  the  crafty  savage.
The sylvan  forests  were not places  of  romance.          The Indian with
arrow  or  gun  lurked  there ;         there  were  no  domestic  animals,    no
tallow for candles to light  the social hour,    if  social hours there were,
and the pine knot was a dangerous element in a thatch cottage on
a windy night.         There were no church gatherings  for  social  inter-
course.        Religion was grim and hard,   for their God was an avenging
one,     " visiting  the iniquity  of  the  fathers  upon the children, "   and
to  be  feared  more  than  to  be  loved.        There  were  no  schools   or
newspapers ,       or any of the daily  recreations  and relaxations  which
we to-day enjoy,     unconscious  that  they  even  exist.          How was  it,
then,    that  in less  than two hundred years  Weymouth had become
the home of  more musicians  of note than any other  New England
town of its  size?
In company with  the valiant  Standish,    Weymouth men helped
to  cut  down the  obnoxious  Maypole at  Merry  Mount  (some  say
 - 366 - 
844                  WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
cutting off  the ears of the leader as well) .     In the glare of the twen-
tieth  century,    its  clash  and clang  of jazz,     one  wonders  how very
dissolute and wicked those Merry Mounters actually were.
But  while  Weymouth  frowned  upon dancing,    it  seems  that  it
did  sing.                 The  North  Parish  had its  clerk  who  " lined  out"   the
hymn,    the people following after him,  singing the words and music,
for hymn books,  or,  indeed,  books of any kind,  were a great rarity
in the colony.         Sometimes queer jumbles occurred;     for instance -
The Lord will come and He will not,
sang first  the clerk,   and then the congregation.
Keep silence,    but speak out,
paradoxically  commanded  the  clerk,     faithfully   followed  by  the
people.         Put both lines  together,     and the meaning at once is  clear.
Had the  humor of  the  situation  struck  any one  of  that  sober
congregation,       the  tithingman would  promptly have stopped  any-
thing like  levity or laughter in the Lord's House,    and on the Lord's
Day.
While the minister turned the hourglass on the two-hour sermon,
who,       I  wonder,   turned  it  on his hour-and-a-half prayer? -,    the
tired  backs of those early stern- purposed exiles  were more inclined
to go home than to linger  longer for song.
Under  the  " lining  out"  system,   all  sang who  chose,      but with
the choirs came a selection of those who had especially good voices.
Church  records  are  full  of  the  vehement  protests  of  those  who
opposed  the  choir.       These quoted  such  Bible  verses  as :          " Let  all
the people sing,"  and " Let everything  which hath breath praise the
Lord."
How often the pendulum swings back,   and those who had crossed
the sea  for  " freedom to worship God,"  became intolerant  in  their
turn.            No,     the choir did not come without a struggle,    and the old
clerk,       ousted  by young  blood,   died hard.         Stringed  instruments
crept  in,     only to be driven out again,   and even the  organ did  not
find favor from all,   but the choir persisted,   and rehearsals  became
necessary  and the singing  school  was born,                     that  greatest  of  all
musical institutions,    which has done more to give foundation to the
soloist   and  to  weld  singers   into  musical  unity  than  any  other
factor in education.
Its  influence  was  far  greater  than  that  of  modern "music  in
schools .   "      Believe me that  I  speak the truth,    when you listen  next
Sunday to  the congregational singing  at your church.
But  I  remember that,     alas,    " Few now go to the solemn feasts "
ofthe church on Sunday morning,   partly because we have so many
churches,      although  we all  sing,    " The  Church's  one  Foundation,  "
and  more,      perhaps,     because  children  are  no  longer  "taken,  "  but
" sent, "  and,       lacking  the  influence  of  example,   they  soon  remain
away of their own volition.        In the times of which we are speaking,
 - 367 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                845
it  was  not  respectable  to  stay  away from  church.            True,      in  the
earlier  days some must stay with gun or axe to protect  the home-
stead from Indians or wild beasts,  and even later the cattle on little
isolated  farms  required  that  some  one  should  be  near  in  case  a
horse or an ox should get " cast, " and out of a large family,   who must
needs all eat,    perhaps one member was required to remain at home
to look out for the inner man.          But the family must attend church,
and each individual,   in some degree at least,   must " remember the
Sabbath  day, "  or such family or individual would be looked upon
by their  neighbors with a scrutiny that bordered  on suspicion.
The late  Mrs.  Charles  Hunt of  the  Landing  ("Aunt Marcia,  "
as we love to call her)  once told me that when she came from Marsh-
field a bride,    and she and her husband took sittings in the old Union
Church of Weymouth and Braintree,    their  choice lay between the
back pew in  the  gallery  and the front  seat  on the floor  with  no
railing  in front of it.          That church must have seated  six hundred.
And I  have also  been  told  that  early  in  the  nineteenth  century,
when that church was both beautiful and new,   and also at that time
the only church in the village,   the sidewalks  on Sunday morning
were  swept  clean by the  long  skirts  of  the women of that  large
congregation.
It  was about  that  time  that  the  late  Jonas  Perkins,     pastor  of
the  church,      said   to  a  supplying  minister,      " I   don't  know  how
large a congregation you will have,  but the singing will be excellent,
the  choir  consisting  almost entirely  of  one family,   and  they  sing
like the birds."
Exactly so.       And like  the birds,    those generations had no train-
ing,       certainly,     but  loads  of  practice.             The  Händel  and  Haydn
society was born in the vestry of  Park Street  Church in  1809,     and
two Weymouth men,     brothers,     sent  to  England for  the  necessary
books.         One was  a charter  member,    and both  walked  to  Boston
and back  every  Sunday night  to  attend  its  rehearsals.            I  doubt,
also,     if   more than  one or two  of  the  charter  members of  that  so-
ciety had what we to-day call  "voice training."     Music as  a  pro-
fession was neither universal nor profitable at that period,    and even
the organist of King's  Chapel had found it  necessary to  advertise
for  dancing  pupils  to  eke  out  his,   therefore,     seemingly  meager
salary.           Those who sang,  "sang like the birds, "  with no conscious-
ness  of  head,     middle or chest  tones;     also  they  sang joyfully  and
open- throated " like  the  birds. "
Not a few of  us now living but remember the  two services  Sun-
day morning and afternoon,   the hurried luncheon,   sometimes eaten
in church  if  the family came from a distance,    the straight-backed
pews,      the   seats   too  high  for  short  legs,    the  long  sermon,        and
the   longer   prayer,        because  one  had  to   keep  even   more  still
during  that.               Not one word of  either  prayer or  sermon ever pene-
trated  the little  bobbing head.         But the choir!       Bolstered  up by a
small  cabinet  organ,     perhaps,    the  self-conscious  girls  in  the  front
row,      the bashful sterner sex behind them,    the leading soprano with
 - 368 - 
846                  WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
half  the  world  on her  shoulders,     standing  next  to  the  first  alto,
who supported  the  other  half,    and the dragging off  at  both  ends
into  more  giggles  than  singing.       " How did  they  get  into  that
place?"  wondered the bobbing head.      Not mine,   however,      I  knew.
Didn't  my father  sing  there,     and,      on  rare  occasions,      when  my
mother  was  kept  away,    didn't  I  sit  there,     also,     and wasn't  I  fed
peppermints by " Uncle"  Ned Bates,   a heavy,    elderly,   but correct
bass singer?
The Union Church of Weymouth and Braintree had a big organ.
I heard it  very seldom,   but never forgot it in between times.         What
tones!       What power!        How did it,     and how did they do it  (for I had
learned that it  took two to make it go) .       Isn't it  singular that my
fingers  were the very last  to  play upon it  on the Sunday in June,
1897,      next  before the fatal Saturday on which it went up in smoke
and flames ?
But to  come back from personalities.          The early records  of  the
North  Parish  have unfortunately  been  destroyed,    though  it  was,
we remember,     the  church  of  the father  of  Abigail  Smith Adams.
Nor have we forgotten that when the first  edifice was destroyed by
fire,      everybody wondered which of his neighbors had been so wicked
as to call down the wrath of God upon the whole parish.          However,
its  experiences  were  like  those of other churches  of  the  Plymouth
Colony.        The South Parish was separated in  1723,    and in 1809 the
Union  Church  of  Weymouth and  Braintree  came  into  being,     so
large  had become the  village  of  Weymouth Landing  and its  little
neighbor,     East Braintree.
But it  is  not with the records of church history that this  chapter
intends  to deal,   except to make clear the perhaps obvious fact  that
music as well as other educational matters in New England had its
origin  in the  church.          It was the meeting-house      no  Massachu-
setts  Bay colonist  would have said  " church. "     If  it  possessed  a
bell,     the  bell  rope hung down to  the  floor  in the handiest way to
call the folks  and to  sound an alarm of fire  or foe.        All  matters  of
public welfare were brought there  and threshed out.          The minister
was  a  great  man there  in  his  proper setting,  rivaled  only  by the
squire,     with  the odds against the latter,    for was not the title  borne
by the former divinely bestowed?
And well  some  of  those  old  divines  deserved  the  respect  and
reverence paid them.       It is  said,    upon good authority  to  back up
the  statement,     that  the  present  high  standards  of  education  in
what was  then  the  Massachusetts  Bay  Colony,    or  perhaps  more
properly  now Plymouth  County,     are  the direct  result  of the stren-
uous  efforts  of one man,   the  Rev.  Mr.  May,    pastor of  the church
in  Norwell  (then South Scituate)   in  the last  part of the eighteenth
century.           Visiting the little  schoolhouses,    he found it  possible to do
so much more than was being done in the process of education that
he made it  his first  business  to  arouse  the  men and women of his
church  to  the great  need  of  better  schools  and  schooling,     and  to
this  day Norwell (my present  home)  still  feels  the vibrations  from
 - 369 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                847
the waves he set in motion.          The good is  not always interred with
a man's bones.
But we are in church.          The choir is  about to sing.          There are  no
viols  nor even any little cabinet organ.            Some one is  holding up the
pitch pipe for " attention,"  and when all  have received  the pitch,
all   sound  " do,     sol,       mi,       do, "       bass,         tenor,        alto,    soprano.            " Ye
tribes  of Aaron join,"  sings  the choir,    while  the  poor,     discomfited
clerk,      robbed  forever  of his  petty  position,  leaves  the  church  in
tears,       never to darken its  doors again.
A well-balanced mixed quartet is  a wonderful  musical  combina-
tion.           I  had rather listen  to  one than to  a soloist  or a chorus,      but
professional singers  have driven the "sing "  out of the congregation
because of the very contrast of trained  and untrained.
There is   a legend  of  a monastery in  northern  Italy  during  the
Middle Ages,     in which the monks were very devout,    and,    although
unskilled in music,   sang their Aves and Matins with great unction.
One day there arrived as  a guest a weary traveler who proved to be
an opera  singer  from  Milan.          The Abbot conceived  the  idea  of
praising God at vespers  by the use of that wonderful and trained
voice.              The silent  monks in their  stalls  listened  entranced  as  their
guest  sang  the  beautiful  vesper  music.         Never  had  those  walls
echoed  to  such wonderful  tones.
But  that  night  the Abbot had  a vision.       He beheld  an  angel
standing  in  his  cell  who inquired  in  a  severe  tone  of  voice  why
vespers had not been celebrated that night.
" Indeed,        but  they  were, "    responded   the  frightened   Abbot,
"and  we had  such  wonderful  music  as  we have  never  enjoyed
before."
"Strange!        Very strange ! "  was the angel's reply,  "not one note
of it  ever penetrated  to  heaven.  "
It  is  good  to  sing  with  the  understanding  as  well  as  with  the
spirit,     but  the  worship  of God comes with  the  spirit,     whether  or
not the voice be trained.
It was my intention to begin here a record of the early families
who sang  and of their descendants  to the present day,   tracing  the
musical inheritance in those who sing or play now,   and,   through the
columns  of  the  " Weymouth Gazette"  and  " Transcript, "   I   have
sought  for  a response from those now living concerning their musi-
cal  ancestors  lately  deceased,    or long  ago departed.        With the  in-
difference  born  of  the  hurried  condition  in  which  we live,     that
response  has been very meager in amount,    and from very few per-
sons,     and  I  must proceed,   therefore,    much less  accurately  than  I
had hoped,    borrowing  from my own memory in many cases,     and
from the stories told me by those who have "passed on"  and can-
not now verify the impressions that they gave.
This,       then,      imperfect record  is  the  cause  of deepening  regret  as
I  turn in this  chapter which is  all  too incomplete.        Before  me lie
the records of the social and religious singing societies of the various
churches,            the  Union  Church,        1817;       the  North  Parish,       1822,

and another  of  1839;     the  Wesleyan Society,   1826;     and the  South

We do hereby individually bind  ourselves  to  strive  earnestly to  promote the
spirit  of mutual affection,   forbearance and long-suffering,  so that no root of bit-
terness  may ever spring  up to  trouble us,    but that we may long  be united as  a
band of brothers evidencing by our conduct that the delightful strains of melody
are not in vain  upon our lips,    but that  our hearts  are  thereby warmed with  a
flame of love,     not only toward our God who gave us these faculties we possess,
but toward each other,     showing itself in acts of mutual and earnest exertion  to
promote each other's spiritual good and temporal prosperity and happiness,    that
eventually,   although the hand of death may arrest us and separate us from em-
ployments for which we now unite,   we may be prepared to join the glorious choir
above whose constant employment is  to praise  the Lord in an eternal anthem of
glad Hosannas to  Him who died and rose again and is  seated on the right hand
of His Father.        Depending upon that  blessing which cometh down from above,
we now declare  by this  public  act  that  we are  determined  zealously  and per-
severingly  to render every aid and assistance in our power both by precept and
example,    to promote the judicious performance by a full  choir of public singing
in the meeting-house of the society.

In 1822,      in  the North Parish,    was formed a musical society  con-
sisting  entirely  of  men.            The blue  paper  record  lies   before  me,
itself a copy of an original.      The copy is the work of the late  Elias
Richards,       Esq. ,    of  Weymouth Landing.
Their  first  meeting was held  in  the schoolhouse  of  the  United
District,       and  Thomas  Bicknell  was  chosen  moderator,       Charles
Bates,      first  chorister,    Edward Blanchard,    second  chorister,     Benja-
min Burrell,     Jr.,    third chorister,    and Deacon Zachri  Nash,    William
Pratt and Jacob Bates,   standing committee.
In  1823  Enos  White was  chosen  chorister,     Edward  Blanchard
following  him in the next year.      James Whitmarsh succeeded him,
Edward  Blanchard  again  serving  in  1829 and  1830,    Albert  Whit-
marsh  following  in  1831  and  1832.    Edward  Blanchard  returned
again in  1833,     William O.  Nash in  1834,     and Mr.  Blanchard  once
more in  1835.
Beginning in 1836,    David Pratt served for  five years,    William O.
Nash  following  him,    and  in  1851  Francis  B.  Bates  was  chosen
chorister.           John  Wildes was elected  in 1853,    and for  some reason
not given,     no first  chorister was chosen until in  1862,   when Joseph
H.  French,       who had served  them as  second chorister  during  that
time,    was elected  first  chorister.         William S.  Collier succeeded him
in  1864,       Edward Blanchard  returning  again  in  1865;       William  O.
Nash,       from  1866  to  1869;        Mr.  French  in  1870;      J.   D.  Wildes  in
1871 ;      F.  D. Cushing in 1872;    Samuel P. Nash in 1873,    and A. F. G.
Hunt in  1874.
In  1865  Lot  W.  Bicknell  was  chosen  secretary  and  held  that
position until 1874,   when the society as a group with functions  and
officers  seems to have been less active.
A meager record  here,     to which many now living  could  perhaps
add  more  accurate  data,     but what a suggestion  of  pleasant  and
profitable evenings,   of social  and musical advantage,   of friendships
made and cemented  in  this,    which was perhaps  the  only  regular
outing of those men of that day.        The schoolhouse was not lighted.
Those living  near must have brought  candles  or  oil  lamps  -lan-
terns,       even,      perhaps      to light  the way home on dark  or  stormy
nights.              In  the following  list  of  members during  more than  fifty
years of the society's life,  few now living in the town,   either of Wey-
mouth birth  or descended from those born there,   but can trace  an
ancestor or  two,   and,  recalling by name a man old and feeble  in my
young days,      I say to  myself,   as I  sit  and think,  " Did he ever sing?"

The facts  concerning the formation  and history of the Wesleyan
Singing  Society  of  East  Weymouth have been made available  by
John W. Bates  in an extended extract from the original  records  of
the society.             The ensuing account has been gleaned largely from his
neat and accurate digest.
In East Weymouth,   on Jan. 23,   1826,   a group of men and women
met  and  drew  up  a  constitution,     not  unlike  that  of  the  Union
Singing Society,     an article of which we quoted on a previous page.
This  latter  company was known as  the Wesleyan Singing Society.
The  original   members   were :           Charles   Bates,        Ruben  Gardner,
Jacob Bates,       Royal Wildes,     David Bates,    Benjamin Burrell,   James
Hawes,       Thomas  Richards,     James  Bicknell,     Cotton  Bates,   Alvah
Raymond,     Asa  Dyer,     3d,     William  French and William  Rice.
A note in  another  hand  on Mr.  Bates'      manuscript  states  that
"At this  time (1884)  none of the fourteen is  living.      Thomas Rich-
ards  and Alvah Raymond were the last survivors. "
In the  succeeding  account  of  the  more important  activities  of
the  Wesleyan  Society,     the  chronological  order  has  been  rather
strictly   observed.          Names  almost  identical       save  for,       perhaps,
one  initial -will  be  found  occurring  at  intervals  in  the  lists   of
members.             It  has been assumed  that  such names refer  to  separate
individuals.
The first  annual meeting of the society was held in the Methodist
chapel  on  Monday,     Feb.  13,      1826,     and at the  annual  first  service
April  6,      1826,     the following  music was sung :         Broomsgrove,     C. M.;
" Lord,     for  Thy Tender Mercies'    Sake," and " The Lord's Prayer, "
 - 373 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                851
both  from  the  Händel  and  Haydn  collection;       " Ninety-Seventh
Psalm,  "   L.   M.,       " Hear  My  Prayer"  and  " Teach  Me,        O  Lord, "
both from the Old Colony collection of anthems.
In 1827 the name of Isaac Sampson was added to the roll.          Abra-
ham Bates and Ruben Gardner were elected in  1828;    Joseph Bates
in  1829,     and Ebenezer Tirrell (who remained a member until 1883)
Urban Bates,     Ephraim W. Whiting and Ezra Tirrell in 1830.
In  1830 the members,    needing a new case for the bass viol,    sub-
scribed  one dollar  and seventy- three  and a half cents .
John Tirrell  joined in  1831 ,     and William  B.  Davis and Warren
Burrell  in  1832.   About the  year  last  mentioned,    Joseph  Bates,
who played the bass viol,   went home across lots one night with the
instrument  over his  shoulder,  fell,    and damaged the viol  consider-
ably.            Money to  repair it  was raised by subscription.          Such names
of  persons  subscribing  to this fund as do not  appear elsewhere  in
the  record  are included in the following list:       Urban  Rice,     Bela  L.
Pratt,       John Tuttle,    Jacob  Lovell,    Thaddeus  Bates,      William  Har-
rington,              Luther   Livingston,        Joshua   Randall,        James   Totman,
Nathaniel  Shaw,    Josiah  Lane,     Ambrose Salisbury,    Ebenezer  Pool,
Elias  Vining,         Minot Harrington,     Benjamin Bates,   John  Peterson,
Albert  Bates,    Nathaniel  Ford,    Josiah  E.  Rice,    Hosea G.  Pool,     Asa
Bates  and Asa Kingman,     Jr.
During  the  next  five  or  six  years  several   persons  joined  the
society:        Cornelius  Bates  and George  Bates in  1834;     Bela  French,
David  French,    and Joseph  French in  1835 ;          William  Harrington,
James Hawes,    Jr. ,    Abiah  W. Salisbury in  1836;      Samuel  P.  Pratt,
Nathan Bates and Ebenezer W. Dean in  1838.
In the latter year the society voted to give " Their humble thanks
to  Ebenezer  Tirrell,      Abraham Bates  and  Ezra Tirrell,      their  past
choristers,      for their past services. "
New  members  again  were  added:         Isaac  P.   Sampson,       Amos
Tirrell  and George  Evans in  1839,    Joseph  Burrell  in  1841,     Zach-
eriah  Bicknell in 1842.    The society  voted also,   in  1842,     to  buy a
violin  which  should  be  their  corporate  property.            They  chose  a
librarian,    George Bates;     they furthermore voted,  " That the chor-
isters  have the privilege of placing the singers as they think best,
both  male and female. "     That  same year,      also,     after  buying  the
violin,  they purchased by subscription six new books,  the "Templi
Carmina.  "    Among those who subscribed  were  the  following,     not
elsewhere   listed:       William   W.   Raymond,       Amos  A.   Raymond,
H.  B.   Ford,       Joseph  Dunbar,     Joseph  P.   Dunbar,       William  Bates,

"To  bring  before  the congregation  the  subject  of purchasing  a
new  bass  viol, "   a  committee  of  three  was  voted  in  1855.    One
wonders  if  the ill-fated  instrument repaired in  1832,   or about that
time,   had served until this year.          The librarian in  1855 was ordered
to  conduct  an  inventory of  property belonging  to  the society and
to report the complete list  of such possessions  to the treasurer .
W. C.  French,   C. P. Joy,    A. J.  Garey and Joseph Bates,     Jr. ,     were
voted into membership in  1856.
What seems  to  us an astoundingly rigorous resolution  " to  meet
for  rehearsal  every Sunday morning at eight and one-half o'clock"
was  adopted  in  1856,    but the society  must have felt  that it  had
ventured  too  far,    for  at the very bottom of the  same page it  was
" Voted,        '      To  reconsider   the  vote  whereby  we  voted  to  have  a
rehearsal.       "    In  1860  the  membership of  the society was enlarged
by  allowing  all  who sat  " in  the  choir"   to  sign  its  constitution.
In  1862  occurs  the  first  mention  of  an  organ;     at  that  time  the
choristers  were made a committee to  see  that the instrument  was
put in tune.          Alphaeus  Bates  and Fannie Burrell were organists  in
1868.
The  church  building  burned  Feb.  23,     1870,    and the  organ  was
destroyed.               Some time later       the exact date is  impossible  to  de-
termine  from  the  record  -a  new church  building was dedicated.
An  organ,       formerly  in  the  Cockerel  Church  in  Hanover  Street,
Boston,      had been installed.       The instrument had three banks  of
keys  and had been made by Appleton.      Some improvements upon
it  were effected  when it  was set  up in the  East Weymouth church
by  " George Ryder,    organ builder."    In the evening of the day of
dedication,       an  organ  recital  or  " organ  concert"  according  to  our
source,      was given.          F.  P.  Ryder,     R.  F.  Ryder and Alphaeus  Bates
seem  to  have been organists  upon that  occasion.
" The  town  chorus  met with  this  society  in  the  vestry  of  the
church,  "   says  a significant  entry in  May,   1872,      " to  practice  the
music to be sung at the Peace Jubilee in  Boston. "
Strange as  it  may seem,   the first mention of any women singers
does not  occur until  1873,   when it  is  recorded  that  " Mrs.  Susan
Stevens,         for   many  years   the  leading  soprano,    being  sick,       Miss
Sarah  French took her place.      In the fall  of the year Mrs. Stevens,
having  recovered  her health,    resumed  her  accustomed  place."
In  1880,     A.  M. Raymond,    Willie  H. Pratt,    T. J.  Evans,     J.  Frank
Porter,    Caleb Benson and Frank Lincoln were admitted as members.
While  the  funeral  of  the  late  President  James A.  Garfield  was

taking place in Cleveland,   Ohio,   the churches  of  East Weymouth

A sermon was preached by the  Rev.  D.  P.  Leavitt,    pastor of  that
church,   and the choirs of the Methodist and Congregational churches
presented a program of music.
"The foregoing  extracts  from the records  of  the  society do not
constitute  a very full history,"  writes  Mr.  Bates.            " No record  in
the earlier  years is  made of any females who sang with them.            We
have tried  to  obtain such  information  as we could,   from some of
the old people of East Weymouth.          We learn that among the early
singers  were:         " Mary Burrell  (Mrs.  Sullivan) ;      Lucy Bates  (Mrs.
Edward  Blanchard) ;          Patience   Bates   (Mrs.   Alvah   Raymond) ;
Lucy Bates  ( Mrs.  Ruben Gardner) ;      Silence  Rice  (Mrs.  John Tir-
rell) ;          Miss  Pratt  (Mrs.  William  Rice) ;      Ruth Burrell  (Mrs.  Sam-

Burrell   ( Mrs.   William  Davis) ;        Lucinda  Bates   (Mrs.   Ebenezer
Tirrell)  ;          and Jane Pratt  (Mrs. Asa Kingman) . "
A glance  at  this  list  leads  inevitably  to just  one conclusion -
the singing school and the church choir must have been an excellent
place to find a wife.          The Bateses,    the Tirrells,   the Burrells  and the
Kingmans of earlier  generations  thought so,    anyway.
"Many who are now living took an active part during the later
years,  "  continues  our record.             Some of  the names given  are  Mrs.
Ruth Lincoln,     Mrs. Ellen Nash,    Mrs.  Mary Pool and Mrs. Augusta

if as much,     as she has,    to further the interests of the society. "
There  were  also   various  musical  instruments.            " Mr.   Charles

"The first  organ was built by Stevens.          It was not a very power-

times for a year or more.          We learn from the old people that it  was

than fifty years ago now - to  have rehearsals in the  large kitchens
of the members'    houses,    and one person relates  that when they met
at  her  father's  house  the  treat  was  'doughnuts'     and mince  pie,
and probably the men had a little  old cider  to clear their  throats.
The society  still  meets for  practice every week.         One notable  fact
connected with its  history is that there has never been any trouble
in its  ranks ;       no dissensions.          It has been harmonious in all  things.
May it  ever be so in the future. "
In  1839 the old  North Village decided to have a musical  society
which should  include both men and women,    and on January 14  in
that year the following-named met and formed a glee  club.           They
were  William  O.  Nash,       Francis  N.  Bates,    George  Dyer,         Robert
Raymond,       Caleb  P.  Joy,      Daniel  P.  Nash and  W.  M. Harrington.
They drew up a constitution,   elected their officers,   and called them-
selves  the  Weymouth North  Parish  Glee  Club.       The " Weymouth
Gazette"   of   March  19,      1885,      has  an  interesting  article  on  the
doings of this  society,   their  semi-annual meetings which continued
until  1863,       and  the  still  more  interesting  annual  excursions  and
dinners  at  Nantasket Beach,   the last  of which took place in  1884.
This article  is from the pen of the late  Henry A.  Newton,    who,     in
closing,       said  that  there  were  still   living   (in   1885)   thirty- three
signers  of  the constitution.

generally  held  in  the  houses  of  members;      occasionally,     however,

used  were  the  " Odeon,"  " Boston  Glee  Book, "   " American  Glee

Occasionally  they appeared in  public,    and it  is  recorded  that  on
Feb.   11 ,         1840,     they  met at  the  Third  District  School  and  that
tickets  were twelve and a half cents.           They placed themselves  on
record  on the temperance question,  for in  1839 it  was " Resolved,
That  we,      the  Glee  Club,    accept  of  no treat,     such  as  intoxicating
drinks,      and we also resolve that we will  not allow  band playing  or
dancing at our sings.  "    The social choir was,   in its  flourishing times,
one of  the most important organizations  of  the north  part  of  the
town,    and it has done much to create good feeling among the people.
In  the  eighties  they gave semi-annual  concerts  in  the  Old  North
Meeting-House,    and invited  other  singers,      not  members  of  the
club,       to  assist  them.         I  remember that  my father was sometimes
asked to sing  with them,   as tenor voices were not very plentiful .
And the South Parish was also singing.          One record says  that as
early  as  1829  concerts  were given both in  the  Old  South  Church
and in Rogers Hall.         A small admission fee was charged,   the money
going  to  pay  for  assistance  rendered  by  Boston  talent.            Among
others  mentioned  were  Mr.  B.  J.   Kendall,    clarinetist ;         Mr.  John

Conquering  Hero  Comes !   "  from  "Judas  Maccabeus, "    and  also
solos   and  choruses  from  the  " Messiah "  were  presented.
concerts  were always opened with prayer by the minister.

Many of  those  named in  the  previously  given  lists  belonged  to
the  old   Stoughton  Musical  Society,      an  organization  antedating
the  Händel   and  Haydn  Society.         The  Stoughton   society   was
formed  in  1776  and  it  still   exists  as   a  name,      with  no  activities .
Trained in  those four early  nineteenth  century choruses,   attending
them because they loved music,    those people became the  ancestry
of  the group that made Weymouth a notable town musically in the
latter  decades of  the  nineteenth century,     and one that is  maintain-
ing its  high musical repute even to the present day.
Weymouth  sent  two  hundred  singers  to  the  Peace  Jubilee  of

1872,        ranking fifteenth  in the list  of choruses,     and being  assigned
seats  directly  behind the  Boston chorus,     so  great,    even then,     was
the  reputation of Weymouth as  a musical  center.
The statement was made earlier in this  chapter that most of the
educational  as well as  the musical beginnings  in this  country had
their birth in the church.         This is  an obvious though perhaps some-
times  forgotten fact,  and is  equally true of all  civic  matters.            The
meeting- house was the one large  building of the little  village,     and
therein many community activities  found their home.     It  is ,       then,
not out of keeping with the historical  trend of this  article  to  turn,
as we begin the alphabetical  records of  our Weymouth singers,    first
to  a church  choir.
Prominent in the choir formed about 1875 in the Roman Catho-
lic  Church of  the  Sacred  Heart in  Weymouth Landing were mem-
bers  of the Ahern family.     Mrs.  Mary E.  Ahern Donovan was one
of the earliest and most helpful singers in that musical organization.
She gave thirty years of musical service,    and was the first  person to
sing the music of the requiem mass in that church.          Mrs. Donovan,
her  brother  John  W. Ahern,     her  sisters  and her children  all  gave
liberally  of  their  talent,    both in the music of the  church  services
and in numerous entertainments of a high order which were a great
help to the church in both social and financial ways.
Two  of  Mrs.   Donovan's  sisters   were  organists  in  the  Sacred
Heart  Church.             One,        Mrs.   Caroline  Ahern  Corridan,       held  that
position  eight  years,    and also  sang,   for  she  possessed  a pure and
musical contralto voice.          The other sister,    Miss Margaret Z.  Ahern,
was organist for twelve years.      She had been a pupil of Miss Susan
M.  Blanchard,    and later  took a course in the New England  Con-
servatory  of  Music,    studying  pianoforte,    the organ,    harmony and
voice  culture.              She  was  a  successful  and  painstaking  teacher  as
well,     and a pupil of whom Miss Blanchard was justly proud.
From the next generation,    two daughters  of Mrs. Donovan have
manifested ability as vocalists,    both in the church and in the musi-
cal  life   of  Greater  Boston.            Mrs.  Nellie  M.  Donovan Kerins  won
numerous scholarships during her student days in the New England
Conservatory  of  Music,    and was for  ten  years  soprano  soloist  in
the  Park  Street  Church  of  Boston.          Possessed  of  a  lyric  soprano
voice of great beauty and range,   she is  one whom Weymouth is glad
to  own as  a  townswoman.          I still remember with pleasure a concert
in which she and the Weber Male Quartet,   I think it was,  sang the
" Miserere "  from  " Il   Trovatore. "    Miss   Elizabeth   Donovan,         a
younger sister,   is well known in the concert hall and in the open air,
where she has sung with orchestra  and band.
Members of  the Ahern family  still  carry on their  musical  tradi-
tion  in  the  Sacred  Heart  Church.            Mr.  John W. Ahern,    baritone,
is  a  member of the Holy Name choir,    and his wife,    Mrs.  Elizabeth
Leary  Ahern,      sings  in the  Sodality  choir,    while  their  son,     John  I.
Ahern,     plays  the violin  in  the church orchestra.          Another violinist
in  that  group is  Mr.  Lawrence  Corridan,     a  son  of  Mrs.  Caroline
Ahern  Corridan.          His  sister,    Miss  Helen  Corridan,     a  graduate  of

the Leland Powers School of Public Expression,   is  a soprano soloist
in  the junior choir.
Miss Mary Donovan,     a cousin of the family on the Ahern side,
and a former pupil of mine,     was organist of the junior choir  until,
a few years  ago,  she entered a convent of the Sisters of St.  Joseph .
The music of  the  Roman Catholic  church,    because  of its  unity
with the service,    offers  a greater opportunity for devotional expres-
sion than that of any of the Protestant churches,   with the exception,
perhaps,     of  the Protestant Episcopal Church.       Much to my regret,
I have but little  information regarding the singers and the music of
the  Catholic churches  in  our town.             The late  Mrs. John W. Hart
(of the Hart family more later)  was a power in the early days of the
Sacred  Heart choir.      I used to hear her sing as I passed the church
on my way to  my own service,    or  perhaps  during  a funeral  on  a
week day,      and I  have heard her sing  in concerts  the tender ballads
and folk songs for which she was at that time famous.         While Mary
Donovan was my pupil,     I  sometimes  attended the 9 o'clock  mass
to  help  her by watching her work.           It  was a great  satisfaction  to
the teacher  in me to  hear the way she handled the  organ and see
her skill  with  the little  choir which was then  her charge.            I  hope
that in  her  new field  she has still  something  to do with  music,    as,
like  all  the Ahern family,    she is  thoroughly musical.
In  the  latter  part  of  the  last  century  the little  village  of  East
Braintree was so small  that  it  came to Weymouth to  buy most of
its  supplies,     and to the great Union Church for its  Sunday worship.
On Commercial Street,     not far  from the East Braintree station,
lived  Abijah  Allen,    his  wife  and children.       I  have  been told  that
after   supper  at  night  they  pushed  their   chairs   back  from  the
table,      and,     seated there,    would sing for an hour or two.          The father
sang tenor ;       Susie,   soprano ;      Inez,    alto;    Will,  tenor;   and John,   bass.
When I   played  the  organ  in  Trinity  Episcopal  Church  on Front
Street,      Weymouth,    in  1885,    Susie  Allen was the  leading  singer  in
the  church  choir.        Inez  had  married,      and  her  daughter,       Fannie
Merrill,         was  a  promising  student  of  the  pianoforte  under  Miss
Susan  Blanchard.         Trinity  Parish  has had many faithful  workers,
many devoted  communicants,     many generous  donors,      but  it  has
never  had a more cheerful  and liberal  giver than  that  same Susie
Allen.               Winter and summer,    through  cold  and heat,    through  rain
or  shine,    Susie was at  her post,    singing  her own part,   helping every
one  else,       ready to give her  services  and her talent at concerts  and
entertainments,     seldom receiving even a " Thank you. "    How much
she did toward the success of my work those four years and a half,
I did not know then.        I  learned it  afterward through many a bitter
experience with  other  singers.        She  has  passed  on to  her  reward,
and  I   am sure  the  choir  angelic was richer  by her  coming.           Both
Will and John often sang with us,   and I  remember one Sunday,   when
copies  of  the  " Te Deum"  were not  all  alike,     I,    failing  to  turn  a
page (not being  so familiar  with the music of the church as  I  have
become since),    cut John out of  a good bass solo,    much to my cha

grin,     but which,   with infinite  kindness  and good  nature,     he pleas-
antly forgave.
With Will  Morrison,    a tenor,     also  of  East  Braintree,       and  Will
Blanchard  of  Weymouth  (see  the  Hunt family),   a heavy  basso,
and the  two Allen brothers,    a quartet was formed and their  initials
composed the  name,     the Maab Quartet.           They gave generously of
themselves,        singing  whenever  they  were  asked,     and,      I  am sure,
usually  without pay.          As I  think of them now they were  rather  a
remarkable organization,    musical to the  finger  tips,   all  having been
brought  up  in  an  atmosphere  of  music.       Their  voices  presented
considerably  more range  than  is  usually  found  in  male  quartets,
and with  pleasing  address  they were a very welcome addition  to
any program.                In  1887,    I  think it  was,   the parish put on an oper-
etta  written  by Leo  Lewis,     the  son of  a Universalist  minister  in
South Boston,    the words by Mrs.  Lewis,   called " The Reporter  and
the  Fairies.   "       Young  Leo,    who afterwards  became an instructor  in
music  in  Tufts  college,      nearly  supported  himself  through  his  own
student days in college,   I have heard,    on the proceeds of that opera,
and by singing  the title  rôle  himself.         Albert  Avery  (a descendant
of the Hunt family)  took the  leading  rôle,      Miss Allen  the  leading
woman's part,     and the Maab Quartet,     as a  unit,    were the  amusing
compositors in the newspaper office.          We all worked hard.          It went
well.             I   have  a program of it  near me,    and I think it  helped  ma-
terially  to give me recognition as a young musician who might have
possibilities.
Not far  from the Abijah Allen homestead lived  Orace Allen  and
his  family.             I   do  not  know that  they  were  at  all  related.          Mrs.
Orace Allen  was a  Faxon.             Her  mother was a Hunt.               Mr.  Orace
Allen himself had a remarkably fine baritone voice,   a pleasing pres-
ence,      and was a valued member of the Union Church choir.       As I
sit  and write,      I  am amazed and astonished  at the good  nature  of
that generation,   I mean the generation next older than I.      Mr. Allen
was always  willing to sing for  the social and religious  organizations
of  that  day,     his  own church,    the  Village  Cemetery  Improvement
Society,       Grand Army fairs,    the  Literary  Society  and the  various
other  organizations  functioning in the decades  between  1880  and
1900.    The Union Religious Society gave " Esther, "  and he was the
gracious  and stately king.     When they gave " Ruth"  he was the
kinsman,     Boaz.           An emotional temperament lent feeling and pathos
to  his  voice,       always  smooth  and  flexible.        His  daughter,      Emma,
though  I  never  heard  her  sing,   became one  of  Miss  Blanchard's
most  satisfactory  piano  pupils,     and a piano solo  by Emma Allen
(Mrs. Frank White)  was a thing to enjoy.         Helen Allen,   the younger
daughter,       almost  as  a child,    sang  alto  in  the  old  Union  Church.
Very wisely,    her father kept her out of the limelight until suddenly
we woke up to the fact  that we had in our midst a young singer of
extraordinary promise,    and when she came back from Europe with
that promise fulfilled,    Weymouth was very glad to  say,   " Yes,     Miss
Allen belongs  to  us. "    When she  married  Russell  Goddard Hunt,

the family genealogy  showed  that  her  grandmother,     a  Hunt,     was
of the same family,    and that her husband,    Russell G.,   was the  same
generation  as  the  mother of  his  wife.             (Of  Mrs.  Helen Allen  Hunt
more later.)
There was another talented Allen family in Weymouth.            Z.  Mer-
ton Allen played in the band,   his solo instrument being a clarinet.
If  the  Baptist  Church gave an entertainment,   they asked  Merton
Allen  to  play.         When the  Episcopal  Church wanted a cornet  obli-
gato  they got  Merton Allen.         The same way proved  easy  to  the
other churches  and the  social  organizations.       With the prices  that
professional  musicians  are  getting  now,    with  the  unions  and  the
strikes ,         I  wonder did he ever  say,    " No.    I  will  not  play for  you. "
Certainly he never refused me,   and my programs show a versatility
when,     with me at  the piano, he played "Ah Che le  Morte,"  from
" Il  Trovatore,"  for  the  Baptist  Church,     and,     in  the  same week,
the  obligato  to   Howard  M.  Dow's  " Christmas  Hymn "   at  the
Episcopal  Church.       Ah,   but those were musical days!       He married
Emma,    the daughter of  Rufus K.  Trott (one of the singers  in  the
Union Singing Society of 1817).          They were a musical family (Mrs.
Trott was a  Dunbar) ,    and they possessed  one of the few pianos  in
Weymouth at  that  time.          There  were  two  daughters  also  in  this
Allen family,     Aria and Alida.          One played the piano and played it
well,      and  the  other,      Alida,    with  a tiny  violin  in  her little  hands,
was not far  from being a musical  prodigy.       I wonder,    do they play
now?    I  hope so,    though so  many drop their music when they grow
older.
There came with her husband and son to live in her native town,
North Weymouth,      Mrs.  E.  W. Arnold,   who had been a Miss Wilde.
Her mother  was a  Lovell of the well-known Weymouth family  of
that  name.             The Arnolds  were  Baptists,   and  in  the  eighties  Mr.
Arnold became a great  power  so  far  as  the music of that  church
was  concerned.           He  spent  his  time  and  money  freely,      and  the
music began to  be an even  more attractive  feature  of  the  service.
He often  brought  with  him his  talented  son,     E.  Walter Arnold,    a
young man with  a glorious  voice,    whose solos  I  feel  sure  reached
persons in the congregation whom the sermon missed.        I  have heard
him sing -
The twilight falls,   the night is near;   I fold  my work away
And bend to one who deigns to hear the story of the day,
The old,    old story,   yet I  kneel to tell it at Thy call;
And cares grow lighter as  I  feel,    Jesus knows it  all.
Then followed  softly  the voices  of the choir  in  the little  refrain,
and the  song closed with the solo  voice again triumphant
Yes,     Jesus knows it  all !
Lewis   E.   Tilden  was  at  the  organ  (see  the  Cushing  family) ,
Eva  (Hender)   Baker singing  soprano,    with  Miss Cora Graves  and

TheArnold element was a great benefit to the music of the church
and the vicinity.     They had come from Neponset which was much
