well,       I  shall  never forget the influence of his singing  upon me,    and
if  I  cannot forget,   may not the  recording  angel also  be somewhat
mindful of his spiritual use of his gift  of song?
The Baptist minister during a part of that  time was the Rev.
Seth  J.  Axtel.           Mrs. Axtel was quite a singer.         Her voice,     while  it
was  not  so  powerful  as   Mrs.  Baker's,      was  very  sweet  and  very
sympathetic,     and she had enjoyed some advantages that we in  our
country  town did  not  possess.           She had  sung  in  musical  festivals
under  the  baton  of  Carl  Zerrahn,     and with such singers  as  M.  B.

Mr3.         Baker and Mrs. Axtel sang authoritatively  and with ability,
but their voices differed  sufficiently  to make a pleasing and musical
contrast,     and when Mr. Arnold  put on big  numbers requiring  two
soprano   soloists,      like   Mendelssohn's   " I   Waited  for   the   Lord, "
Mrs.  Axtel  would sing  with  us.             I,       of  the  chorus,    remember still,
after  these many years,     the effect of their  singing.
What  educational   advantages   rehearsals   with   these   persons
possessed,     I   found later when I  became both organist and director ;
and it  has  proved true of me,   as  I  suppose it  is  true of every one,
that  I   have never given of myself,     my time,    and of what musical
ability  I,       at  the  moment,    have  possessed,     without  gaining  in  ex-
perience,        and  pleasure  too,      certainly   tenfold.        Perhaps  that   is
what made that generation so generous of their  talents .
The Hon.       Edward Avery and his family of East Braintree  were
attendants at Trinity Church,   Mr. Avery often helping in the choir.
The daughter Carrie (afterward  Mrs. William  Claflin)   and the  son
Albert  were  also  members of  the  choir  from  time  to  time.          Their
mother was a daughter of  the late  Caleb Stetson,     and Mrs. Stetson
was a Miss  Hunt of  Weymouth.            Mrs.  Claflin's  voice was  a con-
tralto  of  unusual  range,     and,    being a thorough musician,    she was a
great  asset  to  the musical endeavors of her locality.        With a group
of  South  Weymouth people,     including  Miss  Fannie  Sprague  and
Mr.  J.    Frank  Porter,   she  drilled  and  produced  such  ambitious
operas  as   " Pauline,      the  Belle  of  Saratoga, "   and  " H.M.S.  Pina-
fore,  "   giving  them in  the  music  hall  at  South  Weymouth,     then
much the best hall in the  town.
There were other families moving into  Weymouth who influenced
its  musical life.         When the  Rev.  Mr. Atwood was preaching at  the
Universalist  Church  in  South  Weymouth,     his  wife,      a pianist  and
organist,       was  making  her  influence  felt  musically  throughout  the
town.           She was a talented musician with a high standard,    manifest

not  only  in  her  playing,    but in her  teaching  and in  the  musical

from  Boston,       and  the years  that  she  spent  there  in  South  Wey-

East Weymouth is justly proud of C. Will Bailey,   who,   at seventy
years of age,    is  still an acceptable singer and is in his fifty-third year
of almost continuous service in the White Church (Congregational)
of  East Weymouth.         The first  music he remembers he heard,    when,
sick of a fever,    as a little  boy,   he sought to go to  sleep because the
doctor had said  that sleep would be better than medicine.       But the
constant  barking  of  a  neighbor's  dog  annoyed  him  so  that  his
mother,       sitting  beside him,    sing-songed  these  words :
Go ' long,     go ' long,    you old bow-wow,
We do not want your noise.
We'd rather sing the pretty songs
Of little  girls  and boys.
The little boy with a fever was lulled to sleep by the united power
of music and a mother's  love.          He was at first  a boy soprano,     and
at  nineteen  his  real  voice began to  manifest itself,   having changed
from a high  soprano  to  a  deep low bass,   developing a range of over
two  octaves.                Like others  that I  have mentioned,    Mr.  Bailey  has
given  freely  of  his  vocal  ability,    receiving  great  pleasure  himself.
Besides  his  long service in the church at  East Weymouth,     he sang
in   the   First   Unitarian  Church  of  Waltham  and  in  the  Baptist
Church at  Weymouth Landing.       This last  service was through the
generosity  of  the late  Marshall  C.  Dizer,     who engaged at his  own
expense  Mrs.  George Baker  (Alida  Dizer) ,     Mrs.  Ellen  Drew,     La-
Forest  Lincoln  and  Mr.  Bailey.        My sister,    Angie  M.  G.  Lund,
played  the  organ.           I  remember that  summer well,     and an anthem
they repeated  several times by request,    in which Mr.  Bailey had a
notable  solo.            It  was by the late  Eugene V.  Thayer,     an organist
and  teacher,       under whom some of us had  studied,    and the  words
of Mr.  Bailey's  solo were :      " My Shepherd is  the living God,    I  know
no  craving  need. "    Mr. Bailey's  singing of it  was authoritative and
convincing.                That  last   statement  is   not  surprising   when  Mr.
Bailey  tells  you that his favorite quotation is :       " Music is  the only
art  that  can  calm  the  agitation  of the  soul  and put  the devil  to
flight."
From  the  Pine  Tree  State,     which,     as  you  know,    has  produced
many great  singers,    three brothers  came to Weymouth in the early
part of the nineteenth century.        They were descended from  Francis
Baker,     who came over in the " Planter"  from England in 1635 and
settled  in  Littlefield,     Me.         There  were,     in  all,      nine  brothers  and
sisters,        and Ashford,    William K.  and George S.  Baker came here.
Ashford  was  already  married,     his  wife being Julia Ann Holmes of
Augusta,       Me.            William  K.  married  a  daughter of  Peter  Cushing,

Both  Mary Ellen and Emma Jane were fine  singers.             I  say this
as the unanimous opinion of those who knew them,   for  Mrs. McIn-
tyre had married and left  Weymouth before my day.        I  know that
Mrs.  Pierce had a fine  voice,    because I  heard her in her middle life
and can easily imagine what it  might have been.     Julia  (Mrs.  Lin-
ton)  had three daughters;      Edith  (Mrs.  Hart)   possessed a fine  con-
tralto  voice,       was  a  well-known  singer  before  her  marriage,      and,
her  husband's  death  occurring  not many years  after,    she  returned
to  public  life  and is  well  known as  a  teacher  in  New York  City

the singer for whom several of his vocal compositions were written.
Alice,     the  second  daughter,       has  a  sweet,     clear  soprano  voice  and
studied and sang as a girl.          Little Enid,   born in the old Tufts house
on  Commercial Street  when the family  occupied  it,    now woman-
grown,     ought to sing  if she follows the family tradition.
Of Elliot  C.  Pierce,   who married Mary Ellen  Baker,    more later.
Of their  children,    the  son,      Will,      seemed  to  manifest  no  special
musical  ability.         The daughter,    Kate  (Mrs.  W.  E.  Thayer)    was
many years  a supervisor of drawing in the public schools  both of
Boston and Brooklyn,    N. Y.,    and is  an artist  and teacher of ability.
Her son,      Elliot  Pierce Thayer,    now in college,    turns  many a good
penny as a member of an orchestra.          Ayounger daughter of Elliot C.
and Mary Ellen Baker Pierce,   Madge (now Mrs. Alexander Barnett) ,
spent some of her early life  on the stage where her skilfull dancing
exemplified  in rhythm her musical temperament.
Both Mary Ellen and Emma Jane Baker sang at the Universalist
Church,       but at one time Mary Ellen  and her husband  (Elliot  C.
Pierce)    were  members  of  a  rather   wonderful  choir,      singing   in
Trinity  Episcopal  Church,    then  newly  organized  in  Weymouth.
The late  Edward Avery was one of  the basses,     Lewis  Pratt  sang

before my day of musical enjoyment,   but all who heard them agreed
that  their  music was very  fine.      In the  nineties,   one time  at  my
father's  home on Commercial Street,    Mrs.  Pierce and some others
were  present  when we were  trying  over  some  old  church  music.
We all  sang,      and Mrs.  Pierce's  voice,    even then,    gave  no  contra-
diction  to  her  reputation  for fine  singing.      One anthem  we sang
was  " Come,        Holy Spirit, "  by Warren,    with  a soprano  solo  and  a
soprano and tenor duet,   in which my father joined.     It was thirty
years ago,    but I have not ceased to  remember it .

The  third   brother,        George  S.,    married  Caroline  Binney  (her
father ,        Silas  Binney,    sang in the old  Union  Church choir) .            Their
eldest daughter,   Ella (now the widow of Willard K.  Richards) ,    was
an  early  woman organist  in  this  part  of  the  country,       thorough,
painstaking,     a good student  and an excellent  reader.       She  played
in Hingham at  the  Old Ship,   at  the  Union Church in South Wey-

always  had  a  reputation  for  her  musical  ability  and  attainment.
Hattie (now the widow of Mason Bachelder)  sang for years in the
Congregational choir,    taught music in our public schools,      and has
been an artist  of considerable ability,    both in oils  and water colors .
Willing and executive by nature,   she has coached and put on many
an entertainment  in  the  village,    proving  her directive  as  well  as
her  musical  ability.       George Herbert,    the son,    besides  having skill
as  a musician,     a good  voice  and interpretive  power,    has  followed
out his  artistic  inheritance,   turning to interior  decorating,     because
art,      after  all,     is  not confined  to any one field,   but finds  expression
in  the beautiful way of doing things.        He married Edith Humphrey
of East Weymouth,    and their  daughter  Hazel has  a voice so beau-
tiful   and  promising  that  when  she  sang  before  Melba,      the  diva
urged her  to give  up everything but music,    and to study pianoforte
and voice and study hard because the girl had a fortune in her voice.
Up near  the  Baptist  Church,    some time in the seventies,     Calvin
Baker was making,     repairing and playing violins,    and Nellie Baker,
his daughter,     was the  first  woman violinist  I  had ever seen.
Preaching at the Baptist Church was the Rev. William C.  Wright,
a fine  musician,     and  one  who probably  knew more about  music
from  a  professional  standpoint  than many in the  town who were
earning  a  livelihood  by music.         Not entirely  to  the satisfaction  of
his   congregation,     he  had  some  wonderfully  interesting   musical
Sunday nights at his church.            The Baker father and daughter,   with
Mr. Wright at the piano,  played trios  from the old masters.           Israel
Daley  brought  his  violin;     his  son,   John  Daley,    was  playing  the

organ in  the  church  at  that  time,    and a daughter,     Minnie  (Mrs.
Charles  Bailey),  was singing  alto  in the  choir.        The late  Chester
Shaw,     the man with a wonderful voice,   more like  a woman's  than

Mr.  Wright's stay was not long,   but before he left  town he gath-
ered about him in a singing school a group of people who liked  and
respected  him and admired his  musicianship.        My father  took me
with  him,        and  I   was  put  among  the  altos,      sitting  beside  Mrs.
Eleanor  (Smith)   Holmes  and the  late  Miss Jane Clapp.         We had
some good things that winter.        For the first  time I  began to appre-
ciate what part-singing meant,   -the balance of  the alto,     the  true
meaning  of  the  bass,       and  why  the  tenor  was  sometimes  called
counter.                As  a relaxation  in the  intermission,      Mr.  Wright  would
seat  himself  at the  piano,   and,     throwing  back his head,      with  its
snow-white hair,   sing and play to us some song of his own choosing.
I  remember this :
In the downhill of life,  when I  find I'm declining,
May my fate no less fortunate be,
Than a snug elbow chair can afford for reclining,
And a cot that o'erlooks the wide sea.
That he had a good  voice,      I  feel  very  sure;      that his  style  and
enunciation were excellent,      I  am positive.
In  the  list  of  North Weymouth singers  were  Elizabeth  (Dizer)
Tirrell  and Anne (Dizer)  Canterbury.         They were the daughters  of
John Dizer and his wife,    who was a French,    and there is  record  of
the Frenches also singing.            Their brother,    Marshall Dizer,     married
Delia Denton,     of a musical family,   and the youngest child  of that
marriage,        Alida,    now Mrs.  George W. Baker,     early displayed  more
than usual  musical  ability.         She was given  a most liberal  musical
education,      and  easily  became  a musician  of whom the  village  of
East  Weymouth and the  town at  large  were justly  proud.              Pos-
sessed  of a most pleasing  personality and giving generously of  her-
self   and  her   musical  ability,      while  she  has  moved  away  from
Weymouth,     she is certainly not forgotten by her  native town.
Mention was made of  her as singing at  one time in the quartet of
the  Baptist  Church,      where  her  father  was  a  prominent  member.
Besides  that,     she sang for  years  in  the Methodist  Church  of  East
Weymouth,   at the Old Ship in Hingham,   and in several other places.
She  taught  pianoforte  very  successfully  in  East  Weymouth,     and
to-day  is   a  power in  the  musical  circles  and  in  the  Professional
Woman's Club of Boston.          She belonged to that generous group who
gave unstintingly of their  best  to  Weymouth,    and who helped  to
build  up the  fabric  which  is  the  warp and woof  of  this  chapter.
If  I  am not  mistaken,     Mrs.  Baker  made her  singing  debut at  a
concert in the Baptist Church in Weymouth.       One of her numbers

Mrs.  Baker had a clear,    ringing  soprano voice,    rather of the dra-
matic  quality,       always  sweet,        always  true,       and  she  was  always
pleasant  and obliging when called upon.         Was there a concert  to  be
gotten up?   Ask Eva Baker.          Was there a funeral?      Probably Eva
would sing.             No money was  paid  for  such  funeral  music in  those
days,     and no one was refused.      Many a time when I was attending
the  high  school  in  Weymouth,   my father  called  me out  to  sing

Alphaeus  Bates played  the organ in  the  Union Church of  Wey-
mouth and  Braintree about 1860,   for  my father " took lessons "  of
him about  that  time,     previous  to  the  Saturday evening  choir  re-
hearsal  at  the church.        His father was Frank Bates,     a great  choir
leader  and  organizer  of  singing  schools  in  the  early  nineteenth
century.              Alphaeus  Bates  married  Hannah  Smith,     whose mother
was a  Cushing,   descended from David Cushing  (see Eleanor Smith
Holmes  and Lewis E. Tilden) .       He was a thorough musician,    sing-
ing  and  playing  well  with  his  daughter  Mary,      afterwards  Mrs.
Lyons  of  Brockton and with her forming a part of the clientele  of
the Arion- Cecilias,     of which more later.        Mrs. Lyons is  a contralto
and thoroughly musical as becomes  the daughter of  such a family.
Ayounger daughter,   Anna,    years after,    studied pianoforte with me,
and  used  to  be considerably  amused that  her  father  taught  mine
and  I  was  teaching  her.
A matter  referred  to  earlier which still  puzzles  the writer is  the
fact that,     with a paid music teacher  in  our public schools,     a matter
of  perhaps  forty  years'      standing  in  Weymouth,    there  has  been  a
proportionate  decline  during  those years  in  the available  material
out  of  which  church  choirs  are  made.             My father,       Simeon  W.
Gutterson,       his  predecessors  and  his  immediate successor,    had  no
difficulty in obtaining  a large,    though a changing,  volunteer chorus
choir.               Such a thing  is  now becoming almost an impossibility.          Is
it  a foregone conclusion,     or is  there a remedy?    About thirty years
ago,    in  order to  have any assured singing in the country churches,
it  became necessary to  pay one singer,   at least,    usually a soprano,
and  Miss  Bessie  Bates  of  East  Weymouth,     though  a contralto,
was one of  the  number.         I  think her first  position was at the Uni-
versalist  Church in Weymouth Landing,   where her  fine  singing was
a  great  feature.            Her  coming was much talked  about.           Of  Wey
 - 389 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                867
mouth  ancestry,    we felt  not only justly  proud  of  her,     but  quite
complacent  to claim  her as  ours.            Other churches  were obliged  to
follow,      and  I   think  within  ten years  from that  time nearly  every
church  in   Weymouth  was  paying  at  least  one  singer.        What a
difference  from the voluminous records  of the early chorus  choirs
in  the first  part of the nineteenth  century!      And no soloist  and no
quartet  can  ever  sing  the  wonderful  old  songs  that  we  used  to
hear.
The  Bicknells,      an  old  Weymouth  family,    were  musical  in  all
their   branches.             Stephen  and  two  brothers,       men  older  than  I ,
possessed  fine  natural  tenor  voices,    and were in great demand for
concerts  and  entertainments.          Stephen  married  a Miss  Pertillow
of  Weymouth,   herself a musician.         Of their  two daughters,     Viola,
the younger,     is  the owner of a remarkable contralto voice.          Under
the  teaching  of  Miss Gertrude  Edmands of  Hingham,      Miss  Bick-
nell  came dangerously  near  to  being  a great  artist,     that  danger
having  been  averted  only  by her  attention  to  her  duties  as  a
teacher  in  the  Boston  Public  Schools.           (Of  the  Bicknells   more
later.)
There are many branches of the Blanchard family in Weymouth,
and  I   think  all  are  musical.           Nathaniel  Blanchard  married  Susan
Maria  Hunt.                Their oldest  daughter,     Susan,    was  one  of  the most
thorough  and painstaking  pianoforte teachers  Weymouth has  ever
seen.             In my childhood  Miss Susan Blanchard and a cousin of hers,
Mrs. Rebecca Hunt Thompson,   were teaching about all  the children
of Weymouth Landing and East Braintree who studied  pianoforte.
Miss Blanchard had much the  larger class,    as Mrs. Thompson pre-
ferred spending what time she could devote to music on an advanced
grade  which,        I  am sure,     better  satisfied  her  musical  aestheticism.
Miss  Blanchard  was busy from  early  morning  Monday until  her
Saturday night  choir rehearsal,    and  to  study with  her meant that
one  surely  had  something  to  carry  away
way from one's  lesson,      for   I
don't  think  she  ever  absolutely failed  with  a pupil.       I  know what
she did for  me,    and whatever musical ability I may have displayed
and  all  musical  attainment which  I   ever  achieved  had its  founda-
tion and beginnings in the hours that were spent under her tutelage.
To  this  dispassionate  tribute  many now  living  would  gratefully
subscribe,    and scores passed on,  in their day must have paid her the
same loving  testimony.      She was a power,    and her works  live  after
her.
Her  sisters   all  sang  and  played.        Lizzie,    Annie,     Carrie,        Nellie
and Alice,        all  in  turn,    were  members  of the  Union  Church  choir,
and their  brother Will sang  a heavy bass.        He and his  sister  Alice,
the youngest,     alone  survive  that  large  family.     Alice  sang  almost
before  she  could  talk,     and  possessed  a  sweet,      flexible  and  high
soprano  voice.       Although  she  was younger  than  I,     we were  in  a
small set in high school,   and had the " Pinafore" craze,   Alice singing
" Josephine, "  Wallace Leonard (his  mother was a French),    " Ralph, "
Annie Pratt,    " Buttercup," with Grace Baker,   " Hebe, "  and Charles
 - 390 - 
868                   WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
Garey " Captain Corcoran."     We practised and sang and had a good
time  at  the  various  houses.         One night,      I  remember (it  came out
afterwards   that  the  clock  had  stopped  while  we  were  making
candy) ,    considerably after  1  A.M. ,     a group of apprehensive children
we were called  children in  those days      hurried  out and  to  our
homes under the cold midnight sky,   wondering just what reception
awaited  each.              The Blanchard's  was  a thoroughly  musical  home.
There  were  two  pianos,    an unusual  thing in the country in those
days,    plenty of music for eight hands,    and three or four daughters,
already   skilfull   musicians,       presided   over  by  our  acknowledged
priestess  of  music,      Miss  Susie.          Besides,     all   sang,    for  they  were
true Hunts.
Miss Evelyn Blanchard of North Weymouth was also one of Miss
Susie's  accomplished  pianoforte  pupils.            I  think  she  was  younger
than I ,    but evidently a better  student,    for her numbers were much
harder and therefore came later on the recital  programs which used
to be a musical feature at the closing of the study season,    and were
held  in the lecture  room of the  old  Union Church.           We all  waited
and listened with fascinated  pleasure  to the  " hard "  pieces  Evelyn
could  so  seemingly easily perform.         It was at one of  those  recitals
that  I  attempted my first  presentation  speech.        We had collected
money to give our beloved teacher a black walnut music rack,    and,
as  the  oldest  boy,     I  was selected  to  present  it.             Over  and  over  I
had studied  the four lines  my mother had written  out for  me,     and
over and over I  had said them to her.       But when I came to  speak
them to  our teacher they were not there.      However,    that gracious
lady,     taking the cabinet from my trembling hands said,     I  hope with
as much truth as grace,  " It is  very unexpected,   and I  am very much
obliged."
Louise Blanchard,   the daughter of Isaac and his wife Ruth Willis,
both of  the Landing,   was a schoolmate and friend of  my mother's,
and sang and played,  the family owning one of the few pianos of the
fifties .              The last years of her life  were spent in Haverhill,   but when,
in January,      1917,    I laid  my mother to rest in the village cemetery,
an hour later  the body of  Louise Blanchard was placed not far from
that  of  her  schoolmate of  long ago.       Somehow it  seemed comfort-
ing and less  lonesome that those two old friends should be left  there
together.
With a modesty which certainly has a commendable side,    neither
Mr.  Stephen  C.  Burgoyne  nor  his  sister  Addie  (Mrs.  Charles  H.
Chubbuck)    has  furnished  me much data  regarding  their  musical
work  in  Weymouth.         East  Weymouth,      however,     well  remembers
the musical  life of their mother,    Mrs. Augusta Burgoyne  (she was
a daughter of the late Stephen Cain),   and honorable mention of her
may be found in  the records of the Wesleyan Society.        Both brother
and sister  were  students  of mine,   and their  public  career  was  as
satisfactory  as  were  their  student  days.            Stephen  played  in  the
Methodist  Church  for  years  tunefully  and well,   bringing  out  skil-
fully the tones of that fine  organ.          It was at his instigation that the
 - 391 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                869
instrument  was  thoroughly  overhauled  a few  years  ago.              It  still
stands a monument to the effect of the softening hand of time upon
both wood and metal.         From the writer's  point of view,   it is  such
an unwise  thing  to  replace  a  reclaimable  piano  or  a  mellow  old
organ with  a modern instrument.         The church organs  in  Europe,
many of  them,   are hundreds  of  years  old,    and carefully  repaired
and restored as occasion requires.         That is why the American,   when
he  listens  to  their  tones,    finds  a musical uplift  he does  not  always
experience in his own country,   and likewise it is why the  European
visitor  here gets the impression of noise  rather than of the softened
blending  of  pipes  and reeds  to  which he  is  accustomed  at  home.
This may be a new thought to some reader,   but let me refer such to
the better known fact that the value  of  a violin  increases  with  its
age.             The analogy,   however,   holds,   and it is no slander to the artisan
of to-day to  refer  regretfully to the better and more skilful  work of
his  predecessor  of years  ago.
Further to illustrate :      About thirty years ago it  became necessary
to  make  some  repairs  on  the  tiny  one-manual  organ  in  Trinity
Church,       Weymouth.           It  was my good fortune to be allowed  to  do
that work,      and as  an illustration  of the decadence at least  of  ma-
terials  in  this age,   so valuable was the old metal removed to make
room  for  new  pipes,                 as  the  old  ones  had fallen  from  place  or
become crushed by their  own weight,                  and  so  inferior  was  pipe
metal of thirty years ago,   so full  of alloy as compared with  that of
the day when the  organ was first  built,    that when the repairs  were
completed  the  committee,      if   I   remember  correctly,      found  that
they were not in debt to  the  repairer,    but that he was in debt  to
them because  of the superior  value  of  the metal  removed.              This
fact  Mr.  Burgoyne well knew,   and he was able to take advantage of
his  knowledge when he rebuilt  the organ in the Methodist Church.
Mrs.  Chubbuck,   I think,   is still playing in the Universalist  Church
in  North Weymouth,    where she has been for some time,    and where
her  smooth devotional  organ playing  must be a most helpful  part
of the whole service.        Mrs. S.  C.  Burgoyne was a Garey of the well-
known musical family,   and the Burgoyne children  could  not  help
being  musical  if  they tried .
From  the  earliest  days  the  Burrell  family  and all  its   branches
and  descendants  have been  famous  as  musicians,    particularly  as
instrumentalists.         It was my fortune when but a boy to come under
the teaching of one of that family,    the late William Burrell,     organ-
ist,        pianist   and  clarinetist.             How he  could  play!       And how  he
wanted me to  learn  to  play!      But I  had not then the vision,    my
point of view being that of the average ten-year- old boy.       I wanted
the fruit without tilling  the ground.      But he was both painstaking
and patient,     and the seed sown was not all  lost,    though I  certainly
did  not  then  appreciate  my  opportunity  in  studying  under  so
versatile  and musicianly an instructor.           I  was conscious even then,
however,    that I  loved to hear him play,   and what a treat it  was at
the concerts  of that day to  hear  Mr.  Burrell and his  talented wife
 - 392 - 
870                  WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
(Ida Young)  perform together.         I  still  have a song  that used to be
on their  programs:
Who's at  my window at break of day?
Minstrel or lover?     Say,    Oh say!
How they could sing!     And how the tones of the clarinet used to
follow  her  voice!     Mr.  Burrell played the organ,     first  at  the White
Church  in  East  Weymouth,     and  then  at  the  Porter  Church   in
Brockton.                He must have been  one of  the  first  among the many
Weymouth musicians  to  carry the musical torch outside his  native
village.           A son  of  these  two  famous  people,     Carl,   still   living  in
Brockton,     has  earned quite  a reputation  as  a  pianist,     as,      indeed,
how could he help doing with such an inheritance and the environ-
ment of a musical home?
My generation and the one next older were thrilled,    entertained
and enthused by such as  William  Burrell and their  work,    but like
all  of  us who are passing,    to  this generation we are scarcely even a
name.               But we have had our day,   and with the egotism of middle
age,      which  is   certainly  not  the  egotism  of youth,     standing  here
with so much of life behind me,    I  say with deliberation,      " We did
our work well.  "
From another branch of  the  Burrell  family,    in  the  last  half  of
the  last  century,     came a  well-known violinist,     Oliver  Burrell.             A
daughter,       Mrs. Sadie Burrell Plaisted,   sang both in Weymouth and
in  her  present  home,   California.          Another  daughter,       Mrs.  A.  L.
Flint,     is   a musician of  the  type of which the writer  is justly proud
because she  and many like her have lived their useful lives  contrib-
uting  of  their  best in the town in which they were born.            As she
says  of herself,    " I  remember my first  public  appearance  in  North
Weymouth when I was eight years old.       I played and sang a song.
As my father,     Oliver  Burrell,   used to play the violin,                          he
took me along to play the organ,   for  there were only a few pianos
in  those days,    and often he carried our own little  organ with us. "
She was  organist  of  the  First  Unitarian  Church  of  East  Wey-
mouth from  1888 to 1907,   playing at the services held in the after-
noon.                  In the  meantime she  became organist  for  the  Old  North
Church in  1890,    playing  at the morning services  there for  twenty-
three years.           Mrs.  Flint's   reason  for  resigning  at  the  Old North
Church was that she was getting  too  old  to  play,   but fortunately
for  the  cause  of  music  in  Weymouth,      when,     later,        the  Baptist
Church wanted her,  she went there,    staying two years,     and at  the
present  time is  at the  Universalist  Church in Weymouth Landing.
Mrs.  Flint  was a pupil of Alphaeus Bates,     and her contributions  to
me for  this  article  have been most valuable,    and  I  gratefully  ac-
knowledge  them at  this  time.           Mrs.  Flint's  daughter,       now  Mrs.
Evelyn  Sherman  Philbrook,     began  her  singing  career  while  her
mother was organist in the First  Church of Weymouth.
Miss  Fannie  Burrell  (see  Frank Vining),  daughter  of  John  P.
Burrell,      played the organ that was destroyed by fire  in the Metho-

Another musical family in  East Weymouth,   the Nathan Canter-

Associated  with Merton Allen,    mentioned earlier in this  chapter,
were two musicians  pleasantly  and familiarly  called  Bennie Clapp
and  Sammie Denton.          Both  were instrumentalists  and both  came
good- naturedly to  augment the old folks'   concerts and sings which
were being given in various parts of the town at that time and later.
Mr.  Clapp was a brother both of the late James Henry Clapp and
of  Edwin  Clapp,     and  got  his  musical  ability  from  his  mother's
family.             Mr.  Denton was a cousin of Mrs.  Marshall C.  Dizer,      and
married  Minnie Bicknell  of  East Weymouth.       She sang  for  years
in  the  Baptist Church choir,     and her daughter,    Clara,   was training
to be an organist at the time of her early death .
Of the  Clapp family,    Miss  Emma,    a daughter of Augustus and
Eleanor  Richards  Clapp,    was  perhaps  the  most famous.              Emma
Clapp's  maternal  grandmother  was  Elizabeth  Hunt,     and  people
now living  agree that she was the most famous of the famous Hunt
family.          She had a sweet,   pleasant and well- trained voice,   and sang
for years  in the Union Congregational  Church.         Her name will be
found in the list  of that society's  chorus.           Elizabeth Hunt married
Elias  Richards,    and a son of theirs who left Weymouth and located
in  the South before my remembrance was said to have been a good
singer  and  a  finished  musician.         One daughter,    Eleanor,      became
the mother of Emma Clapp.        Another daughter,    Susan  Richards,
pleasantly known as  " Sunie,"  for  many years was one of the choir
in the Universalist  Church to which reference has been made.          She
sang all  the oratorio solos of which she was especially fond.
Miss  Emma Clapp,    besides  possessing  a  soprano  voice  under
considerable cultivation,    taught piano in  Weymouth and played for
many years  at  the  Universalist  Church,     though  at  a  much  later
date than the sixties of which I  have been speaking.        Mrs.  Eleanor
Smith Holmes (see the Cushing family)   and her brother Dana were
members of  that choir,    having come at  that time from the  Union
Church.                The Baker brothers,      William  and George,    were also  in
this  choir.             They were music lovers  if  not great musicians.            There
was also  a  rather noted soprano whom I heard only in middle age
at old  folks'      concerts  and general sings,   but who was said  to  have
possessed  a  rather  famous  trill;     she  was  Mrs.  Ann  (Williams)
Smith.

Though  not  Weymouth born,      Miss  Ella  Clark  and  her  brother
Fred came to  Weymouth with their sister,    the wife of the late Judge
Louis  A.   Cook,      and  contributed  greatly  to  South  Weymouth's
musical prestige in the late nineties and early part of this century.
Miss  Clark  had a fine  contralto  voice  under excellent  cultivation,
and her brother Fred was the possessor of an equally fine and well-
cultivated  baritone voice.           They were heard always  with  pleasure
in  both  concert  and  church  work,     and  were  great  assets  in  the
musical life  of South Weymouth.
It  has  happened  curiously  that,     in  my recollection  of  musical
Weymouth Landing,    the churches in turn have had their high-water
mark musically.         Of the Union Church and its  famous choir more
will be said as we discuss the various  branches of the Hunt family.
With  the  organization  of  the  Universalist  Church,     and owing  to
some disturbances  in the Union Church at that time,   several  very
prominent families  rallied  around the new creed.         Their music in
the  early  sixties  reached  a very  high  standard.         Mrs.  Elliott  C.
Pierce  (Mary Ellen  Baker)  and Miss Mary Ellen  Cook (later Mrs.
George Field,    and still  later Mrs. Alburn Sterling)  were young women
and in a sense rivals,    though I am sure they were then and always
friends .            At one time when a cantata  was given  two evenings  in
succession,       one young lady sang the title  rôle  the  first  night,    the
other  following  the  next  evening.       Had there  been  an  unhappy
emotion in either of their hearts over that affair,   I am sure that those
arranging  the program would not have permitted the thing  to  be.
Elliott   C.   Pierce,     later  Major  Pierce,     and  the  husband  of  Miss
Baker,     sang  the  leading  man's  part,    and I  am sure  that his  sister
Fannie must have coached  it.
The  Cushing  family  were  also  old-time  singers.            The  name  of
one  ancestor,      Thomas,     will be found in the membership list  of  the
Union Singing Society.       He had one son,    David,   who,    perhaps,    was
better known musically than any member of that choir.     A daugh-
ter,       Rachel,      became Mrs.  Darius  Smith,     and her daughter Eleanor
(Mrs.  Eleanor  Smith  Holmes)    possessed  a  fine   contralto  voice,
studied  under  Julius  Eichberg  at  the  Boston  Conservatory,     and
with  her  brother  Dana  was  a  famous  singer  in  the  Universalist
choir  half  a century  ago.       A brother  of  Rachel,    Simeon,    was  the
father  of  the  late  Mrs.  Francis  Tilden  and the  grandfather of the
talented and lamented Lewis E. Tilden of whom Weymouth Land-
ing  was justly  proud.         Another daughter of  Simeon,      Mrs.  George
Porter,     was the mother of Dr. Charles I.  Porter now of Canton,   and
Susan Hunt Porter,     now Mrs.  Walter E.  Thompson of East Brain-
tree.            This  brother and sister  (the  Porters)  could not escape being
musical,      for  their father's  mother was one of the famous Hunts,     so
that  they possess  a double musical inheritance.         Susie  Porter  sang
in  the Old North Church of Weymouth.
Mrs.  Elizabeth  F.  Leavitt,      formerly  of  Weymouth  and  now a
resident   of  Brooklyn,       N.  Y.,       was  Elizabeth  Cushing  before  her
marriage.          Her son Charles is  prominent as a musician in Brooklyn .

He plays  the  French horn in  the Mecca and Kismet Shrine  bands
and in  the Grotto band.         He also  plays the viola  in  a string quartet
of  the Aurora Grotto  of  Scottish  Rite Masons.           He has also  been
an instructor  of musical classes  in the Y.  M. H. A.,     and plays  the
' cello,    the banjo and the violin.
Abbie Pratt,     Mrs. Dennison of Wollaston,   the daughter of Frank
Pratt,    was born and raised  in Weymouth,   for you will find  her an-
cestry  mentioned  in  the  annals  of  the  North  Weymouth singing
societies .             She began her musical career in the high school,   where her
natural  ability  and some cultivation  made her  a great help in  the
school singing of that day.         With her pleasing manner and pleasant
voice she sang for some years at the Old North Church,     and,     in her
new home,     I  sincerely hope that she is singing now.
The very first  reply to my advertisement in the " Gazette, "  three
years  ago,      was from Mrs.  William  DeNeill in  regard  to her father,
the  late John Viger,    a musician in the Civil  War.         She told me that
he marched away from Weymouth with his company and was never
heard of  again.        He left  a wife,     a daughter Nellie and a son John,
who died in his  school days.          Nellie became Mrs.  DeNeill,     and she
has had an interesting  family of children  who were all  little  folks
together.                    Joseph  studied  violin   at  the   Quincy  Music  School.
William came to me for pianoforte lessons.          Both boys were musical,
as,         indeed,      were  the  whole  family,     and  before  long  Joseph  and
William  were  busy  around  the  neighborhood  playing  pianoforte
and violin for  concerts  and dances,   and playing well,   too.            William
afterwards  became  assistant  United  States  consul  in  Japan,     and
now occupies  a similar  position.       By the operation  of  the  law  of
inheritance,       Mrs.  DeNeill's  grandchildren should be musical.
Over  fifty  years  ago  Howard  M.  Dow,    then  one  of  the  most
prominent  organists   and  accompanists  of  Boston,      purchased  a
house  in  Weymouth  Heights,     then  North  Weymouth,      under  the
eaves of the Old First  Church,     and made his home there for about
thirty  years .               Many of the young people of that day studied with
him,     and,    being a prominent Mason,   and a great friend of the late
Col.  B.  S.  Lovell,   who,   I think,  at that time was commander of the
G.  A.   R.  in  Weymouth,    his  influence  musically  was  tremendous,
and it  is  impossible to estimate what he and the musical friends whom
he  brought  to  Weymouth  accomplished  in  the  cause  of  musical
appreciation.              Never shall I forget the first  time I saw him,    because
it was my first  big concert.         It  was exactly  May 30,    1873.    I  was
not yet nine years old,   but my father took me to the old Town House
for what proved to be the first  and last  time I  ever heard Adelaide
Phillips ,    and the first but not the last time for me to hear and meet
Henry  Clay  Barnabee,      Mrs.  Helen  Carter   (Mrs.  George  Hardy
Wright)    and  Howard  M.  Dow himself,   for  all  three  later  became
my close  friends.         Never  have  I   heard  anything  that  surpassed
Adelaide  Phillips  as she sang a little  " Laughing  Song."    Such rip-
ples,   such manner!       My eyes  must have bulged.      In the  interlude
she  toyed  with  a tiny  bouquet  which  seemed  to  hang  from  her
 - 396 - 
874                 WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
little  finger.             Forty- seven years  after,    when it came in  the way of
the Winslow Associates to  buy some of the effects  of the departed
diva,     there came into  my possession,     as  one of  the  Winslow Asso-
ciates,     a little  gold filigree bouquet-holder with a chain and ring for
the little  finger which probably glittered before my eyes  that night
in 1873.
Besides  the  singers  mentioned,      Mr.  Dow brought  to  those  con-
certs   Camilla  Urso,     then  probably  the  foremost  violinist  of  her
day;     the  famous  Mendelssohn  Male  Quartet,     a  combination  of
four  artists  who,    in the late  seventies,    did  a great deal of Masonic
work;        Mrs.  J.   H.  Long,    who was Geraldine  Farrar's  first  teacher;
Alta Pease,    a famous contralto of the early eighties;   Avon D. Saxon,
a baritone ;         Mrs. Jennie Patrick Walker;      C. N.  Allen and his  wife
(Mrs.  E.  Humphrey Allen) ,                    great persons  in  my day who over-
whelmed me,     hero worshiper as  I  was,   when I  met them from  time
to  time under  Mr.  Dow's  hospitable  roof,     for  I   became  his  son
Arthur's  chum at  school in the late  seventies .
Personally,        I   cannot pay too  great  a tribute  to  the memory of
Howard M.  Dow.           It  was he who gave me my first  engagement in
Boston.               I  played for him the last Sundays in June and the first  in
September while he was away filling  an engagement at the so-called
"Beacon Street Church "  at Nahant,   a position he held for twenty-
five consecutive years.        At the Church of the Unity on West Newton
Street,    where I went first,   there was Charles R. Adams,   tenor,    fresh
from a long engagement as the only American tenor at the Vienna
Opera  House.             Mrs.  Lizzie V.  C.  Richardson  was  soprano,     Annie
Lord (the late  Mrs.  Harry Hooper) ,    alto,    and either Harry Cornell
or  Jacob  Benzing sang bass.         I  shall  never  forget  those  Sundays
and  how kind  those  big  people  were  to  the  twenty-year- old  boy
from the country,    and how big of Howard M. Dow to give me and
other  Weymouth people the  chance to  appear in  Boston,     for  Mrs.
Fannie  Wilde  Preston,     born  in  Weymouth Heights,   sang  at  the
Unity after she was widowed;      Mrs. Ellen Drew of East Weymouth
followed her ;        Percy F.  Baker (see Eva Hender,    Mrs. Willie  Baker)
sang  one or  two  seasons  at Nahant;     and though for  the moment
my memory fails  me,     I  am sure other Weymouth men and women
were the  recipients  of musical favors  at  Mr. Dow's hands.
Never did  I   hear  Mr.  Dow say an unkind word about anybody,
but many pleasant things,    and when,    in  1884,    his  brother,      Deacon
Dow of the South Baptist Church,    South Boston,    asked him about
a young man of good character to  play the organ for their  church,
he said,      in  reply:      "John Gutterson is  just the man if you  can  get
him, "  and they could get him,   and I went to Boston at five times the
salary little  Trinity Church was paying me.           " If you can get him! "
What tact,     what infinite kindness and forethought!      He was always
like that.           In the next few years Weymouth Heights was pleasantly
known as  the home of Howard M. Dow,    and as he at that time was
rivaled  as  an organist  and accompanist perhaps  only by the late
B.  J.   Lange,      it  meant a great musical lift  for Weymouth.         I  could

WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                875
write fifty  chapters as my mind runs back so  pleasantly over those
evenings  at  Weymouth  Heights.         The  talented  daughter,        Lilian
(now the widow of  Albert  W.  Dow,    her cousin) ,    and Arthur  M.
Dow,    her  brother,    were both musical (they could hardly help being
so) ;     they both sang,   and the two younger children sat and listened .
Not least  in  the  happy company was the late  Mrs.  Dow herself,
whom her friends  lovingly called " Mollie."    She was not musical,
but oh,    so charmingly critical of the noises we younger people made
in the name of  music.
Susan  Josephine  Dowse  (see  Mrs.  Albert  Edward  Avery)   was
the daughter of Susan Loud and the late Benjamin Dowse.            Susan
Loud  was  the  daughter  of  the late John  W.  Loud  and  his  wife,
Susan  Torrey,     who was  a distant  cousin  of  Chief Justice  William
Howard Taft.          Susan (Mrs.  Loud)  and her sister,   Deborah Torrey,
were the granddaughters of  Dr. James Torrey of  South Weymouth,
and they,    the two girls,  were famous singers in the Old South choir.
Of the  Loud family,    from  which  Mrs.  Avery is  descended,     more
later.            All  branches of that family are musical.
Mrs. Avery taught singing,  played the organ in Trinity  Church,
Weymouth,     and sang in  the  First  Universalist  Church,     Columbus
Avenue,         Boston,     familiarly  known  as   " Dr.   Miner's  church, "   a
church which has always been noted for its  fine singing.         She was a
concert singer of note up to and after her marriage to Albert Avery.
The children of this marriage,    besides inheriting the musical ability
of  the  Torreys  and the  Louds,      also  derived  advantages  from  the
Averys,          the  Hunts  and  the  Stetsons.         Susan  Avery,       the  oldest
daughter,     is  a cultured soprano;     her voice is  said to be like her ma-
ternal  grandmother's.       She has sung for  fifteen years  in the Union
Church,     and has always been interested  in musical work.            Stetson,
the second son,  took the musical course at Harvard College,      and is
a solo  violinist  and  orchestra  player  as  an  avocation.            Dorothy,
the youngest child,   is  a graduate of the New England Conservatory
of  Music in  organ,    with  a four  years'     course  in  composition,      has
taught  piano,     played  the  organ  in  church,     and  directed  choirs.
Such a family record of musical activity gives notable support to the
theory that musical ability is best developed by training in the home.
Mrs.  Ellen  Drew,   mentioned above,    was not,    I  think,      a native
of Weymouth,   but she resided here for a good many years,   delighting
the various  churches  and organizations  of our town with her  fine
presence,       her  beautiful  contralto  voice  and  her  always   correct
rendition.           Besides singing in East Weymouth regularly and at  the
Church of the Unity with Mr. Dow,   and at the Baptist  Church in
Weymouth  (see  earlier  mention)   she  sang for  a while  at  the  Old
Ship in Hingham,   and during many longer and shorter engagements
elsewhere,     always pleasing  and always gracious.
Mrs.  Cynthia Reed Ellwell of South Weymouth,    daughter of the
late Dea.     Josiah Reed,   one of the members of the South Weymouth
Singing Society,    has been a singer of note and a valued  member of
the  Union  Church  choir,     South  Weymouth.

When  Charles  G.  Estabrook  became  owner  and  editor  of  the
" Weymouth Gazette, "  he brought his  wife,      Flora  D.  Estabrook,
who had been a valued member of the South Baptist choir in South
Boston,      where both Lewis Tilden and I  afterward played,     and the
choir  at  the  Weymouth Baptist  Church  were  very glad  indeed  to
welcome her  into  their midst.          It was at  least  sixty years  ago,      and
she  brought  an element into that organization which had its  influ-
ence.          She read well,    sang every note at the rehearsals,    and helped
to  elevate  a rehearsal  into  a  period of accomplishment as well as a
social  good  time.         My father was the chorister  in  those days,      and
I know how much he appreciated her singing and her co- operation.
Mrs.   Augusta   Hobart,       afterwards   Mrs.   Albert  Sanborn,         Mrs.
Joseph  Richards,     and  later   Mr.  John  Daley  were  the  organists
both on the little cabinet organ and later on the big new organ which
took  its  place  somewhere,      I  think,    about 1872.    Mr.  Daley,     who
was a son of Israel A. Daley,  the violinist,  mentioned in the records
of  the  Wesleyan  Singing  Society,     and  as  playing  in  the Baptist
Church of Weymouth,   married  Miss Augusta Estabrook,     and both
died  early  in  life  of that  New England scourge,    consumption.             A
younger   daughter,       Lilian   Estabrook,      distinguished   herself  as  a
singer,       but  married  young,     becoming  Mrs.  Whittemore  of  South
Hadley  Falls.          With her family and her mother,   who is  still  living
at a great  age,  she spends her summers on the  North Weymouth
shore.
In the records of the South Parish are the names of three Sprague
sisters  who sang,    and of one,    Eunice,    who played the organ.            It was
left  to  Fannie,    the youngest of the Sprague sisters,    to  add to Wey-
mouth's  musical  prestige in the  city  of  Boston.            Fannie  Sprague
Foster,      the  wife  of  Charles  Foster,      also  of  South  Weymouth and
also a singer,    sang soprano for years at the Hawes Unitarian Church
in  South  Boston.          Part  of  that  time  I  was  playing  at  the First
Baptist  Church,    corner of  Broadway and F Streets .          George Bunt-
ing,       the  bass  at  the  Hawes  Church,     a man older  in years  and in
musical  experience  than were we two from Weymouth,    told  me at
that time that he considered there was no finer  church soprano in
Boston than Mrs. Foster,   and he knew of no one whose phrasing was
more correct  and musical.       Middle-aged as  I am,    it  is  exceedingly
difficult  to  avoid being personal  and even garrulous  as  I  think  of
those days and those people.         We were serious and we did our work
well,   which statement has a familiar sound,    as I  am sure I have made
it once before in this chapter,    and while we sang or played for money,
I  know that we also sang and played with a love for the profession
we had espoused.         Mr. Foster sang a good deal in his native town,
and  was  an  excellent  church  choir  tenor.         They  have  a musical
daughter  and  are  grandparents  now,    but they have  been  strong
factors  in  musical  Weymouth.
South Weymouth,     the home of so many fine singers,   at one time
boasted  four  famous girls  who formed  themselves  into  a  quartet
than which I  have heard none better,  -Fannie Sprague Foster,    the

late  lamented  Mrs.  Fobert,     Nellie  Nolan (Mrs. John Carroll)   and
Annie  Dean.             How those  girls  could  sing,     individually  and  to-
gether.              Miss Deane is  still  living in Weymouth,    where,    besides  her
wonderful  singing,   she  is  busy  with  dramatic  entertainments  in

the  first  (I  think Mrs. Foster was the second)   of a large company
of us who,      in the last decades of the nineteenth century,   left  Wey-
mouth  every  Sunday  morning  to  fill   positions  in  Boston  choirs.
There were Howard M. Dow,    Arthur Raymond,  Josie Dowse (Mrs.
Albert  Avery) ,     Lewis  Tilden,     myself,      Frank O.  Nash,       E.  Walter
Arnold,     for a while Mrs. Eva Baker,    Mrs.  Drew,    later  Percy Baker,
Annie Estelle  Powers (Mrs.  Will  Hollis) ,    Lewis  Canterbury,     Helen
Allen  Hunt,      Porter  Pratt,     Stephen  Pratt,    Jennie Barker  Worster,
and more I  am sure I shall think of as  I take them up individually.
One of  the most accomplished musicians  in the near-by town of
Rockland,     Mass. ,    is  Mrs.  Mildred Garey French  Fish,    the wife  of
Arthur L.  Fish.       Her father is  Stephen French,    of a musical family ;
her  mother  was  a  Garey,     with  both  Rice  and Bates  inheritance.
Her maternal grandfather,    John Hutchins  Garey,    was an old-time
singing  school  leader,    and conducted choirs  in  Fairhaven and New
Bedford.                Mrs.  Fish's Aunt Sarah became Mrs. Quinn,     and  was a
famous  soprano  in  East  Weymouth in  the  eighties  and  nineties.
Among Mrs.  Fish's  brothers and sisters  are  a sister,    Lucinda Salis-
bury French,    who has studied the violin,   and two brothers,   Samuel
and Malcolm,     who have sung with Miss French for many years  in
the  South Weymouth Universalist  choir.        Of Mrs.  Fish's  cousins,
one,       Dr.  William  P.  Pratt,    is  an organist,    and another,     Ruth Mil-
dred Pratt,    has for four years been organist of the Porter Methodist
Episcopal  Church,    East Weymouth.
Mrs.  Fish's  musical education was obtained in her own town and
in Boston.          She played in the Universalist churches of Hingham and
South Weymouth,   and at present is organist on the memorial organ
of  the  First  Baptist  Church  in  Rockland.        She  is  pianist  of  the
Mozart  Instrumental  Quartette,    and for  several  years  has been on
the music committee of the  Rockland Woman's Club.          She formed
the Rockland Choral Society,  and has been president of it  since its
organization  in  March,    1921.
Weymouth has  often  been enriched musically by the coming  of
some  family or  families  who have  brought  their singing  members
with  them.           There  came from  the  State  of  Maine,   that home of
notable musicians,      a family by the name of Fuller,    and each of  the
three  daughters  in  turn  became  the  mother of  a  notably  musical
child.
One of  the  Fuller sisters  married James Hender.            Their daughter
Eva has been referred  to  under her maiden name,   and also  as  Mrs.
William  Baker.            Without doubt she was a great singer,     for  I   never
knew or heard of her not making good musically in any of the varied
lines  of  musical  work which  she  essayed.        She must have  been  a
natural  reader,   for in about ten years of rehearsals,   while  I  was also
 - 400 - 
878                   WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
a member of the Baptist choir,    Eva,    as we always pleasantly called
her,      was ever the  leader  and always far and correctly  in advance.
With  infinite  patience  and good  nature  she  sang and sang  again
until all knew their notes.     What tons of unappreciated effort  she
and those like her freely gave!     Her son Percy has been mentioned
for   his  wonderful  baritone  voice  and  his  excellent  professional
work.
Another Fuller girl married Woodbury P. Sanborn.         He possessed
a rather  good tenor voice and loved music.       Their daughter Nellie
played  and  sang  almost  before  she  could  balance  herself  on  the
piano  stool.             She  taught,     and,   in  time,      became  Mrs.  Fred  Sulis .
Until the time of her death,    a few years ago,    she was actively inter-
ested in the musical affairs  of the Baptist Church,   played the organ
for a number of years  (as did also her daughter,   Mrs. Frank Bryant)
and was one of that large group to whom I  have referred who gave
so  freely  of their musical inheritance and of their more or less  val-
uable  time.             Her  cousins   Eva  Hender  and  Laura  North  (Mrs.
Ingham) ,    a daughter of the other Fuller sister who married Leonard
North,      were also  members of  that altruistic company.
The  Sanborns  had  a  son,       Walter,     who  manifested  no  musical
ability.            He married  Etta  Thayer.         Their son  Russell,    to be men-
tioned  later,      perhaps  inheriting  the  Fuller  musical  inclination,      or
perhaps,     more likely,   influenced by Aunt Nellie's constant musical
atmosphere,       has  made a name and  a fame for  himself,    of which
more later.
The Garey family  in  East  Weymouth,     the late  Captain  Garey,
his  son,        Minot  T.  Garey,      his  daughter,     Mrs.  Stephen  Burgoyne,
previously  referred  to,    and another son,   Dr. Charles  P.  Garey,    who
married  Grace,      a daughter  of  the late  William T.  Baker,    were  all
choir  singers.        Dr.  Garey attained quite  a reputation  as  a soloist,
possessing  a good baritone voice  and a pleasing manner.         Wallace
M.  Leonard,       whose  mother was  a  French,     Dr.  Charles  I.   Porter,
previously  referred  to,      Dr.  Garey and the writer  were members of
a quartet that sang during our high school days.
The  Baptist choir in the eighties,  when under the leadership  of
Mr.  E.  W. Arnold,   was augmented by three members of the Graves
family  of   North  Weymouth,     Frank  singing   tenor,     Mr.  Samuel
Graves,     bass,     and the daughter,     Miss Cora,    being a soprano.          They
were all  musicians  as  well,    a combination which does  not  always
follow,       for  I  know musicians  who are  not  singers  or  performers,
and we are obliged  to listen to many who are  not musicians.        They
brought with them at times a very fine  contralto,    Mrs. Sarah New-
comb,      and  I  have pleasant and still  vivid  recollections  of duets by
Mrs.  Baker and Mrs.  Newcomb.
In  Milford,       N.  H.,     in  1795,     John Gutterson was born.            He mar-
ried  very  young,      Martha  Sawtell,      two  years  his  junior,      and  the
couple  were valuable members of the choir in the village in which
they lived.               Of their  twelve children,   two daughters were in great
demand at the country funerals  round about,    and often drove miles
 - 401 - 
WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS                879
to sing their simple duets,  sometimes even for  strangers,    who knew
of them simply as " the singing Gutterson girls. "
Two brothers,    Joseph,    born in 1814,    and Simeon,     1832,      came to
Weymouth.             Adaughter of the former,   Flora ( Mrs. William Alden) ,
is  said to have possessed  a wonderful alto  voice.         She sang in  the
Baptist  Church  until  her  marriage  and  her  early  death  in  1869.
Another daughter,    Frances  ( Mrs.  A.  W.  Preston) ,   sang soprano in
the same church,   and,   going to live in Brookline after her marriage,
became  quite  a power in  the  Baptist  Church  in  that  town.             A
granddaughter  of  Joseph,     Alice  (Mrs.  Edward  Senior) ,      born  in
1869,     has played considerably in Weymouth Landing,   and has also
been organist both at the Episcopal and Universalist Churches there.
My father,     Simeon W. Gutterson,   sang in this town for forty years
with no training but that afforded by the singing school.          He pos-
sessed  a good voice,    however,    and loved to use it.        In his last illness
when he was confined  to his bed,    as  I sat at the piano  in  another
room,     he would sing  tenor to  his  favorite hymns until the pianist
would have to improvise long interludes  in  order  to  recover  com-
posure enough to go on with the hymn singing.
My musical  life  is  too well known and has been so kindly con-
sidered  that  I  do not venture to add any word to  it  at this  time.
I  played both  at  Trinity  Church  and in  the old Union Church of
Weymouth and  Braintree,     at the South Baptist Church in Boston,
at  St.   Barnabas'     Church  in  Falmouth,     at  the  First   Parish  Uni-
tarian  Church,   South Street,     Brighton,    the  Central  Congregational
Church,      Newtonville,    Unity  Church,    North  Easton,     and the  Old
Ship,         Hingham,       twenty- nine  consecutive  years,    with  settlement
work Sunday afternoons,    a Sunday evening chorus in  East Milton
for  about eight years,    and five years at the Ford Hall meetings  on
Beacon  Hill.               There is  scarcely  a church or hall  in  Weymouth in
which I  have not appeared,   and I  have taught children from all  the
villages of my native town.     Perhaps  I  am not a prophet,     but  my
own town has honored me most profitably.        My sister Angie ( 1873) ,
Mrs.  Charles Benson Lund,   sang contralto here and played the organ
for  many years,   and  I feel  sure,    is  pleasantly remembered  for  her
music.            She is  still helpfully at work in her home in Groton,    near
New London,      Conn.         Not feeling  herself too old to learn,    she is  at
present  taking  a weekly lesson  in voice.      Margaret  Deland  said,
"When you feel  that you are too  old to do a thing,   do it, "  and by
that same token,   Mrs. Lund is  still working with her music.          The
writer is  having a pleasant summer singing tenor in a choir of eight-
een persons in St. Andrew's Protestant Episcopal Church,    Hanover.
Charles  F. Gutterson (1876)  had a much better voice than his older
brother,      and enjoyed  the environment to  which  a  musical  father,
brother  and sister  contributed,    but apparently he has  lacked  any
strong musical inclination.

account  of  a funeral  at  the  Sacred  Heart  Church  in  Weymouth.
Mrs.  Hanley  is   still   the  efficient   organist  of  that  church,      and

It  would  seem quite  in  order  here  to  remember  the  late  Dan
Haley,       Weymouth born  and  bred,    who came  into  prominence,         I
think,       as  he  sang,    black-faced,    at  an entertainment given by his
church.          At one time,   it  is  said,     Harry Lauder was paid  more per
minute  than  even  such  singers  as  Melba,     Gadski  and  De Reske.
It  takes  ability to be funny on the  stage.         Haley's fun was always
clean and his  work was  artistic.          I  do not see why he should  not
come under the head of  Weymouth musicians.

Although the details  are  not clear,     I  remember well  the  singing

have been older than I,   for they sang prominently before I had the
least  claim to anything like a musical life.           Years later,    about 1895,

one Sunday for us at the Union Church.      She was a good singer and
had a pleasing  personality.

Elias  (2)   was the father  of  Ebenezer  (3) ,      Edmund (3) ,     Rebecca

James Turner (4) .         Edmund Aubrey,    recently  deceased,     expressed
the  Hunt  artistic  talent  with his  brush,    and left  behind  him  an

Russell (4) ,     my schoolmate and friend,   can play anything,     -   organ,
piano,      ' cello ,      what not?    And he put the crown  upon his  artistry
when  he  became  the  husband  of  Helen  Allen,     and,      as  has  been
mentioned before,     her  maternal grandmother being a Hunt,    joined
together  two branches of that large and musical family.
James  (4)   passed out all  too soon for  us to know what he might
have become,   but I do not think that we who love music will soon
forget  that  small  figure with a violin  tenderly held under his  chin,
almost  oblivious  of  time and space,     and those long  slender  fingers
which  brought  such  music  from  the  instrument  of his  love  and
devotion.
Rebecca  (3) ,          a daughter  of  Elias,       married  Charles  Thompson
and was herself a musician of great note.          She has previously been
referred   to  as  teaching  cotemporaneously  with  her cousin  Susan
Blanchard  (5) ,     a daughter  of Susana  Hunt  (4),   and it  has  been
said  of  her  that  there was almost  no score for  pianoforte or  organ
she could not read.       As a technician probably no one in Weymouth
surpassed  her  in  her  prime,   and she  was  the  notable  teacher  of
Emma Clapp (5) ,    and of Lewis E. Tilden,   that musical descendant
of  the David Cushing family.        Although she was not a great singer,
both she and her husband,  who sang bass,   with her father  (2)  for  a
tenor,      and her cousin " Sunie"  Richards (4)  singing alto,    had many
home musicales in which only the best music was given.

New England stock  who value opportunity and make the  most of

at  one time,    and,     being  exceedingly  musical,    but  most dissimilar,
their  numbers  on my musical  programs  were  always  moments of
great  interest,    and the  query would be,    " Which one is  the better
player ? "     But  with,     I  think,     a just  valuation  of  the  situation,
I  used  to  say,      " They  are  so  unlike,    they  cannot be compared.
They  are  both  '  best.  ' "    Edwin  (5)   married,     for   a  second  wife,
Addie McQuinn,    a famous soprano of  Weymouth,    and at that time
singing  in  the  Union Church of South Weymouth.            This is a record
of  the  Hunt family,    about whom the  remark was  made,     by the

late  Rev.  Jonas  Perkins,    that  no matter how small the congrega-
tion might be on a particularly  rainy Sunday morning,    the singing
would be all  right  because the choir was composed almost entirely
of one family,     and they  " Sang like  the birds. "
It  is   recorded that during the forty-two years'    continuous life  of
the Union Church choir (1817 to 1859)  there was only one break in
the Hunt leadership,   and that was entirely due to political lobby-
ing.          I  have heard my father say that during the time that Richard
Hunt (3)  was organist there,   my father singing  tenor at that time,
he had never heard  smoother organ playing.     But my father was
religious,       and the  smooth  organ  playing  would have  appealed  to
him.          Still,       that organist was a Hunt.
Later,       and  notably  when  Susan  Blanchard  (5)   played  there,

I can see that old choir gallery now.           Its acoustic properties could
not have been worse,    and it was left  for  me (1893-98)   to buy and
install  a set  of screens which not only broke the blinding morning
light as it  fell  upon the congregation,    but also  acted as  a sounding
board  to  concentrate  and throw out into  the  audience room with
some semblance  of unity  the  voices  of  my choir.          These  screens
were cheap and homely,   and were only meant to be an experiment
and temporary,    as various changes in the interior of the church had
been under consideration at the time when the  fire  came.
Of the  North  Weymouth Hunt family,   the  record  shows  that
one member,   A. F. Gilbert  Hunt,    was several times president of the
North Weymouth Singing Society.        His daughter Mercy,   a contralto
singer  of  ability  and cultivation,    writes  me that  her  father  sang
all  his life,    and that he used  to say he would rather sing than eat,
because singing rested him.       As a young man,  he also was a member
of the band,   playing B-flat  cornet;      but singing seemed to appeal to
him more.            He sang  in  both  Peace Jubilees,    led  the  choir  in  the
Old North Church for many years,     was at one time engaged by the
Union Church of Weymouth and Braintree to lead its Sunday school

singing,      and conducted  several  singing  schools  in Weymouth and
Hingham.             In the early days  of temperance  reform  he sang with
the Good Templars,    and was one of the old-time " singing-by-note "
musicians,     as  the daughter writes :
"
" I  doubt if  he could  have been caught by any music that was
put before him so  far  as  reading  was concerned.       Chorus singing
was something of a fine  art  in  those days.          Another great enjoy-
ment of those singers was serenades.         I have heard him tell of groups

know it was my father's life to sing,   and it  sometimes seems to me,
she adds,     " that few people nowadays love to sing as those old- timers
did.            The whole French family,    as you know,   were great singers  in
those  days.              It  was  mostly in  church,     I  suppose,     but  they  sang

it,     there was with them all great pride in being able to sing by note,
in good time and with expression. "
Mrs.  Pauline  Bicknell Osgood and her brother Stephen  Bicknell
were the children of an older sister of  Mr. A. F. G. Hunt;    therefore
they were Hunts.        Mrs. Osgood had a wonderful soprano voice and
sang both at  Christ  Church,    Quincy,     and in the Codman Church,
Dorchester.              She also sang at both jubilees,    and when over eighty
and  blind   (because  both  she  and her  brother  succumbed  to  the
family infirmity)  she was asked to sing  " The Star Spangled Banner "
at a Fourth of July gathering.     Not only did she sing the song,   but
she  also  took the  B-flat  with  a coloratura  that  many a younger
singer  might envy.         Truly,   " There were giants in those days. "
A South Weymouth girl,   Jennie Hocking,   became a member of
the Hunt family when she married John Hunt,   and she has had a
notable  career .              She tells  me that during thirty-four years she  has
served  long  terms  as  organist  in  each  of  three  churches,      among
them  the  Union  Church  of  South  Weymouth.        She  has  taught
pianoforte  twenty- eight years,    and for the last  ten years has given
almost  her  entire  time  to  professional  accompanying,       both  for
vocal  soloists  and for  several  members  of  the  Boston  Symphony
Orchestra.               As becomes  a woman whose mother was a Loud ( for
that  name,     in  Weymouth,    is  only a synonym for  music) ,      she  has
conducted  choruses  and  coached  light  opera.         One of  her  three
children possesses a fine  baritone voice,    another is  a good performer
on the 'cello,    and a third  has that rare  musical endowment which
enables  him to  play a composition  through  after  having  heard  it
once.
There  came from  Boston in the early  eighties  a  Mr.  Kimberly
who had been a bank- note engraver and a portrait  artist,      and who
had sung tenor in  Trinity  Church,     Boston.           Music was evidently
his  hobby,      for  he drew around him a little  group who met weekly
for  practice  in  Old English  glees.          Susie  Allen  and  Mrs.  Richard
Lloyd Hunt sang soprano,   " Sunie "  Richards (daughter of Elizabeth
Hunt  Richards)    and  Josie  Dowse Avery  sang  alto,     Lewis  Pratt
sang  tenor,     and Mr. Kimberly and John J.  Loud sang bass.            Lewis

Tilden,    not more than seventeen or eighteen,   played the piano,    and
probably,     under Mr. Kimberly,   laid the foundation for his musician-
ship.             I  presume there  were others who sang with them at times,
but I  am sure only of that group.           Mr.  Kimberly's was a great in-
fluence musically,  and his friends worked seriously as well as happily.
The organization was one of the musical landmarks of its  time.
Mrs. Frank B. Lewis  (who was Elsie Litchfield) ,  according  to her
own statement,     inherited  her musical ability  from both her  father
and her mother.         Her father's  family was the more musical of the
two.            Mrs.  Lewis studied first  with Mrs. George Baker,     then with
Helen Allen Hunt,   and finally with Clarence Hay.      She began as  a
church singer in the First Methodist Episcopal Church at East Wey-
mouth,       singing also in Bethany Church,    Quincy,    and in the Union
Congregational Church of South Weymouth,   which society retained
her services  after  its  union with the Old South  Church.          She con-
tinued in that position until 1900.
David P.   Lincoln  of  East Weymouth was a violinist  of note  in
the last century.        His name will be found in the lists of instrumental-
ists  earlier  in  this  chapter,    and he was often  to  be found,      also,      a
visiting  artist  in  the group gathered  at  the  Baptist  Church  and
elsewhere in  Weymouth Landing .
LaForest  Lincoln,    not related  to David P.  Lincoln,    was a  tenor
of  note,     singing  in  concerts  and in churches  throughout  the  later
years  of  the nineteenth  century.         His  mother was a sister  of  Otis
Nash and aunt to  Frank Otis  Nash.         He also  was related  to Mrs.
Ruth Cushing,   a prominent singer in the seventies,   about whom I
have been able to  find  little,    though  I  remember having heard her
sing at one of the concerts given in Clapp's Hall under the direction
of the late Henry Webb.
All the members of the Loud family appear to have been musical.
Both South Weymouth choirs had members by that name,   and the
Landing was widely known as the home of the musical Loud family.
John W. Loud,   whose first  wife was a Torrey of South Weymouth,
by that marriage,    through his  daughter Susan,    became the grand-
father  of  Susan  Josephine  Dowse (Mrs.  Albert  E.  Avery) .              His
second wife was a Blanchard,    a sister  of Nathaniel Blanchard who
married  Susanna Hunt (3) .             There were,    I  think,     five  children  of
that  second  marriage,  -Sarah,   Alice (the widow of Alexis  French
of  Brookline) ,    a daughter who died young (Josie,   I think) ,     John J.
and Annie.            Sarah was a wonderful woman,    efficient  and executive,
musical without being a musician.       She played and sang in Sunday
school  and in entertainments,    but was,    perhaps,    overshadowed  by
the greater proficiency of her brother and youngest sister.         I  have
heard Mrs.  French sing  alto  in the Sunday school  quartet,    but  I
do not think that she ever rated herself  as  a musician.
The late John J.  Loud was one of the finest men I  ever knew,   broad
and tolerant  in his criticisms,    manifesting a keen  sense of humor,
withal an excellent citizen and a kindly neighbor -would there were
more such !        He possessed a perfectly natural baritone voice of great
 - 408 - 
886                   WEYMOUTH  MUSIC  AND  MUSICIANS
range.              I  do not think  he  ever  had what is  called  voice  culture,
though  I  am sure that he attended many singing schools,     and that
there  was  singing  in  the home,   for  his  father,     the  late  John  W.
Loud,      was a  member of the old Union Church choir.         Mr. John J.
Loud himself  conducted  that  choir  for  twenty years,     and it  used
to  be my great  pleasure  to  be invited  to sing  with  them at  the
extra  services  which,    from the  eighties  on,     were  an  outstanding
feature of village  life .
What rehearsals we used to have in that old church!      There would
be those whom I  have mentioned as having sung at the time when
Miss Blanchard played,   the younger ones,    like  Helen Allen,    Annie
Hunt and my sister Angie,   sometimes my father,   too,    with various
other members of the Baptist choir,    Dana Smith and Mrs.  Eleanor
Smith  Holmes from the  Universalist  Church,     and Susie Allen and
Mr.  Chessman from  the  Episcopal  Church.          Up near  the  organ
would be Merton Allen with his  B- flat  cornet,     Nat Hunt (4)  play-
ing trombone,    and other instrumentalists.         There would be pleasant
greetings between us,   and then Mr. Loud would hand around music
with a special  and personal word for  each  one.        Perhaps  he would
speak  a  few  words  in  explanation  of  the  music,   then  he would
knock on the casing of the organ for attention,    all would rise,  the
organ would begin,   and our rehearsal was under way.
One Thanksgiving Day,    I  remember,   we sang " Jehovah's Praise,  "
from " The Modern Harp, "  a devotional and yet triumphant chorus
in     time.                A rather  florid  duet in     time for two sopranos,      occurs
in it,     which was assigned to Mrs. Worster and the late Miss Emma
Clapp.             I  realize  I  am middle aged, but it  seems to me no one sings
now.            Those union services were of great benefit to the community,
and I  wonder could such a thing be possible to-day?
The  second  Mrs.   Loud  having  died  when  her  children  were
small,           the  widower  married  for  the  third  time  a  Mrs.   Martha
Vickery,       who  has  been  referred  to  as  a  daughter  of  Rev. Jonas
Perkins .             She  brought  with  her  her daughters  Helen  and  Emily
and her son  Frank  Hermann,   who later  became a famous Boston
physician,      now retired.         Mr. John J.  Loud,   marrying,     chose Emily
Vickery,       the daughter of his  new stepmother.       Of their eight chil-
dren,   two died in infancy.
John Hermann,   the oldest  son,   born in 1873,    has already become
the  leading  organist  in  Boston,   if  not in New England.           With a
musical  inheritance,    and  possessed  of  the  desire  to  work  and  to
become a master,    he has been a most ardent student at home and
abroad.              His  first  teacher  was  his  father's  younger  sister  Annie.
Of her more will  be found herewith.       A thorough musician herself,
an organist,     pianist,    theorist and composer,   she poured her musical
soul  into  the  education  of  that  boy,    so  stimulating  his  love  for
music that,   before he went abroad to study with a French organist,
Guilmant,     then the  organist of  Holy Trinity in the French capital,
John Hermann Loud,    although  young,   was already a performer of
some note.            After  four  years  abroad,    he returned  to  take  up his
