EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
Read before the Society Jan. 5,   1881,   by GILBERT NASH.
There have been many families  resident in this  town for  many
generations,        numerous,      important  and  highly   respected,        whose
blood  yet  runs  in the veins of large  numbers of our citizens,    but
whose names are only known upon our records or  in the memories
of  the present  generation,                remembered  among those  who have
passed  away;      and it  may not be uninteresting  or unprofitable  to
glance briefly over their  history.      Many localities  are still  called by
their  names,      and cherished  remembrances still  linger  in  the tradi-
tions of their descendants.
AGER
Following the alphabetical order,   the first  that comes to our notice
are  the  " Agers,"  as  they are  now called,   but known in  the early
days as  " Eagers. "    The earliest  upon our records  is  Richard,    who
married  Abigail,    eldest  daughter  of  Lieut.     Jacob Nash,    by whom
he had six children,   the first  of whom was born the last day of the
year  1698.    The homestead of  the family  for  several  generations
was  situated  in what is   now wild  pasture  land,   about  two miles
south from the village  of Weymouth Landing,   between Front and
Summer Streets,   about equally distant from each.        The members of
the family have removed from time to time to other towns,   so that
now  the  name is  a strange  one where it  was once  honored  and
esteemed.               A descendant,      Solomon Ager,     of  the  third  generation
from  Richard and Abigail,    is  now residing in Boston,   in the enjoy-
ment of good health,    active and vigorous,    at the age of eighty-four
years.          The homestead long  ago passed  into  other  hands,     and the
family in Weymouth is  among those that were.
BADLAM
The next  name to  be mentioned  is  that of the Badlams,     living
for  many years  upon the estate  at the  corner  of  Green  and  East
Streets,    and extending along the former street  to the  eastward for  a
considerable  distance.          The  stock  still   exists,      but  under  other
names,     being  connected with many of  our old  families  who gladly
claim  the relationship.       The first  whose record  appears  is  that  of
William,      with  Mary his  wife,   who  had  born  to  them  Dec.  20,
1693,       a son  named for his  father,    followed  on July  14,     1699,     by
the birth of a daughter bearing  her mother's name.         Four genera-
tions  have lived  and died in this  town,    the last of the name dying
 - 466 - 
944                     EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
during the present century.         The place fell  into the hands  of  Dr.
Tufts,     where it remained until the death of the last  survivor of his
family,    when,     upon the breaking up of that estate,    it  was purchased
by Charles  Humphrey.
BEAL
Athird name is  that of Beal,   which first appears in the family of
James and Sarah,   who came to Weymouth from Hingham or  Co-
hasset,      probably  the  latter,    soon  after  the  beginning  of  the  last
century;   the birth of their daughter Mary is  recorded as  occurring
Nov.  11,    1713.    For nearly a hundred years  they occupied an im-
portant  position  in  our town,   but they disappear from  its  records
previous  to  the  year  1800.    Their  home was located  upon  Front
Street,     about a mile and three- quarters southward from Weymouth
Landing,      and was afterwards  the residence  of  the late  Ezra  Reed,
Esq.            The present family of that name came into town about the
time the former disappeared .
BOLTER
Thomas Bolter was the head of another of the old families whose
names have disappeared from our records.        He came in among the
early  settlers,    and married  Experience Aldridge Oct.  16,     1660,     the
first birth in the family dating July 27,   1661.   They settled probably
in Summer Street,    just  beyond the half river,    to the west,     towards
the Braintree line.          The property passed into the hands of the Col-
sons ,       Thomas of that name having married a daughter  Mary Dec.
4,     1735.    Four generations  make up the sum of their existence  as
residents  of  Weymouth;     the name,   however,    was perpetuated  into
the present century,     Bolter  Colson,    a son  of Thomas and Mary,
before mentioned,     being well known to persons of middle age now
living  at  Weymouth Landing.      Ebenezer Bolter,    a son of the  first
Thomas,        married  Mary,     the daughter of  Gideon Tirrell,      the  pro-
genitor of all  of that name now living in town.
DRAKE
Next in  order are  the  Drakes,     not so numerous nor so long  resi-
dent as some of the other families  occupying a place in this  fellow-
ship,     yet  three generations  were well known dwellers  of the town,
from  its  early  settlement  until  near the middle of the  eighteenth
century,    Thomas,   the original planter,   and Jane,   his wife,    being the
parents  of  a  large family,   the births  of six of whom are  recorded,
from that of  Thomas,    the eldest,      March 12,    1659,   to that of Benja-
min,       the  youngest,      Jan.   15,      1676.    Their  property  was  situated
probably not  far  from the old tide  mill,    near the corner  of  Com-
mercial  and  Essex  Streets,      North Weymouth.          William,      the  third
son of  the original  Thomas,    married Sarah,    the daughter of  James
Nash,      Jr. ,     who gave to  their son James,   his  namesake,    the tide-mill
 - 467 - 
EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES                    945
property.              During  the third  generation  the name disappears,      the
family  removing  to  the  southwest,   settling  in Taunton and other
towns.
DYER
Another family,  and one of the most important of its time in the
town,       was  that  of Dea.     Thomas  Dyer,     who came to  Weymouth
probably  soon  after  1630,     where  he  married  Agnes,     daughter  of
William and Mary Read,    the latter  family having continued  from
that day to the present to maintain its  position as  one of the most
influential  in the town,   William being its  first  representative to the
General Court.          His wife,    Mary,   died in 1655,   the first death of the
Read name upon the town records.           The Dyers  located upon the
corner of North and Commercial Streets,    to the westward of King
Oak Hill,      where they continued to reside for four generations,    when
the last of the name in that family disappeared,   and the property
passed into  the hands of Samuel Humphrey,   Esq.,   in whose family
it remained for three generations,   and is  now owned by James Jones,
Esq.             This family has  numerous representatives  at  present  among
our citizens of  other names,    and the name itself  is  preserved in the
direct line in other towns.          The present Dyers of Weymouth are of
another and probably a distinct family.
GREEN
Following   these  are  the  Greens,     who  were  among  the  early
settlers,       their  names appearing upon the record April  28,     1658,     in
noting the birth of Joseph,   son of Joseph and Elizabeth (Whitman)
Green.              This  family  also  includes  four  generations  in  its  history
which covers a period of about a century.           It connects also by mar-
riage with many of the oldest and most important families,     among
which occur the names of  Whitman,    Richards,    Ripley,     Humphrey,
Tirrell,        Cushing,    Ford,     Pratt,     Kingman and  Torrey.          The latest
death upon the  record  is  that  of  Zachariah,    which occurred  Feb.
23,         1743.    The homestead  was  situated  upon Summer Street,     on
both  sides  of  the half  river,     the house  standing  upon  the  top  of
the  gravel  bank a little  to  the eastward  of  that  brook,     and some
ten or  fifteen rods to the north of the house lately  belonging  to the
Tufts farm,    which was the same estate.           The last of the family who
lived there,    tradition says,   was Ann,   who married Nathaniel Vinton.
The story further  states  that they lost  nine or ten children by an
epidemic,      and  became  so  disheartened  in  consequence  that  they
sold  their  home and removed to  another town.
GURNEY
The Gurneys were also  an ancient family,   Richard,    of Weymouth,
having children born to  him,    according to the record,    from 1656  to
1667.    The family also continues its  name for four generations,     the
 - 468 - 
946                       EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
last  survivor being Jacob,   who died in 1793,    when the name became
extinct  in Weymouth.         It is  yet green and flourishing  in  towns  to
the  south,        Abington  and  Bridgewater,      branches  from  the  main
trunk that had its  root in this  town.       Hobart's " History of Abing-
ton"  says that John was the original settler,    having sons  Richard,
David and Nathan,    the latter of whom went to that section.        Rich-
ard  settled  in  Weymouth,    but where,    it would perhaps be difficult
now to determine,    possibly on East Street towards Old Spain,     and
extending to Back River.         Quite early,  however,   the family removed
southward,      for about the year 1700 Zechariah,    the son of Richard,
owned the property  afterwards  in possession of his son Jacob,    and
located  on Front  Street,    the  line  dividing  the two parishes  after-
wards passing through it.         The son Jacob married Elizabeth,    widow
of James Richards,    and great-grandmother of the first  president  of
this  society.               They had no children,    and the property passed into
the hands of the widow and was inherited by her children,    a portion
ofwhich is still  owned by their descendants.        The estate was a large
one,     embracing some two hundred or  more acres.
KING
The  " Kings "  owned an estate  on Summer Street beyond those
of  the  Greens  and  the  Bolters,      probably  covering  that  property
afterwards belonging to James Richards.       They are one of the ear-
liest  families  that appear upon our records,   the birth of Mary,     the
daughter  of  John,    dating  June  15,    1639.    Four  generations  are
recorded  to  them before they disappear in the person of Hezekiah,
who died  in  1765.    This  was a notable  family of its  day as  their
intermarriages indicate.     Among these connections occur the names
of  Phillips,      Vinson,     White,      Hovey and others.      In the early days
of the town the farms at a distance from the shore of the bay,    and
now  accounted  of but  little  worth,    were  then  valuable,    and  the
owners  were of  the  substantial  class.            The variation in the impor-
tance of  these  places  indicates,   in  a measure,   some of  the changes
that have been going on in our local society,   in the manner of living
and in ways of obtaining a subsistence.           In  a deed dated Dec.  10,
1649,      Thomas Jenner of Charlestown sold to " Elder Edward Bates
and John Whitman of Waymouth,   one dwelling house in Waymouth,
(now in possession  of  John  King,)   two  orchards  and  twenty-one
acres  adjoining,     more or  less ;  "    possibly  the  same property  that
the  same family  afterwards  occupied.
LUDDEN
The name of Ludden occurs also very early,   even prior to that of
the  Kings,       James  Ludden recording  the  name of a daughter Dec.
17,    1636,    and it  is  quite probable that there were children older than
she.           Their property was situated in Old Spain,    and extended from
Great Hill  and Eastern  Neck to  Back River.        Benjamin,    a grand
 - 469 - 
EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES                    947
son of James,    " entered as a soldier  against the bloody Ffrench and
blondy  Murtherous  and salvage  Indians, "   and  was  killed  in  the
fall  of  1690.     This  family  also  extends  through  four generations,
the last  birth  occurring  Jan.  4,    1719,    and  is  recorded  as  that  of
Benjamin,    the son of Benjamin and Sarah.        It was also a prominent
family,   and one that enjoyed the respect of the community.          Their
estate was probably one of  the original  grants,     and like  many of
that class,     long and comparatively narrow,    laid out from the shore
of the bay and extending for a considerable distance  inland.            Con-
sequently we find many different  owners to  the land upon Eastern
Neck,    Grape Island,    Great Hill,    and so on through the whole extent
of what is  now Old Spain,    but thus far  no plan of these divisions
has been discovered.
PHILLIPS
Phillips  was  a name well known among our ancient  settlers  and
of  very frequent occurrence upon its  records.           Its  possessors  stood
high  in  town and  church,    and  they  were connected  by marriage
with many of the families  of the first  five  generations  of  settlers.
Nicholas  Phillips,   who died in  1672 at the age of sixty  years,      was
one of  the early arrivals.          But two of his  children  stand upon our
records as being of Weymouth birth,   those of Experience and Caleb,
born in  1641  and 1643,   although six  others  are  named in his  will .
Joshua,      the  eldest,     must have been born  previous  to  1635.    The
births  of  only five generations of this family have come down to us
upon the  record,     although  another  is  known to have resided  here,
and the  widow of  the  last  survivor  of  the  name died  only  some
dozen years  since  the widow of  Mr.  Ephraim  Pratt,     at  the age  of
more than one hundred years.        Adaughter,   her child by her former
husband,        William  Phillips,     Mrs.  Sophia  Newcomb,    died  in  Quincy
during  the  present  season  at  the  age  of  nearly  eighty- five  years .
The old  Phillips  homestead  was  situated  upon  Phillips  Creek  in
Old Spain,      and probably extended on both sides  of that stream for
a considerable  distance.         Here upon the  north bank was probably
their  original  settlement,     and very  nearly upon the  identical  spot
where Thomas Weston made his  short  tarry in  1622.  The present
family of the name are of only two generations date in  Weymouth,
although they may have sprung from the same source.
PITTEY
The Pitteys were always proud of their  name and descent,    claim-
ing  and holding  a place among the most influential families of  the
town.            They came with the early planters,     and for  more than one
hundred  and  fifty  years  retained  their  position  and  inheritance.
William,     and Mary his wife,   recorded the birth of a son,    John,    Jan.
28,     1638,     and this record is  followed by that of three other sons and
one daughter.         In this family we find a more extended line  reaching
to  the seventh generation,   the last  survivors dying within the pres
 - 470 - 
948                       EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
ent century and well known to persons  now living.         Their  home-
stead was located to the south of Great Hill,   and extended from the
shore for a considerable distance to the southward,    touching James
Ludden on the east and Samuel Torrey on the south.          It reached to
the water on the northwest of Great Hill,   and also covered a part of
Eastern  Neck.           Probably the General Lovell house,    as it  is  called,
on Neck Street,    just south of the Turnpike,   was near the site of the
original  home.         The property came into  the  General's  possession
through his wife Hannah,   who was the daughter of James and Han-
nah  (Reed)   Pittey.      This,   perhaps,    was the second dwelling of the
family,          and  is   now  occupied  as  a  tenement  house.       The  family
tomb,   standing on the north side of Bridge Street,   at a short distance
from it,     has been removed during the present generation.        The name
is  now wholly extinct in the town.
RANDALL
The patrimony  of John  Randall  extended from  the  water  side
southeast  of the tide mill on Mill Cove,   between the lands of the
Whitmans and the Burrells.        It lay to the west and south of King
Oak Hill,        with  the family dwelling probably  near  the  spot where
James  Jones,       Esq. ,     now lives,     in  North  Weymouth,    whose home-
stead  came into  the hands of his family  as the  inheritance  of  his
great-grandmother,    who was the daughter  of John and Susannah
Randall,       and  the  granddaughter  of  Robert,     the  original  settler.
Of this  family we have account of but three generations,    the family
of John and Susannah the latest,    consisting of nine daughters and
no son.           The last death of the family recorded in this town is  that
of John,    just mentioned,   and occurred Sept. 4,   1730.   The earliest
birth of a child of Robert upon the town records,    and the only one,
is  that of a daughter Mary,    who was born March 20,   1642,     and who
married  Abraham Staple.        They afterwards  removed to  the town
of Mendon,    in which town also resided her sister Hannah,   the wife
of  John  Warfield.        There were also  two  sons,    Thomas and John,
who lived in Weymouth for a time at least,   inheriting a part of their
father's  estate.          The present families of the name are not known to
be of this  line,  although they probably are descendants of the early
Weymouth stock,    returning  to  the original root.         The gravestones
of John and  Susannah  are  a little  to  the  eastward  of  the Tufts
tomb in  the Old North Burying Ground.
RIPLEY
Josiah Ripley came into this town not far from the year  1690,   the
birth  of his daughter Mary occurring  Feb.  18,    1695.    Four genera-
tions  of  the family are  recorded from that time to the close of the
eighteenth  century,       Eliphalet,      Jr.,      and  Rebecca  (Webb)     Ripley
having a family of eight daughters,    the marriages of five of whom
are recorded,    but there is no mention of a son,  and the name became
 - 471 - 
EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES                   949
extinct.            This family came in from Hingham and probably settled
in  East Weymouth.       The records,    however,    fail  to give much infor-
mation.           An entry  in  the  Suffolk  probate  office  mentions  Josiah
Ripley,       innholder,     of  Weymouth,    whose  son,   Josiah  Ripley,      Jr. ,
husbandman,    was appointed to administer upon his estate April 19,
1743.    This must have been the son of Josiah and Joanna,    the origi-
nal  settlers  here.          Mary Ripley,   the widow of the second  Josiah,
lived and died in an old house at the landing at Back River,    on the
western side .           The house was afterwards occupied by Mr. Silvanus
Holbrook.            She was the daughter of Capt.    John and Mary (Hum-
phrey)   Burrell,     and died  Dec.  14,    1802,    at  the age of one hundred
and four  years,    probably the oldest  person whose death was ever
recorded  in  this  town.           Tradition  says  that  at  a party  given  her
on  her  last  birthday she jumped  upon the  table saying  that  she
was four years old that day.        Very likely this was the inn of which
the  father  of her husband was the keeper,     and was the homestead
of  the  family  until  the removal of  the  later  generation  to  South
Weymouth.                No gravestone bearing  the  name of Ripley is  found
in  the Old North graveyard.          The last of this family,  the Eliphalet
before  mentioned,   removed  to  South  Weymouth,   the  daughters
all  marrying in that parish.      They lived a short remove above the
Four Corners,    at a considerable distance from Front Street,    to the
southwest,      in the field.
ROGERS                              1
Dea.      John  Rogers is  one of the most honored  names that stand
upon our record.         He was one of the ancient settlers,    and stood very
high in the town as well as in the church,   of which he was an hon-
ored  officer.        He died  in  1660.    The birth  of but one child  stands
to him upon the town record,    a daughter named Lydia,   born March
27,      1642.    His will,    however,    mentions  the  names of one son John
and four daughters:       Mary,   who married John Rane,    as  our records
have it;        Lydia,    the wife of Joseph  White;     Hannah,   who married
Samuel  Pratt;        and Sarah,  unmarried.         The son John was elder  of
the  Old  North  Church for  many years,    and died  in  1709.    This
family remained in Weymouth but two generations,   the latest birth,
that  of  Hannah,    the daughter of John and Mary (Bates)   Rogers,
being  recorded July 23,    1670.    Their homestead was  situated  be-
tween the properties of Captain Whitman and Mr. Nicholas Phillips ,
and must  have extended  from  near  the present line  of the South
Shore Railroad to Old Spain,  following the shore westerly from the
parsonage property.     Whether or not this  Dea.   John Rogers was a
descendant  of  him who perished  at  the  stake,    with  whose  large
family  the early  generations of this  century were so familiar  from
the pictures  in  the primers,    it  is  not easy  to  say,    since  all  of the
Rogers'      claim that honor and few of them are able to  prove it.

950                      EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
SMITH
No community could  probably  exist  for  any considerable  time
without  representatives  of the Smith family.      In very many local-
ities,    possibly in a majority,   they are the most numerous of any single
name.               Weymouth has  never been without them,   although  never
numerous;       nor has the same family continued its  history  through
all  of its  generations.           Our first  family of that name was an early
and  an important  one,    James,     and Joane his  wife,    recording  the
birth of a son,   Nathaniel,   as early as June 8,   1639.   No other child
is  accredited to them by the town clerk,    but an older son,    James,    is
mentioned in the father's will March 11,   1672-73,    to whom he gives
the  land  on  " Easter  Neck,    Great  Hill  and  Back  River  (formerly
James  Ludden's, ) "  besides  large  tracts  of  land in other  localities,
he to pay his sister Hannah Narramore £20.           There were also Wil-
liam  and Edward,  the births  of children  of whom are recorded  at
about the same time,    1639 to 1642,   perhaps brothers of James,    but
their  families  do not  appear to  have remained in town,    while that
of  James  is  represented  in  five  generations,     and  disappears  with
the family of Jacob and Mercy (Pratt) Smith,  who probably removed
to Abington about 1750.   Their homestead,   as indicated by the will
of James,      Sr. ,   lay along the southern base of Great Hill,    which was
called  from  their ownership,    Smith's  Hill,   and their  property was
a large  one.         The family  of  Rev.  William  Smith,     the  long- time
pastor  of the Old North Church,   and the father of three celebrated
daughters,    - Mary,      the  wife  of  Judge  Richard  Cranch,     Abigail,
the wife of President John Adams,    and Elizabeth,    the wife of Rev.
John Shaw,   -came in about the time or shortly before the disap-
pearance of the James Smith family,   while to succeed his line there
appeared  about  1780 that  of Lemuel Smith from  Roxbury.          The
present race is  not of the primitive stock.
STAPLES
John Staple was also  a very early settler in Weymouth,    the birth
of two children being recorded :       Rebecca,    Nov. 27,   1639,     and Jos-
eph,      Feb.  19,     1641.    There were besides these,   two sons,    John and
Abraham,         and  another  daughter,     Sarah,      who  married   Increase
Sumner,      her  sister  Rebecca having married  Samuel Sumner.           Few
more distinguished families  than those of the two daughters have
been known in the State.          Abraham married Mary,    the daughter of
Robert  Randall,    and removed to Mendon.          There are three genera-
tions  of this  family noted upon the records;    that of Lemuel of  the
third does not show a connection with those of the Johns' ,     Sr. ,      and
Jr. ,       although  he probably  belongs  with  them.          He died  in  1743.
There is  also the death recorded of Martha,  the daughter of Geofrey,
buried  Feb.  17,    1639.    Geofrey was perhaps the father of the elder
John.                The location  of  their  inheritance  is  hardly clear,    although
 - 473 - 
EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES                    951
incidental  notices  upon the Suffolk  Registry  of Deeds would indi-
cate that it lay to the south and west of the Dyers,   the Whites and
the  Burrells,       and  consequently  on the  south  side  of  Commercial
Street,       reaching,    probably,     and covering a part of the  town farm
on  Essex  Street.      The family soon became  scattered,      some going
westward and others to the south,   nor do their descendants appear
ever to have returned to their native town to reside.
TUFTS
Dr.  Cotton Tufts settled in this town near the middle of the last
century,       a  late  comer,    but one memory of whom the citizens  will
not  care  to  lose.         Among the  first  scholars  of his  day,    known and
respected throughout the whole land,   he was at the same time physi-
cian,    statesman and citizen;  one whom his  compatriots delighted  to
honor and of whom his associates had never occasion to be ashamed.
The foremost man of his generation in the town in civil service and
in the church,    he was,    to a degree,   responsible for his leadership,   and
the result proved the wisdom of the choice that placed him in these
positions.        Besides filling  important offices at home,    he several  times
served  his  district  in  the State Senate,    and was always  recognized
in  that body as  one of  its  wisest and most useful  members.             His
family extend  through three  generations,    neither of which was rep-
resented by more than one son.             The last of  the  race passed away
but a few years since in the person of Susan,     the granddaughter of
Dr.  Cotton.                Soon  after  his  settlement  in  town the  Doctor  pur-
chased a part of the Whitman estate in North Weymouth,    situated
between the meeting-house and Burying Hill,   quite near the former,
where he continued to reside until  the day of his death.           His tomb-
stone  bears  the following:     " Cotton  Tufts,      M.D.,     A.A.S.  M.M.S.
|    died  Dec.  8,      1815,    |     aged  84.   |                                                        His  property  was  large  and
descended to  the last  generation of his  family,    Susan,      the  last  of
which,   was buried in the family tomb in 1877,   the date of her death
being March 7.    The tombwas then sealed up to be opened no more.
Although the name is  no longer borne by any member of the family
in the town,    yet it will not soon be extinct,   for the munificent be-
quests  of Quincy Tufts,    Esq.,  the last surviving son,   and his  sister
Miss Susan,      or Susannah,     as it  reads upon the tombstone,     the  last
surviving  daughter of the house,    will keep it  fresh and fragrant  as
long  as  the Tufts  Library shall  be the  messenger  of  good to  this
people in disseminating the accumulated wisdom of the ages through
the volumes that go forth from its  shelves.       May it  ever  be fully
appreciated by a grateful community.
TURNER
The Turners of this town,   although they came here late in the sev-
enteenth century,     are  by no means a recent family,   for Jacob,   the
first  of  the  name in Weymouth,    was  the  grandson  of Humphrey
 - 474 - 
952                      EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
and  Lydia  (Garner)   Turner,    who came  from  Essex,       Eng. ,       about
1626,          and settled  in  Scituate  with their  four  children.        Jacob,   the
grandson,       married Jane Vining  of Weymouth,     and settled  in  this
town.             The family existed  here  for  four generations,     when it  dis-
appears  from  our  records,      the  last  death  recorded  being  that  of
Jacob,     June 20,    1808,    at the age of fifty- two years.          One son,    Seth,
removed  to  that  part  of  Braintree  now known as  Randolph,      and
was a colonel during the Revolutionary War,    his grandson,    Colonel
Royal,      and  great-grandson,     Hon.    Seth Turner of  Randolph,    being
well known and highly respected  in this  community,   the  wife  of
the  former  being the  daughter of  Maj.   John White  of  this  town.
The family dwelling  place was somewhere in East Weymouth,     but
the writer  has thus  far been unable to ascertain the precise locality.
The last  of  the family lived  near  the  river  at  East  Weymouth,     a
little  northerly from  the  iron  foundry,   and not  far  from the  resi-
dence of Oliver Bates,   and it  is probable that the house was the old
Turner homestead.
WARD
Henry Ward is  named in  the division  of the estate  of  Thomas
Bayley as  the husband of his  daughter  Ruth,     May 11,       1698,       and
the part  set  off  to  them was " the  lott  adjoining  Ebenezer  Whit-
marsh twenty five rods on the highway and eighteen and one half in
the  rear  next  to  [ Israel]     Fords  land, "   with  two  intervening  lots
between  that  and  Samuel  Pittee's  land,     one  laid  off  to  the  son
Thomas,         and  the  other,     the  lot  above  mentioned,       to   Ebenezer
Whitmarsh  and his  wife,     Christian,     also  the  daughter  of  Thomas
Bayley.           We hear no more of him,   but John Ward and Hannah his
wife are  recorded as having a daughter Hannah,    born Feb. 2,    1699.
Neither do  they  appear  any more upon the  records,    but  Increase
Bate,      by will,    April  13,     1716,     gives  his  Ebenezer  one  acre of  fresh
meadow next to  John Ward's land.          Samuel Ward,     cooper,    whose
will  dates  Sept.  2,    1717,    gives  his  wife,   Jael,   the  improvement  of
the  " land  adjoining  the  north  side  of  Josiah  Waterman's  home
land.   "     He also bequeaths land in Hingham and Braintree,   besides
other  land  in  Weymouth.           These are  all  probably  of  one family,
and their  homestead lay  to  the north of Josiah  Waterman's place
and extended into Hingham,     with detached lots  in other localities .
The grandson  Samuel  was  a captain  during  the  Revolution,      and
was a man of standing in the town.          The record of his death,    which
took place  Dec.  18,      1778,     styles  him major.         The family  seems  to
have come into town in the latter  part of the seventeenth century,
and  to  have  had  an existence  here  of  three  or  four  generations.
Samuel was undoubtedly the son of the  first  John,   who died  Feb.
9,      1758,      aged  eighty-nine years,     two months and fourteen days,     as
the graves of the family lie in a cluster in the Old North Cemetery.

WATERMAN
The Watermans came from the South Shore,    probably Scituate,
soon after  1700.   Little is said of Deacon Josiah or his wife Elizabeth
(Marsh)  upon the records,   but his nephew,   Josiah,   found a home in
Weymouth,     where he married  Thankful  Humphrey,    by whom he
had a large family.      Only three generations are  noted upon the rec-
ords  of  the town,    although  five have lived  here,    the  last  reaching
well  into  the present  century.         The epitaph  of  Deacon Josiah,     as
found  upon  his  gravestone  in  the  Old  North  cemetery,       runs  as
follows:          "  |    Preety  & Charity  Chear|   fulness  & Sincerity  adorned
|   the  Life  of  Josiah |    Waterman  Dean for  about |   40 years  to  the
church    in  Weymouth whose |        remains  are here interred |    he Died
July ye  27th  |       1773 in  the 86th |  Year of  his Age.   |    "     He was evi-
dently a man of  character  and standing,   a pillar  in the church and
an ornament  to  society,     as  well  as  a  useful  citizen.      Their  estate
extended from Whitman's Pond to the Hingham line,    on both sides
of the road.             The dwelling house was situated  on the east side  of
the highway,    not far from the Burying Ground,    and was afterwards
owned and occupied by Capt.    Robert Bates,   whose second wife was
a daughter of the Watermans.        The house is  now standing.
WHITMARSH
John Whitmarsh,   his wife Alice,    and children John,   Jane,    Nich-
olas  and  Richard,   came over  from  England  with  the  Hull  Com-
pany in  1635.    Another  son,      Simon,    was  probably  born  in  Wey-
mouth  after  their  settlement  in  the  town.         Six  generations  lived
and  died  here,     and  some of  the daughters  of  the  house  are  yet
among our people;    but the name has departed,   as far as that family
is concerned.           They have been a numerous and respected  race,    and
by marriage relation  have connected themselves  with most of  the
prominent families  of  the town.           The homestead was,      for  genera-
tions,    in  East Weymouth,    on  Commercial Street,     nearly  opposite
the  street  leading  to  the  South  Shore  Railroad  station,     and  the
estate extended back for a great distance,   perhaps the whole length
of  Whitman's  or  Fresh  Pond,      as  it  was often  called  in  the  early
records .                       Ezra  Whitmarsh,      a  son  of  the  third  generation,     was  a
graduate of  Harvard  College and a man of very great influence  in
the town for many years.         The sons of the last generation,    of whom
there  were  a  goodly  number,       nearly  all   removed  to  Abington,
where several of them are now living.        The elder John was born in
England  in  1594,    but  there  is  no  record  of his  death.           John,       Jr. ,
was a man of large property and owned much real estate in  various
localities  besides  that  mentioned  above.
Of the families  here enumerated,     none  cover  the  names  of  less
than three generations,   while some are extended enough to include
 - 476 - 
954                     EXTINCT  WEYMOUTH  FAMILIES
seven.           All but three came in during the seventeenth century,    that
in which the original  settlement of the town was made.       Of these
three,    Beal and Waterman came very soon after 1700,  within ten or
fifteen years,     while that of Tufts was some forty or fifty years  later.
Most,      if  not all of them,  although not now in this town,    have vig-
orous  shoots  in other parts of the country,   so they are only  trans-
planted and not extinct.        Some of them,   after a temporary removal,
returned,     to be again exiled.     Some of the older families  who have
representatives  now living  here,   have had their  existence  renewed
in this  manner.            The branches remaining as  permanent  residents,
after  a time becoming extinct,    shoots from other branches,     genera-
tions  before removed,    have returned  to  take their places  and pre-
serve the original stock.        Some,    it  may fairly be presumed,    are truly
extinct and their names unknown to the records of the present time,
although  they  are  very  few.          These  sketches  are  reminders  of
insecure  tenure  of  hereditary  reputation,    and  teach  the  wrongly
estimated  value of blood and lineage,   since they show how true it
is  that the higher classes of to-day were the lower classes  of yester-
day,    and will be the lower classes  of to-morrow.
There are many other families which might almost belong to this
list,     and yet are not quite gone,   like the Kingman's,    having no male
representative,        the  Webbs,        the  Trufants,      the  Colsons  and  the
Jones,      who  are  represented  upon the  voting  list  by but a single
name each;   the Bayleys and Vinsons each by two only;      the Fords
by three;     and the Whitmans by four and they of one family.         These
have been all  large  and important  families  from the early  settle-
ment,     coming in,   with possibly  two exceptions,   before  1700.

THE  HURRICANE  OF  1815
One of  the  severest  gales  that  ever  visited  this  section  of  the
country occurred in September,    1815.    It  is  known as  the " Hurri-
cane  of  1815."     On  Friday,      September  22,     it  began  to  rain,     the
wind being  at  the  time  in  a  northeasterly  direction.           It  rained
moderately during the day,   but at night the rain increased and the
wind  became  more  violent.            On  Saturday,     September  23,        the
wind changed to  the eastward,    and so continued until  11 o'clock,
when  it   changed  to  southeast,    increasing   in  violence  until   12
o'clock  at  noon,  when it  gradually began to subside.             Roofs  were
torn from the houses,    barns  demolished and trees  uprooted.             The
roof  of  the  house occupied  by Jacob  Richards,      on  Front  Street,
was blown off;     a barn belonging  to Joseph  Loud on Commercial
Street  was blown down.        Some of the people occupying houses  in
Middle  Street  left  them  and  assembled  in  a field.         Some of  the
houses   on  that   street   were   blown  down.            The  water  in   the
Monatiquot  River  rose  twelve  feet.           One  Peter   Whitmarsh  was
struck  by  a  piece  of falling  timber  and  seriously  injured.          Our
neighboring  towns also  suffered  in a similar way.       In Quincy,    part
of the roof of the meeting-house was swept away and some of the
houses  unroofed.       At Bent's  Point  nearly  all  the  chimneys  were
blown  down.          In  Hingham  most  of  the  houses  were  damaged,
chimneys  blown  down,     several   barns  leveled   and  two  persons
severely  bruised.       In Dorchester  seventeen  houses  were  unroofed,
sixty  chimneys  blown  over,    about forty  barns  unroofed  and de-
molished,     and upward of five  thousand fruit and forest trees  pros-
trated.           The South Meeting- House was partially  unroofed and the
North  Meeting-House much injured.         The  storm  extended  along
the  entire  length  of  the Atlantic  coast,      from  Florida  to  Maine.
The  Indians  had  a  tradition  that  two  hundred  years  before  a
similar  gale  occurred  in  which  a considerable  number  of  Indians
perished.

SOUTH  WEYMOUTH  TORNADO
On Aug.  31,       1920,     South  Weymouth was visited  by a tornado,
causing considerable damage to property and suffering  to some of
the  inhabitants.           Some of  the citizens  of the village  immediately
formed a Relief Committee,   comprising the following:      Fred Waite,
Frank  C.   Torrey,       Matthew  Sproul,   John  Reidy,      B.  B.  Wright,
Louis  Borlenghi,      Edward  Marr  and  Peter  J.   Healy,     which com-
mittee took action towards securing relief for those in need.         There-
after  a public meeting of the citizens  of the town was held in the
Music Hall Building,   at which meeting it was voted that the select-
men of the town appoint a Relief Committee,    and on Sept. 3,     1920,
the selectmen appointed the following committee:        Hon.     George L.
Wentworth,     Hon.    Kenneth L.  Nash,    Hon.    Edward Hunt,     Frederick
L. Alden,     John H. Tower,    Prince H. Tirrell,   John F. Reardon,    John
Reidy,           D.   Frank  Daley,       James   W.  Santry,      George  Marshall,
Matthew  O'Dowd,     J.   Leonard  Bicknell,      Emerson  R.  Dizer  and
William J.   Holbrook,    which committee immediately organized and
commenced its  duties,    and it  found that various  organizations  and
individuals were raising funds and collecting contributions for relief
purposes.            It found a marked desire upon every one to help in this
worthy cause.           Various articles  for household consumption,   wearing
apparel,      etc. ,     were donated by the local  merchants.
After  the  committee had made a survey of the damaged  area,
they,    in conjunction with the original Relief Committee,   decided to
hold a Field  Day at the Agricultural Society grounds.        Tickets for
the Field Day were printed and distributed to the various organiza-
tions  for  sale.           Much credit  is  due to  the members of St.  Francis
Xavier  Church,     to  the Knights  of  Columbus  of  East  Weymouth,
to  the  American Legion  for  the large  number of tickets  sold  by
them,    and to the Special Aid Society for their splendid work.
The Field Day was held on Sept. 18,    1920,   at which many of the
churches,      societies  and  individuals  participated  with  booths  and
attractions,      and assisted in the sale  of tickets,    programs  and score
cards,      all  of which services  were cheerfully given.      The program in-
cluded horse trotting  under the direction of the Old Colony Driving
Club,      a ball  game between the Knights  of  Columbus and the All
Stars  of  Weymouth,     and foot  races,   the  prizes  for  the  foot  races
being donated by the Stetson Shoe Company,    Edwin Clapp & Son,
Inc.,     and  Weymouth Trust  Company.         Advertising  in  the  local
press  and the  printing  of  the programs were donated.         The town
officials   and  police  and  fire  departments  generously  co-operated
with the work.           The merchants closed  their stores,    and every one
joined  in making the  Field  Day a  success .           Net amount available
for  relief,       $6,105.66.

AN  ACCOUNT  OF  THE  THREE  HUNDREDTH
ANNIVERSARY  CELEBRATION  JUNE 16,       1923
Prepared  by  BATES TORREY
Out of  the labors  of  a committee of shifting membership which
endured  some  vicissitudes  but  finally  achieved  results  of  consid-
erable  importance,                 came  forth   the  exercises   and  parade  that
marked the  celebration  of the three hundredth anniversary  of  the
settlement  of  Weymouth.
At a special  town meeting held June 24,    1921,      it  was voted  to
celebrate   the  three  hundredth  anniversary,       and  the  following
committee of arrangements was appointed:     Mrs. Josephine Barnes,
Mrs.  Abbie  E.  Beals,       Miss  Ida  M.  Cronin,       William  B.  Dasha,
Allan  C.   Emery,       Richard  Halloran,      Ralph  S.   Haskins,        Bradford
Hawes,      Mrs.  Mary E.  Holbrook,    Rev. John B.  Holland,     Robert S.
Hoffman,      Edward W. Hunt,    Rev.  William Hyde,    Howard H.  Joy,
Edward  I.   Loud,      Ralph  Merluzzo,    J.  Edward Mulligan,     Matthew
O'Dowd,         Frank  F.   Prescott,      Josiah   B.   Reed,        C.   Edgar  Stiles ,
Bowdoin B.  Smith,    Lewis C. Strang and Mrs. Kate Pierce Thayer.
Mr. Josiah  B.  Reed was made chairman of this committee.
On Oct.  21 ,        1921 ,     it  was voted to  raise  and appropriate  $1,000
for  the  use  of  this  committee.          (This  obviously  small  sum  was
subsequently  increased  to  $5,000.)      Meetings  of  this  committee
were held at intervals until  March,    1923,    when almost an impasse
was  encountered.       The chairman  resigned,    and the  efforts  of  the
committee up to that point seemed to have been futile.
In  the  meantime  the  Weymouth  Historical  Society,      realizing
that valuable  time was passing,    carried  out a little  celebration  of
its  own,      and on Aug.  19,    1922,    dedicated  two tablets,     one on the
birthplace  site  of Abigail Adams,    the other on the oldest  edifice  in
Weymouth,       namely,    the  Bicknell  House,     and the  same afternoon
listened  to  brief  memorial messages  by  Mr.  H.  H.  Joy and  Rev.
William Hyde,    to  an oration by Hon.   Joseph Belcher  of Randolph
on local  history,   to  a poem by Bates Torrey,    partook of a banquet,
and believed that it had kept the faith and honored tradition.
Perhaps,       under the stimulus  of this  brave impulse,    the germ of
commemoration was revived,   for in the spring of 1923 a call  for  a
meeting of citizens met with an enthusiastic response,    and schemes
were thereupon rife  for  a real  celebration.         The resurrected  Com-
mittee had this  personnel:      Winslow  M.  Tirrell,     Clayton V.  Mer-
chant,         Bradford  Hawes,      Rev.  Chas.       W.  Allen,      Rev.  Wm.      Hyde,
Howard H. Joy,    Edw.    W. Hunt,    Theron V. Tirrell,    Wm.     B.  Dasha,

Stanley  T.  Torrey,     Wm.     J.  Holbrook,     Esq. ,    Frank E.  Loud,       Maj .
Francis  A.  Bicknell,     Col.  F.  G.  Bauer,     Prince H. Tirrell,     Esq.  ,     and
many others,    including  ladies.           Mr.  Howard  H.  Joy  was  made
chairman,     and Colonel Bauer chief marshal of the day.
The plans  for  a worthy  celebration,    which in the earlier  stages
outlined  the  production  of  an historical  pageant,    were  afterward
modified to fit  the appropriation made by the town,   and in place of
a monument to  surmount Great Hill,   as  was first  proposed,     it  was
finally  decided  to  establish  a memorial  boulder there,   upon which
it  came to  pass  was  set  a  tablet  contributed by The Society  of
Colonial Wars of Massachusetts,  and dedicated to the first recorded
battle  on these shores,    the  fight  of Capt.      Miles  Standish with  the
Indians  in  1623.    Thus  were  dates  reconciled,     and  the unveiling
of this  tablet  on Great Hill,    and the  spectacular  parade  through
the  streets  of  Weymouth which  followed,    together  with  the  pro-
gram of addresses at the David Bates Clapp Memorial Field,    made
up in  abundant  measure  the  doings  of  a busy June  afternoon.
The balcony of the Memorial edifice furnished an excellent speaking
stand,     and the Field with its human picture of uniformed soldiery,
white- garbed  children  and  listening   populace,    made  a  scene  of
color  and movement long to be remembered.
One of  the  happiest  thoughts  of  the  Committee  was  to  send
Town Counsel  William  J.   Holbrook,    Esq. ,    to  Washington,      D.  C.,
to  interview  Chief Justice William  Howard Taft,    who,     on account
of  his  Weymouth ancestry,    was known to  cherish  a warm regard
for  the  old  town.     Having secured  Mr.  Taft's  promise to  attend
the celebration,   all good fortune followed in its train,   and a brilliant
assemblage of notables was insured to honor the occasion.
The presence of the second most distinguished official  in the na-
tion made possible the assembling of an impressive array of military.
The entire  101st  Infantry,      Battery  C,     101st  Field Artillery,      and
Troop C,     110th Cavalry from the National Guard,   was the contri-
bution of the Commonwealth;     while the United States government
was  represented  by a  Provisional  Battalion,    13th  U.  S.  Infantry,
a section  of armored tanks,    a company of the U.  S.  Marine Corps
with  a  naval  band,     and  a detachment of  Blue Jackets  from  the
U.  S.  S.  " Utah,"      in all  numbering about fifteen  hundred.
This display was augmented by survivors of the Grand Army of
the  Republic,    now much reduced in numbers,     Spanish  War Vet-
erans  resident  in  the  town,    the young and stalwart  soldiers  of the
American  Legion,    not  so  long  home from the  more recent World
War,      as well as  by semi- military pageantry exemplified by fraternal
societies  with  colors  and music.          Conspicuously standing  forth  in
the beauty of banners was the new flag  of the town of Weymouth
in  blue  and  gold,     emblazoned  with  appropriate  heraldry,     which
attracted  much attention.
The celebration  began  at  12.30 noon,   when Lieut.     Melville  F.
Cate and  Mr.  William A.  Hodges,       as  representatives  of  the  Chief
Marshal  and  the  selectmen,       met  Governor   Cox,       Chief  Justice

Taft,     Chief Justice Rugg,  Judge Morton,   and their party in Boston
and entertained them at an informal luncheon at the Hotel Somer-

was begun,     under escort  of a patrol from the  Massachusetts State

It was  a cog in the wheel of arrangements  that the principals
should  fit   into  the  program  of  entertainment  and dedication  in
various  ways.            The Governor was to enter the town by way of the
bridge  from Quincy,   and be greeted by a salvo of seventeen  guns
from  the  battery.        Chief Justice Taft,    in  his  personification  of  a
son  of Weymouth in its  colonial  line,   was to  embark in a launch
at the Quincy Yacht Club and land on the shore as near the landing-
place of the pioneers  as could be arranged,   and his arrival  be her-
alded by a salute.          This was done,   and the roar of twenty- one guns
announced his  coming.
In the meantime the military and other orders had been deployed
on the seaward slope of Great Hill,    awaiting the arrival of the dig-
nitaries,       and  presenting  a martial  front  warranted  to  excite  the
enthusiasm of any beholder,    the  assembled school children  singing
patriotic  airs  under the leadership  of  Mr.  James  W.  Calderwood,
supervisor  of music.      Perhaps the hill will never again quite dupli-
cate its  appearance of June 16,     1923.
Straightway  the  celebrants  and  invited  guests  coming  to  take
part in  the exercises  reached the summit,   where nature had set the
scene  magnificently for purposes  of  theatric display.        A well-built
road  led  to  the  top  of the  hill.      The town had been given  carte
blanche to take possession of all its  verdant slopes.       At the foot on
the North Street side lay broad acres -the site of the Capt.   William
Torrey  farm.            The  reservation  upon  the  summit was  ample  for
every accommodation,    and the view in panoramic breadth,    embrac-
ing every point of the compass,   was that of a beautiful bay dotted
with  islands,     the  town of  Hull in  full  view (and even Gloucester
on a clearer  day),    Hough's  Neck,     the  Milton  Blue Hills,     Quincy
city,     the woods and hamlets of Weymouth,     and over all  the broad
canopy  of  high  heaven.          Surely  there  could  have been  designed
no  better  spot for  the dedication,   and the eminent fitness  of the
place for the occasion cast its  influence upon the character of every
utterance.
The situation  at  the  top  of  Great  Hill  was that  of a flagstaff
newly set  at  the apex,  with a boulder and a bronze tablet  thereon
established  close  by.       Numerous soldiery  were aligned  about  the
slopes  of  the  hill  and round about the  stone,    where also  function-
aries  and invited guests stood.        Among those present were Governor
Channing  H.   Cox,        Chief  Justice  William  Howard  Taft  of  the

TERCENTENARY  CELEBRATION                   965
Mr.  Jov:        " My friends,   Weymouth welcomes this joyous multi-
tude  to-day on this  occasion  of the celebration  of the  three  hun-
dredth anniversary of the settlement of the town,  the second oldest
town in the Commonwealth,    and the first  municipality in America
to  adopt  the  democratic  form  of  government,      -for  the  people ,
by the people,    and of the people.
"And we are honored to-day by State and Nation in the presence
of our distinguished  guests.
" Three  hundred  years  ago  there  sailed  up this  river  one  June
day two little  sloops,    the ' Charity'    and the 'Swan,'   and from them
landed  a sturdy band of pioneers;     and after  due deliberation  they
decided  that  this  was  ' a pleasant  place  to  sit  down.'       And then
and there the corner stone of this  ancient town was formally laid.
"This  colony,   under the leadership  of Thomas Weston,    suffered
much  from  the  animosity  of  the  Pilgrims,   being  denounced  by
them as '  rude and profane, '    but before we judge them too severely
I think it  is  only fair  that we should understand the meaning of the
words applied to them.         Three hundred years  ago among the Pil-
grims a man who was strong and husky was termed a ' rude fellow,  '
and any one who supported the  Church of England and did  not
subscribe to the Pilgrim doctrines was called ' profane,'    and thus the
first  settlers  were described by Bradford.
" The Indians whom they found here were decidedly hostile,    and
they  planned  an attack  which  should  annihilate  the  whites,      but
through  the  friendly  interference  of  one of the  Indians  this  plan
was revealed in time to obtain aid from Plymouth,   and on March 27
Capt.       Myles  Standish  arrived here with his army(?)  of eight men,
and in  the  fight which followed,    which was the first  encounter  of
armed troops in New England,    the Indians were overcome and the
destiny of the colony was preserved.
" It  was that  landing  three  hundred years  ago and that  Indian
encounter which we commemorate to- day,    treading the same shores
where the  first  settlers  landed,     roaming over the very  hills  which
were first  peopled by them,    and looking down eastward of this  hill
to  those broad  acres  which were the ancestral  home of  our distin-
guished guest,     the Honorable Chief Justice of the United States.
"Realizing that the first  settlers founded this colony on the  firm
rock of  the church,   and believing  that much of our prosperity  has
come from  a consistent  adherence  to  those  principles,      it  is   emi-
nently  fitting  that we turn  our hearts  and lift  our  voices  to  the
Supreme Ruler of the universe,    and I  now ask the Reverend Father
Holland to  offer  a  prayer.   "
Rev.  JOHN  B.   HOLLAND.             " Our  Father  in  Heaven,         we,        Thy
children,      gathered  here  to-day beneath  the  flag  of our country on
ground that is  sacred with many relations  of history  and religion,
ask Thy blessing.
"Three hundred years ago  this  great  Republic,    of which we are
citizens  now,     by Thy all-merciful  providence was  established,     and
Thou  Almighty  God hast  watched  over  us  and  hast  blessed  it
 - 488 - 
966                         TERCENTENARY  CELEBRATION
among all  the nations of the world,   so that the oppressed in  every
land can turn longing eyes  and outstretched hands hitherward for
relief and comfort,   and we have never failed them.         But O Heavenly
Father,    we know that anything of permanent value in this life  must
be built  on Thee;     we cannot forget  that  the Almighty God,      the
Giver of  all  good gifts,     watches over the smallest  creature,     and so
we ask Thy blessing this day that we may walk in the paths of our
forefathers ;       that we may regard life  as  a sacred  trust and not our
own,      but  something  loaned  to  us  by Thee,     Almighty  God,       the
bountiful  Giver of all  things.          Make us,    Heavenly Father,    to walk
in the way of Thy guidance;    teach us to know Thee in Jesus Christ,
Thy Son,      and when the battle of life  is  over,    and when the death
angels call us,   may we hear those consoling words :       ' Well done thou
faithful  servants,    enter into the joy of Thy Lord and receive in all
eternity  the golden crown.'     "
WILLIAM  ROTCH,      Esq.:      " Your  Excellency,     Mr.  Chief  Justice,
Ladies  and Gentlemen:     Three hundred years ago and a little  more
the first  two settlements  were established  on the shores  of  Massa-
chusetts  which  have  persisted  to  this  day.           The first,      of  course,
was historic  Plymouth;    the second was at  Wessagusset,    the Indian
name for Weymouth,    which,    as has just been stated,   was the place
where democratic government was first  proclaimed.
" I  will  not go very much into  the history  of  those  early days,
but will say that perhaps in those times the Indians were not always
fairly  treated;     at any rate,    they believed they had cause for  com-
plaint,   and they planned to make an attack on this little settlement
of Wessagusset,   and even went so  far  as  to  say that they would
extend  that attack to Plymouth and wipe out all the white settlers.
"But Massasoit,    the great chief of the Wampanoags and a friend
also  of  the  Puritans,    had made a treaty of friendship with the  in-
habitants of the  Plymouth Colony,   which was perhaps the first  act
of diplomacy  recorded  in  this  country.       Massasoit  heard  of  this
plot and proposed attack and gave warning to the Plymouth people.
A council  was held,    and  Capt.    Myles Standish was appointed  to
take charge of proceedings  necessary  to  preserve the safety  of  the
two settlements.
"Myles  Standish had received a commission from Queen  Eliza-
beth.          He had served in  the Netherlands in  the outrageous wars of
the Inquisition,    and was the only man among the Pilgrims who had
any  training  in  military  affairs,      and  was  among  all  others  the
principal man of the community when anything very decided had
to  be adopted.          He assembled,    as has been said,   eight men,    which
he considered  was a large enough army to do what was necessary,
and they marched  immediately towards  the settlement  of  Wessa-
gusset  because that was where the  Indians  were;       and after  one or
two short  engagements,    and you would hardly call them that,     two
Indians  were  killed  and  one  captured.            One  Indian  escaped  and
gave warning to  the  rest  of the  tribe.         Standish  straightway  took
his men and marched to the place where he knew the Indians to be,
 - 489 - 
TERCENTENARY  CELEBRATION                    967
for he was determined to carry the war into the enemy's precinct.
He saw the Indians;    they saw him.           There was a high hill they both
tried  to  gain  possession  of.       Standish  evidently  outgeneraled  the
Indians,      and although  a few scattered  volleys were fired  they were
finally defeated and driven off,    and the settlements were preserved.
"Now,    in  commemoration of the three hundredth anniversary
of  the arrival  on these shores  of those  hardy settlers,     and in com-
memoration of the historic  fight  by Myles Standish and his  army,
the Society of Colonial  Wars of  Massachusetts presents  this  tablet
to  the  citizens  of  Weymouth;      and in  after  years  when you may
ascend  to  the top  of  this  Great  Hill  may your hearts  thrill  with
admiration for the men and women who crossed  the sea,    and may
you  also  admire  Capt.      Miles  Standish,    whose  courage probably
saved those early settlers  from destruction. "
Mr.  FRANCIS  W.  REA ( Chairman of  the  Park  Commissioners) :
"Responding for the town of Weymouth to the presentation of our
honored guest,     the  representative of  the Society  of  Colonial  Wars,
I would say that the gift of this tablet has been made more inter-
esting  and valuable  by the touch  of  the hand of  one of the  first
ladies of the land.
"We accept it,    first,   in commemoration of events which marked
the  beginning  of the  greatest  nation  on the  earth,     and  also  the
beginning  of  the  settlement  which  makes  Weymouth  what it  is
to-day,      and we hope as we look upon this tablet in the future that
not only the occurrences of three hundred years  ago will be remem-
bered,       but  that  the  16th  of June,     1923 ,       was  a  great  day  in  the
history of Weymouth.
"We thank the Society of Colonial  Wars for  this  tablet,      and we
hope that the citizens  of Massachusetts and of Weymouth will  for
the  next  three hundred years continue in progress  and in loyalty
to this country and its  institutions. "    (Applause. )

EXERCISES  AT  THE  CLAPP  MEMORIAL
As soon as  the parade had passed the  reviewing  stand the  Cav-
alry and Field Artillery proceeded via Charles Street  to the grounds
of  the James Humphrey School,     where they camped for  the night,
marching to  their armory at Allston the following day.      The floats
and  other  vehicles  proceeded  along  Middle  and  Charles  Streets,
and the remainder of the parade turned  into  the  Clapp Memorial
Grounds,     where a luncheon was served  to the troops and ice-cream
distributed  to  all  the  marchers.           On the balcony of the  Memorial
Building,     which was draped in the national colors,     were the invited
guests,      members of  the Grand Army,    town officials,    the chief mar-
shal  and  staff,       and  other  prominent  citizens,    among them  Mrs.
Edward  B.  Nevin,     daughter of  Brevet  Brig.   Gen. James  L.  Bates ,
who  had  presided  at  the  two  hundred  and  fiftieth   anniversary
exercises  in 1874.
When all  were in their places,     High Sheriff  Samuel H.  Capen of
Norfolk County stepped to the front of  the platform,   and,    rapping
three  times  with his  sword,    said:       " This  assemblage is  now called
to order."
 - 501 - 
TERCENTENARY  CELEBRATION                   979
Chairman Theron L. Tirrell of the board of selectmen then came
forward and announced:      " In the name of the town of  Weymouth,
the  oldest  town  save  Plymouth  in  this  ancient  Commonwealth,
and the scene of the first  battle by troops  of  this  State,     I  extend a
cordial  welcome to  our honored guests  and to  all  visitors  both civil
and military.
" I  will  now appoint Col.  Frederic G.  Bauer to officiate  as  master
of  ceremonies."
Colonel  Bauer thereupon  took the chair,     and the  exercises  pro-
ceeded  as  follows :
Colonel  BAUER:          " Although  the  first   settlers   of  our  town  are
said to have been men of somewhat fast lives,    who did not like the
strict   régime  at  Plymouth,    the  permanent  colonization  of  Wey-
mouth was a part of the great Puritan movement which sought to
find  on  these  shores  a  place  to  worship God freely,     as  we enjoy
that  privilege  to-day.
"The one  thing  they  reverenced  most  was  the  Bible;        indeed,
the standard of the  Puritan army in England had the Bible repre-
sented  upon it.           The  Rev.  William  Hyde will  now read  a lesson
from the Scriptures.         The passage which he will read is  that which
was  read  at  the three hundredth  anniversary  of  Emmanuel  Col-
lege,      Cambridge,   the college  from which graduated  nearly  all  the
Puritan  leaders  of  New England  who had a University  training;
and the book from which he will  read was originally  the property
of John William Shute,     a soldier in the War of  1812."
Rev.  WILLIAM  HYDE:        " The passage  of Scripture  appointed  to
be read  is  taken  from  the  forty-fourth  chapter  of  the  Book  of
Ecclesiasticus,    the first  to the fifteenth  verses,    inclusive :
Let us now praise famous men,   and our fathers  that begat us.
The Lord hath wrought great glory by them through His great power from the
beginning.
Such as did bear rule in their  kingdoms,    men renowned for their power,    giving
counsel by their understanding,    and declaring prophesies :
Leaders  of the  people  by their  counsels,    and by their knowledge  of learning
meet for  the people,   wise and eloquent  in  their instructions :
Such as found out musical tunes,    and recited verses in writing :
Rich menfurnished with ability,  living peaceably in their habitations :
All these were honored in  their generations,    and were the glory of their times.
There be of them,    that have left  a name behind them,   that their praises  might
be reported.
And some there be which have no memorial ;      who are perished,   as  though they
had never been;   and are become as  though they had never been born ;         and their
children  after them.
But these were merciful men,    whose righteousness hath not been forgotten.
With their  seed  shall  continually remain a  good inheritance,    and their children
are within the covenant.
Their seed standeth fast,    and their children for their  sakes.
Their seed shall  remain forever,    and their glory shall  not be blotted out.
Their bodies are  buried in  peace;      but their  name liveth  forevermore.
The people will tell of their wisdom,   and the congregation will show forth their
praise.
"Here endeth  the lesson. "
